item.title: Genie 4 开卖：一句话改天气、加角色、上原生音频；Genie 3 还补了长会话、全景锚定与「连起来的世界序列」 ｜ Genie 4 is now available
item.description:
一句话：这一次的卖点不是画质，而是「实时可编辑 + 可分享可 remix」。

要点：

  • 能力变化：向 Google AI Ultra 订阅用户开放 Genie 4，可以用**自然语言实时修改环境**（改天气、加角色）、加入**原生音频**，并把作品发布到新的社区画廊供他人探索与 remix
  • 同时更新了 Genie 3：支持**更长会话、全景锚定（panorama grounding）与「联动世界序列」**——后者意味着多个世界可以互相链接
  • 配套的 Project Genie agent 让人通过日常对话构建复杂环境，而不是手写参数；未在 Ultra 档的 AI Pro 用户可以排 waitlist

为什么值得看：这是「生成式世界」第一次以订阅产品的形态交付：实时编辑 + 音频 + 分享/remix 三件套，等于把「制作」与「分发」压进同一个界面。对引擎团队的启示很直接——如果世界可被自然语言实时改，那「关卡编辑」这件事的产品形态会被重写。

中文摘要：DeepMind 把 Genie 4 推向符合条件的 Google AI Ultra 订阅用户，强调更快的响应、更强的社交与交互式世界生成：用户可以用自然语言实时修改环境（例如改天气、加角色）、加入原生音频，并把创作发布到新的社区画廊，让别人探索与 remix。同时 Genie 3 获得更新，支持更长会话、全景锚定以及「联动的世界序列」（即多个世界可以串接）。新的 Project Genie agent 则让人通过简单的自然语言对话来构建复杂环境。对业界而言，这次的重点不在画质，而在于「实时可编辑 + 可分享可复用」——生成式世界第一次以完整产品形态交付，也让「关卡编辑」这个环节的产品形态有了被重写的可能。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：DeepMind（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Genie 4 is now available

Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery.

Diego Rivas

Group Product Manager, Google DeepMind

Pavan Kumar

Group Product Manager, Google Labs

We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.
  • We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers for creating interactive worlds.
  • You can now modify environments in real time using text prompts and native audio features.
  • Our updated Genie 3 model supports longer sessions, panorama grounding, and linked world sequences today.
  • The new Project Genie agent helps you build custom worlds through simple natural language conversations.
  • You can publish your creations to our community gallery for others to explore and remix.
    • Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

    We are updating Project Genie to help you create and explore interactive digital worlds. With our new Genie 4 model, you can change weather, add characters, and hear adaptive audio in real time just by typing prompts. You can also use our new creative agent to build complex environments through simple conversation. If you subscribe to Google AI Ultra, you can start building, sharing, and remixing these custom worlds in our community gallery today.

    Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

    Explore other styles:

    Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie, an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them.

    So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds.

    Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser.

    Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie

    With Genie 4, our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue.

    Discover new Genie 3 capabilities

    While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include:

  • Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys.
  • 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images.
  • Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore.

    • Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas.

    See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around.

    Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command.

    Create new interactive experiences

    The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood.

    You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds.

    Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command

    Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert.

    Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix.

    Explore the new gallery

    When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.”

    Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring.

    “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery.

    “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective.

    The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism.

    Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix.

    Learn how we are building responsibly

    We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.

    Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview.

    Try Project Genie today

    Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can try the new Project Genie experience starting today, and Google AI Pro members can join the waitlist on the same page.

    Posted in:

item.title: 代理视频粗到只有布局、细到带关节：Code World Model 2.0 让渲染器在「几步因果推理」内接住两种极端 ｜ Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：视觉代理把「显式世界状态模拟」与「真实感视频合成」解耦，但渲染器得同时扛住两种输入尺度。

要点：

  • 分工前提：视觉代理（visual proxy）把**显式的世界状态模拟**与**真实感视频合成**解耦，从而给离线片段生成与实时交互流都提供一个可控接口
  • 两个工程难点：其一，上游代理的粒度**从粗糙布局一直到带关节的精细几何**，取决于具体交互；其二，流式推理必须在**少数几个因果步**内完成，且不能损失精度
  • Code World Model 2.0 针对这两点设计，目标是「无限长且可控」的视频生成

为什么值得看：这是 GameWM/WorldDraft 那条线里最工程化的一篇：它承认「代理视频的质量是变化的」，并要求渲染器对这种变化鲁棒。做「引擎出代理、模型出最终帧」的团队，这条正好补上「代理质量参差怎么办」这个缺口。

中文摘要：视觉代理把「显式世界状态模拟」与「真实感视频合成」解耦，从而为离线片段创作与实时交互流提供可控接口。但一个实用的渲染器必须解决两个问题：一是上游代理的粒度会随交互而变化，从粗糙的布局一直到带关节的精细几何；二是流式推理必须在少数几个因果步内完成，且不能牺牲准确性。Code World Model 2.0 针对这两点提出方案，目标是实现「无限长且可控」的视频生成。对已经在做「引擎输出代理、模型输出最终帧」这条链路的团队，它补的正是「代理质量参差不齐时渲染器如何兜住」这个现实缺口。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Code World Model 2.0:
Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation

Abstract

Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned ∼200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

Project Page•GitHub•Hugging Face

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models must synthesize coherent observations as user actions alter the environment [2, 52, 70, 51]. Rather than simulating both dynamics and appearance in one network, an emerging paradigm maintains explicit state in an upstream engine and delegates visual synthesis to a generative renderer [8, 20, 56]. Visual and geometric proxies bridge the two stages by prescribing camera paths, layout, and entity motion while leaving photorealistic appearance to the video model [27, 41, 7, 26]. Recent systems pair such structural cues with appearance references for offline authoring and real-time rendering [12, 34, 31, 19, 67].

In practice, the structural detail appropriate for conditioning depends on the interaction. Broad navigation often requires only coarse scene geometry and root trajectories, whereas close-range interactions demand articulated poses or finer surface structure. Detailed proxies supply tighter constraints at higher construction and transmission cost, while coarse proxies are lightweight to produce yet leave local geometry and motion under-specified. A capable renderer must interpret both regimes faithfully. For example, a rigid mannequin that tracks a character’s root pose should constrain global position and heading without imposing a frozen limb posture on the generated motion.

We introduce Invoker-Render, a proxy-conditioned rendering framework comprising a bidirectional creation model and a causal four-step streaming model. Both accept structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language through a shared interface. Training covers different proxy families, such as semantic layouts and shaded geometry, and multiple granularities within a family. Each checkpoint can follow fine constraints when supplied and synthesize plausible local motion when omitted, supporting different input granularities with the same weights.

For video creation, users edit complete proxy sequences to refine camera paths, trajectories, and event timing. The bidirectional model attends across the full clip. During streaming, future states depend on actions yet to occur. The causal model therefore consumes proxy chunks and local text incrementally, generating each chunk in four steps using retained visual history.

We build on MiniMax-H3 [42] and adopt Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6] to adapt its guidance-distilled backbone to proxy conditioning. Converting the resulting bidirectional model to a streaming renderer requires both fewer denoising steps and tolerance to errors in generated history. Progressive Forcing (ProForcing) addresses these changes in stages (Figure 4). Teacher forcing (TF) first trains block-causal prediction on clean video prefixes. Resampling forcing (RF) then constructs imperfect histories by adding noise to observed prefixes and refining them sequentially with the current model.

RF-DMD retains these resampled histories while learning four-step generation through distribution matching distillation (DMD) [64, 63] and an auxiliary GAN loss [23]. The student, trainable score model, and GAN discriminator then continue training on continuous self-generated histories in SF-DMD [18, 61, 14]. Long-rollout training thus starts with a four-step generator and supervision models already trained alongside it.

We train on an aligned ∼200-hour multi-granularity corpus with hierarchical text. Persistent history caching and pipelined proxy encoding and video decoding reduce serving overhead. Across 140 streaming rollouts, Invoker-Render outperforms recent streaming baselines in visual quality, structural adherence, and reference preservation, and maintains stable scene and subject appearance across 30-minute racing rollouts.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Mixed-granularity proxy conditioning. A shared conditioning interface lets each creation or streaming checkpoint accept coarse and fine proxies.

  • •

    Progressive Forcing. A curriculum progresses from TF/RF causal adaptation to four-step DMD with GAN supervision, then continues the trained student, score model, and discriminator under self-generated histories.

  • •

    Long-horizon controllable generation. Our four-step causal renderer outperforms recent streaming baselines and maintains scene and subject appearance across 30-minute racing rollouts.

  • •

    Multi-granularity corpus and serving stack. An aligned ∼200-hour dataset and a low-latency distributed serving engine support multi-granularity training and continuous interactive streaming.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Interactive Worlds and Generative Rendering

    Action-conditioned video models often internalize world dynamics and visual synthesis in one network, learning latent or discrete action transitions from gameplay and video corpora [2, 52, 10, 4, 54, 57, 70, 40]. LingBot-Video studies mixture-of-experts video pretraining for embodied intelligence, combining web videos with robot-oriented footage [39]. Streaming architectures extend interactive horizons across open-world interactions and explicit context or 3D-aware memory, including the Matrix-Game series, WorldPlay, WorldCrafter, and related streaming world models [16, 53, 44, 68, 51, 66, 46, 13, 62]. Because one visual transition model governs both state evolution and rendering, modifying scene structure or enforcing persistent physical rules remains challenging.

    A complementary paradigm maintains explicit state in an executable engine or agentic controller and delegates synthesis to a conditioned video model. Code World Model, Programmable World Model, and AgentGarten compile structured program state into visual signals [8, 20, 9], Marionette decouples state prediction, geometry rendering, and appearance painting [41], and Wizard supports real-time world manipulation via agentic control [55]. StreamRender-H3, Streaming CWM, Magpie, and BoxWorld likewise couple game or simulator backends with neural renderers through semantic, white-box, or bounding-box streams [34, 28, 67, 56]. Treating proxies as an explicit state-to-renderer contract, Invoker-Render studies controllable granularity across creation and streaming.

    2.2 Proxy-Conditioned Video Generation

    Building on spatial control, camera conditioning, and unified video creation frameworks [69, 15, 22], proxy-conditioned video models ground synthesis in geometric or semantic structure across several regimes. Paired methods learn directly from dense geometry, lighting, material buffers, or animated meshes, as in DiffusionRenderer, Generative World Renderer, and native 4D mesh rendering [26, 21, 7]. Proxy2World relaxes paired supervision via posed RGB-D clips [59], whereas training-free methods such as Code Video Model restrict proxy injection to early denoising steps so appearance follows the reference image [27].

    Recent renderers broaden representation diversity, customization, and structural fidelity. SolarRenderer reuses the backbone’s reference pathway across heterogeneous structural videos with a four-step acceleration LoRA [12], EdenLive and Mundo support real-time reference-driven rendering and customized world synthesis [19, 36], Fight World Model controls combat interactions via visual proxies [25], and AnyGameRenderer preserves cross-game entity counts and timing [31]. Invoker-Render targets an orthogonal axis: structural granularity within one representation family, enabling a single model to honor fine constraints when supplied and synthesize natural local motion under lightweight coarse proxies.

    2.3 Streaming Video Diffusion and Few-Step Distillation

    While training-free queue scheduling such as FIFO-Diffusion enables continuous generation via diagonal denoising [24], interactive streaming requires block-causal attention and few-step sampling. Diffusion Forcing trains causal models with independent token noise levels [5], CausVid distills a bidirectional teacher into an autoregressive student [65], and Self Forcing rolls out the student on its own predictions [18]. LongLive stabilizes rollouts via streaming tuning and a persistent frame sink [61, 58], SANA-WM and minWM scale minute-horizon and full-stack world modeling [77, 71], and AlayaRenderer-Flash and StreamRender-H3 co-design few-step causal rendering with low-latency serving [29, 34].

    To compress flow-matching trajectories [30, 32], consistency distillation maps states directly to clean targets [49], score-based distribution matching [35, 64, 75] aligns distributions via auxiliary score differences, and DMD2, ADD, and LADD pair score or diffusion distillation with discriminator supervision [63, 48, 47]. Multi-step variants refine supervision across steps, with Trajectory Distribution Matching (TDM) and VA-TDM aligning multi-step trajectories and velocity fields [37, 38] and Endpoint Distribution Matching (eDMD) anchoring the fake score model on final clean outputs [73]. For causal video, Causal Forcing uses an autoregressive ODE teacher, Causal Forcing++ and Causal-rCM adopt consistency-based causal initialization [78, 72, 74], and Salt++ aligns streaming generation and scoring contexts [14]. ProForcing instead distills a four-step student with teacher-feature relativistic GAN supervision [23, 47] on resampled data-anchored histories (RF-DMD) before continuing the coupled student, fake score model, discriminator, and optimizer states on continuous self-generated rollouts (SF-DMD).

    3 Data Curation and Proxy Construction

    Controllable rendering requires aligned training pairs that cleanly separate the geometry prescribed by a proxy from the appearance and local dynamics synthesized by the model. Our corpus comprises approximately 200 hours of footage, combining 150 hours of self-collected data with 50 hours from public datasets, and associates each usable RGB clip with structural conditions, an appearance reference, and hierarchical text annotations. We design the pipeline around three core requirements: spatial-temporal correspondence between proxies and RGB targets, multi-granularity structural representations of the same event, and language descriptions tailored to both whole-window creation and block-causal streaming.

    3.1 Data Sources and Coverage

    Table 1 summarizes the corpus composition. Self-collected recordings allow us to render matched coarse and fine proxies from a shared reconstructed scene state, whereas public datasets broaden environment diversity and contribute native structural modalities. Reported durations count unique source footage prior to extracting overlapping training windows or multiple proxy variants. Figure 2 illustrates representative source frames alongside their paired structural conditions.

    Self-collected data.

    We capture gameplay across diverse 3D environments (including Grand Theft Auto V, Cyberpunk 2077, Elden Ring, and Forza Horizon 5), spanning navigation, urban driving, and character interactions under varied camera trajectories, weather, and illumination. Automated navigation and driving scripts yield sustained, smooth trajectories, while human gameplay contributes unscripted interactions and rapid viewpoint transitions. RGB frames and accessible engine buffers are recorded synchronously, with camera poses and dynamic object states recovered offline where engine exports are incomplete, preserving continuous multi-action trajectories for long-horizon training.

    Public sources.

    Public subsets contribute white-box geometry, semantic layouts, and dense depth, and Figure 2 additionally includes Virtual KITTI 2 [3] to illustrate RGB paired with dense semantic segmentation. Source-specific preprocessing aligns native annotations to a unified frame rate and conditioning interface, applying geometric and temporal validity checks before enabling structural supervision. Clips lacking reliable structural alignment are retained solely for reference-and-text appearance supervision. Recording available condition types per sample allows public datasets to contribute their native modalities without requiring synthetic coarse/fine pairs for every source.

    3.2 Aligned Scene States and Multi-Granularity Proxies

    Figure 3 outlines capture and proxy construction for our self-collected corpus. While recorded RGB serves as the supervision target, synchronized engine buffers and reconstructed 3D scene states (comprising camera intrinsics and extrinsics, static environment geometry, and tracked dynamic entities) allow us to render multiple structural granularities of the exact same visual event.

    Capture and reconstruction.

    Starting from synchronized RGB and engine depth capture, our reconstruction pipeline recovers camera calibration, scene semantics, and 3D entity motion. Instance segmentation and multi-object tracking [45] isolate moving actors and vehicles from the static scene, which is labeled via semantic segmentation and completed across invalid depth regions [60], while camera pose estimation and background point tracking recover globally consistent trajectories. For dynamic actors, human motion recovery estimates both global root trajectories and articulated body poses, and 3D bounding-box fitting tracks rigid vehicle motion. Retaining per-frame camera parameters, track IDs, and confidence masks alongside the video enables automated reprojection and tracking verification prior to proxy rendering.

    Coarse structural control.

    Coarse proxies encode global scene layout, camera motion, and entity placement and heading while omitting fine local geometry. Humans are rendered as canonical rigid mannequins driven solely by root pose, vehicles as oriented 3D boxes, and backgrounds as simplified geometry or semantic regions. Because a canonical mannequin conveys root translation and orientation without limb articulation, the paired RGB target and action text teach the generator to synthesize natural gait and posture consistent with the trajectory.

    Fine geometric and motion control.

    Fine proxies augment this representation with articulated human poses (rendered as depth-tested volumetric body parts) and shaded local surface geometry, while preserving rigid vehicle boxes. Wherever both variants are constructed, coarse and fine proxies share identical camera parameters, timestamps, entity identities, and RGB targets, directly supervising the renderer across constraint strengths for the same event. Throughout this work, we distinguish granularity, meaning the level of geometric and kinematic detail within a representation, from representation family, such as semantic maps, shaded depth, or white-box renders.

    Separating structure from appearance.

    To prevent appearance leakage, both granularities strip away surface textures, materials, and scene lighting. Before compositing dynamic entities, foreground masks are excised from background depth and semantic buffers and inpainted from temporally adjacent background views, suppressing silhouette cues from clothing, hair, or accessories. Reprojecting the simplified dynamic primitives onto this cleaned background with depth occlusion ensures that proxies convey pure spatial and motion structure, leaving appearance to the reference frame, language, and learned video prior.

    3.3 Sequence Lengths and Hierarchical Language

    Short windows and continuous sequences.

    Self-collected and public recordings are standardized at 24 fps into 158-frame windows (∼6.6 s) and 328-frame continuous sequences (∼13.7 s). RGB targets use 1344×768, while aligned proxies are stored at 672×384 and encoded at 672×384 or 448×256 using nearest-neighbor resizing for semantic maps and anti-aliased filtering for continuous geometry. Short windows support bidirectional GFT, supervised TF/RF, and RF-DMD, whereas 328-frame sequences support variable-length SF-DMD rollouts across uninterrupted trajectories.

    Whole-window descriptions.

    Text annotations combine clip-level scene descriptions with timestamped local actions (“Scene + local actions” in Figure 3). Each window pairs its opening RGB anchor with a vision-language caption covering environment, subject appearance, lighting, events, and camera motion. The bidirectional creation model and the bidirectional teacher and fake score models each receive independent whole-window captions rather than concatenated local tags.

    Streaming action annotations.

    Timestamped local annotations track action progression, motion directions, interactions, and camera shifts across block boundaries so that TF/RF and the distilled student observe text strictly up to the current block, without future labels or clip summaries. For coarse proxies, local text disambiguates behaviors whose articulation is omitted from rigid root geometry.

    Condition organization.

    A system instruction defines the roles of structural proxies and the appearance reference alongside sample captions, while automated validation checks reference tags, temporal order, and entity-action agreement.

    3.4 Quality Control and Evaluation Separation

    Quality control screens both video and proxies for corrupted or frozen frames, exposure failures, shot cuts, reprojection outliers, tracking switches, and timing drift. Automated geometric checks and manual review evaluate each proxy against its intended constraints, distinguishing omitted coarse articulation from root-trajectory or camera errors.

    Records track source identifiers, frame ranges, proxy variants, captions, and encoding provenance, with cross-source deduplication across shared game worlds. Training and held-out splits are partitioned by recording (and by scene or map where identifiable), keeping overlapping windows, coarse/fine pairs, and alternative views of one recording in the same split to prevent leakage.

    4 Invoker-Render

    Invoker-Render adapts MiniMax-H3 [42] into both a bidirectional video creation model and a causal four-step streaming renderer. We first formalize the shared conditioning interface and linear flow parameterization, then present bidirectional proxy adaptation via Guidance-Free Training, and finally detail Progressive Forcing (ProForcing), which distills few-step causal rendering on data-anchored histories before transitioning to continuous self-generated rollouts.

    4.1 Rendering Formulation and Proxy Conditioning

    Let x₀=(x₀¹,…,x₀^B) denote clean video latents partitioned into B contiguous temporal blocks (corresponding to streaming chunks at inference time). Conditioning inputs consist of an independently encoded appearance anchor a, structural proxies p=p_1:B, a system instruction s, and text annotations ℓ=ℓ_1:B. Whereas the bidirectional creation model attends over the full proxy sequence p_1:B and a clip-level caption, the causal streaming model observes c_b=(a,s,p_≤b,ℓ_≤b) at block b and factorizes the joint distribution autoregressively across blocks:

    p_θ(x₀|a,p,s,ℓ)=∏_b=1^Bp_θ(x₀ᵇ|hᵇ,c_b),

    		(1)

    where hᵇ denotes the retained visual history prior to block b and ℓ_≤b collects text annotations revealed through block b. Target attention in the streaming model is bidirectional within each block and strictly causal across blocks. Both models preserve the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [43] backbone’s native reference pathway and rotary positional embedding (RoPE) [50] indexing, keeping the appearance anchor a fixed outside the training loss.

    Control across granularities.

    Coarse and fine proxies enter through an identical conditioning pathway, trained jointly on mixed-granularity examples. Coarse inputs prescribe scene layout, camera trajectory, and entity root motion, while fine inputs further constrain limb articulation and local surface geometry. At inference time, downstream applications can select the structural detail suited to each interaction while relying on the appearance reference, text, and video prior to supply visual texture and unconstrained local motion.

    Flow parameterization.

    Given clean latents x₀, Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), and noise level t∈(0,1], we adopt the linear flow-matching trajectory and velocity target [30, 32]

    xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tε, v=ε-x₀.

    		(2)

    We write v_θ for the velocity network and f_θ=xₜ-tv_θ for the induced clean-latent denoiser, omitting shared conditioning arguments where unambiguous. Here θ⁻ indicates evaluation at current weights with gradients detached, and all squared-error objectives below are implicitly averaged over valid non-anchor latent elements.

    4.2 Bidirectional Creation Model

    Because MiniMax-H3 already incorporates distilled classifier-free guidance [17], we adapt it to structural proxy control using Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6]. Pairing the full conditioning tuple c⁺ with a weakened counterpart c⁻ that drops the structural proxy while retaining the appearance anchor, we blend their velocity predictions at guidance scale β=2 with 10% condition dropout:

    \begingatheredṽ_θ=1/βv_θ(xₜ,t|c⁺)+(1-1/β)v_θ⁻(xₜ,t|c⁻), [3.0pt] L_GFT(θ)=𝔼_x₀,ε,t [w(t)\lVertṽ_θ-v\rVert₂²].\endgathered

    		(3)

    Here w(t) denotes the backbone’s time-dependent loss weighting. Detaching the weak-condition branch v_θ⁻(xₜ,t|c⁻) routes gradients exclusively through the proxy-conditioned pathway, sharpening structural adherence without inference-time CFG overhead. Trained under full bidirectional attention with complete proxy sequences and whole-window captions, the resulting checkpoint serves directly as our offline creation renderer and provides the initialization for causal adaptation and distillation critics.

    4.3 Progressive Forcing for Few-Step Rendering

    Directly distilling a bidirectional model into a few-step autoregressive renderer conflates trajectory compression with exposure to self-generated rollout errors. ProForcing disentangles these challenges across progressive stages (Figure 4). Supervised TF and RF first adapt attention to block-causal histories anchored to ground-truth video, RF-DMD then distills a four-step generator alongside learned score and adversarial critics under those data-anchored histories, and SF-DMD (Section 4.4) finally transitions the jointly trained system to continuous self-generated rollouts.

    Causal adaptation with TF and RF.

    Replacing bidirectional target attention with block-causal attention, both Teacher Forcing (TF) and Resampling Forcing (RF) optimize the GFT objective of Eq. (3) under β=2 and 10% condition dropout. TF first conditions each block on clean ground-truth history h_TFᵇ=x₀^
    x̃_ρᵇ=(1-ρ)x₀ᵇ+ρεᵇ,(4)
    x̃₀ᵇ=f_θ⁻ (x̃_ρᵇ,ρ|x̃₀^

    Conditioning each one-step refinement on previously refined blocks x̃₀^

    RF-conditioned distribution matching.

    Initialized from the supervised RF checkpoint, RF-DMD compresses sampling to four steps via distribution matching distillation [64, 63, 37, 73] while retaining detached RF history construction (h_RFᵇ). Keeping histories anchored to observed video during distillation isolates four-step trajectory learning from open-loop autoregressive drift. To score student outputs, a frozen bidirectional teacher f_teacher and a trainable bidirectional fake score model f_fake (both initialized from the bidirectional GFT checkpoint) evaluate re-noised student predictions under complete scoring-window conditions, while the student itself remains strictly block-causal. Meanwhile, f_fake is updated online via flow matching on detached, re-noised student samples.

    Specifically, let x₀^θ denote the clean prediction tapped from a selected step of the student’s four-step denoising rollout, and let xₜ=(1-t)x₀^θ⁻+tε be its detached re-noised input shared by both score models. We apply the DMD gradient through the surrogate objective

    L_DMD(θ)=1/2 𝔼 [\lVertx₀^θ-x₀^θ⁻+g\rVert₂²].

    		(5)

    Writing g=(g¹,…,g^B), the target-seeking displacement on block b is gᵇ=(f_fakeᵇ-f_teacherᵇ)/Z_b, where Z_b normalizes by the mean absolute discrepancy between detached student and teacher predictions (clamped to a positive floor). Treating g as a stop-gradient target ensures that differentiation of Eq. (5) propagates the exact normalized score difference into x₀^θ across all valid blocks.

    Teacher-feature relativistic GAN.

    To sharpen perceptual detail and suppress few-step over-smoothing, we pair DMD with a discriminator D_φ comprising frozen teacher backbone features [47, 63] followed by lightweight trainable projections and a noise-conditioned scalar head. Ground-truth windows x₀ and generated windows x₀^θ are perturbed with identical (t,ε) via Eq. (2) under matched conditions and the shared appearance anchor, producing scalar logits r_φ and q_φ. We optimize paired relativistic logistic losses [23, 63] alongside the combined student objective:

    L_D(φ)=λ_D 𝔼 [\log (1+e^q_φ-r_φ)],(6)
    L_GAN(θ)=𝔼 [\log (1+e^sg(r_φ)-q_φ)],
    L_student(θ)=L_DMD(θ)+λ_advL_GAN(θ).

    Here λ_D and λ_adv weight the discriminator and adversarial terms, and sg(·) denotes the stop-gradient operator on scalar logits. Discriminator updates detach generated latents x₀^θ, whereas student updates detach the real-branch logit r_φ and freeze both teacher and discriminator parameters while backpropagating through the generated-branch input q_φ. Note that D_φ and f_fake remain separate networks trained under distinct objectives.

    4.4 Long-Sequence Self-Forcing

    Building on self-forcing and streaming long tuning [18, 61], SF-DMD replaces data-anchored RF prefixes with continuous student-generated histories. Starting from the appearance anchor a, the student sequentially denoises each block in four steps and commits its detached terminal prediction x̂₀ᵇ to the causal history cache (h_SFᵇ=x̂₀^

    Local scoring of a continuous stream.

    To supervise rollouts longer than the bidirectional teacher’s native window, we tile the continuous student stream with overlapping local scoring windows. Each window pairs preceding generated blocks (serving purely as detached temporal context) with a disjoint interval of newly generated target blocks, always retaining the original appearance anchor a. The teacher, fake score model, and discriminator observe complete conditions within each local window while the student remains causal, and DMD and GAN input gradients are masked to apply strictly once per non-anchor target block, weighted by target coverage.

    Coordinated continuation from RF-DMD.

    Crucially, transitioning from RF-DMD to SF-DMD carries forward the entire coupled training state (student weights, fake score model f_fake, discriminator D_φ, their respective AdamW moments [33], and the student EMA) against the same frozen teacher. Because RF-DMD already converges a capable four-step causal generator together with calibrated supervision models tailored to its output distribution, SF-DMD avoids cold-start critic instability and focuses optimization on mitigating long-horizon error accumulation under self-generated histories.

    5 Streaming Serving Infrastructure

    To deploy the causal world model as an online interactive rendering service, each streaming step must encode incoming visual proxies, update retained clean history H and current proxy conditioning C within a bounded KV window, run four-step causal denoising, and return decoded RGB frames within a strict latency budget. Starting from a standard streaming baseline, we streamline the inference stack across three levels: (i) an asymmetric streaming codec pairing a lightweight Tiny AutoEncoder (TAE) for online proxy encoding with a causal video decoder for RGB reconstruction; (ii) intra-window invariant reuse and fused execution across DiT layers, KV workspaces, and prefill/denoising passes; and (iii) cross-packet codec overlap and asynchronous CPU delivery (Figure 5). On an eight-GPU node at 1344×768 resolution, these optimizations reduce the steady-state per-chunk period from 1770 ms to 930 ms and increase throughput from 9.9 FPS to 18.0 FPS (1.82× speedup; Figure 6).

    5.1 Efficient Asymmetric Streaming Codec

    Interactive streaming places asymmetric demands on the visual codec: incoming proxy frames must be encoded at every chunk with minimal latency, whereas generated latents must be decoded into temporally continuous RGB video. Encoding online proxies with the full video encoder is slower than output decoding and dominates the inter-chunk codec interval.

    We therefore adopt an asymmetric codec design. The static reference frame is encoded once at session start with the full encoder to preserve anchor detail, while online proxy packets are encoded independently by a lightweight TAE proxy encoder directly into normalized 16× spatially compressed, 24-channel conditioning latents. On the output side, we retain the tensor-parallel Causal Video Decoder to preserve temporal continuity across chunks. Replacing the online proxy encoder with TAE makes input encoding an order of magnitude faster than causal decoding (T_enc≪T_dec), reducing the steady-state chunk period from 1770 ms to 1410 ms and raising throughput from 9.9 FPS to 12.4 FPS.

    5.2 Intra-Window Reuse and Fused Execution

    Within each DiT window, we eliminate redundant per-layer preparation, projection compute, memory allocation, and separate prefill launches:

  • •

    Cross-layer structural sharing. Within a single forward pass, all DiT layers share identical token layout plans, sliding-window crop indices, and frame-aligned RoPE position tensors. We construct these plans and index tensors once at backbone entry and reuse them across all layers.

  • •

    Per-layer AdaLN projection caching. Because session conditioning is stationary and the four-step Euler timestep schedule repeats across chunks, we cache each DiT block’s projected AdaLN modulation parameters by timestep and reuse them across subsequent chunks.

  • •

    Transactional KV workspace reuse. Instead of allocating fresh output and concatenation buffers at every layer, we reuse pre-allocated KV result backplanes and temporary forward workspaces across the transaction lifecycle (Figure 5, top). Combining structural invariant and workspace reuse reduces the steady-state chunk period from 1410 ms to 1180 ms and lifts throughput from 12.4 FPS to 14.4 FPS.

  • •

    Fused prefill-and-denoise pass (H/C/D₁). In ordinary continuation windows, we defer committing prior clean history Hₙ₋₁ and pack it with incoming proxy tokens Cₙ and the first denoising state D₁ into a single block-causal composite forward (Pass 1 in Figure 5), followed by three denoising-only passes (D₂–D₄). Reducing backbone launches from six to four trims the chunk period from 1180 ms to 1165 ms and raises throughput to 14.8 FPS.

    • 5.3 Cross-Packet Pipelining and RGB Delivery

    With intra-window DiT execution compressed, we pipeline codec execution and host frame delivery across packet boundaries to remove inter-chunk idle gaps:

  • •

    Cross-packet codec overlap. Between consecutive DiT windows, causal video decoding for chunk n and TAE proxy encoding for chunk n+1 run concurrently on disjoint GPU subsets (Figure 5, center and bottom). Because TAE encoding finishes well within the causal decoding window, next-packet proxy encoding is hidden behind current-packet decoding.

  • •

    Pipelined CPU delivery. Once causal decoding and the device-to-host copy into shared RGB memory complete, frame packing and socket emission are offloaded to an asynchronous CPU worker. The GPU pool immediately starts chunk n+1’s DiT passes while host delivery proceeds in parallel, cutting the steady-state chunk period from 1165 ms to 930 ms and reaching 18.0 FPS.

    • 6 Experiments

    We evaluate Invoker-Render through systematic pairwise preference comparisons on causal streaming rollouts alongside qualitative studies of multi-granularity creation, camera control, and long-horizon streaming. Section 6.1 details the held-out benchmark and evaluation protocol, Section 6.2 compares our four-step causal renderer against representative streaming baselines, and Section 6.3 illustrates control across proxy families, structural granularities, camera paths, and extended rollouts.

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmark and baselines.

    We evaluate causal streaming rendering on a held-out benchmark of 140 test sequences spanning 6.58 s to 20 s across diverse 3D environments, multi-entity interactions, and proxy representation families, covering both single-window clips and multi-window streaming rollouts. We compare our ProForcing-trained Invoker-Render (Causal, 4-step) checkpoint against three representative few-step causal and streaming proxy-conditioned renderers: SolarRenderer (Causal, 4-step)[12], StreamRender-H3 (2-step)[34], and Streaming CWM (4-step)[28]. Every method receives the identical structural proxy video and appearance reference image on each test sequence.

    Pairwise preference protocol and Elo metrics.

    Effective streaming proxy rendering demands sharp per-frame synthesis, faithful spatial-temporal alignment to the driving proxy, and sustained reference fidelity across sliding windows. Following SolarRenderer [12], we use Gemini 3.8 Flash to conduct blinded pairwise evaluations along four criteria. Each query presents the ground-truth structural proxy sequence, the appearance reference image, and two anonymized candidate renderings A and B (uniformly sampled as timestamped frame sequences at 672×384 and 12 fps with randomized order balancing), eliciting an independent win, tie, or loss judgment along four axes:

  • •

    Visual Quality: per-frame detail sharpness, suppression of synthesis artifacts, and temporal smoothness.

  • •

    Structure & Motion: adherence of scene geometry, subject trajectories, action timing, and camera motion to the input proxy.

  • •

    Reference Preservation: stability of palette, illumination, material appearance, and subject identity relative to the reference frame.

  • •

    Overall Preference: holistic quality as a coherent, deliverable rendered sequence.

    • Pairwise preferences are summarized as Elo ratings using the Bradley–Terry model [1], with ties counted as half a win and the mean rating across methods set to 1000. Overall Preference is evaluated independently of the three component criteria.

    6.2 Quantitative Streaming Comparison

    Table 2 reports Elo ratings across four criteria, and Figure 7 shows Overall outcomes on 140 sequences per baseline. Invoker-Render ranks first on all four criteria, with an Overall rating of 1232.0.

    Against Streaming CWM, Invoker-Render records 130 wins, 8 ties, and 2 losses, giving a 92.9% win rate and an Overall margin of +539.6 Elo. Against StreamRender-H3, it records 116 wins, 4 ties, and 20 losses (82.9% wins and +291.8 Overall Elo). Its margins over StreamRender-H3 are +300.7 in Visual Quality, +197.6 in Structure & Motion, and +281.6 in Reference Preservation.

    SolarRenderer (Causal) is the strongest baseline across all four criteria. Invoker-Render leads by +61.5 in Visual Quality, +56.1 in Structure & Motion, and +46.0 in Reference Preservation. Its 88 wins, 2 ties, and 50 losses against SolarRenderer (62.9% wins vs. 35.7% losses) correspond to an Overall advantage of +96.7 Elo.

    Figure 8 illustrates seven held-out sequences at matched late-rollout timestamps. Other works exhibit scene-geometry loss, severe texture artifacts, visible proxy geometry and flat proxy colors, or drift from the appearance reference at longer horizons: the underwater scene shifts into a bright sky, the winged character loses its wings, the deer loses its antlers, the red car turns beige, the road surface becomes blotchy, half of the ruined street turns black, and a narrow alley fades almost completely to black. Across all seven sequences, Invoker-Render preserves both structural alignment and reference identity.

    6.3 Qualitative Results

    Figures 9–11 further demonstrate how the bidirectional creation checkpoint and the causal four-step checkpoint operate across representations, granularities, camera trajectories, and rollout horizons:

  • •

    Proxy families and geometric granularity (Figure 9). Across five structural families (semantic maps, sparse 3D boxes, subject masks, shaded geometry, and boxes with skeletons), the creation model adheres to prescribed layouts and actor motion while synthesizing coherent lighting and surface detail (Figure 9a). Under a shared appearance reference, varying geometric granularity within one family (Figure 9b) transitions smoothly from global layout guidance under coarse geometry to exact surface anchoring under detailed geometry.

  • •

    Camera-path control (Figure 10). Each row pairs two views of the same scene and event at a matched timestamp, using a shared appearance reference and different proxy-defined camera routes. Coastal driving contrasts tunnel following with an overhead bypass. The rocket launch pairs ground tracking with an ascending drone, and the racing replay pairs a broadcast view with FPV following. These examples show how the supplied camera trajectory changes the viewpoint while retaining the scene and subject appearance.

  • •

    Long-horizon causal streaming (Figure 11). Two racing sequences are compared at six matched timestamps each, extending to 298 s and 299 s. Driven incrementally by incoming proxies, the four-step causal model preserves vehicle appearance and follows the prescribed trajectories across successive streaming windows. These examples complement longer 30-minute racing sessions with consistent scene and vehicle appearance.

    • 7 Conclusion

    We presented Invoker-Render, a proxy-conditioned video rendering framework that unifies bidirectional video creation and four-step causal streaming under a shared multi-granularity interface. Built on a ∼200-hour multi-granularity video-proxy corpus, Progressive Forcing decouples causal adaptation and four-step DMD and GAN distillation on data-anchored histories from stateful continuation on self-generated rollouts, mitigating long-horizon drift while preserving structural fidelity and reference identity. Co-designing this renderer with a fused, KV-persistent, and codec-pipelined serving stack enables low-latency chunked execution, yielding consistent gains in visual quality, structural tracking, and reference preservation across streaming evaluations and sustaining coherent 30-minute racing rollouts toward infinite controllable generation.

    Several directions remain open for scaling proxy-conditioned world rendering. First, although our static prefix sink and sliding KV window bound inference cost and sustain appearance over extended sessions, visual details outside the active window are eventually evicted once they leave the local context. Incorporating explicit long-term memory mechanisms directly into causal training and distillation, such as learnable memory compression, spatial-temporal context retrieval, or persistent 3D-aware state caches, would allow the renderer to recall previously visited environments and maintain multi-entity appearance consistency across revisits. Second, because current training uses a fixed proxy granularity within each rollout window, supporting dynamic mid-stream level-of-detail transitions and coupling Invoker-Render with interactive state engines in closed loop remain promising avenues for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：视觉代理把「显式世界状态模拟」与「真实感视频合成」解耦，但渲染器得同时扛住两种输入尺度。

要点：

  • 分工前提：视觉代理（visual proxy）把**显式的世界状态模拟**与**真实感视频合成**解耦，从而给离线片段生成与实时交互流都提供一个可控接口
  • 两个工程难点：其一，上游代理的粒度**从粗糙布局一直到带关节的精细几何**，取决于具体交互；其二，流式推理必须在**少数几个因果步**内完成，且不能损失精度
  • Code World Model 2.0 针对这两点设计，目标是「无限长且可控」的视频生成

为什么值得看：这是 GameWM/WorldDraft 那条线里最工程化的一篇：它承认「代理视频的质量是变化的」，并要求渲染器对这种变化鲁棒。做「引擎出代理、模型出最终帧」的团队，这条正好补上「代理质量参差怎么办」这个缺口。

中文摘要：视觉代理把「显式世界状态模拟」与「真实感视频合成」解耦，从而为离线片段创作与实时交互流提供可控接口。但一个实用的渲染器必须解决两个问题：一是上游代理的粒度会随交互而变化，从粗糙的布局一直到带关节的精细几何；二是流式推理必须在少数几个因果步内完成，且不能牺牲准确性。Code World Model 2.0 针对这两点提出方案，目标是实现「无限长且可控」的视频生成。对已经在做「引擎输出代理、模型输出最终帧」这条链路的团队，它补的正是「代理质量参差不齐时渲染器如何兜住」这个现实缺口。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Code World Model 2.0:
Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation

Abstract

Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned ∼200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models must synthesize coherent observations as user actions alter the environment [2, 52, 70, 51]. Rather than simulating both dynamics and appearance in one network, an emerging paradigm maintains explicit state in an upstream engine and delegates visual synthesis to a generative renderer [8, 20, 56]. Visual and geometric proxies bridge the two stages by prescribing camera paths, layout, and entity motion while leaving photorealistic appearance to the video model [27, 41, 7, 26]. Recent systems pair such structural cues with appearance references for offline authoring and real-time rendering [12, 34, 31, 19, 67].

In practice, the structural detail appropriate for conditioning depends on the interaction. Broad navigation often requires only coarse scene geometry and root trajectories, whereas close-range interactions demand articulated poses or finer surface structure. Detailed proxies supply tighter constraints at higher construction and transmission cost, while coarse proxies are lightweight to produce yet leave local geometry and motion under-specified. A capable renderer must interpret both regimes faithfully. For example, a rigid mannequin that tracks a character’s root pose should constrain global position and heading without imposing a frozen limb posture on the generated motion.

We introduce Invoker-Render, a proxy-conditioned rendering framework comprising a bidirectional creation model and a causal four-step streaming model. Both accept structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language through a shared interface. Training covers different proxy families, such as semantic layouts and shaded geometry, and multiple granularities within a family. Each checkpoint can follow fine constraints when supplied and synthesize plausible local motion when omitted, supporting different input granularities with the same weights.

For video creation, users edit complete proxy sequences to refine camera paths, trajectories, and event timing. The bidirectional model attends across the full clip. During streaming, future states depend on actions yet to occur. The causal model therefore consumes proxy chunks and local text incrementally, generating each chunk in four steps using retained visual history.

We build on MiniMax-H3 [42] and adopt Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6] to adapt its guidance-distilled backbone to proxy conditioning. Converting the resulting bidirectional model to a streaming renderer requires both fewer denoising steps and tolerance to errors in generated history. Progressive Forcing (ProForcing) addresses these changes in stages (Figure 4). Teacher forcing (TF) first trains block-causal prediction on clean video prefixes. Resampling forcing (RF) then constructs imperfect histories by adding noise to observed prefixes and refining them sequentially with the current model.

RF-DMD retains these resampled histories while learning four-step generation through distribution matching distillation (DMD) [64, 63] and an auxiliary GAN loss [23]. The student, trainable score model, and GAN discriminator then continue training on continuous self-generated histories in SF-DMD [18, 61, 14]. Long-rollout training thus starts with a four-step generator and supervision models already trained alongside it.

We train on an aligned ∼200-hour multi-granularity corpus with hierarchical text. Persistent history caching and pipelined proxy encoding and video decoding reduce serving overhead. Across 140 streaming rollouts, Invoker-Render outperforms recent streaming baselines in visual quality, structural adherence, and reference preservation, and maintains stable scene and subject appearance across 30-minute racing rollouts.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Mixed-granularity proxy conditioning. A shared conditioning interface lets each creation or streaming checkpoint accept coarse and fine proxies.

  • •

    Progressive Forcing. A curriculum progresses from TF/RF causal adaptation to four-step DMD with GAN supervision, then continues the trained student, score model, and discriminator under self-generated histories.

  • •

    Long-horizon controllable generation. Our four-step causal renderer outperforms recent streaming baselines and maintains scene and subject appearance across 30-minute racing rollouts.

  • •

    Multi-granularity corpus and serving stack. An aligned ∼200-hour dataset and a low-latency distributed serving engine support multi-granularity training and continuous interactive streaming.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Interactive Worlds and Generative Rendering

    Action-conditioned video models often internalize world dynamics and visual synthesis in one network, learning latent or discrete action transitions from gameplay and video corpora [2, 52, 10, 4, 54, 57, 70, 40]. LingBot-Video studies mixture-of-experts video pretraining for embodied intelligence, combining web videos with robot-oriented footage [39]. Streaming architectures extend interactive horizons across open-world interactions and explicit context or 3D-aware memory, including the Matrix-Game series, WorldPlay, WorldCrafter, and related streaming world models [16, 53, 44, 68, 51, 66, 46, 13, 62]. Because one visual transition model governs both state evolution and rendering, modifying scene structure or enforcing persistent physical rules remains challenging.

    A complementary paradigm maintains explicit state in an executable engine or agentic controller and delegates synthesis to a conditioned video model. Code World Model, Programmable World Model, and AgentGarten compile structured program state into visual signals [8, 20, 9], Marionette decouples state prediction, geometry rendering, and appearance painting [41], and Wizard supports real-time world manipulation via agentic control [55]. StreamRender-H3, Streaming CWM, Magpie, and BoxWorld likewise couple game or simulator backends with neural renderers through semantic, white-box, or bounding-box streams [34, 28, 67, 56]. Treating proxies as an explicit state-to-renderer contract, Invoker-Render studies controllable granularity across creation and streaming.

    2.2 Proxy-Conditioned Video Generation

    Building on spatial control, camera conditioning, and unified video creation frameworks [69, 15, 22], proxy-conditioned video models ground synthesis in geometric or semantic structure across several regimes. Paired methods learn directly from dense geometry, lighting, material buffers, or animated meshes, as in DiffusionRenderer, Generative World Renderer, and native 4D mesh rendering [26, 21, 7]. Proxy2World relaxes paired supervision via posed RGB-D clips [59], whereas training-free methods such as Code Video Model restrict proxy injection to early denoising steps so appearance follows the reference image [27].

    Recent renderers broaden representation diversity, customization, and structural fidelity. SolarRenderer reuses the backbone’s reference pathway across heterogeneous structural videos with a four-step acceleration LoRA [12], EdenLive and Mundo support real-time reference-driven rendering and customized world synthesis [19, 36], Fight World Model controls combat interactions via visual proxies [25], and AnyGameRenderer preserves cross-game entity counts and timing [31]. Invoker-Render targets an orthogonal axis: structural granularity within one representation family, enabling a single model to honor fine constraints when supplied and synthesize natural local motion under lightweight coarse proxies.

    2.3 Streaming Video Diffusion and Few-Step Distillation

    While training-free queue scheduling such as FIFO-Diffusion enables continuous generation via diagonal denoising [24], interactive streaming requires block-causal attention and few-step sampling. Diffusion Forcing trains causal models with independent token noise levels [5], CausVid distills a bidirectional teacher into an autoregressive student [65], and Self Forcing rolls out the student on its own predictions [18]. LongLive stabilizes rollouts via streaming tuning and a persistent frame sink [61, 58], SANA-WM and minWM scale minute-horizon and full-stack world modeling [77, 71], and AlayaRenderer-Flash and StreamRender-H3 co-design few-step causal rendering with low-latency serving [29, 34].

    To compress flow-matching trajectories [30, 32], consistency distillation maps states directly to clean targets [49], score-based distribution matching [35, 64, 75] aligns distributions via auxiliary score differences, and DMD2, ADD, and LADD pair score or diffusion distillation with discriminator supervision [63, 48, 47]. Multi-step variants refine supervision across steps, with Trajectory Distribution Matching (TDM) and VA-TDM aligning multi-step trajectories and velocity fields [37, 38] and Endpoint Distribution Matching (eDMD) anchoring the fake score model on final clean outputs [73]. For causal video, Causal Forcing uses an autoregressive ODE teacher, Causal Forcing++ and Causal-rCM adopt consistency-based causal initialization [78, 72, 74], and Salt++ aligns streaming generation and scoring contexts [14]. ProForcing instead distills a four-step student with teacher-feature relativistic GAN supervision [23, 47] on resampled data-anchored histories (RF-DMD) before continuing the coupled student, fake score model, discriminator, and optimizer states on continuous self-generated rollouts (SF-DMD).

    3 Data Curation and Proxy Construction

    Controllable rendering requires aligned training pairs that cleanly separate the geometry prescribed by a proxy from the appearance and local dynamics synthesized by the model. Our corpus comprises approximately 200 hours of footage, combining 150 hours of self-collected data with 50 hours from public datasets, and associates each usable RGB clip with structural conditions, an appearance reference, and hierarchical text annotations. We design the pipeline around three core requirements: spatial-temporal correspondence between proxies and RGB targets, multi-granularity structural representations of the same event, and language descriptions tailored to both whole-window creation and block-causal streaming.

    3.1 Data Sources and Coverage

    Table 1 summarizes the corpus composition. Self-collected recordings allow us to render matched coarse and fine proxies from a shared reconstructed scene state, whereas public datasets broaden environment diversity and contribute native structural modalities. Reported durations count unique source footage prior to extracting overlapping training windows or multiple proxy variants. Figure 2 illustrates representative source frames alongside their paired structural conditions.

    Self-collected data.

    We capture gameplay across diverse 3D environments (including Grand Theft Auto V, Cyberpunk 2077, Elden Ring, and Forza Horizon 5), spanning navigation, urban driving, and character interactions under varied camera trajectories, weather, and illumination. Automated navigation and driving scripts yield sustained, smooth trajectories, while human gameplay contributes unscripted interactions and rapid viewpoint transitions. RGB frames and accessible engine buffers are recorded synchronously, with camera poses and dynamic object states recovered offline where engine exports are incomplete, preserving continuous multi-action trajectories for long-horizon training.

    Public sources.

    Public subsets contribute white-box geometry, semantic layouts, and dense depth, and Figure 2 additionally includes Virtual KITTI 2 [3] to illustrate RGB paired with dense semantic segmentation. Source-specific preprocessing aligns native annotations to a unified frame rate and conditioning interface, applying geometric and temporal validity checks before enabling structural supervision. Clips lacking reliable structural alignment are retained solely for reference-and-text appearance supervision. Recording available condition types per sample allows public datasets to contribute their native modalities without requiring synthetic coarse/fine pairs for every source.

    3.2 Aligned Scene States and Multi-Granularity Proxies

    Figure 3 outlines capture and proxy construction for our self-collected corpus. While recorded RGB serves as the supervision target, synchronized engine buffers and reconstructed 3D scene states (comprising camera intrinsics and extrinsics, static environment geometry, and tracked dynamic entities) allow us to render multiple structural granularities of the exact same visual event.

    Capture and reconstruction.

    Starting from synchronized RGB and engine depth capture, our reconstruction pipeline recovers camera calibration, scene semantics, and 3D entity motion. Instance segmentation and multi-object tracking [45] isolate moving actors and vehicles from the static scene, which is labeled via semantic segmentation and completed across invalid depth regions [60], while camera pose estimation and background point tracking recover globally consistent trajectories. For dynamic actors, human motion recovery estimates both global root trajectories and articulated body poses, and 3D bounding-box fitting tracks rigid vehicle motion. Retaining per-frame camera parameters, track IDs, and confidence masks alongside the video enables automated reprojection and tracking verification prior to proxy rendering.

    Coarse structural control.

    Coarse proxies encode global scene layout, camera motion, and entity placement and heading while omitting fine local geometry. Humans are rendered as canonical rigid mannequins driven solely by root pose, vehicles as oriented 3D boxes, and backgrounds as simplified geometry or semantic regions. Because a canonical mannequin conveys root translation and orientation without limb articulation, the paired RGB target and action text teach the generator to synthesize natural gait and posture consistent with the trajectory.

    Fine geometric and motion control.

    Fine proxies augment this representation with articulated human poses (rendered as depth-tested volumetric body parts) and shaded local surface geometry, while preserving rigid vehicle boxes. Wherever both variants are constructed, coarse and fine proxies share identical camera parameters, timestamps, entity identities, and RGB targets, directly supervising the renderer across constraint strengths for the same event. Throughout this work, we distinguish granularity, meaning the level of geometric and kinematic detail within a representation, from representation family, such as semantic maps, shaded depth, or white-box renders.

    Separating structure from appearance.

    To prevent appearance leakage, both granularities strip away surface textures, materials, and scene lighting. Before compositing dynamic entities, foreground masks are excised from background depth and semantic buffers and inpainted from temporally adjacent background views, suppressing silhouette cues from clothing, hair, or accessories. Reprojecting the simplified dynamic primitives onto this cleaned background with depth occlusion ensures that proxies convey pure spatial and motion structure, leaving appearance to the reference frame, language, and learned video prior.

    3.3 Sequence Lengths and Hierarchical Language

    Short windows and continuous sequences.

    Self-collected and public recordings are standardized at 24 fps into 158-frame windows (∼6.6 s) and 328-frame continuous sequences (∼13.7 s). RGB targets use 1344×768, while aligned proxies are stored at 672×384 and encoded at 672×384 or 448×256 using nearest-neighbor resizing for semantic maps and anti-aliased filtering for continuous geometry. Short windows support bidirectional GFT, supervised TF/RF, and RF-DMD, whereas 328-frame sequences support variable-length SF-DMD rollouts across uninterrupted trajectories.

    Whole-window descriptions.

    Text annotations combine clip-level scene descriptions with timestamped local actions (“Scene + local actions” in Figure 3). Each window pairs its opening RGB anchor with a vision-language caption covering environment, subject appearance, lighting, events, and camera motion. The bidirectional creation model and the bidirectional teacher and fake score models each receive independent whole-window captions rather than concatenated local tags.

    Streaming action annotations.

    Timestamped local annotations track action progression, motion directions, interactions, and camera shifts across block boundaries so that TF/RF and the distilled student observe text strictly up to the current block, without future labels or clip summaries. For coarse proxies, local text disambiguates behaviors whose articulation is omitted from rigid root geometry.

    Condition organization.

    A system instruction defines the roles of structural proxies and the appearance reference alongside sample captions, while automated validation checks reference tags, temporal order, and entity-action agreement.

    3.4 Quality Control and Evaluation Separation

    Quality control screens both video and proxies for corrupted or frozen frames, exposure failures, shot cuts, reprojection outliers, tracking switches, and timing drift. Automated geometric checks and manual review evaluate each proxy against its intended constraints, distinguishing omitted coarse articulation from root-trajectory or camera errors.

    Records track source identifiers, frame ranges, proxy variants, captions, and encoding provenance, with cross-source deduplication across shared game worlds. Training and held-out splits are partitioned by recording (and by scene or map where identifiable), keeping overlapping windows, coarse/fine pairs, and alternative views of one recording in the same split to prevent leakage.

    4 Invoker-Render

    Invoker-Render adapts MiniMax-H3 [42] into both a bidirectional video creation model and a causal four-step streaming renderer. We first formalize the shared conditioning interface and linear flow parameterization, then present bidirectional proxy adaptation via Guidance-Free Training, and finally detail Progressive Forcing (ProForcing), which distills few-step causal rendering on data-anchored histories before transitioning to continuous self-generated rollouts.

    4.1 Rendering Formulation and Proxy Conditioning

Conditioning inputs consist of an independently encoded appearance anchor a, structural proxies p=p_1:B, a system instruction s, and text annotations ℓ=ℓ_1:B. Whereas the bidirectional creation model attends over the full proxy sequence p_1:B and a clip-level caption, the causal streaming model observes c_b=(a,s,p_≤b,ℓ_≤b) at block b and factorizes the joint distribution autoregressively across blocks:

    where hᵇ denotes the retained visual history prior to block b and ℓ_≤b collects text annotations revealed through block b. Target attention in the streaming model is bidirectional within each block and strictly causal across blocks. Both models preserve the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [43] backbone’s native reference pathway and rotary positional embedding (RoPE) [50] indexing, keeping the appearance anchor a fixed outside the training loss.

    Control across granularities.

    Coarse and fine proxies enter through an identical conditioning pathway, trained jointly on mixed-granularity examples. Coarse inputs prescribe scene layout, camera trajectory, and entity root motion, while fine inputs further constrain limb articulation and local surface geometry. At inference time, downstream applications can select the structural detail suited to each interaction while relying on the appearance reference, text, and video prior to supply visual texture and unconstrained local motion.

    4.2 Bidirectional Creation Model

    Because MiniMax-H3 already incorporates distilled classifier-free guidance [17], we adapt it to structural proxy control using Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6]. Pairing the full conditioning tuple c⁺ with a weakened counterpart c⁻ that drops the structural proxy while retaining the appearance anchor, we blend their velocity predictions at guidance scale β=2 with 10% condition dropout:

    \begingatheredṽ_θ=1/βv_θ(xₜ,t|c⁺)+(1-1/β)v_θ⁻(xₜ,t|c⁻), [3.0pt] L_GFT(θ)=𝔼_x₀,ε,t [w(t)\lVertṽ_θ-v\rVert₂²].\endgathered

Detaching the weak-condition branch v_θ⁻(xₜ,t|c⁻) routes gradients exclusively through the proxy-conditioned pathway, sharpening structural adherence without inference-time CFG overhead. Trained under full bidirectional attention with complete proxy sequences and whole-window captions, the resulting checkpoint serves directly as our offline creation renderer and provides the initialization for causal adaptation and distillation critics.

    4.3 Progressive Forcing for Few-Step Rendering

    Directly distilling a bidirectional model into a few-step autoregressive renderer conflates trajectory compression with exposure to self-generated rollout errors. ProForcing disentangles these challenges across progressive stages (Figure 4). Supervised TF and RF first adapt attention to block-causal histories anchored to ground-truth video, RF-DMD then distills a four-step generator alongside learned score and adversarial critics under those data-anchored histories, and SF-DMD (Section 4.4) finally transitions the jointly trained system to continuous self-generated rollouts.
