    RF-conditioned distribution matching.

    Initialized from the supervised RF checkpoint, RF-DMD compresses sampling to four steps via distribution matching distillation [64, 63, 37, 73] while retaining detached RF history construction (h_RFᵇ). Keeping histories anchored to observed video during distillation isolates four-step trajectory learning from open-loop autoregressive drift. To score student outputs, a frozen bidirectional teacher f_teacher and a trainable bidirectional fake score model f_fake (both initialized from the bidirectional GFT checkpoint) evaluate re-noised student predictions under complete scoring-window conditions, while the student itself remains strictly block-causal. Meanwhile, f_fake is updated online via flow matching on detached, re-noised student samples.

    Specifically, let x₀^θ denote the clean prediction tapped from a selected step of the student’s four-step denoising rollout, and let xₜ=(1-t)x₀^θ⁻+tε be its detached re-noised input shared by both score models. We apply the DMD gradient through the surrogate objective

    L_DMD(θ)=1/2 𝔼 [\lVertx₀^θ-x₀^θ⁻+g\rVert₂²].

    		(5)

    Writing g=(g¹,…,g^B), the target-seeking displacement on block b is gᵇ=(f_fakeᵇ-f_teacherᵇ)/Z_b, where Z_b normalizes by the mean absolute discrepancy between detached student and teacher predictions (clamped to a positive floor). Treating g as a stop-gradient target ensures that differentiation of Eq. (5) propagates the exact normalized score difference into x₀^θ across all valid blocks.

    Teacher-feature relativistic GAN.

    To sharpen perceptual detail and suppress few-step over-smoothing, we pair DMD with a discriminator D_φ comprising frozen teacher backbone features [47, 63] followed by lightweight trainable projections and a noise-conditioned scalar head. Ground-truth windows x₀ and generated windows x₀^θ are perturbed with identical (t,ε) via Eq. (2) under matched conditions and the shared appearance anchor, producing scalar logits r_φ and q_φ. We optimize paired relativistic logistic losses [23, 63] alongside the combined student objective:

    L_D(φ)=λ_D 𝔼 [\log (1+e^q_φ-r_φ)],(6)
    L_GAN(θ)=𝔼 [\log (1+e^sg(r_φ)-q_φ)],
    L_student(θ)=L_DMD(θ)+λ_advL_GAN(θ).

    Here λ_D and λ_adv weight the discriminator and adversarial terms, and sg(·) denotes the stop-gradient operator on scalar logits. Discriminator updates detach generated latents x₀^θ, whereas student updates detach the real-branch logit r_φ and freeze both teacher and discriminator parameters while backpropagating through the generated-branch input q_φ. Note that D_φ and f_fake remain separate networks trained under distinct objectives.

    4.4 Long-Sequence Self-Forcing

    Building on self-forcing and streaming long tuning [18, 61], SF-DMD replaces data-anchored RF prefixes with continuous student-generated histories. Starting from the appearance anchor a, the student sequentially denoises each block in four steps and commits its detached terminal prediction x̂₀ᵇ to the causal history cache (h_SFᵇ=x̂₀^

    Local scoring of a continuous stream.

    To supervise rollouts longer than the bidirectional teacher’s native window, we tile the continuous student stream with overlapping local scoring windows. Each window pairs preceding generated blocks (serving purely as detached temporal context) with a disjoint interval of newly generated target blocks, always retaining the original appearance anchor a. The teacher, fake score model, and discriminator observe complete conditions within each local window while the student remains causal, and DMD and GAN input gradients are masked to apply strictly once per non-anchor target block, weighted by target coverage.

    Coordinated continuation from RF-DMD.

    Crucially, transitioning from RF-DMD to SF-DMD carries forward the entire coupled training state (student weights, fake score model f_fake, discriminator D_φ, their respective AdamW moments [33], and the student EMA) against the same frozen teacher. Because RF-DMD already converges a capable four-step causal generator together with calibrated supervision models tailored to its output distribution, SF-DMD avoids cold-start critic instability and focuses optimization on mitigating long-horizon error accumulation under self-generated histories.

    5 Streaming Serving Infrastructure

    To deploy the causal world model as an online interactive rendering service, each streaming step must encode incoming visual proxies, update retained clean history H and current proxy conditioning C within a bounded KV window, run four-step causal denoising, and return decoded RGB frames within a strict latency budget. Starting from a standard streaming baseline, we streamline the inference stack across three levels: (i) an asymmetric streaming codec pairing a lightweight Tiny AutoEncoder (TAE) for online proxy encoding with a causal video decoder for RGB reconstruction; (ii) intra-window invariant reuse and fused execution across DiT layers, KV workspaces, and prefill/denoising passes; and (iii) cross-packet codec overlap and asynchronous CPU delivery (Figure 5). On an eight-GPU node at 1344×768 resolution, these optimizations reduce the steady-state per-chunk period from 1770 ms to 930 ms and increase throughput from 9.9 FPS to 18.0 FPS (1.82× speedup; Figure 6).

    5.1 Efficient Asymmetric Streaming Codec

    Interactive streaming places asymmetric demands on the visual codec: incoming proxy frames must be encoded at every chunk with minimal latency, whereas generated latents must be decoded into temporally continuous RGB video. Encoding online proxies with the full video encoder is slower than output decoding and dominates the inter-chunk codec interval.

    We therefore adopt an asymmetric codec design. The static reference frame is encoded once at session start with the full encoder to preserve anchor detail, while online proxy packets are encoded independently by a lightweight TAE proxy encoder directly into normalized 16× spatially compressed, 24-channel conditioning latents. On the output side, we retain the tensor-parallel Causal Video Decoder to preserve temporal continuity across chunks. Replacing the online proxy encoder with TAE makes input encoding an order of magnitude faster than causal decoding (T_enc≪T_dec), reducing the steady-state chunk period from 1770 ms to 1410 ms and raising throughput from 9.9 FPS to 12.4 FPS.

    5.2 Intra-Window Reuse and Fused Execution

    Within each DiT window, we eliminate redundant per-layer preparation, projection compute, memory allocation, and separate prefill launches:

  • •

    Cross-layer structural sharing. Within a single forward pass, all DiT layers share identical token layout plans, sliding-window crop indices, and frame-aligned RoPE position tensors. We construct these plans and index tensors once at backbone entry and reuse them across all layers.

  • •

    Per-layer AdaLN projection caching. Because session conditioning is stationary and the four-step Euler timestep schedule repeats across chunks, we cache each DiT block’s projected AdaLN modulation parameters by timestep and reuse them across subsequent chunks.

  • •

    Transactional KV workspace reuse. Instead of allocating fresh output and concatenation buffers at every layer, we reuse pre-allocated KV result backplanes and temporary forward workspaces across the transaction lifecycle (Figure 5, top). Combining structural invariant and workspace reuse reduces the steady-state chunk period from 1410 ms to 1180 ms and lifts throughput from 12.4 FPS to 14.4 FPS.

  • •

    Fused prefill-and-denoise pass (H/C/D₁). In ordinary continuation windows, we defer committing prior clean history Hₙ₋₁ and pack it with incoming proxy tokens Cₙ and the first denoising state D₁ into a single block-causal composite forward (Pass 1 in Figure 5), followed by three denoising-only passes (D₂–D₄). Reducing backbone launches from six to four trims the chunk period from 1180 ms to 1165 ms and raises throughput to 14.8 FPS.

    • 5.3 Cross-Packet Pipelining and RGB Delivery

    With intra-window DiT execution compressed, we pipeline codec execution and host frame delivery across packet boundaries to remove inter-chunk idle gaps:

  • •

    Cross-packet codec overlap. Between consecutive DiT windows, causal video decoding for chunk n and TAE proxy encoding for chunk n+1 run concurrently on disjoint GPU subsets (Figure 5, center and bottom). Because TAE encoding finishes well within the causal decoding window, next-packet proxy encoding is hidden behind current-packet decoding.

  • •

    Pipelined CPU delivery. Once causal decoding and the device-to-host copy into shared RGB memory complete, frame packing and socket emission are offloaded to an asynchronous CPU worker. The GPU pool immediately starts chunk n+1’s DiT passes while host delivery proceeds in parallel, cutting the steady-state chunk period from 1165 ms to 930 ms and reaching 18.0 FPS.

    • 6 Experiments

    We evaluate Invoker-Render through systematic pairwise preference comparisons on causal streaming rollouts alongside qualitative studies of multi-granularity creation, camera control, and long-horizon streaming. Section 6.1 details the held-out benchmark and evaluation protocol, Section 6.2 compares our four-step causal renderer against representative streaming baselines, and Section 6.3 illustrates control across proxy families, structural granularities, camera paths, and extended rollouts.

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmark and baselines.

    We evaluate causal streaming rendering on a held-out benchmark of 140 test sequences spanning 6.58 s to 20 s across diverse 3D environments, multi-entity interactions, and proxy representation families, covering both single-window clips and multi-window streaming rollouts. We compare our ProForcing-trained Invoker-Render (Causal, 4-step) checkpoint against three representative few-step causal and streaming proxy-conditioned renderers: SolarRenderer (Causal, 4-step)[12], StreamRender-H3 (2-step)[34], and Streaming CWM (4-step)[28]. Every method receives the identical structural proxy video and appearance reference image on each test sequence.

    Pairwise preference protocol and Elo metrics.

    Effective streaming proxy rendering demands sharp per-frame synthesis, faithful spatial-temporal alignment to the driving proxy, and sustained reference fidelity across sliding windows. Following SolarRenderer [12], we use Gemini 3.8 Flash to conduct blinded pairwise evaluations along four criteria. Each query presents the ground-truth structural proxy sequence, the appearance reference image, and two anonymized candidate renderings A and B (uniformly sampled as timestamped frame sequences at 672×384 and 12 fps with randomized order balancing), eliciting an independent win, tie, or loss judgment along four axes:

  • •

    Visual Quality: per-frame detail sharpness, suppression of synthesis artifacts, and temporal smoothness.

  • •

    Structure & Motion: adherence of scene geometry, subject trajectories, action timing, and camera motion to the input proxy.

  • •

    Reference Preservation: stability of palette, illumination, material appearance, and subject identity relative to the reference frame.

  • •

    Overall Preference: holistic quality as a coherent, deliverable rendered sequence.

    • Pairwise preferences are summarized as Elo ratings using the Bradley–Terry model [1], with ties counted as half a win and the mean rating across methods set to 1000. Overall Preference is evaluated independently of the three component criteria.

    6.2 Quantitative Streaming Comparison

    Table 2 reports Elo ratings across four criteria, and Figure 7 shows Overall outcomes on 140 sequences per baseline. Invoker-Render ranks first on all four criteria, with an Overall rating of 1232.0.

    Against Streaming CWM, Invoker-Render records 130 wins, 8 ties, and 2 losses, giving a 92.9% win rate and an Overall margin of +539.6 Elo. Against StreamRender-H3, it records 116 wins, 4 ties, and 20 losses (82.9% wins and +291.8 Overall Elo). Its margins over StreamRender-H3 are +300.7 in Visual Quality, +197.6 in Structure & Motion, and +281.6 in Reference Preservation.

    SolarRenderer (Causal) is the strongest baseline across all four criteria. Invoker-Render leads by +61.5 in Visual Quality, +56.1 in Structure & Motion, and +46.0 in Reference Preservation. Its 88 wins, 2 ties, and 50 losses against SolarRenderer (62.9% wins vs. 35.7% losses) correspond to an Overall advantage of +96.7 Elo.

    Figure 8 illustrates seven held-out sequences at matched late-rollout timestamps. Other works exhibit scene-geometry loss, severe texture artifacts, visible proxy geometry and flat proxy colors, or drift from the appearance reference at longer horizons: the underwater scene shifts into a bright sky, the winged character loses its wings, the deer loses its antlers, the red car turns beige, the road surface becomes blotchy, half of the ruined street turns black, and a narrow alley fades almost completely to black. Across all seven sequences, Invoker-Render preserves both structural alignment and reference identity.

    6.3 Qualitative Results

    Figures 9–11 further demonstrate how the bidirectional creation checkpoint and the causal four-step checkpoint operate across representations, granularities, camera trajectories, and rollout horizons:

  • •

    Proxy families and geometric granularity (Figure 9). Across five structural families (semantic maps, sparse 3D boxes, subject masks, shaded geometry, and boxes with skeletons), the creation model adheres to prescribed layouts and actor motion while synthesizing coherent lighting and surface detail (Figure 9a). Under a shared appearance reference, varying geometric granularity within one family (Figure 9b) transitions smoothly from global layout guidance under coarse geometry to exact surface anchoring under detailed geometry.

  • •

    Camera-path control (Figure 10). Each row pairs two views of the same scene and event at a matched timestamp, using a shared appearance reference and different proxy-defined camera routes. Coastal driving contrasts tunnel following with an overhead bypass. The rocket launch pairs ground tracking with an ascending drone, and the racing replay pairs a broadcast view with FPV following. These examples show how the supplied camera trajectory changes the viewpoint while retaining the scene and subject appearance.

  • •

    Long-horizon causal streaming (Figure 11). Two racing sequences are compared at six matched timestamps each, extending to 298 s and 299 s. Driven incrementally by incoming proxies, the four-step causal model preserves vehicle appearance and follows the prescribed trajectories across successive streaming windows. These examples complement longer 30-minute racing sessions with consistent scene and vehicle appearance.

    • 7 Conclusion

    We presented Invoker-Render, a proxy-conditioned video rendering framework that unifies bidirectional video creation and four-step causal streaming under a shared multi-granularity interface. Built on a ∼200-hour multi-granularity video-proxy corpus, Progressive Forcing decouples causal adaptation and four-step DMD and GAN distillation on data-anchored histories from stateful continuation on self-generated rollouts, mitigating long-horizon drift while preserving structural fidelity and reference identity. Co-designing this renderer with a fused, KV-persistent, and codec-pipelined serving stack enables low-latency chunked execution, yielding consistent gains in visual quality, structural tracking, and reference preservation across streaming evaluations and sustaining coherent 30-minute racing rollouts toward infinite controllable generation.

    Several directions remain open for scaling proxy-conditioned world rendering. First, although our static prefix sink and sliding KV window bound inference cost and sustain appearance over extended sessions, visual details outside the active window are eventually evicted once they leave the local context. Incorporating explicit long-term memory mechanisms directly into causal training and distillation, such as learnable memory compression, spatial-temporal context retrieval, or persistent 3D-aware state caches, would allow the renderer to recall previously visited environments and maintain multi-entity appearance consistency across revisits. Second, because current training uses a fixed proxy granularity within each rollout window, supporting dynamic mid-stream level-of-detail transitions and coupling Invoker-Render with interactive state engines in closed loop remain promising avenues for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 镜头转开再转回来，世界就冻住了：PanoEvo 用全景潜空间做「世界状态演化」，只在当前视角渲染 ｜ Evolve in Panorama, Render in View: Panoramic World State Evolution for Video World Models
item.description:
一句话：视野之外没有任何「继续变化」的表示，所以一转回来就冻结、丢物体或变样。

要点：

  • 现象精准：视频世界模型本应维持一个**随视角变化持续演化**的世界，但当前模型在镜头转开再转回时，常常把未观察的场景**冻结**、丢掉物体，或让外观改变
  • 根因：**视野之外的内容没有任何能持续变化的表示**
  • PanoEvo 的做法是用一个 Panoramic Evolver，在全景视频扩散模型的**潜空间**里演化世界状态，再把「当前视角」渲染出来——即「在全景里演化、在视角里渲染」

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线里最直白的一篇：它把 11-12 期 Evoke 的「外置状态库」换成「全景潜空间」，指出同一件事——不表示画外，画外就不会动。引擎开发者对此再熟悉不过：这就是「视锥外剔除」与「世界仍在 tick」的区别。

中文摘要：视频世界模型本应维持一个随视角变化而持续演化的世界，但作者发现当前模型有一个共性失败：当相机转开再转回来时，未观察到的场景常常被冻结、物体丢失，或者外观发生变化。根因在于，视野之外的内容没有任何能够持续变化的表示。PanoEvo 因此提出「在全景里演化、在视角里渲染」：用一个 Panoramic Evolver 在全景视频扩散模型的潜空间中演化世界状态，再从中渲染出当前视角的画面。这条思路与把世界状态外置到显式结构中的做法同源——不表示画外，画外就不会动。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Evolve in Panorama, Render in View:
Panoramic World State Evolution for Video World Models

Abstract

Video world models should maintain a world that keeps evolving as the viewpoint changes. Yet when the camera turns away and returns, current models often freeze the unobserved scene, lose objects, or change their appearance, because content outside the view has no representation that keeps changing. We present PanoEvo, which uses a Panoramic Evolver to evolve the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model, where every viewing direction is present at every time step, so the scene evolves whether or not it is observed. Existing panoramic video models are not trained to evolve a scene from a single image or the objects within it, so we build PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360∘ videos, and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine as an image-to-panoramic-video model. Since each view covers only a small part of the low-resolution panorama, directly projected views are blurry and often show low-quality details or structural errors. A Perspective Renderer, built on a perspective video diffusion model, reads this state via latent-space projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to render sharp, high-quality views. PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench. Code, models, and data will be released.

1 Introduction

Video world models generate future observations of a scene from an initial image and a sequence of viewpoints or actions [33, 38, 35, 31]. As they move toward interactive exploration, they are expected to maintain a persistent world. Persistence, however, is more than geometric consistency. The world keeps evolving: a person keeps walking, a dog keeps playing, and an action that has started keeps unfolding, whether or not the camera looks at it. Recent benchmarks test this by turning the camera away and back [29, 30, 8], and show that current models fall short. On return, the unobserved scene is frozen in its last observed state, objects vanish, or their appearance changes.

The root cause lies in what a perspective video model represents. It models the content inside the current view, and once content leaves it, nothing in the model represents it, let alone advances it. Existing remedies mainly retain what has been seen. Geometry caches and 3D memories [34, 53, 52, 44] keep the scene geometry, source-video re-rendering [3, 19] reuses observed frames, and memory or state mechanisms [9, 10, 50, 5] retrieve past observations or reason about entities explicitly. These approaches preserve how the world looked when observed, but few densely represent unobserved content that keeps changing.

We observe that, for a rotating camera, a panoramic video latent provides exactly such a representation. Every viewing direction is present at every time step, so a panoramic video diffusion model evolves the whole scene jointly in its latent space, regardless of where the camera points, and any requested view is a projection of this state. Directly projected views, however, are poor. At a typical 512×1024 resolution, a 90^∘ view covers only about 256 pixels horizontally and must be upsampled over three times to 480×832, blurring the view and degrading object structures. We therefore assign the two roles to two models (Fig.1). A panoramic video diffusion model maintains the evolving world state, and a perspective video diffusion model reads it to render high-quality views. We call this framework PanoEvo: evolve in panorama, render in view.

Realizing this idea requires two components. First, the panoramic model has to work like a conventional image-to-video model, the common interface of video world models [33, 38, 19]: given a single image, it should evolve the whole scene. Existing panoramic video models are text-driven [46, 49, 12] or complete panoramas from video observations [20, 39], panoramic world models start from a full panoramic image [44], and how individual objects evolve remains underexplored. Zero-shot, a strong panoramic model completes the scene but evolves it poorly (Sec.5.4). We build PanoEvo-Data from real 360∘ videos and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine. A Completion stage on about 20K curated clips teaches image-conditioned panoramic completion, and an Evolution stage on 1.4K verified event clips teaches object-level state evolution. Second, the Perspective Renderer has to read the state faithfully and improve visual quality. Built on a perspective video model, it projects the panoramic latent into each view in latent space, reads further context through frustum cross-attention, and is guided by an auxiliary read-out loss.

PanoEvo achieves the best overall score on WRBench among 23 publicly evaluated models (.753 vs. .741 for the strongest baseline), together with the best scores on visible state and both re-observation metrics. On STEVO-Bench, it attains the highest total score (364.7 vs. 300.9). Compared with direct projection of the panorama, the Perspective Renderer raises VBench imaging quality from .538 to .729 while largely preserving the evolved states.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose PanoEvo, which evolves the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model and renders views from it with a perspective one.

  • •

    We build PanoEvo-Data from real 360∘ videos and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine to evolve object-level states from a single image.

  • •

    We design a Perspective Renderer that reads the state through latent-space projection and frustum cross-attention. PanoEvo is state of the art on both benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video world models with memory and state.

    Interactive and camera-controlled video world models [33, 38, 23, 35, 22, 31] generate long explorations from an initial image. Camera control is usually injected into video diffusion models [40, 21, 51] through Plücker embeddings [37, 14, 47, 2], with open-source variants available [1]. To add memory, geometry-based methods maintain point clouds or 3D caches and condition generation on their renderings [34, 53, 52, 44]. Source-video methods re-render a given video along a new trajectory [3, 19]. These methods keep revisited regions geometrically consistent but treat dynamic content as static or remove it. Closer to our goal, HyDRA [9] tracks dynamic subjects over a static memory, LiveWorld [10] advances dynamic entities with an evolution engine, and ReMind [50] recovers evolving states across interruptions. Other works reason about out-of-view events with a vision-language model [5] or control objects along trajectories planned by a language model [43]. Recent evaluations expose the remaining gap through camera look-away, occlusion, and illumination changes [29, 30, 8], where unobserved content is often frozen, lost, or altered. Unlike these methods, PanoEvo keeps a dense panoramic latent of the whole scene that evolves at every time step, so unobserved content advances without explicit entity modeling, memory retrieval, or event reasoning.

    Panoramic video generation.

    Panoramic video models generate 360∘ videos from text [46, 49, 12], outpaint perspective videos to panoramas [39], use cube-map representations for high resolution [24], or support roaming and world modeling [28, 20, 54, 44], and panoramic image models [13] provide static first frames. PanoWorld [20] treats the panoramic latent as a geometrically consistent world representation, and we build the Panoramic Evolver on its released weights. These works focus on the panorama itself and its spatial consistency. We instead use a panoramic model as the state of a perspective world model, start from a single image, and target object-level evolution.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Setting and Overview

    Given a perspective frame I₀, an optional text prompt y, and a camera trajectory C={Rₜ}ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹, we generate a perspective video V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹ that starts at I₀ and follows C.

    Why a panoramic state.

    For a rotating camera, every perspective frame is a deterministic function of the panoramic frame at the same time,

    Iₜ=Π(Pₜ,Rₜ),

    		(1)

    where Pₜ is the 360^∘ frame at time t and Π is the perspective projection. Content outside the current view is not missing, only not projected. Generating P_0:T-1 from I₀ amounts to evolving the whole world, and the trajectory only selects which part is shown. A perspective model, in contrast, has to decide what an unobserved region looks like when it re-enters the view, without having represented it in between, which is where frozen scenes and vanishing objects arise.

    Factorization.

    PanoEvo factorizes generation through a panoramic world state W, generated by the Panoramic Evolver 𝔼 and rendered by the Perspective Renderer ℝ (Fig.2):

    W∼𝔼(I₀,y), V∼ℝ(W,I₀,y,C),

    		(2)

    where W is the latent of an equirectangular (ERP) panoramic video under the Wan2.1 VAE [40], the latent space that ℝ reads. 𝔼 determines what happens in the world, including outside the view, and ℝ reads it faithfully along C and renders coherent, high-quality views. 𝔼 and ℝ are trained separately, and at inference 𝔼 generates W once and ℝ renders any number of views from it.

    3.2 Panoramic Evolver

    Conditioning and observation write-back.

    We build 𝔼 on PanoWorld [20], a panoramic video diffusion transformer based on Cosmos [31], and reuse its native completion pathway without adding input channels. We place I₀ at the front of the ERP canvas (yaw 0^∘, pitch 0^∘) to obtain a sparse observation X_obs and its visibility mask M. Unobserved pixels are filled with Gaussian noise, X_cond=M⊙X_obs+(1-M)⊙ε_fill with ε_fill∼ℕ(0,0.5²I), and X_cond is encoded into a reference latent z_ref, which is concatenated with the latent-resolution mask along the channel dimension. SigLIP2 [41] features of I₀ enter through cross-attention, and the text y is encoded by Cosmos-Reason1 [32]. The condition is encoded independently of the target panorama, so it never contains unobserved content. Before every network evaluation, the fully observed latent cells M̄ (coverage above 0.99) are replaced by the clean z_ref and excluded from the loss, and the replacement is applied once more after sampling. Partially covered cells are generated and supervised. This native write-back is essential for single-image inputs, since without it the fine-tuned model learns to ignore the observed image.

    Objective.

    Let z₀ be the latent of the target panoramic video. Following rectified flow [27, 25], we sample a noise level σ with logit-normal sampling and a shift of 5 [11], form z_σ=σε+(1-σ)z₀ with ε∼ℕ(0,I), and minimize

    \beginsplitr_θ&=v_θ(z_σ,σ,c)-(ε-z₀), L_𝔼&=𝔼_σ,ε[ ∥(1-M̄)⊙r_θ∥²],\endsplit

    		(3)

    where v_θ is the velocity predicted by 𝔼, r_θ its residual, and c the conditions (z_ref with its mask, I₀, and y).

    Coarse-to-fine training.

    We train 𝔼 in two stages on the subsets of PanoEvo-Data (Sec.4). The Completion stage adapts the model to image conditions on the Coarse subset. Besides single-image conditions, it uses trajectory-video conditions as an auxiliary task, in which observations along a random yaw trajectory are back-projected to the canvas, so that the model sees content entering and leaving the view. The Evolution stage starts from the Completion-stage weights and trains on the Event subset with image conditions only. Its prompts are detailed, brief, or empty, so that the model learns to evolve the scene under different amounts of textual guidance. Completion needs scale but tolerates loosely matched text, whereas object-level evolution needs verified events and matching prompts, which limits the amount of data. Starting from the Completion stage lets the Evolution stage focus on how objects change rather than on how to complete a panorama (Tab.4).

    3.3 Perspective Renderer

    ℝ is built on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [40] and renders the view from W, I₀, y, and C. The trajectory enters through Plücker embeddings [37, 14] at the input and a zero-initialized per-block camera injection, and I₀ replaces the first latent frame. ℝ reads W through two complementary pathways.

    Projected latent maps.

    Each latent frame k of the video corresponds to a group Gₖ of four RGB frames (one for k=0). For each frame j∈Gₖ, we cast the rays of the perspective latent grid, rotate them by Rⱼ, and bilinearly sample the panoramic latent frame Wₖ:

    \beginsplitW̃ₖ⁽ʲ⁾(u)&=Wₖ(π_ERP(Rⱼ d̂(u))), d̂(u)&=K⁻¹ũ / ∥K⁻¹ũ∥,\endsplit

    		(4)

    where u is a perspective latent grid location, ũ the homogeneous coordinate of its center, d̂(u) its unit ray in camera coordinates, K the intrinsics at latent resolution, and π_ERP maps a unit direction to panoramic latent coordinates. The four maps are stacked along channels and added to the video tokens by a zero-initialized patch embedding. The projection needs no decoding, and per-frame rotation aligns it with every RGB frame. It gives every output token a pixel-aligned estimate of the panorama in its direction, which anchors the view geometry under large rotations.

    Frustum cross-attention.

    To aggregate panoramic context beyond this pixel-aligned estimate, every block contains a cross-attention from video tokens to panoramic tokens p, obtained by patchifying W and adding a Fourier encoding of their center directions dₚ. A query token u of latent frame k attends only to the set ℕₖ(u) of panoramic tokens of the same latent frame that lie within an angular radius ρ=15^∘ of its viewing direction in any frame of Gₖ:

    ℕₖ(u)={ p:\min_j∈Gₖ∠(dₚ, Rⱼ d̂(u))≤ρ }.

    		(5)

    where ∠ is the angle between unit vectors. Defined on the sphere, the window covers a consistent solid angle at all latitudes despite the ERP distortion. The attention output passes through a zero-initialized channel-wise gate, so ℝ starts as the original model. A linear read-out head h_b on each frustum block b∈B maps the attended features a_b to latent channels,

    L_read=(1)/(|B|)∑_b∈B∥h_b(a_b)-D(z₀)∥²,

    		(6)

    where z₀ is the target view latent and D is 2×2 average pooling to tokens. It encourages the attention to retrieve panoramic content rather than stay inactive behind its gate.

    Training conditions.

    Following cascaded generation practice [15, 36], ℝ is trained on ground-truth panoramic latents and views projected from the same high-resolution panorama, and reads the generated panorama at inference. During training, the condition is perturbed as W←(1-s)W+s ε with a random level s, which is embedded and added to the timestep embedding, and s=0 at inference. The perturbation teaches ℝ to treat the panorama as an estimate to be refined rather than a signal to be copied, since generated panoramas are softer than ground truth. The panorama and the text are also dropped at random.

    Objective.

    Following the flow-matching parameterization of the base model [40, 25], we form z_σ=σε+(1-σ)z₀ and minimize

    \beginsplitr_φ&=v_φ(z_σ,σ,c^′)-(ε-z₀), L_ℝ&=𝔼_σ,ε[ ω(σ) ∥(1-m₀)⊙r_φ∥²]+λ L_read,\endsplit

    		(7)

    where v_φ is the velocity predicted by ℝ, r_φ its residual, c^′=(W,I₀,y,C), m₀ a mask that excludes the first latent frame, which holds I₀, from the loss, ω(σ) a Gaussian noise-level weight centered at σ=0.5, and λ=0.1.

    4 PanoEvo-Data

    Both models are trained on real panoramic videos with a fixed camera center, which we build from 360-1M [42] and 360+x [7] (Figs.3 and 1). All clips are 77-frame, 16 fps windows of continuous static-camera footage that pass a shared quality gate. Three principles guide the construction. (i) Real footage only, avoiding the domain gap of simulated scenes. (ii) Scale where it suffices, verification where it matters. The Coarse and Render subsets favor scale with inexpensive rules, while the Event subset admits only samples with verified events. (iii) Supervision matched to each model. The Panoramic Evolver is supervised by complete panoramas at its world-state resolution, and the Perspective Renderer by views projected from native-resolution sources. Details are in the supplementary material.

    Coarse subset.

    The Coarse subset teaches image-conditioned completion at scale, with inexpensive rules against three failure cases. Camera motion is measured from the global panoramic flow. Freezing is limited by capping static and low-motion windows by their dynamic area. Duplicated subjects arise when the text mentions a subject outside the cropped first frame, which teaches the model to generate it elsewhere. For 360+x, whose text is a scene and action label, the crop is oriented toward the subject detected by Grounding DINO [26]. 360-1M has no text, so its crop is oriented by motion and Qwen3-VL [4] captions the crop, naming only subjects that Grounding DINO detects in it.

    Event subset.

    The Event subset teaches object-level evolution with verified events. Qwen3-VL annotates each candidate on multi-directional previews, using the video as evidence and the original caption only as a hint, and records the event, the entities to check and their expected changes, those required in the first frame, and the timing. Each verified event yields up to three prompts of decreasing detail. For a person who walks to a bench and sits down, the detailed prompt describes the walk and the sitting, the brief prompt only says that the person heads toward the bench, and the sample without a prompt starts once the walk is visible in the first frame. The first frame shows the required entities within a 90^∘ field of view, and the target is verified against SAM 3 [6] tracks. We further reject close-ups, moving cameras, and prompt–video mismatches, and audit every remaining sample with Claude Opus 5.5. The final 1,400 samples from 846 source videos cover in-place actions (42%), walking toward a target (26%), holding a state (25%), and walking to then interacting with an object (6%).

    Render subset.

    The Render subset supervises ℝ at high resolution. Since a 90^∘ view at 832 pixels needs a 3,300-pixel-wide ERP, we keep only sources at least 3,840 pixels wide. Each of the 20,526 clips has five trajectories, three look-aways (90^∘–150^∘) and 30^∘ and 60^∘ round trips. Target views are projected from the native-resolution source to 480×832, while conditions are 512×1024 ERP latents. Consecutive samples often share a clip but differ in trajectory, so only the camera tells ℝ which part to render.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks and metrics.

    WRBench[29] tests whether the spatial layout and object states stay consistent when hidden by camera rotation and re-observed. It covers static views and yaw rotations of two magnitudes in both directions, and reports camera alignment (Cam Align.), integrity (Integ.), visible and re-observed spatial and state consistency, and their average (Avg.). We re-score all baselines (Tab.2) with the official code on their released videos, since it differs from that behind the published table. STEVO-Bench[30] tests whether an ongoing process continues unobserved to a later state. We report its five metrics and their sum (Total) as in ReMind [50]. VBench[17, 18] measures visual quality on WRBench videos with eight dimensions of its image-to-video mode (excluding camera motion), plus CLIP-IQA+ [45] and Laplacian sharpness.

    Implementation details.

    We generate 77 frames at 16 fps and 480×832, placing I₀ with a nominal 90^∘ horizontal field of view, and W∈ℝ^16×20×64×128 is the latent of a 512×1024 ERP video. 𝔼 is fine-tuned from PanoWorld with rank-64 LoRA [16], for 3 epochs in the Completion stage (batch 32, constant learning rate 10⁻⁴, single-image and trajectory-video conditions at 0.8:0.2) and 11 epochs in the Evolution stage (batch 8, cosine schedule). ℝ is fine-tuned from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with rank-64 LoRA and fully trained new modules for 5 epochs (batch 8). The condition is perturbed with probability 0.8 and s∼U(0,0.5), and the panorama and the text are each dropped with probability 0.1. 𝔼 samples with 35 steps and CFG 7.0, and ℝ with 50 steps and text CFG 5.0. For each test case, 𝔼 generates one panorama from I₀ and the benchmark text without prompt rewriting, and ℝ renders every camera setting from it. Full settings are in the supplementary material.

    5.2 Main Results

    WRBench.

    As shown in Tab.2, PanoEvo attains the best official average (.753, vs. .741 for InSpatio-World 14B) and the best visible-state, re-observed spatial, and re-observed state scores, as well as both content averages. Its camera alignment (.950) is close to that of the strongest geometry-cache and source-video models, and its two diffusion transformers (2.4B and 1.8B, including our added modules) are smaller than the backbones of most competitive baselines. The prompt-only Wan2.6 I2V obtains high integrity and visible-spatial scores, but its camera alignment of .121 shows that the camera barely turns, so little content leaves the view and these scores are inflated. Among models conditioned only on the input frame and the trajectory, PanoEvo improves the official average by .061 over the strongest one.
