  • PanoEvo 的做法是用一个 Panoramic Evolver，在全景视频扩散模型的**潜空间**里演化世界状态，再把「当前视角」渲染出来——即「在全景里演化、在视角里渲染」

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线里最直白的一篇：它把 11-12 期 Evoke 的「外置状态库」换成「全景潜空间」，指出同一件事——不表示画外，画外就不会动。引擎开发者对此再熟悉不过：这就是「视锥外剔除」与「世界仍在 tick」的区别。

中文摘要：视频世界模型本应维持一个随视角变化而持续演化的世界，但作者发现当前模型有一个共性失败：当相机转开再转回来时，未观察到的场景常常被冻结、物体丢失，或者外观发生变化。根因在于，视野之外的内容没有任何能够持续变化的表示。PanoEvo 因此提出「在全景里演化、在视角里渲染」：用一个 Panoramic Evolver 在全景视频扩散模型的潜空间中演化世界状态，再从中渲染出当前视角的画面。这条思路与把世界状态外置到显式结构中的做法同源——不表示画外，画外就不会动。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Evolve in Panorama, Render in View:
Panoramic World State Evolution for Video World Models

Abstract

Video world models should maintain a world that keeps evolving as the viewpoint changes. Yet when the camera turns away and returns, current models often freeze the unobserved scene, lose objects, or change their appearance, because content outside the view has no representation that keeps changing. We present PanoEvo, which uses a Panoramic Evolver to evolve the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model, where every viewing direction is present at every time step, so the scene evolves whether or not it is observed. Existing panoramic video models are not trained to evolve a scene from a single image or the objects within it, so we build PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360∘ videos, and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine as an image-to-panoramic-video model. Since each view covers only a small part of the low-resolution panorama, directly projected views are blurry and often show low-quality details or structural errors. A Perspective Renderer, built on a perspective video diffusion model, reads this state via latent-space projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to render sharp, high-quality views. PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench. Code, models, and data will be released.

1 Introduction

Video world models generate future observations of a scene from an initial image and a sequence of viewpoints or actions [33, 38, 35, 31]. As they move toward interactive exploration, they are expected to maintain a persistent world. Persistence, however, is more than geometric consistency. The world keeps evolving: a person keeps walking, a dog keeps playing, and an action that has started keeps unfolding, whether or not the camera looks at it. Recent benchmarks test this by turning the camera away and back [29, 30, 8], and show that current models fall short. On return, the unobserved scene is frozen in its last observed state, objects vanish, or their appearance changes.

The root cause lies in what a perspective video model represents. It models the content inside the current view, and once content leaves it, nothing in the model represents it, let alone advances it. Existing remedies mainly retain what has been seen. Geometry caches and 3D memories [34, 53, 52, 44] keep the scene geometry, source-video re-rendering [3, 19] reuses observed frames, and memory or state mechanisms [9, 10, 50, 5] retrieve past observations or reason about entities explicitly. These approaches preserve how the world looked when observed, but few densely represent unobserved content that keeps changing.

We observe that, for a rotating camera, a panoramic video latent provides exactly such a representation. Every viewing direction is present at every time step, so a panoramic video diffusion model evolves the whole scene jointly in its latent space, regardless of where the camera points, and any requested view is a projection of this state. Directly projected views, however, are poor. At a typical 512×1024 resolution, a 90^∘ view covers only about 256 pixels horizontally and must be upsampled over three times to 480×832, blurring the view and degrading object structures. We therefore assign the two roles to two models (Fig.1). A panoramic video diffusion model maintains the evolving world state, and a perspective video diffusion model reads it to render high-quality views. We call this framework PanoEvo: evolve in panorama, render in view.

Realizing this idea requires two components. First, the panoramic model has to work like a conventional image-to-video model, the common interface of video world models [33, 38, 19]: given a single image, it should evolve the whole scene. Existing panoramic video models are text-driven [46, 49, 12] or complete panoramas from video observations [20, 39], panoramic world models start from a full panoramic image [44], and how individual objects evolve remains underexplored. Zero-shot, a strong panoramic model completes the scene but evolves it poorly (Sec.5.4). We build PanoEvo-Data from real 360∘ videos and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine. A Completion stage on about 20K curated clips teaches image-conditioned panoramic completion, and an Evolution stage on 1.4K verified event clips teaches object-level state evolution. Second, the Perspective Renderer has to read the state faithfully and improve visual quality. Built on a perspective video model, it projects the panoramic latent into each view in latent space, reads further context through frustum cross-attention, and is guided by an auxiliary read-out loss.

PanoEvo achieves the best overall score on WRBench among 23 publicly evaluated models (.753 vs. .741 for the strongest baseline), together with the best scores on visible state and both re-observation metrics. On STEVO-Bench, it attains the highest total score (364.7 vs. 300.9). Compared with direct projection of the panorama, the Perspective Renderer raises VBench imaging quality from .538 to .729 while largely preserving the evolved states.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose PanoEvo, which evolves the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model and renders views from it with a perspective one.

  • •

    We build PanoEvo-Data from real 360∘ videos and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine to evolve object-level states from a single image.

  • •

    We design a Perspective Renderer that reads the state through latent-space projection and frustum cross-attention. PanoEvo is state of the art on both benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video world models with memory and state.

    Interactive and camera-controlled video world models [33, 38, 23, 35, 22, 31] generate long explorations from an initial image. Camera control is usually injected into video diffusion models [40, 21, 51] through Plücker embeddings [37, 14, 47, 2], with open-source variants available [1]. To add memory, geometry-based methods maintain point clouds or 3D caches and condition generation on their renderings [34, 53, 52, 44]. Source-video methods re-render a given video along a new trajectory [3, 19]. These methods keep revisited regions geometrically consistent but treat dynamic content as static or remove it. Closer to our goal, HyDRA [9] tracks dynamic subjects over a static memory, LiveWorld [10] advances dynamic entities with an evolution engine, and ReMind [50] recovers evolving states across interruptions. Other works reason about out-of-view events with a vision-language model [5] or control objects along trajectories planned by a language model [43]. Recent evaluations expose the remaining gap through camera look-away, occlusion, and illumination changes [29, 30, 8], where unobserved content is often frozen, lost, or altered. Unlike these methods, PanoEvo keeps a dense panoramic latent of the whole scene that evolves at every time step, so unobserved content advances without explicit entity modeling, memory retrieval, or event reasoning.

    Panoramic video generation.

    Panoramic video models generate 360∘ videos from text [46, 49, 12], outpaint perspective videos to panoramas [39], use cube-map representations for high resolution [24], or support roaming and world modeling [28, 20, 54, 44], and panoramic image models [13] provide static first frames. PanoWorld [20] treats the panoramic latent as a geometrically consistent world representation, and we build the Panoramic Evolver on its released weights. These works focus on the panorama itself and its spatial consistency. We instead use a panoramic model as the state of a perspective world model, start from a single image, and target object-level evolution.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Setting and Overview

    Given a perspective frame I₀, an optional text prompt y, and a camera trajectory C={Rₜ}ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹, we generate a perspective video V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹ that starts at I₀ and follows C.

    Why a panoramic state.

    For a rotating camera, every perspective frame is a deterministic function of the panoramic frame at the same time,

    Iₜ=Π(Pₜ,Rₜ),

    		(1)

    where Pₜ is the 360^∘ frame at time t and Π is the perspective projection. Content outside the current view is not missing, only not projected. Generating P_0:T-1 from I₀ amounts to evolving the whole world, and the trajectory only selects which part is shown. A perspective model, in contrast, has to decide what an unobserved region looks like when it re-enters the view, without having represented it in between, which is where frozen scenes and vanishing objects arise.

    Factorization.

    PanoEvo factorizes generation through a panoramic world state W, generated by the Panoramic Evolver 𝔼 and rendered by the Perspective Renderer ℝ (Fig.2):

    W∼𝔼(I₀,y), V∼ℝ(W,I₀,y,C),

    		(2)

    where W is the latent of an equirectangular (ERP) panoramic video under the Wan2.1 VAE [40], the latent space that ℝ reads. 𝔼 determines what happens in the world, including outside the view, and ℝ reads it faithfully along C and renders coherent, high-quality views. 𝔼 and ℝ are trained separately, and at inference 𝔼 generates W once and ℝ renders any number of views from it.

    3.2 Panoramic Evolver

    Conditioning and observation write-back.

    We build 𝔼 on PanoWorld [20], a panoramic video diffusion transformer based on Cosmos [31], and reuse its native completion pathway without adding input channels. We place I₀ at the front of the ERP canvas (yaw 0^∘, pitch 0^∘) to obtain a sparse observation X_obs and its visibility mask M. Unobserved pixels are filled with Gaussian noise, X_cond=M⊙X_obs+(1-M)⊙ε_fill with ε_fill∼ℕ(0,0.5²I), and X_cond is encoded into a reference latent z_ref, which is concatenated with the latent-resolution mask along the channel dimension. SigLIP2 [41] features of I₀ enter through cross-attention, and the text y is encoded by Cosmos-Reason1 [32]. The condition is encoded independently of the target panorama, so it never contains unobserved content. Before every network evaluation, the fully observed latent cells M̄ (coverage above 0.99) are replaced by the clean z_ref and excluded from the loss, and the replacement is applied once more after sampling. Partially covered cells are generated and supervised. This native write-back is essential for single-image inputs, since without it the fine-tuned model learns to ignore the observed image.

    Objective.

    Let z₀ be the latent of the target panoramic video. Following rectified flow [27, 25], we sample a noise level σ with logit-normal sampling and a shift of 5 [11], form z_σ=σε+(1-σ)z₀ with ε∼ℕ(0,I), and minimize

    \beginsplitr_θ&=v_θ(z_σ,σ,c)-(ε-z₀), L_𝔼&=𝔼_σ,ε[ ∥(1-M̄)⊙r_θ∥²],\endsplit

    		(3)

    where v_θ is the velocity predicted by 𝔼, r_θ its residual, and c the conditions (z_ref with its mask, I₀, and y).

    Coarse-to-fine training.

    We train 𝔼 in two stages on the subsets of PanoEvo-Data (Sec.4). The Completion stage adapts the model to image conditions on the Coarse subset. Besides single-image conditions, it uses trajectory-video conditions as an auxiliary task, in which observations along a random yaw trajectory are back-projected to the canvas, so that the model sees content entering and leaving the view. The Evolution stage starts from the Completion-stage weights and trains on the Event subset with image conditions only. Its prompts are detailed, brief, or empty, so that the model learns to evolve the scene under different amounts of textual guidance. Completion needs scale but tolerates loosely matched text, whereas object-level evolution needs verified events and matching prompts, which limits the amount of data. Starting from the Completion stage lets the Evolution stage focus on how objects change rather than on how to complete a panorama (Tab.4).

    3.3 Perspective Renderer

    ℝ is built on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [40] and renders the view from W, I₀, y, and C. The trajectory enters through Plücker embeddings [37, 14] at the input and a zero-initialized per-block camera injection, and I₀ replaces the first latent frame. ℝ reads W through two complementary pathways.

    Projected latent maps.

    Each latent frame k of the video corresponds to a group Gₖ of four RGB frames (one for k=0). For each frame j∈Gₖ, we cast the rays of the perspective latent grid, rotate them by Rⱼ, and bilinearly sample the panoramic latent frame Wₖ:

    \beginsplitW̃ₖ⁽ʲ⁾(u)&=Wₖ(π_ERP(Rⱼ d̂(u))), d̂(u)&=K⁻¹ũ / ∥K⁻¹ũ∥,\endsplit

    		(4)

    where u is a perspective latent grid location, ũ the homogeneous coordinate of its center, d̂(u) its unit ray in camera coordinates, K the intrinsics at latent resolution, and π_ERP maps a unit direction to panoramic latent coordinates. The four maps are stacked along channels and added to the video tokens by a zero-initialized patch embedding. The projection needs no decoding, and per-frame rotation aligns it with every RGB frame. It gives every output token a pixel-aligned estimate of the panorama in its direction, which anchors the view geometry under large rotations.

    Frustum cross-attention.

    To aggregate panoramic context beyond this pixel-aligned estimate, every block contains a cross-attention from video tokens to panoramic tokens p, obtained by patchifying W and adding a Fourier encoding of their center directions dₚ. A query token u of latent frame k attends only to the set ℕₖ(u) of panoramic tokens of the same latent frame that lie within an angular radius ρ=15^∘ of its viewing direction in any frame of Gₖ:

    ℕₖ(u)={ p:\min_j∈Gₖ∠(dₚ, Rⱼ d̂(u))≤ρ }.

    		(5)

    where ∠ is the angle between unit vectors. Defined on the sphere, the window covers a consistent solid angle at all latitudes despite the ERP distortion. The attention output passes through a zero-initialized channel-wise gate, so ℝ starts as the original model. A linear read-out head h_b on each frustum block b∈B maps the attended features a_b to latent channels,

    L_read=(1)/(|B|)∑_b∈B∥h_b(a_b)-D(z₀)∥²,

    		(6)

    where z₀ is the target view latent and D is 2×2 average pooling to tokens. It encourages the attention to retrieve panoramic content rather than stay inactive behind its gate.

    Training conditions.

    Following cascaded generation practice [15, 36], ℝ is trained on ground-truth panoramic latents and views projected from the same high-resolution panorama, and reads the generated panorama at inference. During training, the condition is perturbed as W←(1-s)W+s ε with a random level s, which is embedded and added to the timestep embedding, and s=0 at inference. The perturbation teaches ℝ to treat the panorama as an estimate to be refined rather than a signal to be copied, since generated panoramas are softer than ground truth. The panorama and the text are also dropped at random.

    Objective.

    Following the flow-matching parameterization of the base model [40, 25], we form z_σ=σε+(1-σ)z₀ and minimize

    \beginsplitr_φ&=v_φ(z_σ,σ,c^′)-(ε-z₀), L_ℝ&=𝔼_σ,ε[ ω(σ) ∥(1-m₀)⊙r_φ∥²]+λ L_read,\endsplit

    		(7)

    where v_φ is the velocity predicted by ℝ, r_φ its residual, c^′=(W,I₀,y,C), m₀ a mask that excludes the first latent frame, which holds I₀, from the loss, ω(σ) a Gaussian noise-level weight centered at σ=0.5, and λ=0.1.

    4 PanoEvo-Data

    Both models are trained on real panoramic videos with a fixed camera center, which we build from 360-1M [42] and 360+x [7] (Figs.3 and 1). All clips are 77-frame, 16 fps windows of continuous static-camera footage that pass a shared quality gate. Three principles guide the construction. (i) Real footage only, avoiding the domain gap of simulated scenes. (ii) Scale where it suffices, verification where it matters. The Coarse and Render subsets favor scale with inexpensive rules, while the Event subset admits only samples with verified events. (iii) Supervision matched to each model. The Panoramic Evolver is supervised by complete panoramas at its world-state resolution, and the Perspective Renderer by views projected from native-resolution sources. Details are in the supplementary material.

    Coarse subset.

    The Coarse subset teaches image-conditioned completion at scale, with inexpensive rules against three failure cases. Camera motion is measured from the global panoramic flow. Freezing is limited by capping static and low-motion windows by their dynamic area. Duplicated subjects arise when the text mentions a subject outside the cropped first frame, which teaches the model to generate it elsewhere. For 360+x, whose text is a scene and action label, the crop is oriented toward the subject detected by Grounding DINO [26]. 360-1M has no text, so its crop is oriented by motion and Qwen3-VL [4] captions the crop, naming only subjects that Grounding DINO detects in it.

    Event subset.

    The Event subset teaches object-level evolution with verified events. Qwen3-VL annotates each candidate on multi-directional previews, using the video as evidence and the original caption only as a hint, and records the event, the entities to check and their expected changes, those required in the first frame, and the timing. Each verified event yields up to three prompts of decreasing detail. For a person who walks to a bench and sits down, the detailed prompt describes the walk and the sitting, the brief prompt only says that the person heads toward the bench, and the sample without a prompt starts once the walk is visible in the first frame. The first frame shows the required entities within a 90^∘ field of view, and the target is verified against SAM 3 [6] tracks. We further reject close-ups, moving cameras, and prompt–video mismatches, and audit every remaining sample with Claude Opus 5.5. The final 1,400 samples from 846 source videos cover in-place actions (42%), walking toward a target (26%), holding a state (25%), and walking to then interacting with an object (6%).

    Render subset.

    The Render subset supervises ℝ at high resolution. Since a 90^∘ view at 832 pixels needs a 3,300-pixel-wide ERP, we keep only sources at least 3,840 pixels wide. Each of the 20,526 clips has five trajectories, three look-aways (90^∘–150^∘) and 30^∘ and 60^∘ round trips. Target views are projected from the native-resolution source to 480×832, while conditions are 512×1024 ERP latents. Consecutive samples often share a clip but differ in trajectory, so only the camera tells ℝ which part to render.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks and metrics.

    WRBench[29] tests whether the spatial layout and object states stay consistent when hidden by camera rotation and re-observed. It covers static views and yaw rotations of two magnitudes in both directions, and reports camera alignment (Cam Align.), integrity (Integ.), visible and re-observed spatial and state consistency, and their average (Avg.). We re-score all baselines (Tab.2) with the official code on their released videos, since it differs from that behind the published table. STEVO-Bench[30] tests whether an ongoing process continues unobserved to a later state. We report its five metrics and their sum (Total) as in ReMind [50]. VBench[17, 18] measures visual quality on WRBench videos with eight dimensions of its image-to-video mode (excluding camera motion), plus CLIP-IQA+ [45] and Laplacian sharpness.

    Implementation details.

    We generate 77 frames at 16 fps and 480×832, placing I₀ with a nominal 90^∘ horizontal field of view, and W∈ℝ^16×20×64×128 is the latent of a 512×1024 ERP video. 𝔼 is fine-tuned from PanoWorld with rank-64 LoRA [16], for 3 epochs in the Completion stage (batch 32, constant learning rate 10⁻⁴, single-image and trajectory-video conditions at 0.8:0.2) and 11 epochs in the Evolution stage (batch 8, cosine schedule). ℝ is fine-tuned from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with rank-64 LoRA and fully trained new modules for 5 epochs (batch 8). The condition is perturbed with probability 0.8 and s∼U(0,0.5), and the panorama and the text are each dropped with probability 0.1. 𝔼 samples with 35 steps and CFG 7.0, and ℝ with 50 steps and text CFG 5.0. For each test case, 𝔼 generates one panorama from I₀ and the benchmark text without prompt rewriting, and ℝ renders every camera setting from it. Full settings are in the supplementary material.

    5.2 Main Results

    WRBench.

    As shown in Tab.2, PanoEvo attains the best official average (.753, vs. .741 for InSpatio-World 14B) and the best visible-state, re-observed spatial, and re-observed state scores, as well as both content averages. Its camera alignment (.950) is close to that of the strongest geometry-cache and source-video models, and its two diffusion transformers (2.4B and 1.8B, including our added modules) are smaller than the backbones of most competitive baselines. The prompt-only Wan2.6 I2V obtains high integrity and visible-spatial scores, but its camera alignment of .121 shows that the camera barely turns, so little content leaves the view and these scores are inflated. Among models conditioned only on the input frame and the trajectory, PanoEvo improves the official average by .061 over the strongest one.

item.title: 自回归视频扩散慢好几个数量级：FastFrames 先 profile 推理再动手，做到交互延迟且不掉质量 ｜ FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
item.description:
一句话：模型能力够用，但延迟差几个数量级——这就是交互式视觉体验卡住的地方。

要点：

  • 定位：自回归视频扩散模型根据新观测与新输入生成帧，天然适合交互式视觉体验
  • 判词很重：现有模型**慢了若干个数量级**，达不到「流畅交互」的要求
  • FastFrames 是「快自回归视频扩散」的一个模型家族，宣称在**不牺牲质量**的前提下达到交互延迟；方法是先对推理过程做 profile，再针对瓶颈下手

为什么值得看：「差异在数量级」意味着这不是调参能解决的，必须动架构/调度。对做实时生成内容的团队，这类「先 profile 再重构」的工作比再提一个 FVD 新低更有参考价值。

中文摘要：自回归视频扩散模型依据新的观测与输入逐帧生成，因而很适合承载交互式视觉体验；但作者指出，现有模型的推理速度慢了若干个数量级，远达不到流畅交互的要求。FastFrames 提出一族「快速自回归视频扩散模型」，目标是在不牺牲质量的前提下达到交互级延迟。其做法是先剖析（profile）推理过程中的开销构成，再针对真正的瓶颈下手，而不是笼统地减少采样步数。对需要把生成式内容送进实时管线的团队，这种「先测量、再重构」的路径比再刷一项画质指标更有参考价值。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

FastFrames: Video Generation at
Interactive Latency

Abstract

Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models can be orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8× slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8× B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation. See our project page for videos, code, and model weights.

https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-fastframes/

1 Introduction

Video diffusion models [(Ho et al., 2022b; Ho et al., 2022a; Singer et al., 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023)] synthesize realistic videos [(Wang et al., 2025; Seedance Team et al., 2026; Black Forest Labs, 2026; MiniMax, 2026)], compose diverse scenes and visual concepts [(Deng et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026)], and respond to camera and action controls [(Wang et al., 2024; He et al., 2025)]. In particular, autoregressive (AR) models [(Jin et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Teng et al., 2025)] generate videos incrementally, allowing them to incorporate new controls or observations. They are a promising medium for interactive visual applications, such as world simulation [(Chou et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026)], games [(Yu et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], and predictive models for robotics [(Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026)].

Recent works have significantly accelerated AR video diffusion models, primarily through distillation and few-step sampling [(Yin et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2025)]. Some now report real-time generation speeds based on frames per second (FPS) [(Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)]. However, FPS alone does not establish whether a model can respond to user inputs in real time. For instance, a model that generates a 30-frame clip as a single batch in one second achieves 30 FPS, but the user must still wait one second to see a response. Seamless real-time interactivity demands low input-to-response latency, as established in interactive systems research [(Miller, 1968)]. Human-computer interaction studies have reported delay-detection thresholds of approximately 50 to 60 ms [(Annett et al., 2014; Deber et al., 2015; Forch et al., 2017)].

Thus, we target end-to-end per-frame latency below 50 ms. We define this latency as the delay between the arrival of a new input signal (e.g., a steering command) and the presentation of the first RGB frame that depicts its effects. In the baseline methods we study [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a)], the inference pipeline consists of KV cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. Measuring latency requires accounting for the complete critical path through these operations.

We also report the corresponding responses per second (RPS), defined as RPS=1/Lₛ=1,000/Lₘₛ, where Lₛ and Lₘₛ denote this latency in seconds and milliseconds, respectively. Each generation unit counts as one response, regardless of how many frames it produces. Unlike FPS, which amortizes generation time over the frames in a batch, RPS directly measures responsiveness for interactive applications; an interactive latency target of 50 ms corresponds to 20 RPS. As shown in Fig. 1, the fastest baselines remain well below the target response rate.

To close this gap, we introduce FastFrames, a family of autoregressive video diffusion models that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to take end-to-end per-frame latency into the interactive regime (≤ 50 ms). We analyze the limiting factors of existing models by profiling the critical inference path of a reference 1.3B-parameter model, a common model size that balances speed and generation quality (Fig. 2). We find that dominant costs lie not in diffusion denoising steps, but rather in operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates. For instance, a single VAE decoding step takes as long as 3.5 DiT passes.

We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. First, we replace the VAE decoder with a ConvNeXt-based [(Liu et al., 2022)] head that operates only in low spatial resolution, followed by a single linear layer that unpatchifies and upsamples the latents to pixel dimensions, reducing decoding latency by 147× while matching quality. Furthermore, because the head is lightweight, training the model end-to-end in pixel-space (e.g., perceptual [(Zhang et al., 2018)] and GAN [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] losses) becomes practical, bypassing the reconstruction bottleneck of the VAE. Second, the baseline inference pipeline includes an additional DiT evaluation on each fully denoised latent solely to refine the KV cache (Sec. 3.3); we replace the DiT evaluation with a lightweight network, reducing cache-update latency 10x without measurable degradation in quality. Finally, we perform multiple system-level, hardware-aware optimizations that specifically target the end-to-end per-frame critical path. Our techniques target components shared by many AR video diffusion models and are therefore complementary to advances in backbone architecture, such as hybrid transformers [(Chen et al., 2026a)], and improved distillation methods [(Liu et al., 2026a)].

In the standard text-to-video (T2V) setting, where the model simply treats the current generated frame as input for generating the next, our quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that FastFrames establishes a new Pareto frontier between generation quality and speed (Fig. 1). The 1.3B variant achieves an end-to-end per-frame latency of 36 ms (28 RPS) on a single B200 GPU at 832×480 resolution (480p), matching the visual quality of a state-of-the-art baseline [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] that is 7.6× slower. Scaling FastFrames to 14B improves visual fidelity while achieving 45 ms (22 RPS) on an 8× B200 GPU node.

The T2V AR pipeline can be extended to accept controls between generation steps, such as camera poses [(Jiang et al., 2026)], 2D tracks [(Shin et al., 2026)], and 3D dynamics [(Li et al., 2025b)]. We show that FastFrames enables fluid interactive experiences in two applications: camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

2 Related Work

Accelerating diffusion sampling. Diffusion models require iterative sampling [(Ho et al., 2020)]. Earlier work reduces the number of sampling steps using training-free accelerated samplers [(Song et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2025)] or by training models to take larger steps along their sampling trajectories [(Frans et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025; Shaul et al., 2026)]. The state of the art relies on distribution matching [(Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Cui et al., 2026)], where a few-step student generator approximates the distribution of a teacher network. Another line of work focuses on the inference cost of DiTs, including hybrid attention [(Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)], sliding-window attention for long context [(Xiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025)], and layer pruning or model-size distillation [(Fang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025b)]. A smaller line of work focuses specifically on compressing or sparsifying the KV cache of autoregressive video diffusion models to reduce attention overhead [(Ji et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2026)]. However, these methods are generally model-specific, so instead we target other components on the critical path. Our work builds on state-of-the-art few-step models, but we observe that the iterative denoising process is no longer the latency bottleneck.

Reducing VAE decoding time. State-of-the-art video diffusion models perform diffusion in latent space [(Blattmann et al., 2023)], generally encoded via a variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma & Welling, 2014)]. For instance, the Wan VAE [(Wang et al., 2025)] can perform up to a 48× reduction in dimensionality. This makes generation cheaper but pixel decoding becomes expensive. VAE decoders repeatedly upsample features in space and time, and apply dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, a tensor containing four 480×832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions. A line of work aims to speed up VAEs [(Boer Bohan, 2023; Buzovkin & Shilov, 2025)] by reducing the number of parameters and removing expensive operations like attention and wide 3D convolutions. These methods gain up to 4× speedup but incur degradation in visual quality [(Boer Bohan, 2025; Huang et al., 2025)]. Instead, we treat the pixel decoder as a lightweight readout specific to a frozen DiT, rather than a general-purpose reconstruction problem. Our pixel head maintains visual quality while being two orders of magnitude faster.

Systems-level optimizations. Systems-level techniques accelerate diffusion inference through more efficient scheduling and hardware utilization. [Kodaira et al. (2025)] and [Bandyopadhyay et al. (2026)] use batching and pipeline parallelism to improve streaming throughput but do not improve per-frame latency. StreamDiffusionV2 [(Feng et al., 2026)] emphasizes non-amortized time-to-first-frame but to the best of our understanding, this metric focuses on the start of a stream, in contrast to our steady-state measurements. Optimized attention kernels [(Dao, 2024)], compilation and operator fusion [(Ansel et al., 2024)], and CUDA graph execution [(Ghosh et al., 2025)] reduce memory traffic and execution overhead. Weight and activation quantization [(Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Su et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b)] reduce memory requirements and can accelerate computation with suitable hardware support. Distributed inference spreads computation across multiple GPUs through patch, sequence, and pipeline parallelism [(Li et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2024)]. Our work incorporates many of these techniques.

3 Method

3.1 Preliminaries: Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion Models

Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate a video one latent chunk at a time, using diffusion to synthesize each chunk conditioned on previously generated ones. We represent a video sequence as z^1:N=(z¹,z²,…,z^N), where each chunk zⁱ∈ℝ^C×T×H×W contains T≥1 latent frames with C channels and spatial resolution H×W. Each latent frame corresponds to K RGB frames, where K is the temporal compression factor of the VAE. Generating larger chunks (e.g., one chunk = three latent frames, as in Self-Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)]) is closer to bidirectional models and empirically easier to optimize, while generating a smaller chunk (e.g., one chunk = one latent frame, as in Causal Forcing++ (CF++) [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] and FastFrames) is faster. The joint distribution factorizes autoregressively as p(z^1:N)=∏ᵢ₌₁^Np(zⁱ|z^

To examine the inference cost, we profile CF++, the fastest few-step AR video diffusion model at the time of writing. It is built on the Wan 2.1 1.3B-parameter backbone. Fig. 2 shows its inference latency on a single B200 GPU, decomposed into three stages: KV-cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. We use its two-diffusion-step variant, which provides the best speed-quality tradeoff; reducing sampling steps to one significantly degrades visual quality while merely reducing latency by 15%. Each DiT evaluation takes 41.6 ms using BF16 precision, cuDNN attention backend [(NVIDIA Corporation, 2026)], and torch.compile[(Ansel et al., 2024)]. The KV cache update is an additional DiT evaluation. Finally, the VAE decoder takes 147 ms to decode each generated latent into four RGB frames, resulting in a total end-to-end latency of 271.8 ms.

This profile suggests that our latency budget of 50 ms leaves room for only a single diffusion sampling step. Instead, we replace the VAE with lightweight pixel rendering (Sec. 3.2) and accelerate KV cache updates (Sec. 3.3). Then, by reducing the latency of each DiT evaluation through systems-level optimizations (Sec. 3.4), we fit the full inference pipeline within the target latency. Our final 1.3B model runs in 36 ms on a single B200 GPU, making it 7.6× faster than CF++. Our 14B model runs 10.6× faster than the fastest open-source AR model of the same parameter count and achieves a further 3.5× speedup when distributed across eight B200 GPUs.

3.2 Removing the VAE Decoder

We first target the VAE decoder since it accounts for more than half of the end-to-end inference latency and alone exceeds our real-time budget 3×. The VAE decoder only has 73M parameters (compared to the DiT’s 1.3B) but repeatedly upsamples its features in space and time and applies dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, a tensor containing four 480×832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions.

In light of recent advances in pixel diffusion models, we question whether such a decoder is necessary when the DiT already produces rich and spatially contextualized features. For instance, JiT [(Li & He, 2026)] produces sharp images by mapping between image patches and transformer features using only linear projections. Thus, we first attempt replacing the VAE with a single linear layer and train it with an MSE loss against the VAE decoded output, keeping the DiT frozen. We found that the outputs were blurry yet recognizable (Fig. 3).

We then increase the size of the pixel decoder, until arriving at our final architecture consisting of three causal 3D ConvNeXt-style blocks [(Liu et al., 2022)]. Each block uses a causal 3×3×3 depthwise convolution followed by a channel-mixing MLP. All blocks operate only on the transformer’s low-resolution 21×30×52 token grid. A final linear layer converts each token into a 4×16×16 RGB patch, yielding an 84-frame, 480×832 video. We discard the first three frames following the conventions of the Wan VAE, which does not temporally upsample the first frame. The total number of parameters is comparable (63.9M for ours vs. 73.3M), yet two orders of magnitude faster (1 ms vs. 147 ms).

We train the pixel decoder using spatial and temporal reconstruction objectives. Let ŷₚᵢₓ denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let y_VAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x₀ with the frozen VAE. We optimize

L_rec(ŷₚᵢₓ,y_VAE)=λ₁L₁+λ_MSEL_MSE+λ_gradL_grad+λₜₑₘₚLₜₑₘₚ+λₘₒₜᵢₒₙLₘₒₜᵢₒₙ.

(1)

Here, λ₁=0.5, λ_MSE=5.0, λ_grad=λₜₑₘₚ=0.05, and λₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=0.5. All five terms are computed between ŷₚᵢₓ and y_VAE. The L₁ and L_MSE terms enforce pixel-level fidelity, while L_grad matches spatial image gradients and Lₜₑₘₚ matches frame-to-frame changes. The motion-weighted term Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ emphasizes reconstruction errors in regions exhibiting motion in the VAE target. Complete definitions of the loss terms are provided in the supplement.

In addition to reducing latency, our pixel decoder is less memory-intensive to optimize. For a batch-size-one, 81-frame video at 832×480 resolution, a VAE decoder update with BF16 precision and activation checkpointing requires approximately 68 GB of peak GPU memory, compared with approximately 5 GB for our pixel decoder. This makes it practical to optimize the decoder directly in pixel space with adversarial losses to improve sharpness and realism.

We curated an internal dataset of 10K real videos and used a frozen DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] ViT-S/16 backbone as our discriminator. On each of layers 4, 8, and 12, we train two lightweight token-level discriminator heads: a spatial classifier and a temporal classifier that receives both the current patch feature and its change from the preceding frame. Let H denote the six discriminator heads, let y denote a real video crop, and let ŷ denote a generated crop. We use the following relativistic softplus discriminator objective [(Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2019)]:

L_D=(1)/(|H|)∑_h∈H⟨softplus (Dₕ(ŷ)-Dₕ(y))+λ_center[Dₕ(y)+Dₕ(ŷ)]²⟩+λₛₗₒₚₑ(R₁+R₂),

(2)

where ⟨·⟩ denotes averaging over clips, frames, and patch tokens, λ_center=0.01, and λₛₗₒₚₑ=0.25. The terms R₁ and R₂ are finite-difference slope penalties on real and generated inputs, respectively [(Lin et al., 2026)]. We estimate them on 25% of the clips by adding Gaussian RGB perturbations with standard deviation ε=0.01.

The generator consists of the frozen DiT and the trainable ConvNeXt pixel decoder. We continue using the reconstruction objective (Eq. 1) with the reverse relativistic comparison:

L_adv=(1)/(|H|)∑_h∈H⟨softplus(-[Dₕ(ŷ)-sg (Dₕ(y))])⟩,

(3)

where sg denotes stop-gradient. We cap the adversarial RGB-gradient magnitude relative to the reconstruction gradient for stable optimization. We also tried finetuning the DiT with low learning rate, but observed training instability.

As seen in Fig. 3, our pixel decoder faithfully reconstructs thin structures like hair and raindrops. However, unlike the Wan VAE decoder, which can be shared across models of the same family (e.g., 1.3B and 14B variants), our pixel decoder must be finetuned for each individual model. Our main takeaway is that we can turn pixel decoding into a lightweight readout rather than a general-purpose reconstruction problem.

3.3 Faster KV Cache Updates

Autoregressive video diffusion models attend to earlier frames through a KV cache [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025)]. Each DiT layer maintains its own cache, which holds an attention sink plus a sliding window of recent entries. During each generation, the final denoising pass leaves the current chunk’s cache entries computed from a noisy input. The baselines therefore run an additional DiT pass on the predicted clean latent ẑᵢ at t=0 and replace those entries with its keys and values (the KV cache write in Fig. 2). They discard the pass’s output prediction.

In a two-step diffusion setup, KV refinement accounts for one-third of DiT evaluations. We first investigate whether refinement is necessary. Naively removing the refinement leads to substantial degradation and training the model to use noisy cached features still produces noticeable artifacts (see supplement for visualizations). However, we hypothesize that a lightweight network can replace the expensive DiT pass. We design a KV refinement network with a shared feature extractor and per-layer KV-repair heads. The feature extractor takes ẑᵢ and applies the DiT’s frozen patch embedding followed by four lightweight transformer blocks trained from scratch. Each repair head takes these output features and its layer’s noisy keys and values to predict residual corrections.

During training, we freeze the DiT and use the keys and values produced by the original DiT refinement pass to supervise residual corrections to the noisy cache. We train our network with two losses: a direct KV reconstruction loss combining cosine distance and relative ℓ₂ error, and an attention-output loss that compares the outputs obtained when subsequent chunks attend to the predicted versus target cache. The network performs comparably to the original refinement pass in terms of quantitative and qualitative comparisons, while taking approximately 2 ms for the 1.3B model and 6 ms for the 14B model on a B200 GPU, around 20× and 12× faster respectively than the baselines’ refinement. We provide details in the supplement.

3.4 Systems-level Optimizations

After reducing non-denoising overhead, DiT evaluations remain the main bottleneck to real-time generation. “Free” optimizations, including faster attention backends and torch.compile(), are already accounted for in the baseline profiling (Fig. 2). First, we observe that the repeated structure of DiT evaluations offers opportunities to reuse computation. We maintain persistent KV-cache buffers and write new entries directly into their designated slots; precompute and store RoPE tables, text and timestep conditions; and fuse QKV projections into one larger matrix multiplication.

Second, we find that per-frame AR generation can provide too few query tokens to fully utilize the GPU. We therefore split the KV sequence into segments processed in parallel, then combine their attention outputs using a softmax merge. Concretely, for a full KV cache of length 32,760, we found that splitting it into five segments of 6,552 each led to a 13% latency reduction. Third, we reduce the overhead of launching and coordinating GPU work via CUDA graphs. Together, these optimizations bring the DiT evaluation latency from 41.6 ms to 16.4 ms for the 1.3B model on one B200 GPU at the full 32,760-token KV prefix and from 89.2 to 75.6 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to approximately 2.5× and 1.2× speedups.

Next, we distribute computation across 8× B200 GPUs. We experimented with tensor parallelism, attention-head parallelism, KV sharding, joint query–KV partitioning, and context parallelism (CP). Among them, only CP reduced computation sufficiently to justify communication overhead. CP partitions query tokens across GPUs and distributes both attention and feed-forward computation, requiring only one exchange of computed keys and values per transformer layer. We implement these exchanges using CUDA-graph-compatible NVLink symmetric-memory gathers. This configuration reduces DiT latency from 16.4 to 5.8 ms for the 1.3B model and from 75.6 to 20.3 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to 2.8× and 3.7× speedups over their optimized single-GPU implementations.

4 Experiments

Models and baselines. We build FastFrames on the Wan 2.1 backbone at two model sizes: FastFrames-S with 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with 14B. We initialize FastFrames-S from the two-step Causal Forcing++ (CF++) checkpoint and finetune it using our method. We freeze the DiT and train our pixel decoder and KV refinement network against their respective targets. FastFrames-L required starting from the base bidirectional model. Following the training recipe in CF++, we converted Wan 2.1 14B into an autoregressive model, distilled it into a few-step model, and trained it with DMD. Both FastFrames-S and FastFrames-L perform two-step diffusion sampling and generate one latent frame per autoregressive step.

Quantitative comparisons. Tab. 1 provides a quantitative comparison against bidirectional video generators and autoregressive models. The bidirectional models provide a broader reference for generation quality and latency, while the autoregressive models provide direct comparisons. We report model size, latency, and VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)] scores. All models are evaluated using the same VBench prompts and seeds. We report end-to-end latency and compute RPS as its reciprocal in seconds, following the definitions in the introduction. For AR models, one response corresponds to an autoregressive generation unit; for bidirectional models, it corresponds to a complete generated clip. Consequently, RPS does not credit a method for producing multiple frames within one generation unit. We account for diffusion sampling, KV cache updates where applicable, and pixel rendering. For AR models, we measure latency at steady state after warm-up and with a full KV cache. For bidirectional models, we let the model warm up and then generate the configured native clip lengths. All models are evaluated on a B200 GPU unless otherwise specified, at approximately 480p using the model’s officially supported resolutions.

We find that FastFrames matches corresponding baselines with the same Wan 2.1 backbone (Krea-Realtime vs. FastFrames-L, CF++ vs. FastFrames-S). Between FastFrames-S and CF++, which use the same DiT weights, we attribute the higher visual quality to end-to-end adversarial training in pixel space, which boosts realism and sharpness.

None of the baselines meet the 50 ms latency target required for interactive applications. The fastest baseline, CF++, reaches 3.68 RPS at 272 ms, falling 5.4× short of the 20 RPS target. In contrast, FastFrames-S attains a latency of 36 ms (27.8 RPS) on a single B200 GPU and FastFrames-L attains 45 ms (22.2 RPS) on an 8-GPU node. FastFrames-S on 8 GPUs reaches 14 ms (71.4 RPS), while FastFrames-L on a single GPU reaches 158 ms (6.33 RPS).

Qualitative comparisons. Fig. 4 shows a side-by-side comparison between FastFrames-S, FastFrames-L, and their respective baselines. FastFrames-S maintains visual sharpness relative to CF++, capturing fine details like sculptures and leaves while being nearly 8× faster. FastFrames-L achieves realism, prompt adherence, composition, and text rendering capabilities comparable to Krea-Realtime while being over 10× faster.

Fig. 4 also illustrates the improved capabilities of the 14B models relative to their 1.3B counterparts. The larger models produce more realistic lighting and shadows in the first two examples, better capture the folded-paper appearance of the origami dragon in the third, and render more legible text in the fourth. We encourage readers to view the supplementary videos on the project website.

Interactive applications. We showcase FastFrames in interactive settings by accelerating camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation: LingBot [(Gao et al., 2026)], a family of camera-conditioned video models with 1.3B and 14B variants, and RealWonder [(Liu et al., 2026c)], a 1.3B physics-conditioned video model. Our techniques transfer directly to these off-the-shelf models and yield large speedups, even over official code that already includes optimizations such as Ulysses sequence parallelism [(Jacobs et al., 2024)]. Fig. 5 summarizes the latency profiles.

On LingBot 1.3B, we reduce latency from 842 ms (the fastest official configuration, 2 GPUs) to 52 ms on 8 GPUs, a 16× speedup. On RealWonder, latency drops from 1141 ms (official, 1 GPU) to 51 ms (22×), so both models approximately reach our target interactive latency. On LingBot 14B, latency drops from 1373 ms to 233 ms on 8 GPUs (5.9×). These models remain slower than our T2V models because they require more diffusion sampling steps, predict multiple latent frames per autoregressive step, and need extra DiT computation to process additional conditioning.

We show a side-by-side comparison between the interactive demos on the project website; the original models exhibit noticeable lag while our optimized versions of LingBot 1.3B and RealWonder respond to user inputs fluidly.

5 Conclusion

We presented FastFrames, a family of autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency by rethinking components of the inference pipeline often treated as fixed implementation details. Both our 1.3B and 14B variants achieve generation quality comparable to or better than their respective baselines.

While our evaluation focuses on text-to-video generation at 480p on high-end GPUs, important directions for future work include adding action conditioning without increasing latency, scaling to higher resolutions, and supporting lighter hardware form factors. Improving long-term consistency and physical plausibility will further broaden the utility of video world models.

Appendix

We organize the appendix into the following sections: (A) Limitations and future work, (B) Additional latency profiling, (C) Architecture and training details of pixel decoder, (D) Architecture and training details of KV refinement network, and (E) Adaptation details of interactive applications.

We encourage readers to view the videos on our website.

Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

Resolution. Most baselines and base video models use 480p resolution, which we finetune from. Higher resolution like 720p or even 4K is desired for a variety of applications like gaming and content creation. In the next section, we find that increasing resolution to 720p increases latency significantly; further optimization is required to bring high-res video generation into the interactive regime.

Accessible hardware. We use B200 GPUs for our latency measurements in the main paper. While we assume compute will continue to become cheaper and more accessible, being able to run interactive video models on-device is an exciting possibility.

Action conditions designed for lower latency. We applied FastFrames to off-the-shelf autoregressive models that were slower than their T2V counterparts. Training base models with lower latency in mind, such as concatenating camera poses in the channel dimension rather than the sequence dimension, without compromising quality, is essential for reducing latency.

Appendix B Additional Latency Profiling

In Tab. 2, we include detailed profiling of each operation on B200 and H100 GPUs, and at 480p and 720p resolution. In short, FastFrames-S runs at 36 ms at 480p and 127 ms at 720p on a B200 GPU, and FastFrames-L runs at 45 ms at 480p and 116 ms at 720p on 8 B200 GPUs. Savings from our lightweight networks are more noticeable at 720p. H100s are approximately 25% to 50% slower depending on the configuration.

Some baselines like Self-Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)] report latency in their paper. However, we did not find detailed descriptions or breakdowns of those numbers and can only infer their profiling from source code. We found that Self-Forcing measured latency by generating a video sequence of N latent chunks (where each chunk ≥ 1 latent frame(s)), then dividing the total time by the number of chunks. However, earlier chunks are faster to generate due to an initially empty KV cache that gradually fills, so this average does not represent steady-state latency at long contexts. Occasionally, baselines provide ambiguous latency numbers without explanation; Causal Forcing++ [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] reports 270 ms for its 1, 2, and 4 step models without explanation.

All of our profiling numbers include a breakdown of the specific operation, and are measured at steady-state with a full KV cache where applicable based on officially released configurations (e.g., KV=32760 for Self-Forcing and its follow-up works).

Appendix C Architecture and Training Details of Pixel Decoder

Our pixel decoder is a causal ConvNeXt model operating directly on the pre-head features of the frozen two-step DiTs. For a 21-frame latent sequence, the DiT produces 32,760 tokens on a (21×30×52) spatiotemporal grid with channel width 1536. The head applies per-frame adaptive shift/scale modulation, a (1×1) channel projection, and three ConvNeXt-style causal 3D residual blocks—two low-resolution blocks followed by one output block—using depthwise (3×3×3) convolutions, channel-wise layer normalization, and width-4 pointwise GELU expansions. All convolutional processing remains at the DiT token resolution; the selected configuration has no learned temporal or spatial upsampler, latent adapter, displacement branch, auxiliary feature fusion, or post-RGB refiner. A final per-token linear projection maps the 1536-dimensional features to (4×16×16×3) RGB values, which are unpatchified into 84 frames at (480×832) and aligned to the VAE convention by dropping the first three frames, yielding 81 output frames. The decoder contains 63.87M parameters and is causal in time, so each output block depends only on the current and preceding latent blocks.

We train the pixel decoder using a paired spatial-temporal reconstruction objective. Let ŷₚᵢₓ denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let y_VAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x₀ with the frozen VAE. Both videos are represented in the range [-1,1]. Our reconstruction objective is

L_rec=0.5 L₁+5.0 L_MSE+0.05 L_grad+0.05 Lₜₑₘₚ+0.50 Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ.

(4)

The pixelwise terms are L₁=mean(|ŷₚᵢₓ-y_VAE|) and L_MSE=mean((ŷₚᵢₓ-y_VAE)²). To preserve spatial structure, we match horizontal and vertical finite differences:

L_grad=mean (|Δₕŷₚᵢₓ-Δₕy_VAE|)+mean (|Δ_wŷₚᵢₓ-Δ_wy_VAE|).

(5)

To preserve temporal dynamics, we match consecutive-frame differences:

Lₜₑₘₚ=mean (|Δₜŷₚᵢₓ-Δₜy_VAE|).

(6)

Finally, we place greater reconstruction weight on regions that move in the VAE target:

Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=mean_t>1,p [(1+γ mean_c|Δₜy_VAE,t,c,p|)mean_c|ŷ_pix,t,c,p-y_VAE,t,c,p|], γ=10.

(7)

Here, Δₕ, Δ_w, and Δₜ denote vertical, horizontal, and temporal finite-difference operators, respectively; c indexes RGB channels; and p indexes spatial locations. The multiplier γ controls how strongly moving target regions are emphasized within Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ, while the coefficient 0.50 controls the overall contribution of this term to L_rec.

Using the 

vidprom_filtered_extended.txt
file provided in Self-Forcing’s repo, we roll out the frozen DiT and VAE 150k times to get the input and output targets, running 4 optimization steps per rollout. We train on 32 B200 GPUs for about a week; we find that validation loss and metrics (PSNR and SSIM) continue to improve steadily though slowly.

We take the last checkpoint and train with the adversarial setup as described in the main paper (Sec. 3.2). We train on 8 B200 GPUs and run 5000 rollouts per GPU and 4 optimization steps per rollout. Training completes in a few hours.

Appendix D Architecture and Training Details of KV Refinement Network

As described in the main paper, we first investigate whether KV refinement is necessary, given that the last diffusion sampling step writes a noisy KV cache for free. In Fig. 6, we find that removing KV refinement, even after training the model to learn to use the noisy KV cache, leads to drift and artifacts. These experiments motivate our design.

Our KV refinement network is a cache-repair module that replaces the expensive DiT evaluation of the baselines. Each DiT layer maintains its own KV cache, partitioned into one slice for each generated latent frame. During every diffusion evaluation for frame i, the KV tensors for that frame overwrite its current cache slice, while the slices for earlier frames remain available as causal context. At the final denoising step, the DiT still receives a nonzero-noise latent, although it predicts the clean latent z₀; consequently, the KV written to the current slice correspond to the noisy input. The baseline therefore performs an additional, non-denoising DiT forward pass on z₀ with zero-noise time conditioning (t=0), overwriting the same slice with clean-context KV.

Instead, our network consumes the noisy K/V tensors from the final denoising pass together with the predicted z₀, predicts corrected K/V tensors, and overwrites the same cache slice. Subsequent latent frames therefore attend to the repaired context without requiring the additional full DiT forward pass. A shared stem maps the 1,560 patch tokens per frame from 1,536 to 768 channels, then applies four lightweight 8-head spatial self-attention blocks with 4× GELU MLPs and timestep-conditioned adaptive layer normalization. Each of the DiT layers has a separate repair head that projects its noisy K/V, concatenates them with the shared per-token z₀ features, and predicts residual corrections. Keys are corrected in post-RoPE space and renormalized per attention head, while values receive a learned residual and per-channel scale. All residual outputs are zero-initialized so the adapter initially behaves like the no-prime baseline.

During inference, frame 0 retains a real clean-prime anchor, while subsequent frames use the repaired K/V to overwrite their cache slots before the next frame is processed. The adapter is trained with the DiT and VAE frozen using teacher-forced targets from the real prime pass: the primary objective matches future attention outputs, supplemented by direct K/V reconstruction with approximately three times more weight on value than key errors, since we found that value corruption dominates the degradation.

Appendix E Adaptation Details of Interactive Applications

We use the official model and weights released by the authors. We follow the procedure described in Sec. 3 to train both the pixel decoder and the KV refinement network. Neither component requires large-scale training data. We simply roll out the models to create target pixels and clean keys and values on-the-fly.

LingBot requires four diffusion sampling steps per autoregressive generation, and generates four latent frames at once. RealWonder requires three sampling steps and generates three latent frames at once. Both are substantially more expensive than our setup in FastFrames, which performs two sampling steps, and generates one latent frame at a time. Thus, even the 1.3B models require 8 GPUs to reach interactive latency. RealWonder is slower than LingBot at the same parameter count due to its more expensive processing of its action conditions. Distilling these models to fewer steps and fewer latent frames per generation while maintaining output quality and adherence to conditions is important future work.
