一句话：模型能力够用，但延迟差几个数量级——这就是交互式视觉体验卡住的地方。

要点：

  • 定位：自回归视频扩散模型根据新观测与新输入生成帧，天然适合交互式视觉体验
  • 判词很重：现有模型**慢了若干个数量级**，达不到「流畅交互」的要求
  • FastFrames 是「快自回归视频扩散」的一个模型家族，宣称在**不牺牲质量**的前提下达到交互延迟；方法是先对推理过程做 profile，再针对瓶颈下手

为什么值得看：「差异在数量级」意味着这不是调参能解决的，必须动架构/调度。对做实时生成内容的团队，这类「先 profile 再重构」的工作比再提一个 FVD 新低更有参考价值。

中文摘要：自回归视频扩散模型依据新的观测与输入逐帧生成，因而很适合承载交互式视觉体验；但作者指出，现有模型的推理速度慢了若干个数量级，远达不到流畅交互的要求。FastFrames 提出一族「快速自回归视频扩散模型」，目标是在不牺牲质量的前提下达到交互级延迟。其做法是先剖析（profile）推理过程中的开销构成，再针对真正的瓶颈下手，而不是笼统地减少采样步数。对需要把生成式内容送进实时管线的团队，这种「先测量、再重构」的路径比再刷一项画质指标更有参考价值。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

FastFrames: Video Generation at
Interactive Latency

Abstract

Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models can be orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8× slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8× B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation. See our project page for videos, code, and model weights.

https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-fastframes/

1 Introduction

Video diffusion models [(Ho et al., 2022b; Ho et al., 2022a; Singer et al., 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023)] synthesize realistic videos [(Wang et al., 2025; Seedance Team et al., 2026; Black Forest Labs, 2026; MiniMax, 2026)], compose diverse scenes and visual concepts [(Deng et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026)], and respond to camera and action controls [(Wang et al., 2024; He et al., 2025)]. In particular, autoregressive (AR) models [(Jin et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Teng et al., 2025)] generate videos incrementally, allowing them to incorporate new controls or observations. They are a promising medium for interactive visual applications, such as world simulation [(Chou et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026)], games [(Yu et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], and predictive models for robotics [(Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026)].

Recent works have significantly accelerated AR video diffusion models, primarily through distillation and few-step sampling [(Yin et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2025)]. Some now report real-time generation speeds based on frames per second (FPS) [(Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)]. However, FPS alone does not establish whether a model can respond to user inputs in real time. For instance, a model that generates a 30-frame clip as a single batch in one second achieves 30 FPS, but the user must still wait one second to see a response. Seamless real-time interactivity demands low input-to-response latency, as established in interactive systems research [(Miller, 1968)]. Human-computer interaction studies have reported delay-detection thresholds of approximately 50 to 60 ms [(Annett et al., 2014; Deber et al., 2015; Forch et al., 2017)].

Thus, we target end-to-end per-frame latency below 50 ms. We define this latency as the delay between the arrival of a new input signal (e.g., a steering command) and the presentation of the first RGB frame that depicts its effects. In the baseline methods we study [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a)], the inference pipeline consists of KV cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. Measuring latency requires accounting for the complete critical path through these operations.

We also report the corresponding responses per second (RPS), defined as RPS=1/Lₛ=1,000/Lₘₛ, where Lₛ and Lₘₛ denote this latency in seconds and milliseconds, respectively. Each generation unit counts as one response, regardless of how many frames it produces. Unlike FPS, which amortizes generation time over the frames in a batch, RPS directly measures responsiveness for interactive applications; an interactive latency target of 50 ms corresponds to 20 RPS. As shown in Fig. 1, the fastest baselines remain well below the target response rate.

To close this gap, we introduce FastFrames, a family of autoregressive video diffusion models that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to take end-to-end per-frame latency into the interactive regime (≤ 50 ms). We analyze the limiting factors of existing models by profiling the critical inference path of a reference 1.3B-parameter model, a common model size that balances speed and generation quality (Fig. 2). We find that dominant costs lie not in diffusion denoising steps, but rather in operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates. For instance, a single VAE decoding step takes as long as 3.5 DiT passes.

We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. First, we replace the VAE decoder with a ConvNeXt-based [(Liu et al., 2022)] head that operates only in low spatial resolution, followed by a single linear layer that unpatchifies and upsamples the latents to pixel dimensions, reducing decoding latency by 147× while matching quality. Furthermore, because the head is lightweight, training the model end-to-end in pixel-space (e.g., perceptual [(Zhang et al., 2018)] and GAN [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] losses) becomes practical, bypassing the reconstruction bottleneck of the VAE. Second, the baseline inference pipeline includes an additional DiT evaluation on each fully denoised latent solely to refine the KV cache (Sec. 3.3); we replace the DiT evaluation with a lightweight network, reducing cache-update latency 10x without measurable degradation in quality. Finally, we perform multiple system-level, hardware-aware optimizations that specifically target the end-to-end per-frame critical path. Our techniques target components shared by many AR video diffusion models and are therefore complementary to advances in backbone architecture, such as hybrid transformers [(Chen et al., 2026a)], and improved distillation methods [(Liu et al., 2026a)].

In the standard text-to-video (T2V) setting, where the model simply treats the current generated frame as input for generating the next, our quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that FastFrames establishes a new Pareto frontier between generation quality and speed (Fig. 1). The 1.3B variant achieves an end-to-end per-frame latency of 36 ms (28 RPS) on a single B200 GPU at 832×480 resolution (480p), matching the visual quality of a state-of-the-art baseline [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] that is 7.6× slower. Scaling FastFrames to 14B improves visual fidelity while achieving 45 ms (22 RPS) on an 8× B200 GPU node.

The T2V AR pipeline can be extended to accept controls between generation steps, such as camera poses [(Jiang et al., 2026)], 2D tracks [(Shin et al., 2026)], and 3D dynamics [(Li et al., 2025b)]. We show that FastFrames enables fluid interactive experiences in two applications: camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

2 Related Work

Accelerating diffusion sampling. Diffusion models require iterative sampling [(Ho et al., 2020)]. Earlier work reduces the number of sampling steps using training-free accelerated samplers [(Song et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2025)] or by training models to take larger steps along their sampling trajectories [(Frans et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025; Shaul et al., 2026)]. The state of the art relies on distribution matching [(Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Cui et al., 2026)], where a few-step student generator approximates the distribution of a teacher network. Another line of work focuses on the inference cost of DiTs, including hybrid attention [(Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)], sliding-window attention for long context [(Xiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025)], and layer pruning or model-size distillation [(Fang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025b)]. A smaller line of work focuses specifically on compressing or sparsifying the KV cache of autoregressive video diffusion models to reduce attention overhead [(Ji et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2026)]. However, these methods are generally model-specific, so instead we target other components on the critical path. Our work builds on state-of-the-art few-step models, but we observe that the iterative denoising process is no longer the latency bottleneck.

Reducing VAE decoding time. State-of-the-art video diffusion models perform diffusion in latent space [(Blattmann et al., 2023)], generally encoded via a variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma & Welling, 2014)]. For instance, the Wan VAE [(Wang et al., 2025)] can perform up to a 48× reduction in dimensionality. This makes generation cheaper but pixel decoding becomes expensive. VAE decoders repeatedly upsample features in space and time, and apply dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, a tensor containing four 480×832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions. A line of work aims to speed up VAEs [(Boer Bohan, 2023; Buzovkin & Shilov, 2025)] by reducing the number of parameters and removing expensive operations like attention and wide 3D convolutions. These methods gain up to 4× speedup but incur degradation in visual quality [(Boer Bohan, 2025; Huang et al., 2025)]. Instead, we treat the pixel decoder as a lightweight readout specific to a frozen DiT, rather than a general-purpose reconstruction problem. Our pixel head maintains visual quality while being two orders of magnitude faster.

Systems-level optimizations. Systems-level techniques accelerate diffusion inference through more efficient scheduling and hardware utilization. [Kodaira et al. (2025)] and [Bandyopadhyay et al. (2026)] use batching and pipeline parallelism to improve streaming throughput but do not improve per-frame latency. StreamDiffusionV2 [(Feng et al., 2026)] emphasizes non-amortized time-to-first-frame but to the best of our understanding, this metric focuses on the start of a stream, in contrast to our steady-state measurements. Optimized attention kernels [(Dao, 2024)], compilation and operator fusion [(Ansel et al., 2024)], and CUDA graph execution [(Ghosh et al., 2025)] reduce memory traffic and execution overhead. Weight and activation quantization [(Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Su et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b)] reduce memory requirements and can accelerate computation with suitable hardware support. Distributed inference spreads computation across multiple GPUs through patch, sequence, and pipeline parallelism [(Li et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2024)]. Our work incorporates many of these techniques.

3 Method

3.1 Preliminaries: Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion Models

Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate a video one latent chunk at a time, using diffusion to synthesize each chunk conditioned on previously generated ones. We represent a video sequence as z^1:N=(z¹,z²,…,z^N), where each chunk zⁱ∈ℝ^C×T×H×W contains T≥1 latent frames with C channels and spatial resolution H×W. Each latent frame corresponds to K RGB frames, where K is the temporal compression factor of the VAE. Generating larger chunks (e.g., one chunk = three latent frames, as in Self-Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)]) is closer to bidirectional models and empirically easier to optimize, while generating a smaller chunk (e.g., one chunk = one latent frame, as in Causal Forcing++ (CF++) [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] and FastFrames) is faster. The joint distribution factorizes autoregressively as p(z^1:N)=∏ᵢ₌₁^Np(zⁱ|z^

To examine the inference cost, we profile CF++, the fastest few-step AR video diffusion model at the time of writing. It is built on the Wan 2.1 1.3B-parameter backbone. Fig. 2 shows its inference latency on a single B200 GPU, decomposed into three stages: KV-cache updates, diffusion sampling, and pixel rendering. We use its two-diffusion-step variant, which provides the best speed-quality tradeoff; reducing sampling steps to one significantly degrades visual quality while merely reducing latency by 15%. Each DiT evaluation takes 41.6 ms using BF16 precision, cuDNN attention backend [(NVIDIA Corporation, 2026)], and torch.compile[(Ansel et al., 2024)]. The KV cache update is an additional DiT evaluation. Finally, the VAE decoder takes 147 ms to decode each generated latent into four RGB frames, resulting in a total end-to-end latency of 271.8 ms.

This profile suggests that our latency budget of 50 ms leaves room for only a single diffusion sampling step. Instead, we replace the VAE with lightweight pixel rendering (Sec. 3.2) and accelerate KV cache updates (Sec. 3.3). Then, by reducing the latency of each DiT evaluation through systems-level optimizations (Sec. 3.4), we fit the full inference pipeline within the target latency. Our final 1.3B model runs in 36 ms on a single B200 GPU, making it 7.6× faster than CF++. Our 14B model runs 10.6× faster than the fastest open-source AR model of the same parameter count and achieves a further 3.5× speedup when distributed across eight B200 GPUs.

3.2 Removing the VAE Decoder

We first target the VAE decoder since it accounts for more than half of the end-to-end inference latency and alone exceeds our real-time budget 3×. The VAE decoder only has 73M parameters (compared to the DiT’s 1.3B) but repeatedly upsamples its features in space and time and applies dense 3D convolutions at each resolution. For example, a tensor containing four 480×832 frames requires convolution at approximately 1.6 million spatiotemporal positions.

In light of recent advances in pixel diffusion models, we question whether such a decoder is necessary when the DiT already produces rich and spatially contextualized features. For instance, JiT [(Li & He, 2026)] produces sharp images by mapping between image patches and transformer features using only linear projections. Thus, we first attempt replacing the VAE with a single linear layer and train it with an MSE loss against the VAE decoded output, keeping the DiT frozen. We found that the outputs were blurry yet recognizable (Fig. 3).

We then increase the size of the pixel decoder, until arriving at our final architecture consisting of three causal 3D ConvNeXt-style blocks [(Liu et al., 2022)]. Each block uses a causal 3×3×3 depthwise convolution followed by a channel-mixing MLP. All blocks operate only on the transformer’s low-resolution 21×30×52 token grid. A final linear layer converts each token into a 4×16×16 RGB patch, yielding an 84-frame, 480×832 video. We discard the first three frames following the conventions of the Wan VAE, which does not temporally upsample the first frame. The total number of parameters is comparable (63.9M for ours vs. 73.3M), yet two orders of magnitude faster (1 ms vs. 147 ms).

We train the pixel decoder using spatial and temporal reconstruction objectives. Let ŷₚᵢₓ denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let y_VAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x₀ with the frozen VAE. We optimize

L_rec(ŷₚᵢₓ,y_VAE)=λ₁L₁+λ_MSEL_MSE+λ_gradL_grad+λₜₑₘₚLₜₑₘₚ+λₘₒₜᵢₒₙLₘₒₜᵢₒₙ.

(1)

Here, λ₁=0.5, λ_MSE=5.0, λ_grad=λₜₑₘₚ=0.05, and λₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=0.5. All five terms are computed between ŷₚᵢₓ and y_VAE. The L₁ and L_MSE terms enforce pixel-level fidelity, while L_grad matches spatial image gradients and Lₜₑₘₚ matches frame-to-frame changes. The motion-weighted term Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ emphasizes reconstruction errors in regions exhibiting motion in the VAE target. Complete definitions of the loss terms are provided in the supplement.

In addition to reducing latency, our pixel decoder is less memory-intensive to optimize. For a batch-size-one, 81-frame video at 832×480 resolution, a VAE decoder update with BF16 precision and activation checkpointing requires approximately 68 GB of peak GPU memory, compared with approximately 5 GB for our pixel decoder. This makes it practical to optimize the decoder directly in pixel space with adversarial losses to improve sharpness and realism.

We curated an internal dataset of 10K real videos and used a frozen DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] ViT-S/16 backbone as our discriminator. On each of layers 4, 8, and 12, we train two lightweight token-level discriminator heads: a spatial classifier and a temporal classifier that receives both the current patch feature and its change from the preceding frame. Let H denote the six discriminator heads, let y denote a real video crop, and let ŷ denote a generated crop. We use the following relativistic softplus discriminator objective [(Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2019)]:

L_D=(1)/(|H|)∑_h∈H⟨softplus (Dₕ(ŷ)-Dₕ(y))+λ_center[Dₕ(y)+Dₕ(ŷ)]²⟩+λₛₗₒₚₑ(R₁+R₂),

(2)

where ⟨·⟩ denotes averaging over clips, frames, and patch tokens, λ_center=0.01, and λₛₗₒₚₑ=0.25. The terms R₁ and R₂ are finite-difference slope penalties on real and generated inputs, respectively [(Lin et al., 2026)]. We estimate them on 25% of the clips by adding Gaussian RGB perturbations with standard deviation ε=0.01.

The generator consists of the frozen DiT and the trainable ConvNeXt pixel decoder. We continue using the reconstruction objective (Eq. 1) with the reverse relativistic comparison:

L_adv=(1)/(|H|)∑_h∈H⟨softplus(-[Dₕ(ŷ)-sg (Dₕ(y))])⟩,

(3)

where sg denotes stop-gradient. We cap the adversarial RGB-gradient magnitude relative to the reconstruction gradient for stable optimization. We also tried finetuning the DiT with low learning rate, but observed training instability.

As seen in Fig. 3, our pixel decoder faithfully reconstructs thin structures like hair and raindrops. However, unlike the Wan VAE decoder, which can be shared across models of the same family (e.g., 1.3B and 14B variants), our pixel decoder must be finetuned for each individual model. Our main takeaway is that we can turn pixel decoding into a lightweight readout rather than a general-purpose reconstruction problem.

3.3 Faster KV Cache Updates

Autoregressive video diffusion models attend to earlier frames through a KV cache [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025)]. Each DiT layer maintains its own cache, which holds an attention sink plus a sliding window of recent entries. During each generation, the final denoising pass leaves the current chunk’s cache entries computed from a noisy input. The baselines therefore run an additional DiT pass on the predicted clean latent ẑᵢ at t=0 and replace those entries with its keys and values (the KV cache write in Fig. 2). They discard the pass’s output prediction.

In a two-step diffusion setup, KV refinement accounts for one-third of DiT evaluations. We first investigate whether refinement is necessary. Naively removing the refinement leads to substantial degradation and training the model to use noisy cached features still produces noticeable artifacts (see supplement for visualizations). However, we hypothesize that a lightweight network can replace the expensive DiT pass. We design a KV refinement network with a shared feature extractor and per-layer KV-repair heads. The feature extractor takes ẑᵢ and applies the DiT’s frozen patch embedding followed by four lightweight transformer blocks trained from scratch. Each repair head takes these output features and its layer’s noisy keys and values to predict residual corrections.

During training, we freeze the DiT and use the keys and values produced by the original DiT refinement pass to supervise residual corrections to the noisy cache. We train our network with two losses: a direct KV reconstruction loss combining cosine distance and relative ℓ₂ error, and an attention-output loss that compares the outputs obtained when subsequent chunks attend to the predicted versus target cache. The network performs comparably to the original refinement pass in terms of quantitative and qualitative comparisons, while taking approximately 2 ms for the 1.3B model and 6 ms for the 14B model on a B200 GPU, around 20× and 12× faster respectively than the baselines’ refinement. We provide details in the supplement.

3.4 Systems-level Optimizations

After reducing non-denoising overhead, DiT evaluations remain the main bottleneck to real-time generation. “Free” optimizations, including faster attention backends and torch.compile(), are already accounted for in the baseline profiling (Fig. 2). First, we observe that the repeated structure of DiT evaluations offers opportunities to reuse computation. We maintain persistent KV-cache buffers and write new entries directly into their designated slots; precompute and store RoPE tables, text and timestep conditions; and fuse QKV projections into one larger matrix multiplication.

Second, we find that per-frame AR generation can provide too few query tokens to fully utilize the GPU. We therefore split the KV sequence into segments processed in parallel, then combine their attention outputs using a softmax merge. Concretely, for a full KV cache of length 32,760, we found that splitting it into five segments of 6,552 each led to a 13% latency reduction. Third, we reduce the overhead of launching and coordinating GPU work via CUDA graphs. Together, these optimizations bring the DiT evaluation latency from 41.6 ms to 16.4 ms for the 1.3B model on one B200 GPU at the full 32,760-token KV prefix and from 89.2 to 75.6 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to approximately 2.5× and 1.2× speedups.

Next, we distribute computation across 8× B200 GPUs. We experimented with tensor parallelism, attention-head parallelism, KV sharding, joint query–KV partitioning, and context parallelism (CP). Among them, only CP reduced computation sufficiently to justify communication overhead. CP partitions query tokens across GPUs and distributes both attention and feed-forward computation, requiring only one exchange of computed keys and values per transformer layer. We implement these exchanges using CUDA-graph-compatible NVLink symmetric-memory gathers. This configuration reduces DiT latency from 16.4 to 5.8 ms for the 1.3B model and from 75.6 to 20.3 ms for the 14B model, corresponding to 2.8× and 3.7× speedups over their optimized single-GPU implementations.

4 Experiments

Models and baselines. We build FastFrames on the Wan 2.1 backbone at two model sizes: FastFrames-S with 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with 14B. We initialize FastFrames-S from the two-step Causal Forcing++ (CF++) checkpoint and finetune it using our method. We freeze the DiT and train our pixel decoder and KV refinement network against their respective targets. FastFrames-L required starting from the base bidirectional model. Following the training recipe in CF++, we converted Wan 2.1 14B into an autoregressive model, distilled it into a few-step model, and trained it with DMD. Both FastFrames-S and FastFrames-L perform two-step diffusion sampling and generate one latent frame per autoregressive step.

Quantitative comparisons. Tab. 1 provides a quantitative comparison against bidirectional video generators and autoregressive models. The bidirectional models provide a broader reference for generation quality and latency, while the autoregressive models provide direct comparisons. We report model size, latency, and VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)] scores. All models are evaluated using the same VBench prompts and seeds. We report end-to-end latency and compute RPS as its reciprocal in seconds, following the definitions in the introduction. For AR models, one response corresponds to an autoregressive generation unit; for bidirectional models, it corresponds to a complete generated clip. Consequently, RPS does not credit a method for producing multiple frames within one generation unit. We account for diffusion sampling, KV cache updates where applicable, and pixel rendering. For AR models, we measure latency at steady state after warm-up and with a full KV cache. For bidirectional models, we let the model warm up and then generate the configured native clip lengths. All models are evaluated on a B200 GPU unless otherwise specified, at approximately 480p using the model’s officially supported resolutions.

We find that FastFrames matches corresponding baselines with the same Wan 2.1 backbone (Krea-Realtime vs. FastFrames-L, CF++ vs. FastFrames-S). Between FastFrames-S and CF++, which use the same DiT weights, we attribute the higher visual quality to end-to-end adversarial training in pixel space, which boosts realism and sharpness.

None of the baselines meet the 50 ms latency target required for interactive applications. The fastest baseline, CF++, reaches 3.68 RPS at 272 ms, falling 5.4× short of the 20 RPS target. In contrast, FastFrames-S attains a latency of 36 ms (27.8 RPS) on a single B200 GPU and FastFrames-L attains 45 ms (22.2 RPS) on an 8-GPU node. FastFrames-S on 8 GPUs reaches 14 ms (71.4 RPS), while FastFrames-L on a single GPU reaches 158 ms (6.33 RPS).

Qualitative comparisons. Fig. 4 shows a side-by-side comparison between FastFrames-S, FastFrames-L, and their respective baselines. FastFrames-S maintains visual sharpness relative to CF++, capturing fine details like sculptures and leaves while being nearly 8× faster. FastFrames-L achieves realism, prompt adherence, composition, and text rendering capabilities comparable to Krea-Realtime while being over 10× faster.

Fig. 4 also illustrates the improved capabilities of the 14B models relative to their 1.3B counterparts. The larger models produce more realistic lighting and shadows in the first two examples, better capture the folded-paper appearance of the origami dragon in the third, and render more legible text in the fourth. We encourage readers to view the supplementary videos on the project website.

Interactive applications. We showcase FastFrames in interactive settings by accelerating camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation: LingBot [(Gao et al., 2026)], a family of camera-conditioned video models with 1.3B and 14B variants, and RealWonder [(Liu et al., 2026c)], a 1.3B physics-conditioned video model. Our techniques transfer directly to these off-the-shelf models and yield large speedups, even over official code that already includes optimizations such as Ulysses sequence parallelism [(Jacobs et al., 2024)]. Fig. 5 summarizes the latency profiles.

On LingBot 1.3B, we reduce latency from 842 ms (the fastest official configuration, 2 GPUs) to 52 ms on 8 GPUs, a 16× speedup. On RealWonder, latency drops from 1141 ms (official, 1 GPU) to 51 ms (22×), so both models approximately reach our target interactive latency. On LingBot 14B, latency drops from 1373 ms to 233 ms on 8 GPUs (5.9×). These models remain slower than our T2V models because they require more diffusion sampling steps, predict multiple latent frames per autoregressive step, and need extra DiT computation to process additional conditioning.

We show a side-by-side comparison between the interactive demos on the project website; the original models exhibit noticeable lag while our optimized versions of LingBot 1.3B and RealWonder respond to user inputs fluidly.

5 Conclusion

We presented FastFrames, a family of autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency by rethinking components of the inference pipeline often treated as fixed implementation details. Both our 1.3B and 14B variants achieve generation quality comparable to or better than their respective baselines.

While our evaluation focuses on text-to-video generation at 480p on high-end GPUs, important directions for future work include adding action conditioning without increasing latency, scaling to higher resolutions, and supporting lighter hardware form factors. Improving long-term consistency and physical plausibility will further broaden the utility of video world models.

Acknowledgments

We thank Hongyu Wen, Boyang Deng, Alejandro Newell, Aleksei Bochkovskii, JunYoung Gwak, Lahav Lipson, Marcel Santos, Marko Mihajlovic, Peiyun Hu, Lyndon Duong, Amael Delaunoy, Jackson Hamburger, and Philipp Kraehenbuehl for discussions and support.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix

We organize the appendix into the following sections: (A) Limitations and future work, (B) Additional latency profiling, (C) Architecture and training details of pixel decoder, (D) Architecture and training details of KV refinement network, and (E) Adaptation details of interactive applications.

We encourage readers to view the videos on our website.

Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

Resolution. Most baselines and base video models use 480p resolution, which we finetune from. Higher resolution like 720p or even 4K is desired for a variety of applications like gaming and content creation. In the next section, we find that increasing resolution to 720p increases latency significantly; further optimization is required to bring high-res video generation into the interactive regime.

Accessible hardware. We use B200 GPUs for our latency measurements in the main paper. While we assume compute will continue to become cheaper and more accessible, being able to run interactive video models on-device is an exciting possibility.

Action conditions designed for lower latency. We applied FastFrames to off-the-shelf autoregressive models that were slower than their T2V counterparts. Training base models with lower latency in mind, such as concatenating camera poses in the channel dimension rather than the sequence dimension, without compromising quality, is essential for reducing latency.

Appendix B Additional Latency Profiling

In Tab. 2, we include detailed profiling of each operation on B200 and H100 GPUs, and at 480p and 720p resolution. In short, FastFrames-S runs at 36 ms at 480p and 127 ms at 720p on a B200 GPU, and FastFrames-L runs at 45 ms at 480p and 116 ms at 720p on 8 B200 GPUs. Savings from our lightweight networks are more noticeable at 720p. H100s are approximately 25% to 50% slower depending on the configuration.

Some baselines like Self-Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)] report latency in their paper. However, we did not find detailed descriptions or breakdowns of those numbers and can only infer their profiling from source code. We found that Self-Forcing measured latency by generating a video sequence of N latent chunks (where each chunk ≥ 1 latent frame(s)), then dividing the total time by the number of chunks. However, earlier chunks are faster to generate due to an initially empty KV cache that gradually fills, so this average does not represent steady-state latency at long contexts. Occasionally, baselines provide ambiguous latency numbers without explanation; Causal Forcing++ [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] reports 270 ms for its 1, 2, and 4 step models without explanation.

All of our profiling numbers include a breakdown of the specific operation, and are measured at steady-state with a full KV cache where applicable based on officially released configurations (e.g., KV=32760 for Self-Forcing and its follow-up works).

Appendix C Architecture and Training Details of Pixel Decoder

Our pixel decoder is a causal ConvNeXt model operating directly on the pre-head features of the frozen two-step DiTs. For a 21-frame latent sequence, the DiT produces 32,760 tokens on a (21×30×52) spatiotemporal grid with channel width 1536. The head applies per-frame adaptive shift/scale modulation, a (1×1) channel projection, and three ConvNeXt-style causal 3D residual blocks—two low-resolution blocks followed by one output block—using depthwise (3×3×3) convolutions, channel-wise layer normalization, and width-4 pointwise GELU expansions. All convolutional processing remains at the DiT token resolution; the selected configuration has no learned temporal or spatial upsampler, latent adapter, displacement branch, auxiliary feature fusion, or post-RGB refiner. A final per-token linear projection maps the 1536-dimensional features to (4×16×16×3) RGB values, which are unpatchified into 84 frames at (480×832) and aligned to the VAE convention by dropping the first three frames, yielding 81 output frames. The decoder contains 63.87M parameters and is causal in time, so each output block depends only on the current and preceding latent blocks.

We train the pixel decoder using a paired spatial-temporal reconstruction objective. Let ŷₚᵢₓ denote the RGB video predicted by the ConvNeXt decoder, and let y_VAE denote the output obtained by decoding the same final latent x₀ with the frozen VAE. Both videos are represented in the range [-1,1]. Our reconstruction objective is

L_rec=0.5 L₁+5.0 L_MSE+0.05 L_grad+0.05 Lₜₑₘₚ+0.50 Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ.

(4)

The pixelwise terms are L₁=mean(|ŷₚᵢₓ-y_VAE|) and L_MSE=mean((ŷₚᵢₓ-y_VAE)²). To preserve spatial structure, we match horizontal and vertical finite differences:

L_grad=mean (|Δₕŷₚᵢₓ-Δₕy_VAE|)+mean (|Δ_wŷₚᵢₓ-Δ_wy_VAE|).

(5)

To preserve temporal dynamics, we match consecutive-frame differences:

Lₜₑₘₚ=mean (|Δₜŷₚᵢₓ-Δₜy_VAE|).

(6)

Finally, we place greater reconstruction weight on regions that move in the VAE target:

Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=mean_t>1,p [(1+γ mean_c|Δₜy_VAE,t,c,p|)mean_c|ŷ_pix,t,c,p-y_VAE,t,c,p|], γ=10.

(7)

Here, Δₕ, Δ_w, and Δₜ denote vertical, horizontal, and temporal finite-difference operators, respectively; c indexes RGB channels; and p indexes spatial locations. The multiplier γ controls how strongly moving target regions are emphasized within Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ, while the coefficient 0.50 controls the overall contribution of this term to L_rec.

Using the 

vidprom_filtered_extended.txt
file provided in Self-Forcing’s repo, we roll out the frozen DiT and VAE 150k times to get the input and output targets, running 4 optimization steps per rollout. We train on 32 B200 GPUs for about a week; we find that validation loss and metrics (PSNR and SSIM) continue to improve steadily though slowly.

We take the last checkpoint and train with the adversarial setup as described in the main paper (Sec. 3.2). We train on 8 B200 GPUs and run 5000 rollouts per GPU and 4 optimization steps per rollout. Training completes in a few hours.

Appendix D Architecture and Training Details of KV Refinement Network

As described in the main paper, we first investigate whether KV refinement is necessary, given that the last diffusion sampling step writes a noisy KV cache for free. In Fig. 6, we find that removing KV refinement, even after training the model to learn to use the noisy KV cache, leads to drift and artifacts. These experiments motivate our design.

Our KV refinement network is a cache-repair module that replaces the expensive DiT evaluation of the baselines. Each DiT layer maintains its own KV cache, partitioned into one slice for each generated latent frame. During every diffusion evaluation for frame i, the KV tensors for that frame overwrite its current cache slice, while the slices for earlier frames remain available as causal context. At the final denoising step, the DiT still receives a nonzero-noise latent, although it predicts the clean latent z₀; consequently, the KV written to the current slice correspond to the noisy input. The baseline therefore performs an additional, non-denoising DiT forward pass on z₀ with zero-noise time conditioning (t=0), overwriting the same slice with clean-context KV.

Instead, our network consumes the noisy K/V tensors from the final denoising pass together with the predicted z₀, predicts corrected K/V tensors, and overwrites the same cache slice. Subsequent latent frames therefore attend to the repaired context without requiring the additional full DiT forward pass. A shared stem maps the 1,560 patch tokens per frame from 1,536 to 768 channels, then applies four lightweight 8-head spatial self-attention blocks with 4× GELU MLPs and timestep-conditioned adaptive layer normalization. Each of the DiT layers has a separate repair head that projects its noisy K/V, concatenates them with the shared per-token z₀ features, and predicts residual corrections. Keys are corrected in post-RoPE space and renormalized per attention head, while values receive a learned residual and per-channel scale. All residual outputs are zero-initialized so the adapter initially behaves like the no-prime baseline.

During inference, frame 0 retains a real clean-prime anchor, while subsequent frames use the repaired K/V to overwrite their cache slots before the next frame is processed. The adapter is trained with the DiT and VAE frozen using teacher-forced targets from the real prime pass: the primary objective matches future attention outputs, supplemented by direct K/V reconstruction with approximately three times more weight on value than key errors, since we found that value corruption dominates the degradation.

Appendix E Adaptation Details of Interactive Applications

We use the official model and weights released by the authors. We follow the procedure described in Sec. 3 to train both the pixel decoder and the KV refinement network. Neither component requires large-scale training data. We simply roll out the models to create target pixels and clean keys and values on-the-fly.

LingBot requires four diffusion sampling steps per autoregressive generation, and generates four latent frames at once. RealWonder requires three sampling steps and generates three latent frames at once. Both are substantially more expensive than our setup in FastFrames, which performs two sampling steps, and generates one latent frame at a time. Thus, even the 1.3B models require 8 GPUs to reach interactive latency. RealWonder is slower than LingBot at the same parameter count due to its more expensive processing of its action conditions. Distilling these models to fewer steps and fewer latent frames per generation while maintaining output quality and adherence to conditions is important future work.

item.title: π⁴：一个模型从随手拍的图或视频里同时给出几何、位姿、度量尺度、点轨迹与运动物体掩码 ｜ π⁴: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
item.description:
一句话：几何分支 + 几何条件化的运动分支，把 4D 理解压进一个统一模型。

要点：

  • 输入很宽容：野外的、**未标定**的 RGB 观测——单张图、无序集合，或一段视频
  • 输出很全：稠密几何、相机位姿与**度量尺度**，多图输入下还给 2D/3D 点轨迹与**运动物体掩码**
  • 结构上是「几何分支 + 由几何条件化的运动分支」，其中运动分支预测图像空间的对应关系，从而实现 4D 一致的解

为什么值得看：引擎要消费「4D 场景」，最缺的就是「一份统一的、带度量尺度的表示」。把位姿、稠密度量、轨迹与运动掩码一次给全，等于把重建、跟踪与场景解析三件事合到同一个输出上——这对做 real-to-sim 或视频转场景的管线是直接可用的接口。

中文摘要：π⁴ 是一个面向 4D 场景感知的统一基础模型：从野外采集、未标定的 RGB 观测出发——可以是单张图像、一组无序图像，也可以是一段视频——同时恢复稠密几何、相机位姿与度量尺度，并在多图输入下给出 2D/3D 点轨迹以及运动物体的掩码。架构上它把几何分支与一个由几何条件化的运动分支耦合起来，运动分支预测图像空间的对应关系，从而得到 4D 一致的解。对需要把真实拍摄内容转成引擎可消费场景的管线而言，这种「一份带度量尺度的统一表示」恰好补上了位姿、稠密几何、轨迹与运动解析之间的缝隙。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

\uppi⁴: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion

Abstract

\uppi⁴ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild—a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence—it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, \uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters—less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at Pi4.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward models have established a powerful paradigm for reconstructing scenes directly from RGB observations [(Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b)]. More recently, this paradigm has been extended beyond scene reconstruction to encompass motion recovery [(Lu et al., 2026; Fradlin et al., 2026)]. A key question, however, is how well these capabilities generalize to in-the-wild observations, where scene content, camera configurations, temporal continuity, and the number of observations are unconstrained. Maintaining high-quality geometric reconstruction while robustly recovering motion from such diverse inputs remains a significant practical challenge.

To address this challenge, we present \uppi⁴, a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception from RGB observations. It handles single images, unordered image collections, and videos, recovering dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D and 3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. Across the geometry benchmarks in Table 2, \uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank among the compared methods, while delivering competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D tracking and moving-object segmentation (Figure 2). Despite this broad functionality, the model employs a shared backbone across these capabilities and contains approximately 0.5B parameters in total—less than half the size of most baselines. Beyond benchmark results, Figure 1 showcases joint geometry and motion reconstruction across diverse in-the-wild observations, including aerial footage, casual handheld recordings, driving and sports scenes, and stylized content. These reconstruction and tracking results are all produced in a single forward pass per scene. This combination of accuracy, efficiency, and generality is enabled by coordinated choices in model architecture, training, and data.

At the architectural level, the geometry network of \uppi⁴ retains the permutation-equivariant formulation of π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], treating all input views symmetrically without designating a reference view. Both the geometry and motion branches employ looped Transformer decoding [(Burzio et al., 2026)], which we adopt for its strong cross-benchmark performance and parameter efficiency. We choose loop weight sharing partly to reduce memory usage, freeing capacity for larger within-sequence contexts. Training stochastically samples view counts from single images, 2–24-view sets, and 32/48/64-view sets, with short contexts dominating the mixture. A sparse 3D refiner [(Kong et al., 2026)] further enhances local surface structure and geometric detail.

To incorporate motion estimation without compromising reconstruction, we freeze the geometry network and train a separate geometry-conditioned motion decoder. Direct 3D tracking couples correspondence estimation with geometry, camera placement, and scene scale in the regression target. We instead keep motion prediction in image space and delegate 3D reasoning to the reconstruction branch, composing the two analytically.

This yields a simple correspondence objective that is independent of scene scale, while placing every visible 3D track point on the reconstructed target-view surface. Geometry features also provide useful context for correspondence prediction.

Complementing these architectural and modeling choices, our data construction pipeline addresses gaps in scene and camera coverage, as well as the difficulty of obtaining geometric supervision for foreground-dominated videos. We render scene-level assets from Funes [(FUNES.WORLD, n.d.)] and Sketchfab [(Sketchfab, n.d.)], covering architectural environments and other large-scale scenes rather than isolated objects alone. Coverage-aware view selection and connected view sampling balance broad scene coverage with local cross-view matchability, while complementary natural and counterbias camera configurations expand the range of roll angles and focal lengths encountered during training. We further apply field-of-view and lens augmentation to diversify image-to-ray mappings beyond those induced by conventional pinhole or rectified imagery. For Internet videos dominated by moving foregrounds, we infer background geometry following foreground suppression and video inpainting. We retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels and pair the resulting pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames. GameRealm[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)], developed jointly with collaborators, further provides complementary engine-native geometry and persistent point trajectories as supervision for dynamic scenes.

Together, these architectural, data, and training choices enable coherent joint reconstruction and tracking from thousands of images in large-scale scenes despite a maximum training context of 64 views (Figure 1). We further examine the architecture and training strategy of \uppi⁴ through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that motivate these choices.

2 Related Work

2.1 Visual Geometry Reconstruction

Classical structure-from-motion (SfM) estimates cameras and sparse structure through image matching and bundle adjustment, while multi-view stereo (MVS) reconstructs dense surfaces from calibrated views. COLMAP exemplifies this modular pipeline [(Schönberger and Frahm, 2016; Schönberger et al., 2016)]. Learned MVS methods such as MVSNet [(Yao et al., 2018)] learn cost-volume regularization while retaining camera calibration as input. More recently, DUSt3R [(Wang et al., 2024a)] predicts pairwise pointmaps without supplied cameras, and MASt3R [(Leroy et al., 2024)] combines this 3D representation with learned matching descriptors, bridging reconstruction and correspondence estimation.

Feed-forward multi-view models increasingly estimate geometry and cameras jointly. VGGT [(Wang et al., 2025a)] predicts cameras, depth, pointmaps, and tracks from image sets, while π³ and its released Pi3X variant [(Wang et al., 2025b)] use permutation-equivariant modeling without a privileged input reference. MapAnything [(Keetha et al., 2026)] targets metric reconstruction with flexible geometric inputs, whereas Depth Anything 3 [(Lin et al., 2025)] uses depth and ray prediction across arbitrary views. VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)] incorporates matching supervision, and DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)] reuses Transformer blocks through looped decoding. Monocular models provide complementary components: MoGe2 [(Wang et al., 2025c)] separates metric-scale prediction from relative geometry, and MoGe3 [(Kong et al., 2026)] refines surface detail with sparse volumetric processing. Together, these methods provide complementary designs for joint camera–geometry estimation, reference-free reconstruction, metric prediction, and iterative decoding.

2.2 Image Correspondence and Point Tracking

Classical image tracking estimates motion through local appearance alignment, as in Lucas–Kanade [(Lucas and Kanade, 1981)]. Modern optical-flow models such as RAFT [(Teed and Deng, 2020)] learn dense two-frame correspondence, while TAPIR [(Doersch et al., 2023)] and CoTracker3 [(Karaev et al., 2024)] follow queried points over videos and estimate visibility. CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)] replaces correlation-volume lookup with iterative feature warping. Optical flow and query-based tracking thus provide dense or sparse image-space correspondences, typically within ordered video sequences.

2.3 Dynamic Scene Reconstruction and 4D Perception

Dynamic scene reconstruction extends geometry estimation to scenes with moving and deforming content. Shape of Motion [(Wang et al., 2025d)] reconstructs 4D scenes from monocular videos using compact SE(3) motion bases and data-driven geometric and tracking priors. MonST3R [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] instead adapts pointmap reconstruction to dynamic videos by estimating per-timestep geometry without an explicit motion representation. These approaches connect scene geometry with temporal variation, but differ in how motion is represented and how reconstruction and tracking are coupled.

Recent methods further extend tracking to 3D and connect it to scene reconstruction. D4RT [(Zhang et al., 2026)] and ARROW [(Fradlin et al., 2026)] use query-based decoding to recover point positions across time and reference cameras; ARROW additionally supports unordered and multiview observations. MoSE3 [(Cheng et al., 2026)] models dense world-space motion through per-pixel SE(3) transformations, while Track4World [(Lu et al., 2026)] combines dense correspondences, geometry, and camera estimation for world-centric tracking.

Moving-object segmentation provides a complementary object-level characterization of scene dynamics by identifying regions that undergo motion [(Tokmakov et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2026a)]. Across these directions, methods differ in their supported input configurations, output representations, and the degree to which geometry and motion are modeled jointly.

3 Method

\uppi⁴ combines geometric reconstruction and motion estimation within a single feed-forward model (Figure 3). A shared image encoder provides features to two task-specific looped Transformer decoders. The geometry branch predicts dense pointmaps, camera poses, and metric scale; a sparse 3D refiner then improves the predicted pointmaps. Conditioned on geometry features, the motion branch predicts image-space point tracks and moving-object masks. The predicted tracks are lifted to 3D using the reconstructed target-view geometry.

3.1 Task Formulation and Output Representations

Given N RGB images I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, with Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, \uppi⁴ predicts scene geometry and, for multi-image inputs, point tracks and moving-object masks. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are not required as inputs, and the images need not follow a chronological ordering.

The geometric outputs comprise a dense local pointmap Pᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, a camera-to-world pose Tᵢ=(Rᵢ,tᵢ)∈SE(3), and a confidence map cᵢ(u)∈[0,1] for each image, together with a positive scale m shared across the inputs. Points are expressed in their respective camera coordinates; the camera poses relate these local reconstructions through a common scene frame, and m converts the reconstruction to metric units.

For motion tracking, a query view q specifies the points to track. The model predicts dense image-space correspondences U_q→i:Ω_q→ℝ², together with visibility and tracking confidence. Here Ω_q is the query pixel grid, and U_q→i(u) gives the corresponding location in image i. World-space tracks Y_q→i(u) combine these correspondences with the reconstructed geometry. The model also predicts a moving-object mask for each image, independently of the query selection.

3.2 Shared Encoding and Looped Decoding

Image encoder.

A shared DINOv3 encoder [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] extracts per-image patch features for both branches. We combine intermediate and late-layer encoder features, project them into the decoder feature space, and append shared learnable register tokens. We examine the choice of encoder layers in Section 6.3.

Looped decoders.

Both the geometry and motion decoders alternate frame and cross-view attention [(Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b)]. Following Déjà View [(Burzio et al., 2026)], each decoder repeatedly applies the same pair of blocks, sharing their weights across its loop steps. The two decoders have independent parameters; weight sharing occurs within each branch, not between branches. Starting from encoded tokens Z⁰, the geometry decoder applies

Z^ℓ+1=B_cross (B_frame (Z^ℓ;τ_ℓ);τ_ℓ), ℓ=0,…,L-1,

(1)

where B_frame is a Transformer block that processes each image independently, and B_cross is a Transformer block that aggregates information across input views. The conditioning variable τ_ℓ encodes the normalized current and next loop positions. The geometry loop count L is sampled between 8 and 16 during training, whereas motion decoding uses a fixed M=8. Evaluation uses L=16 and M=8. Task heads read only the final decoder state.

Geometry-conditioned motion decoding.

The motion decoder starts from image tokens and adopts the same frame- and cross-view-attention block design as the geometry decoder, but with independent parameters. It follows the same looped attention structure, with additional geometry conditioning: spatial adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) conditions its attention and feed-forward sublayers on detached geometry features at the same view and patch, together with loop progress. A final within-image readout supplies the tracking and moving-object mask heads. The motion decoder uses no temporal positional embeddings.

3.3 Geometric Reconstruction

Reference-free geometry.

\uppi⁴ retains the permutation-equivariant geometry formulation of π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)]: reordering the images only reorders the corresponding geometry and camera predictions. The geometry decoder uses no view-order or reference-view embeddings. Rather than prescribing a reference camera or world coordinate frame, we use relative camera supervision to let the network learn a consistent common frame from the relations between views.

Point and camera prediction.

For a pixel u, we parameterize its local point by a positive depth zᵢ(u) and a camera-local ray rᵢ(u):

rᵢ(u)=\beginbmatrixrᵢˣ(u)&rᵢʸ(u)&1\endbmatrix^⊤, Pᵢ⁽⁰⁾(u)=zᵢ(u)rᵢ(u).

(2)

The ray is not unit-normalized, and zᵢ denotes camera-axis depth. A within-image readout feeds a convolutional upsampling head that predicts (rᵢˣ,rᵢʸ,\logzᵢ), yielding the coarse pointmap Pᵢ⁽⁰⁾. A shallow camera decoder regresses per-image poses, and a context-attending decoder predicts one log-scale ℓₘ per input set, giving m=\expℓₘ.

Sparse geometry refinement.

Following MoGe3 [(Kong et al., 2026)], a sparse 3D U-Net refines each view’s geometry in ray/log-depth coordinates, conditioned at its bottleneck on projected geometry-decoder features. Starting from the coarse depth zᵢ⁽⁰⁾, it updates log-depth while retaining the predicted rays:

\logzᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾=\logzᵢ⁽ˢ⁾+Δᵢ⁽ˢ⁾, Pᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾=zᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾rᵢ, s=0,…,S-1.

(3)

The final pointmap is Pᵢ=Pᵢ^(S).

Metric reconstruction and confidence.

The predicted camera poses and scale place the local geometry in a common metric frame:

Xᵢᵐᵉᵗʳⁱᶜ(u)=m(RᵢPᵢ(u)+tᵢ).

(4)

No ground-truth alignment is required at inference. A convolutional confidence branch shares early local-point features and estimates the reliability of the final refined geometry.

3.4 Motion Estimation and 3D Tracking

Image-space tracking.

The tracking head predicts correspondences from the geometry-conditioned motion features. We adapt CoWTracker’s iterative warping head [(Lai et al., 2026)] for arbitrary-view tracking by removing its temporal positional embeddings. The head takes upsampled motion features concatenated with 128-channel features from a shallow convolutional RGB encoder, and retains zero-displacement initialization and visibility/confidence outputs, without assuming a chronological ordering of the input views. Outputs satisfy the query anchor U_q→q(u)=u. Sparse query tracks are obtained by sampling the dense correspondence maps.

Lifting to 3D.

Rather than directly regressing 3D motion vectors or endpoint coordinates, we obtain world-space tracks by sampling the target-view metric pointmap from Eq. (4):

Y_q→i(u)=Xᵢᵐᵉᵗʳⁱᶜ (U_q→i(u)).

(5)

This keeps correspondence regression in image space while placing every visible 3D track point on the reconstructed target-view surface.

Moving-object masks.

Inspired by the foreground–background mask head of GMOS [(Xie et al., 2026a)], our query-independent mask head fuses the motion readout with features from a frozen SAM 2 image encoder [(Ravi et al., 2024)]. A convolutional decoder with higher-resolution SAM skip features predicts image-aligned moving-object probabilities. Labels describe sequence-level object motion: an object that moves within the annotated sequence remains positive in each frame where it appears, including during pauses.

3.5 Training Objectives

We train the geometry branch before training the geometry-conditioned motion branch. Geometry and metric prediction are optimized jointly once metric-scale estimation is introduced. For motion training, the pretrained geometry model remains frozen, and we optimize the motion decoder and prediction heads. The geometry confidence branch is trained separately with geometry fixed. Data mixtures and the progressive training schedule are described in Section 4.6.

Geometric supervision.

We normalize both predicted and ground-truth local points by their respective sequence-wide mean valid point norms. For predictions, the factor s(P)=⟨∥Pᵢ(u)∥₂⟩_i,u gives normalized points P̃ᵢ=Pᵢ/s(P). This same factor normalizes camera translations: it remains differentiable on the local-point path but is detached on the camera-translation path, as discussed in Section 6.6 and Eq. (11). Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], we then fit an additional positive alignment scale a using depth-weighted L₁ alignment, without a shift, using the robust, optimal, and efficient (ROE) solver of MoGe [(Wang et al., 2025e)]. Camera translations are multiplied by the same fitted alignment scale. Hats below denote scale-aligned predictions, with P̂ᵢ=aP̃ᵢ, and stars denote normalized ground truth.

After this alignment, the local-point objective is a depth-weighted coordinate error:

L_local=⟨wᵢ(u)∥P̂ᵢ(u)-Pᵢ^*(u)∥₁⟩_i,u,

(6)

where ⟨·⟩ averages over valid pixels and wᵢ is a bounded inverse-depth weight. Following SurGe [(Knaebel et al., 2026)], point-gradient matching (PGM) additionally compares depth-normalized spatial point differences using a Euclidean penalty, excluding invalid neighborhoods and ground-truth depth discontinuities.

Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], L_cam combines rotation-angle and L₁ translation errors over all distinct camera pairs. Relative poses are T̂_j←i=T̂ⱼ⁻¹T̂ᵢ. This supervision constrains inter-view geometry without fixing an absolute world frame. We also supervise points transformed into another camera’s coordinates. Defining Q̂_j←i=T̂_j←iP̂ᵢ and Q_j←i^*=T_j←i^*Pᵢ^*, the relative-point objective is

Lᵣₑₗ=⟨wᵢ(u)∥Q̂_j←i(u)-Q_j←i^*(u)∥₁⟩_(i,j),u.

(7)

This jointly constrains points and poses wherever the original pixel has valid geometry, irrespective of visibility in image j. On overlapping views, point-to-point consistency compares Q̂_j←i with the predicted point sampled at its ground-truth correspondence in image j. Relative PGM compares spatial point differences in a common camera frame. Both use cross-view visibility masks, unlike Eq. (7).

Following the released Pi3X implementation [(Wang et al., 2025b)], the ray loss L_ray supervises the predicted camera-local ray coordinates (rᵢˣ,rᵢʸ) in Eq. (2) against targets computed from ground-truth camera intrinsics. It is the mean absolute coordinate error over pixels with valid ray targets and does not depend on metric scale.

Inspired by the matching proxy in VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)], we use a row-wise softmax objective to supervise patch matching. For a directed image pair (i,j), query–key descriptor similarities are normalized with a row-wise softmax over destination patches to give πᵢⱼ(b|a). The negative log-likelihood (NLL) is

L_match=-⟨\logπᵢⱼ (b^*(a)|a)⟩.

(8)

Here a indexes query patches and b^*(a) is the ground-truth destination patch. Only visible, in-bounds correspondences contribute.

Following the separate scale-supervision strategy of MoGe2 [(Wang et al., 2025c)], we supervise the predicted metric scale against a ground-truth-derived target m^* using squared error in \log(1+m) space:

L_metric=⟨[\log(1+m)-\log(1+m^*)]²⟩.

(9)

The average is over sequences with native metric ground truth, and m^* is treated as constant during optimization.

Let Lₚₜₛ denote the weighted sum of the local-point, point-gradient, relative-point, cross-view point-consistency, and relative-PGM terms. The geometry objective supervises the coarse prediction and averages point losses across refinement rounds:

\beginsplitL_geom=&Lₚₜₛ (P⁽⁰⁾)+1/S∑ₛ₌₁^SLₚₜₛ (P⁽ˢ⁾) &+λ_camL_cam+λ_rayL_ray+λ_matchL_match+λ_metricL_metric.\endsplit

(10)

Both coarse and refined predictions receive point supervision, with refined losses also propagating through the predicted rays and cameras. Refinement supervision uses reliable dense geometry; direct camera, ray, and matching terms are evaluated once on the coarse branch. Each term uses only available annotations.

Geometry confidence.

Following Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2025b)], we freeze the geometry model and train the confidence branch with continuous targets that reflect reconstruction quality, rather than binary valid/invalid labels. The branch estimates per-pixel reliability of the final refined geometry.

Motion supervision.

We follow CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)] for tracking supervision, combining iterative coordinate regression with binary cross-entropy for visibility and tracking confidence. We additionally supervise static-region correspondences using ground-truth geometry and cameras. Moving-object masks are supervised with binary cross-entropy on annotated moving/static pixels, ignoring unknown labels. We optimize the motion decoder and prediction heads with geometry and the SAM image encoder frozen, applying each loss only where annotations are available.

4 Training Data and Curation

4.1 Data Sources and Mixture

We combine public datasets with scene-level synthetic renderings, curated Internet videos, and game-based supervision to broaden scene and camera coverage and provide complementary supervision for dynamic scenes. Motion training uses point trajectories, static geometric correspondences, and real-video masks. Table 1 summarizes the data sources and sampling probabilities in the final geometry and motion training stages.

4.2 Scene-Level Synthetic Data

Scene assets.

We curate approximately 10,000 scene-level 3D assets from Funes [(FUNES.WORLD, n.d.)] and Sketchfab [(Sketchfab, n.d.)] for synthetic multi-view rendering. These assets include architectural environments and other large-scale scenes, rather than only isolated objects. They support exterior observations and, where the geometry permits, interior views. Our goal is to broaden the diversity of scene layouts and camera configurations represented during training, rather than simply increase the number of rendered images.

Candidate views and validation.

We generate candidate cameras across positions, elevations, viewing directions, and distances using surrounding-space and surface-guided proposals. Exterior views capture both overall structure and local detail; interior views require sufficient free space and renderable surfaces. Visibility and RGB-D quality checks reject invalid cameras and degenerate observations, including views dominated by open mesh backsides.

Coverage-aware views and connected chains.

We select views by their incremental coverage of observable surfaces, balancing surface area with spatial and orientation diversity so that large planar regions do not dominate. Depth-consistent reprojections then define a view-overlap graph, from which we sample connected view chains. Neighboring views retain reliable common geometry, while distant views may have little or no direct overlap. This design decouples global scene coverage from local cross-view connectivity: views need not all overlap a single reference or follow a smooth temporal trajectory.

Camera-distribution coverage.

We construct independent natural and counterbias view sets. Natural sets use modest camera roll and shared intrinsics, whereas counterbias sets explicitly cover broader roll angles and vary focal length across views. The two sets use independently sampled camera positions, diversifying viewpoints and occlusions rather than forming view-by-view pairs. Both sets follow the same geometric-validity principles. RGB and depth are rendered with the assigned camera parameters, followed by final quality validation and depth-based overlap computation. Figure 4 illustrates the two camera-sampling regimes on a scene-level asset.

4.3 Sequence-Consistent Projection Augmentation

Geometry training data are dominated by pinhole or rectified imagery, limiting the camera projections encountered during training. To counter this bias, we apply sequence-consistent lens and crop-and-resize augmentation. Each sequence receives an identity, barrel, blended equidistant (fisheye-like), or pincushion mapping with probability 40%, 35%, 20%, or 5%, respectively. Lens parameters and the final crop and resize are shared across frames.

The augmentation transforms RGB and prepared geometric supervision together. For each output pixel, an inverse warp identifies a source location whose calibrated ray and camera-axis depth define the new point target, without approximating the distorted view with a new pinhole camera. Correspondence targets, visibility, and cross-view overlap are recomputed under the same mapping, while camera poses and scene scale remain unchanged. We crop to valid source-image support and resize, reducing distortion strength when necessary to satisfy a zoom limit.

These transforms diversify image-to-ray mappings within the observed field of view, complementing genuine camera diversity.

4.4 Foreground-Suppressed Supervision from Internet Videos

Foreground-dominated reconstruction failures.

Large moving foregrounds in Internet videos can disrupt geometry reconstruction, especially in egocentric sequences where the foreground dominates the view. These failures motivate suppressing the foreground and completing the video before geometry inference.

Foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling.

We first mask moving foreground regions and complete the video using generative video inpainting [(Team Wan et al., 2025; Alibaba PAI, n.d.)]. An earlier geometry-only checkpoint of \uppi⁴ then infers a background reconstruction from the completed video. We filter the resulting point clouds using the moving-object masks and retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels. This avoids placing pseudo-labels directly on inpainted content. We pair these pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames, rather than the completed video, for subsequent geometry training. Figure 5 summarizes this pipeline.

4.5 GameRealm: Game-Based Geometry and Motion

To broaden supervision for joint geometry and motion learning in dynamic environments, we use GameRealm[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)], a game-based dataset developed jointly with collaborators. It provides engine-native geometric and motion annotations, including posed multi-view RGB-D observations for reconstruction and persistent 2D/3D point trajectories for tracking. Covering diverse scenes, viewpoints, characters, and interactions, these data complement our static scene renderings and real-video pseudo-labels with supervision for both spatial reconstruction and temporal correspondence.

4.6 Training Protocol

\uppi⁴ is trained progressively on 64 NVIDIA A800 GPUs, with approximately 300,000 optimizer updates across geometry-training stages. Starting from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder, early stages train the image encoder, looped decoder, and point, camera, and matching heads. Later stages introduce sparse 3D refinement and metric-scale estimation while expanding the data mixture with curated Internet videos. Successive stages inherit the preceding model weights.

Separately, motion training spans approximately 100,000 updates, including joint optimization of the motion decoder, tracking head, and moving-object mask head, with geometry frozen throughout. The SAM image encoder remains frozen during mask training, and the confidence head is trained separately with geometry fixed.

Optimization uses AdamW and BF16 mixed precision. In the final geometry stage, images have a long side of 512 pixels and varying aspect ratios, with at most 64 images per GPU and no gradient accumulation. For sets of K views (Section 6.2), each GPU packs ⌊64/K⌋ independent examples per batch. The base and encoder learning rates are 1.5×10⁻⁵ and 2×10⁻⁶, respectively, with cosine decay. All update counts denote optimizer steps under weighted data sampling, rather than dataset epochs.

5 Evaluation

5.1 Geometry Evaluation

Standard benchmarks.

Table 2 compares \uppi⁴ with nine baselines across 16 settings spanning depth [(Butler et al., 2012; Palazzolo et al., 2019; Geiger et al., 2012; Silberman et al., 2012)], pose and trajectory [(Zhou et al., 2018; Reizenstein et al., 2021; Sturm et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2017a)], and multiview reconstruction [(Shotton et al., 2013; Azinović et al., 2022; Jensen et al., 2014; Schöps et al., 2017)]. Monocular depth uses per-frame median-scale alignment, whereas video depth uses sequence-level scale-and-shift alignment. The full geometry-and-motion system has approximately 0.5B parameters, including frozen modules; Table 2 instead reports 343M loaded parameters for the geometry model used in this comparison.

\uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank (3.00, compared with 3.10 for Pi3X), with the best panel-average ranks for video depth, pose/trajectory, and multiview reconstruction. It attains the lowest Sintel video-depth AbsRel and the lowest reconstruction accuracy error on DTU and ETH3D. Metric-scale performance is evaluated separately in Table 2.

Long-sequence reconstruction.

We evaluate long-sequence reconstruction on six Oxford Spires [(Tao et al., 2025)] routes with 361–800 frames per route, using the ATE, RRE, RTE, CD, and F1 metric definitions of Scal3R [(Xie et al., 2026b)]. All input images of each route are processed in a single forward pass.

As shown in Table 3, \uppi⁴ achieves the best reported results on all five metrics, reducing ATE by 47.2% and CD by 24.1% relative to DVLT.

5.2 2D and 3D Tracking

We follow Track4World [(Lu et al., 2026)] on its released subsets of Aria Digital Twin (ADT) [(Pan et al., 2023)], PointOdyssey [(Zheng et al., 2023)], and Panoptic Studio (PStudio) [(Joo et al., 2015)], with ADT and PStudio annotations from TAPVid-3D [(Koppula et al., 2024)]. These datasets cover 298 clip–horizon cases, equally averaging 16- and 50-frame settings. We compare with Track4World, MoSE3 [(Cheng et al., 2026)], ARROW [(Fradlin et al., 2026)], CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)], and TAPIP3D [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], reporting APD and AJ for 2D and world-space 3D tracking.

For the methods marked †, CoWTracker lifts its unchanged 2D tracks using predicted depth and cameras, retaining its original visibility; TAPIP3D tracks natively in 3D and projects to 2D. All 3D results use scale-and-shift alignment fitted to ground-truth-visible points; geometry confidence does not filter evaluated predictions.

GameRealm (Long)[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)] contains 45 clips from 15 source sequences in games unseen during motion training, with 256 consecutive native frames per clip. Scores average clips within source sequence, sequences within game, and games equally. Its 3D scoring uses alignment, median rescaling, and approximate metric units. \uppi⁴ leads Average 2D AJ and ranks second in the other three metrics (Table 4(a)).

5.3 Multiview Tracking

We evaluate RGB-only multiview tracking on 58 scene–rig cases: 10 DexYCB [(Chao et al., 2021)], 30 Kubric [(Greff et al., 2022)], and 18 Panoptic Studio [(Joo et al., 2015)], with four cameras and 24 synchronized timesteps. Each time–camera observation uses all registered queries and the same geometry sources as single-view tracking. 3D scoring uses scale-and-translation alignment followed by median rescaling; Kubric units are approximate. Scores average cases within each dataset.

As shown in Table 4(b), \uppi⁴ leads dataset-average 2D AJ and ranks second in 2D APD and both 3D metrics.

5.4 Moving-Object Segmentation

Following GMOS [(Xie et al., 2026a)], we evaluate binary moving-object segmentation on SegTrackv2, the FBMS test split, and YTVOS19-M using region similarity J, contour accuracy F, and their average J&F.

As shown in Table 5, \uppi⁴ achieves the best region similarity on SegTrackv2 and the second-highest mean J&F of 85.04.

5.5 Qualitative Results

Figures 1, 6, and 7 show reconstructed geometry and motion across scenes and visual styles. Figure 7 illustrates the geometric consistency of the lifted tracks. In the 64-frame example (second row), ARROW’s trajectories at later frames with cameras farther from the first-frame origin deviate visibly from the geometry reconstructed for the corresponding frames, whereas our lifted trajectories remain registered with the reconstructed surfaces. This observation is consistent with the error coupling that arises when independently regressed 3D endpoints are composed with camera estimates in a first-frame reference system.

6 Design Choices and Empirical Observations

We study the architectural and training choices underlying \uppi⁴ through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that inform our final design. For loss-based ablations, we use matched model-development configurations, and percentage changes refer to relative differences in validation loss unless otherwise stated.

6.1 Looped Transformers: Training Dynamics and Step Conditioning

Following DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)], we use a looped Transformer decoder with explicit loop-step conditioning. The looped and non-looped reconstruction models follow similar early training trajectories, but the looped model’s advantage emerges later in training and is more pronounced with step conditioning. Figure 8 shows the training and validation objectives of these decoder variants. A separate comparison within the looped architecture isolates the effect of conditioning: adding the step signal reduces local point loss by 2.8% and camera loss by 10.2% relative to the unconditioned baseline. These results support the use of step conditioning in our decoder.

6.2 Training View Counts and Memory Allocation

We allocate part of the training memory budget to larger joint-view contexts, rather than using it only to pack more independent short examples. Our training recipe spans single-image inputs, short view sets of 2–24 images, and long view sets of 32, 48, or 64 images. View counts are sampled stochastically: short view sets receive most of the probability mass, with additional mass assigned to single-image inputs and the long-view buckets. This mixture combines frequent small-context updates with regular exposure to larger sets of observations.

The view count refers to images from one scene or sequence, not the aggregate image count across independent examples in a batch. Including larger view sets gives the model direct training exposure to combining evidence across many observations, rather than relying exclusively on extrapolation from short inputs. This training choice complements weight sharing in the looped architecture. Figure 9 reports the measured training-memory footprint for input sets up to 64 views.

6.3 Encoder Layer Selection and Fine-Tuning

Layer selection.

UFM [(Zhang et al., 2025c, Appendix E)] shows that intermediate features from a frozen encoder can outperform its final-layer features for dense prediction. Our geometry ablations using DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] show a consistent trend. Jointly using layers 11 and 17 gives the best local point reconstruction and camera estimation among the combinations evaluated. This pair, also used in RoMa v2 [(Edstedt et al., 2025)], supplies the input to our multi-view decoder.

Freezing and learning rate.

Fine-tuning the encoder at 10⁻⁴ initially reduces the loss faster than freezing the encoder, but performs worse later in training. By contrast, fine-tuning at 10⁻⁵ reduces local point loss by 8.1% and camera loss by 4.5% relative to freezing. The comparison therefore depends on both learning rate and training duration. Our encoder remains trainable, with a lower learning rate than the decoder and prediction heads.

6.4 Output Factorization and Geometric Consistency

Local geometry and camera placement.

Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], we predict camera-local pointmaps and camera poses rather than directly regressing a global pointmap. Global point errors mix errors in local surface geometry with errors in its cross-view placement. Image evidence may constrain local surface structure even when the relative camera configuration remains uncertain. Separate local-point and camera supervision preserves this distinction, allowing local geometry to be learned without requiring global placement to be equally accurate.

Correspondence and 3D tracking.

Factorizing 3D tracking into image-space correspondence prediction and geometric lifting avoids asking the motion head to independently reproduce target-view geometry and camera placement when predicting 3D endpoints or displacements. For visible tracks, lifting enforces agreement with the target geometry at the predicted correspondence by construction; independently predicted 3D positions need not satisfy this constraint.
