一句话：几何分支 + 几何条件化的运动分支，把 4D 理解压进一个统一模型。

要点：

  • 输入很宽容：野外的、**未标定**的 RGB 观测——单张图、无序集合，或一段视频
  • 输出很全：稠密几何、相机位姿与**度量尺度**，多图输入下还给 2D/3D 点轨迹与**运动物体掩码**
  • 结构上是「几何分支 + 由几何条件化的运动分支」，其中运动分支预测图像空间的对应关系，从而实现 4D 一致的解

为什么值得看：引擎要消费「4D 场景」，最缺的就是「一份统一的、带度量尺度的表示」。把位姿、稠密度量、轨迹与运动掩码一次给全，等于把重建、跟踪与场景解析三件事合到同一个输出上——这对做 real-to-sim 或视频转场景的管线是直接可用的接口。

中文摘要：π⁴ 是一个面向 4D 场景感知的统一基础模型：从野外采集、未标定的 RGB 观测出发——可以是单张图像、一组无序图像，也可以是一段视频——同时恢复稠密几何、相机位姿与度量尺度，并在多图输入下给出 2D/3D 点轨迹以及运动物体的掩码。架构上它把几何分支与一个由几何条件化的运动分支耦合起来，运动分支预测图像空间的对应关系，从而得到 4D 一致的解。对需要把真实拍摄内容转成引擎可消费场景的管线而言，这种「一份带度量尺度的统一表示」恰好补上了位姿、稠密几何、轨迹与运动解析之间的缝隙。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

\uppi⁴: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion

Abstract

\uppi⁴ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild—a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence—it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, \uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters—less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at Pi4.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward models have established a powerful paradigm for reconstructing scenes directly from RGB observations [(Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b)]. More recently, this paradigm has been extended beyond scene reconstruction to encompass motion recovery [(Lu et al., 2026; Fradlin et al., 2026)]. A key question, however, is how well these capabilities generalize to in-the-wild observations, where scene content, camera configurations, temporal continuity, and the number of observations are unconstrained. Maintaining high-quality geometric reconstruction while robustly recovering motion from such diverse inputs remains a significant practical challenge.

To address this challenge, we present \uppi⁴, a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception from RGB observations. It handles single images, unordered image collections, and videos, recovering dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D and 3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. Across the geometry benchmarks in Table 2, \uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank among the compared methods, while delivering competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D tracking and moving-object segmentation (Figure 2). Despite this broad functionality, the model employs a shared backbone across these capabilities and contains approximately 0.5B parameters in total—less than half the size of most baselines. Beyond benchmark results, Figure 1 showcases joint geometry and motion reconstruction across diverse in-the-wild observations, including aerial footage, casual handheld recordings, driving and sports scenes, and stylized content. These reconstruction and tracking results are all produced in a single forward pass per scene. This combination of accuracy, efficiency, and generality is enabled by coordinated choices in model architecture, training, and data.

At the architectural level, the geometry network of \uppi⁴ retains the permutation-equivariant formulation of π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], treating all input views symmetrically without designating a reference view. Both the geometry and motion branches employ looped Transformer decoding [(Burzio et al., 2026)], which we adopt for its strong cross-benchmark performance and parameter efficiency. We choose loop weight sharing partly to reduce memory usage, freeing capacity for larger within-sequence contexts. Training stochastically samples view counts from single images, 2–24-view sets, and 32/48/64-view sets, with short contexts dominating the mixture. A sparse 3D refiner [(Kong et al., 2026)] further enhances local surface structure and geometric detail.

To incorporate motion estimation without compromising reconstruction, we freeze the geometry network and train a separate geometry-conditioned motion decoder. Direct 3D tracking couples correspondence estimation with geometry, camera placement, and scene scale in the regression target. We instead keep motion prediction in image space and delegate 3D reasoning to the reconstruction branch, composing the two analytically.

This yields a simple correspondence objective that is independent of scene scale, while placing every visible 3D track point on the reconstructed target-view surface. Geometry features also provide useful context for correspondence prediction.

Complementing these architectural and modeling choices, our data construction pipeline addresses gaps in scene and camera coverage, as well as the difficulty of obtaining geometric supervision for foreground-dominated videos. We render scene-level assets from Funes [(FUNES.WORLD, n.d.)] and Sketchfab [(Sketchfab, n.d.)], covering architectural environments and other large-scale scenes rather than isolated objects alone. Coverage-aware view selection and connected view sampling balance broad scene coverage with local cross-view matchability, while complementary natural and counterbias camera configurations expand the range of roll angles and focal lengths encountered during training. We further apply field-of-view and lens augmentation to diversify image-to-ray mappings beyond those induced by conventional pinhole or rectified imagery. For Internet videos dominated by moving foregrounds, we infer background geometry following foreground suppression and video inpainting. We retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels and pair the resulting pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames. GameRealm[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)], developed jointly with collaborators, further provides complementary engine-native geometry and persistent point trajectories as supervision for dynamic scenes.

Together, these architectural, data, and training choices enable coherent joint reconstruction and tracking from thousands of images in large-scale scenes despite a maximum training context of 64 views (Figure 1). We further examine the architecture and training strategy of \uppi⁴ through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that motivate these choices.

2 Related Work

2.1 Visual Geometry Reconstruction

Classical structure-from-motion (SfM) estimates cameras and sparse structure through image matching and bundle adjustment, while multi-view stereo (MVS) reconstructs dense surfaces from calibrated views. COLMAP exemplifies this modular pipeline [(Schönberger and Frahm, 2016; Schönberger et al., 2016)]. Learned MVS methods such as MVSNet [(Yao et al., 2018)] learn cost-volume regularization while retaining camera calibration as input. More recently, DUSt3R [(Wang et al., 2024a)] predicts pairwise pointmaps without supplied cameras, and MASt3R [(Leroy et al., 2024)] combines this 3D representation with learned matching descriptors, bridging reconstruction and correspondence estimation.

Feed-forward multi-view models increasingly estimate geometry and cameras jointly. VGGT [(Wang et al., 2025a)] predicts cameras, depth, pointmaps, and tracks from image sets, while π³ and its released Pi3X variant [(Wang et al., 2025b)] use permutation-equivariant modeling without a privileged input reference. MapAnything [(Keetha et al., 2026)] targets metric reconstruction with flexible geometric inputs, whereas Depth Anything 3 [(Lin et al., 2025)] uses depth and ray prediction across arbitrary views. VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)] incorporates matching supervision, and DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)] reuses Transformer blocks through looped decoding. Monocular models provide complementary components: MoGe2 [(Wang et al., 2025c)] separates metric-scale prediction from relative geometry, and MoGe3 [(Kong et al., 2026)] refines surface detail with sparse volumetric processing. Together, these methods provide complementary designs for joint camera–geometry estimation, reference-free reconstruction, metric prediction, and iterative decoding.

2.2 Image Correspondence and Point Tracking

Classical image tracking estimates motion through local appearance alignment, as in Lucas–Kanade [(Lucas and Kanade, 1981)]. Modern optical-flow models such as RAFT [(Teed and Deng, 2020)] learn dense two-frame correspondence, while TAPIR [(Doersch et al., 2023)] and CoTracker3 [(Karaev et al., 2024)] follow queried points over videos and estimate visibility. CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)] replaces correlation-volume lookup with iterative feature warping. Optical flow and query-based tracking thus provide dense or sparse image-space correspondences, typically within ordered video sequences.

2.3 Dynamic Scene Reconstruction and 4D Perception

Dynamic scene reconstruction extends geometry estimation to scenes with moving and deforming content. Shape of Motion [(Wang et al., 2025d)] reconstructs 4D scenes from monocular videos using compact SE(3) motion bases and data-driven geometric and tracking priors. MonST3R [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] instead adapts pointmap reconstruction to dynamic videos by estimating per-timestep geometry without an explicit motion representation. These approaches connect scene geometry with temporal variation, but differ in how motion is represented and how reconstruction and tracking are coupled.

Recent methods further extend tracking to 3D and connect it to scene reconstruction. D4RT [(Zhang et al., 2026)] and ARROW [(Fradlin et al., 2026)] use query-based decoding to recover point positions across time and reference cameras; ARROW additionally supports unordered and multiview observations. MoSE3 [(Cheng et al., 2026)] models dense world-space motion through per-pixel SE(3) transformations, while Track4World [(Lu et al., 2026)] combines dense correspondences, geometry, and camera estimation for world-centric tracking.

Moving-object segmentation provides a complementary object-level characterization of scene dynamics by identifying regions that undergo motion [(Tokmakov et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2026a)]. Across these directions, methods differ in their supported input configurations, output representations, and the degree to which geometry and motion are modeled jointly.

3 Method

\uppi⁴ combines geometric reconstruction and motion estimation within a single feed-forward model (Figure 3). A shared image encoder provides features to two task-specific looped Transformer decoders. The geometry branch predicts dense pointmaps, camera poses, and metric scale; a sparse 3D refiner then improves the predicted pointmaps. Conditioned on geometry features, the motion branch predicts image-space point tracks and moving-object masks. The predicted tracks are lifted to 3D using the reconstructed target-view geometry.

3.1 Task Formulation and Output Representations

Given N RGB images I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, with Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, \uppi⁴ predicts scene geometry and, for multi-image inputs, point tracks and moving-object masks. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are not required as inputs, and the images need not follow a chronological ordering.

The geometric outputs comprise a dense local pointmap Pᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, a camera-to-world pose Tᵢ=(Rᵢ,tᵢ)∈SE(3), and a confidence map cᵢ(u)∈[0,1] for each image, together with a positive scale m shared across the inputs. Points are expressed in their respective camera coordinates; the camera poses relate these local reconstructions through a common scene frame, and m converts the reconstruction to metric units.

For motion tracking, a query view q specifies the points to track. The model predicts dense image-space correspondences U_q→i:Ω_q→ℝ², together with visibility and tracking confidence. Here Ω_q is the query pixel grid, and U_q→i(u) gives the corresponding location in image i. World-space tracks Y_q→i(u) combine these correspondences with the reconstructed geometry. The model also predicts a moving-object mask for each image, independently of the query selection.

3.2 Shared Encoding and Looped Decoding

Image encoder.

A shared DINOv3 encoder [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] extracts per-image patch features for both branches. We combine intermediate and late-layer encoder features, project them into the decoder feature space, and append shared learnable register tokens. We examine the choice of encoder layers in Section 6.3.

Looped decoders.

Both the geometry and motion decoders alternate frame and cross-view attention [(Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b)]. Following Déjà View [(Burzio et al., 2026)], each decoder repeatedly applies the same pair of blocks, sharing their weights across its loop steps. The two decoders have independent parameters; weight sharing occurs within each branch, not between branches. Starting from encoded tokens Z⁰, the geometry decoder applies

Z^ℓ+1=B_cross (B_frame (Z^ℓ;τ_ℓ);τ_ℓ), ℓ=0,…,L-1,

(1)

where B_frame is a Transformer block that processes each image independently, and B_cross is a Transformer block that aggregates information across input views. The conditioning variable τ_ℓ encodes the normalized current and next loop positions. The geometry loop count L is sampled between 8 and 16 during training, whereas motion decoding uses a fixed M=8. Evaluation uses L=16 and M=8. Task heads read only the final decoder state.

Geometry-conditioned motion decoding.

The motion decoder starts from image tokens and adopts the same frame- and cross-view-attention block design as the geometry decoder, but with independent parameters. It follows the same looped attention structure, with additional geometry conditioning: spatial adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) conditions its attention and feed-forward sublayers on detached geometry features at the same view and patch, together with loop progress. A final within-image readout supplies the tracking and moving-object mask heads. The motion decoder uses no temporal positional embeddings.

3.3 Geometric Reconstruction

Reference-free geometry.

\uppi⁴ retains the permutation-equivariant geometry formulation of π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)]: reordering the images only reorders the corresponding geometry and camera predictions. The geometry decoder uses no view-order or reference-view embeddings. Rather than prescribing a reference camera or world coordinate frame, we use relative camera supervision to let the network learn a consistent common frame from the relations between views.

Point and camera prediction.

For a pixel u, we parameterize its local point by a positive depth zᵢ(u) and a camera-local ray rᵢ(u):

rᵢ(u)=\beginbmatrixrᵢˣ(u)&rᵢʸ(u)&1\endbmatrix^⊤, Pᵢ⁽⁰⁾(u)=zᵢ(u)rᵢ(u).

(2)

The ray is not unit-normalized, and zᵢ denotes camera-axis depth. A within-image readout feeds a convolutional upsampling head that predicts (rᵢˣ,rᵢʸ,\logzᵢ), yielding the coarse pointmap Pᵢ⁽⁰⁾. A shallow camera decoder regresses per-image poses, and a context-attending decoder predicts one log-scale ℓₘ per input set, giving m=\expℓₘ.

Sparse geometry refinement.

Following MoGe3 [(Kong et al., 2026)], a sparse 3D U-Net refines each view’s geometry in ray/log-depth coordinates, conditioned at its bottleneck on projected geometry-decoder features. Starting from the coarse depth zᵢ⁽⁰⁾, it updates log-depth while retaining the predicted rays:

\logzᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾=\logzᵢ⁽ˢ⁾+Δᵢ⁽ˢ⁾, Pᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾=zᵢ⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾rᵢ, s=0,…,S-1.

(3)

The final pointmap is Pᵢ=Pᵢ^(S).

Metric reconstruction and confidence.

The predicted camera poses and scale place the local geometry in a common metric frame:

Xᵢᵐᵉᵗʳⁱᶜ(u)=m(RᵢPᵢ(u)+tᵢ).

(4)

No ground-truth alignment is required at inference. A convolutional confidence branch shares early local-point features and estimates the reliability of the final refined geometry.

3.4 Motion Estimation and 3D Tracking

Image-space tracking.

The tracking head predicts correspondences from the geometry-conditioned motion features. We adapt CoWTracker’s iterative warping head [(Lai et al., 2026)] for arbitrary-view tracking by removing its temporal positional embeddings. The head takes upsampled motion features concatenated with 128-channel features from a shallow convolutional RGB encoder, and retains zero-displacement initialization and visibility/confidence outputs, without assuming a chronological ordering of the input views. Outputs satisfy the query anchor U_q→q(u)=u. Sparse query tracks are obtained by sampling the dense correspondence maps.

Lifting to 3D.

Rather than directly regressing 3D motion vectors or endpoint coordinates, we obtain world-space tracks by sampling the target-view metric pointmap from Eq. (4):

Y_q→i(u)=Xᵢᵐᵉᵗʳⁱᶜ (U_q→i(u)).

(5)

This keeps correspondence regression in image space while placing every visible 3D track point on the reconstructed target-view surface.

Moving-object masks.

Inspired by the foreground–background mask head of GMOS [(Xie et al., 2026a)], our query-independent mask head fuses the motion readout with features from a frozen SAM 2 image encoder [(Ravi et al., 2024)]. A convolutional decoder with higher-resolution SAM skip features predicts image-aligned moving-object probabilities. Labels describe sequence-level object motion: an object that moves within the annotated sequence remains positive in each frame where it appears, including during pauses.

3.5 Training Objectives

We train the geometry branch before training the geometry-conditioned motion branch. Geometry and metric prediction are optimized jointly once metric-scale estimation is introduced. For motion training, the pretrained geometry model remains frozen, and we optimize the motion decoder and prediction heads. The geometry confidence branch is trained separately with geometry fixed. Data mixtures and the progressive training schedule are described in Section 4.6.

Geometric supervision.

We normalize both predicted and ground-truth local points by their respective sequence-wide mean valid point norms. For predictions, the factor s(P)=⟨∥Pᵢ(u)∥₂⟩_i,u gives normalized points P̃ᵢ=Pᵢ/s(P). This same factor normalizes camera translations: it remains differentiable on the local-point path but is detached on the camera-translation path, as discussed in Section 6.6 and Eq. (11). Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], we then fit an additional positive alignment scale a using depth-weighted L₁ alignment, without a shift, using the robust, optimal, and efficient (ROE) solver of MoGe [(Wang et al., 2025e)]. Camera translations are multiplied by the same fitted alignment scale. Hats below denote scale-aligned predictions, with P̂ᵢ=aP̃ᵢ, and stars denote normalized ground truth.

After this alignment, the local-point objective is a depth-weighted coordinate error:

L_local=⟨wᵢ(u)∥P̂ᵢ(u)-Pᵢ^*(u)∥₁⟩_i,u,

(6)

where ⟨·⟩ averages over valid pixels and wᵢ is a bounded inverse-depth weight. Following SurGe [(Knaebel et al., 2026)], point-gradient matching (PGM) additionally compares depth-normalized spatial point differences using a Euclidean penalty, excluding invalid neighborhoods and ground-truth depth discontinuities.

Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], L_cam combines rotation-angle and L₁ translation errors over all distinct camera pairs. Relative poses are T̂_j←i=T̂ⱼ⁻¹T̂ᵢ. This supervision constrains inter-view geometry without fixing an absolute world frame. We also supervise points transformed into another camera’s coordinates. Defining Q̂_j←i=T̂_j←iP̂ᵢ and Q_j←i^*=T_j←i^*Pᵢ^*, the relative-point objective is

Lᵣₑₗ=⟨wᵢ(u)∥Q̂_j←i(u)-Q_j←i^*(u)∥₁⟩_(i,j),u.

(7)

This jointly constrains points and poses wherever the original pixel has valid geometry, irrespective of visibility in image j. On overlapping views, point-to-point consistency compares Q̂_j←i with the predicted point sampled at its ground-truth correspondence in image j. Relative PGM compares spatial point differences in a common camera frame. Both use cross-view visibility masks, unlike Eq. (7).

Following the released Pi3X implementation [(Wang et al., 2025b)], the ray loss L_ray supervises the predicted camera-local ray coordinates (rᵢˣ,rᵢʸ) in Eq. (2) against targets computed from ground-truth camera intrinsics. It is the mean absolute coordinate error over pixels with valid ray targets and does not depend on metric scale.

Inspired by the matching proxy in VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)], we use a row-wise softmax objective to supervise patch matching. For a directed image pair (i,j), query–key descriptor similarities are normalized with a row-wise softmax over destination patches to give πᵢⱼ(b|a). The negative log-likelihood (NLL) is

L_match=-⟨\logπᵢⱼ (b^*(a)|a)⟩.

(8)

Here a indexes query patches and b^*(a) is the ground-truth destination patch. Only visible, in-bounds correspondences contribute.

Following the separate scale-supervision strategy of MoGe2 [(Wang et al., 2025c)], we supervise the predicted metric scale against a ground-truth-derived target m^* using squared error in \log(1+m) space:

L_metric=⟨[\log(1+m)-\log(1+m^*)]²⟩.

(9)

The average is over sequences with native metric ground truth, and m^* is treated as constant during optimization.

Let Lₚₜₛ denote the weighted sum of the local-point, point-gradient, relative-point, cross-view point-consistency, and relative-PGM terms. The geometry objective supervises the coarse prediction and averages point losses across refinement rounds:

\beginsplitL_geom=&Lₚₜₛ (P⁽⁰⁾)+1/S∑ₛ₌₁^SLₚₜₛ (P⁽ˢ⁾) &+λ_camL_cam+λ_rayL_ray+λ_matchL_match+λ_metricL_metric.\endsplit

(10)

Both coarse and refined predictions receive point supervision, with refined losses also propagating through the predicted rays and cameras. Refinement supervision uses reliable dense geometry; direct camera, ray, and matching terms are evaluated once on the coarse branch. Each term uses only available annotations.

Geometry confidence.

Following Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2025b)], we freeze the geometry model and train the confidence branch with continuous targets that reflect reconstruction quality, rather than binary valid/invalid labels. The branch estimates per-pixel reliability of the final refined geometry.

Motion supervision.

We follow CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)] for tracking supervision, combining iterative coordinate regression with binary cross-entropy for visibility and tracking confidence. We additionally supervise static-region correspondences using ground-truth geometry and cameras. Moving-object masks are supervised with binary cross-entropy on annotated moving/static pixels, ignoring unknown labels. We optimize the motion decoder and prediction heads with geometry and the SAM image encoder frozen, applying each loss only where annotations are available.

4 Training Data and Curation

4.1 Data Sources and Mixture

We combine public datasets with scene-level synthetic renderings, curated Internet videos, and game-based supervision to broaden scene and camera coverage and provide complementary supervision for dynamic scenes. Motion training uses point trajectories, static geometric correspondences, and real-video masks. Table 1 summarizes the data sources and sampling probabilities in the final geometry and motion training stages.

4.2 Scene-Level Synthetic Data

Scene assets.

We curate approximately 10,000 scene-level 3D assets from Funes [(FUNES.WORLD, n.d.)] and Sketchfab [(Sketchfab, n.d.)] for synthetic multi-view rendering. These assets include architectural environments and other large-scale scenes, rather than only isolated objects. They support exterior observations and, where the geometry permits, interior views. Our goal is to broaden the diversity of scene layouts and camera configurations represented during training, rather than simply increase the number of rendered images.

Candidate views and validation.

We generate candidate cameras across positions, elevations, viewing directions, and distances using surrounding-space and surface-guided proposals. Exterior views capture both overall structure and local detail; interior views require sufficient free space and renderable surfaces. Visibility and RGB-D quality checks reject invalid cameras and degenerate observations, including views dominated by open mesh backsides.

Coverage-aware views and connected chains.

We select views by their incremental coverage of observable surfaces, balancing surface area with spatial and orientation diversity so that large planar regions do not dominate. Depth-consistent reprojections then define a view-overlap graph, from which we sample connected view chains. Neighboring views retain reliable common geometry, while distant views may have little or no direct overlap. This design decouples global scene coverage from local cross-view connectivity: views need not all overlap a single reference or follow a smooth temporal trajectory.

Camera-distribution coverage.

We construct independent natural and counterbias view sets. Natural sets use modest camera roll and shared intrinsics, whereas counterbias sets explicitly cover broader roll angles and vary focal length across views. The two sets use independently sampled camera positions, diversifying viewpoints and occlusions rather than forming view-by-view pairs. Both sets follow the same geometric-validity principles. RGB and depth are rendered with the assigned camera parameters, followed by final quality validation and depth-based overlap computation. Figure 4 illustrates the two camera-sampling regimes on a scene-level asset.

4.3 Sequence-Consistent Projection Augmentation

Geometry training data are dominated by pinhole or rectified imagery, limiting the camera projections encountered during training. To counter this bias, we apply sequence-consistent lens and crop-and-resize augmentation. Each sequence receives an identity, barrel, blended equidistant (fisheye-like), or pincushion mapping with probability 40%, 35%, 20%, or 5%, respectively. Lens parameters and the final crop and resize are shared across frames.

The augmentation transforms RGB and prepared geometric supervision together. For each output pixel, an inverse warp identifies a source location whose calibrated ray and camera-axis depth define the new point target, without approximating the distorted view with a new pinhole camera. Correspondence targets, visibility, and cross-view overlap are recomputed under the same mapping, while camera poses and scene scale remain unchanged. We crop to valid source-image support and resize, reducing distortion strength when necessary to satisfy a zoom limit.

These transforms diversify image-to-ray mappings within the observed field of view, complementing genuine camera diversity.

4.4 Foreground-Suppressed Supervision from Internet Videos

Foreground-dominated reconstruction failures.

Large moving foregrounds in Internet videos can disrupt geometry reconstruction, especially in egocentric sequences where the foreground dominates the view. These failures motivate suppressing the foreground and completing the video before geometry inference.

Foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling.

We first mask moving foreground regions and complete the video using generative video inpainting [(Team Wan et al., 2025; Alibaba PAI, n.d.)]. An earlier geometry-only checkpoint of \uppi⁴ then infers a background reconstruction from the completed video. We filter the resulting point clouds using the moving-object masks and retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels. This avoids placing pseudo-labels directly on inpainted content. We pair these pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames, rather than the completed video, for subsequent geometry training. Figure 5 summarizes this pipeline.

4.5 GameRealm: Game-Based Geometry and Motion

To broaden supervision for joint geometry and motion learning in dynamic environments, we use GameRealm[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)], a game-based dataset developed jointly with collaborators. It provides engine-native geometric and motion annotations, including posed multi-view RGB-D observations for reconstruction and persistent 2D/3D point trajectories for tracking. Covering diverse scenes, viewpoints, characters, and interactions, these data complement our static scene renderings and real-video pseudo-labels with supervision for both spatial reconstruction and temporal correspondence.

4.6 Training Protocol

\uppi⁴ is trained progressively on 64 NVIDIA A800 GPUs, with approximately 300,000 optimizer updates across geometry-training stages. Starting from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder, early stages train the image encoder, looped decoder, and point, camera, and matching heads. Later stages introduce sparse 3D refinement and metric-scale estimation while expanding the data mixture with curated Internet videos. Successive stages inherit the preceding model weights.

Separately, motion training spans approximately 100,000 updates, including joint optimization of the motion decoder, tracking head, and moving-object mask head, with geometry frozen throughout. The SAM image encoder remains frozen during mask training, and the confidence head is trained separately with geometry fixed.

Optimization uses AdamW and BF16 mixed precision. In the final geometry stage, images have a long side of 512 pixels and varying aspect ratios, with at most 64 images per GPU and no gradient accumulation. For sets of K views (Section 6.2), each GPU packs ⌊64/K⌋ independent examples per batch. The base and encoder learning rates are 1.5×10⁻⁵ and 2×10⁻⁶, respectively, with cosine decay. All update counts denote optimizer steps under weighted data sampling, rather than dataset epochs.

5 Evaluation

5.1 Geometry Evaluation

Standard benchmarks.

Table 2 compares \uppi⁴ with nine baselines across 16 settings spanning depth [(Butler et al., 2012; Palazzolo et al., 2019; Geiger et al., 2012; Silberman et al., 2012)], pose and trajectory [(Zhou et al., 2018; Reizenstein et al., 2021; Sturm et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2017a)], and multiview reconstruction [(Shotton et al., 2013; Azinović et al., 2022; Jensen et al., 2014; Schöps et al., 2017)]. Monocular depth uses per-frame median-scale alignment, whereas video depth uses sequence-level scale-and-shift alignment. The full geometry-and-motion system has approximately 0.5B parameters, including frozen modules; Table 2 instead reports 343M loaded parameters for the geometry model used in this comparison.

\uppi⁴ achieves the best overall average rank (3.00, compared with 3.10 for Pi3X), with the best panel-average ranks for video depth, pose/trajectory, and multiview reconstruction. It attains the lowest Sintel video-depth AbsRel and the lowest reconstruction accuracy error on DTU and ETH3D. Metric-scale performance is evaluated separately in Table 2.

Long-sequence reconstruction.

We evaluate long-sequence reconstruction on six Oxford Spires [(Tao et al., 2025)] routes with 361–800 frames per route, using the ATE, RRE, RTE, CD, and F1 metric definitions of Scal3R [(Xie et al., 2026b)]. All input images of each route are processed in a single forward pass.

As shown in Table 3, \uppi⁴ achieves the best reported results on all five metrics, reducing ATE by 47.2% and CD by 24.1% relative to DVLT.

5.2 2D and 3D Tracking

We follow Track4World [(Lu et al., 2026)] on its released subsets of Aria Digital Twin (ADT) [(Pan et al., 2023)], PointOdyssey [(Zheng et al., 2023)], and Panoptic Studio (PStudio) [(Joo et al., 2015)], with ADT and PStudio annotations from TAPVid-3D [(Koppula et al., 2024)]. These datasets cover 298 clip–horizon cases, equally averaging 16- and 50-frame settings. We compare with Track4World, MoSE3 [(Cheng et al., 2026)], ARROW [(Fradlin et al., 2026)], CoWTracker [(Lai et al., 2026)], and TAPIP3D [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], reporting APD and AJ for 2D and world-space 3D tracking.

For the methods marked †, CoWTracker lifts its unchanged 2D tracks using predicted depth and cameras, retaining its original visibility; TAPIP3D tracks natively in 3D and projects to 2D. All 3D results use scale-and-shift alignment fitted to ground-truth-visible points; geometry confidence does not filter evaluated predictions.

GameRealm (Long)[(GameRealm Contributors, 2026)] contains 45 clips from 15 source sequences in games unseen during motion training, with 256 consecutive native frames per clip. Scores average clips within source sequence, sequences within game, and games equally. Its 3D scoring uses alignment, median rescaling, and approximate metric units. \uppi⁴ leads Average 2D AJ and ranks second in the other three metrics (Table 4(a)).

5.3 Multiview Tracking

We evaluate RGB-only multiview tracking on 58 scene–rig cases: 10 DexYCB [(Chao et al., 2021)], 30 Kubric [(Greff et al., 2022)], and 18 Panoptic Studio [(Joo et al., 2015)], with four cameras and 24 synchronized timesteps. Each time–camera observation uses all registered queries and the same geometry sources as single-view tracking. 3D scoring uses scale-and-translation alignment followed by median rescaling; Kubric units are approximate. Scores average cases within each dataset.

As shown in Table 4(b), \uppi⁴ leads dataset-average 2D AJ and ranks second in 2D APD and both 3D metrics.

5.4 Moving-Object Segmentation

Following GMOS [(Xie et al., 2026a)], we evaluate binary moving-object segmentation on SegTrackv2, the FBMS test split, and YTVOS19-M using region similarity J, contour accuracy F, and their average J&F.

As shown in Table 5, \uppi⁴ achieves the best region similarity on SegTrackv2 and the second-highest mean J&F of 85.04.

5.5 Qualitative Results

Figures 1, 6, and 7 show reconstructed geometry and motion across scenes and visual styles. Figure 7 illustrates the geometric consistency of the lifted tracks. In the 64-frame example (second row), ARROW’s trajectories at later frames with cameras farther from the first-frame origin deviate visibly from the geometry reconstructed for the corresponding frames, whereas our lifted trajectories remain registered with the reconstructed surfaces. This observation is consistent with the error coupling that arises when independently regressed 3D endpoints are composed with camera estimates in a first-frame reference system.

6 Design Choices and Empirical Observations

We study the architectural and training choices underlying \uppi⁴ through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that inform our final design. For loss-based ablations, we use matched model-development configurations, and percentage changes refer to relative differences in validation loss unless otherwise stated.

6.1 Looped Transformers: Training Dynamics and Step Conditioning

Following DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)], we use a looped Transformer decoder with explicit loop-step conditioning. The looped and non-looped reconstruction models follow similar early training trajectories, but the looped model’s advantage emerges later in training and is more pronounced with step conditioning. Figure 8 shows the training and validation objectives of these decoder variants. A separate comparison within the looped architecture isolates the effect of conditioning: adding the step signal reduces local point loss by 2.8% and camera loss by 10.2% relative to the unconditioned baseline. These results support the use of step conditioning in our decoder.

6.2 Training View Counts and Memory Allocation

We allocate part of the training memory budget to larger joint-view contexts, rather than using it only to pack more independent short examples. Our training recipe spans single-image inputs, short view sets of 2–24 images, and long view sets of 32, 48, or 64 images. View counts are sampled stochastically: short view sets receive most of the probability mass, with additional mass assigned to single-image inputs and the long-view buckets. This mixture combines frequent small-context updates with regular exposure to larger sets of observations.

The view count refers to images from one scene or sequence, not the aggregate image count across independent examples in a batch. Including larger view sets gives the model direct training exposure to combining evidence across many observations, rather than relying exclusively on extrapolation from short inputs. This training choice complements weight sharing in the looped architecture. Figure 9 reports the measured training-memory footprint for input sets up to 64 views.

6.3 Encoder Layer Selection and Fine-Tuning

Layer selection.

UFM [(Zhang et al., 2025c, Appendix E)] shows that intermediate features from a frozen encoder can outperform its final-layer features for dense prediction. Our geometry ablations using DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] show a consistent trend. Jointly using layers 11 and 17 gives the best local point reconstruction and camera estimation among the combinations evaluated. This pair, also used in RoMa v2 [(Edstedt et al., 2025)], supplies the input to our multi-view decoder.

Freezing and learning rate.

Fine-tuning the encoder at 10⁻⁴ initially reduces the loss faster than freezing the encoder, but performs worse later in training. By contrast, fine-tuning at 10⁻⁵ reduces local point loss by 8.1% and camera loss by 4.5% relative to freezing. The comparison therefore depends on both learning rate and training duration. Our encoder remains trainable, with a lower learning rate than the decoder and prediction heads.

6.4 Output Factorization and Geometric Consistency

Local geometry and camera placement.

Following π³[(Wang et al., 2025b)], we predict camera-local pointmaps and camera poses rather than directly regressing a global pointmap. Global point errors mix errors in local surface geometry with errors in its cross-view placement. Image evidence may constrain local surface structure even when the relative camera configuration remains uncertain. Separate local-point and camera supervision preserves this distinction, allowing local geometry to be learned without requiring global placement to be equally accurate.

Correspondence and 3D tracking.

Factorizing 3D tracking into image-space correspondence prediction and geometric lifting avoids asking the motion head to independently reproduce target-view geometry and camera placement when predicting 3D endpoints or displacements. For visible tracks, lifting enforces agreement with the target geometry at the predicted correspondence by construction; independently predicted 3D positions need not satisfy this constraint.

item.title: 看过摸过的东西，转开就忘了：EPM 给世界模型加了一份「可执行的感知记忆」，还会随动作更新含义 ｜ Perception into Imagination: Executable Memory for World Models
item.description:
一句话：记忆不是静态快照——动作会改变这些记住的事实的含义。

要点：

  • 需求很具体：物理智能体必须在**可见性或接触丢失之后**，仍然用得上此前看到或摸到的东西
  • 难在语义会变：它们的动作会**改变这些被记住事实的含义**，所以记忆不能是静态快照
  • EPM（可执行感知记忆）是一个世界模型框架：在想象过程中，让**显式的感知状态**与神经潜动态并行推进，并用其不断演化的读出去支撑奖励预测、价值估计与策略学习

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」在智能体侧的版本：显式状态 + 神经动态并行。它对 AI NPC 的直接含义是——NPC 得有「记得住且会变」的世界认知，而不是每帧重新看一遍画面。

中文摘要：物理智能体必须在可见性或接触丢失之后，仍然能够使用此前看到或触摸到的东西；而这些被记住事实的含义又会随智能体的动作而改变，因此记忆不能是静态快照。这篇提出「可执行感知记忆」（EPM），一个世界模型框架：在想象过程中，让显式的感知状态与神经潜动态并行推进，并利用不断演化的读出结果去支撑奖励预测、价值估计与策略学习。换句话说，记忆不只是一份存档，而是一个参与决策、并随行动更新的可执行结构——这也正是「显式状态 + 神经动态」这一分工在智能体侧的体现。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Perception into Imagination:
Executable Memory for World Models

Abstract

Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze 13×13, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on 9×9 and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.

1 Introduction

A robot can lose sight of a landmark when it turns, or lose tactile contact with an object when it withdraws. What it previously perceived remains useful, but the implications change with its actions: the landmark acquires a new bearing, and the remembered contact a new relative position. For Physical AI, using perception therefore requires both preserving facts and reasoning about their consequences in possible futures.

World models provide a setting for this reasoning: they predict action consequences and train behaviors on imagined trajectories [17, 19, 18, 21, 23]. Recurrent states encode history, while spatial memories and maps maintain explicit structure [36, 8, 29]. A further question is how maintained facts enter the futures used for learning: their relations to the agent change along a rollout, and these changes must inform predicted rewards and values as well as actions.

We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM). A perceptual writer maintains explicit state during real interaction. At an imagination anchor, a local state is initialized from that history and advanced using candidate actions and predicted motion. Its read-out complements the neural latent state in reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning (Fig. 1). A remembered fact can thus affect both the action under consideration and the return target used to learn that action.

The learning interface connects this joint state to the signals that train behavior. In our DreamerV3 implementation, a transition-aligned read-out refers to the fact relevant to each reward, before the next observation writes new evidence or changes the goal. An additional open-loop loss trains the reward head on prior rollouts of recorded actions. Together, these inputs and objectives make remembered relations available when learning rewards from real transitions and predicting them in imagination.

EPM improves control over a policy/value-only memory interface on a common front end in Memory Maze 9×9 and 13×13, and in MiniWorld. At 13×13, it reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 for that interface and 14.18 for observation-only memory access. Controlled probes in both visual implementations show stronger reward anticipation at remembered, out-of-view arrivals. Comparisons with DreamerV3 and R2I establish the approach’s competitive context. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames test the same perception–memory–decision principle through complementary tasks.

We make three contributions. First, we formulate executable perceptual memory: explicit perceptual state that candidate actions advance alongside neural world-model dynamics, with its read-outs available throughout imagination. Second, we connect these read-outs to reward and actor–critic learning through transition-aligned reward inputs and open-loop supervision. Third, matched-information comparisons establish control gains and conditional component effects in two visual implementations, while symbolic and tactile tasks test complementary uses of persistent facts.

2 Related work

World models and learning through imagination.

World Models [17], PlaNet [19] and Dreamer [18, 20, 21] learn predictive representations for planning or imagined behavior learning. Value Prediction Networks [35], MuZero [42] and TD-MPC2 [23] emphasize reward and value predictions for control. Dreamer 4 [22], iVideoGPT [44], Navigation World Models [4], V-JEPA 2 [3] and Cosmos [1] extend predictive modeling toward video and physical interaction. Multi-step objectives shape latent dynamics and belief states [19, 14]; DreamSmooth studies reward prediction under sparse rewards [28]. EPM connects persistent perceptual facts to the predicted rewards and values used for learning.

Memory under partial observability.

Transformer policies [37], structured sequence models [15], S4WM [11] and R2I [40] strengthen neural memory. Long-context video models preserve past observations [39, 46, 45]; concurrent TT-MBRL encodes episode memory in model parameters at test time [6]. DIACRITIC studies recurrent memory sufficient to reproduce expert behavior [31]. Cognitive Mapping and Planning [16], Neural Map [36], Active Neural SLAM [8] and MemoNav [29] organize spatial history; Memoir retrieves history using imagined futures [47]. GTM-SM couples spatial memory to agent dynamics [12], and FloWM transforms latent memory with self-motion and object motion [32]. Concurrent ScanDreamer advances pose over a frozen map and analytically computes selected reward and termination signals [13]. EPM instead supplies executed fact read-outs to a learned reward model, using transition-aligned and open-loop training. Our comparisons hold the memory observation common and isolate how its read-outs enter imagination and learning.

Structured dynamics and grounded prediction.

Interaction Networks [5], SE3-Nets [7] and structured world models [27] exploit object and geometric structure. Code world models [10] and Programmable World Model [25] express transitions as executable structure. SearchWorld grounds search in spatial values [26]; DreamLedger uses execution outcomes to assess reliance on model predictions [30]. EPM specifies how perceptually maintained facts are executed and read by reward and behavior-learning interfaces.

Touch as persistent perceptual evidence.

Optical tactile sensors recover local geometry and contact information [48]. Tactile Gym [33], Taxim [43] and TacSL [2] support simulation and learning, while Tactile MNIST [41] supplies real observations for active perception. Visuo-tactile world models improve object permanence in predicted rollouts [24]. We study how tactile information persists beyond contact: explicit state advances along candidate motions, and compact sensory memory preserves content for later queries.

3 Executable perceptual memory

3.1 Persistent facts and action-dependent relations

Consider a partially observed process with observations oₜ, actions aₜ, rewards yₜ and an optional goal gₜ. We represent history by a neural state zₜ and explicit perceptual state mₜ. The latter stores quantities with defined persistence and update rules: landmark estimates, object-relative poses or observed card identities. At interaction time, their values are estimated from the agent’s observation stream. Privileged simulator state is not supplied to the policy.

Real interaction combines state propagation with a perceptual write:

mₜ=W (C(mₜ₋₁,δₜ),E(oₜ)), uₜ=R(mₜ,gₜ).

(1)

Here E extracts sensory evidence, δₜ is measured motion, C carries the stored state, and W incorporates new evidence. The query R gives a task-relevant read-out uₜ. A landmark may remain fixed in world coordinates while its bearing changes with the agent’s pose. This distinction lets the model preserve a fact while executing its consequences under movement.

3.2 Joint imagination

At a real anchor t, the posterior initializes z̃₀, and a projection of history initializes local state m̃₀=P(mₜ,gₜ). The policy acts on their joint read-out. Each imagined step advances both components:

ãₕ∼π_ψ(·|z̃ₕ,uₕ),(2)
z̃ₕ₊₁∼p_θ(·|z̃ₕ,ãₕ),
δ̂ₕ=G_θ(z̃ₕ,ãₕ),
m̃ₕ₊₁=F(m̃ₕ,δ̂ₕ,ãₕ), uₕ₊₁=R(m̃ₕ₊₁,gₜ).

The neural model learns dynamics from experience; the executable update applies candidate actions to selected history. The paths interact through policy actions and predicted motion. The neural transition is conditioned on the latent state and action.

In navigation, P extracts the current target’s relative geometry and age. Predicted translation and rotation advance this local relation; new observations and target switches are outside that short-rollout update. A shared motion head learns the subsequent odometry measurement from the pre-action neural feature and action with a squared-error objective. Motion predictions used by F are stopped-gradient. In the tactile instance, the carried quantity is object-relative pose; in Concentration, known identities constrain a simulator of the public rules. The framework specifies where executable structure enters, while each instance defines the structure it can propagate.

3.3 From imagined facts to learning signals

The navigation method supplies [z̃ₕ,uₕ] to both the reward head q_ω and actor–critic. Continuation c_θ reads neural features alone:

ŷₕ=q_ω(z̃ₕ,uₕ), ĉₕ=c_θ(z̃ₕ), v̂ₕ=v_ξ(z̃ₕ,uₕ).

(3)

Predicted rewards, continuation and bootstrapped values form the usual Dreamer returns. The explicit state therefore informs the learning target as well as the behavior being optimized. Policy, critic, slow critic and replay value computation all retain direct read-out access.

Aligning facts with rewards.

Reward yₜ₊₁ is produced by action aₜ. Its replay-side read-out must refer to that transition, before the new observation writes evidence or switches the target. We obtain it by advancing the preceding memory with measured motion:

ūₜ₊₁=R (F(P(mₜ,gₜ),δₜ₊₁,aₜ),gₜ).

(4)

The posterior reward loss pairs (zₜ₊₁,ūₜ₊₁) with yₜ₊₁. At episode starts and at the first replay-sequence position, the additional slots are zeroed. In imagination, the head instead uses the read-out advanced with predicted motion along the imagined trajectory.

Training rewards on open-loop futures.

From replay posterior anchors t∈S, we roll the prior along the recorded actions for H steps without further observations, and propagate the local memory in the same way. Let b_t,h indicate that no episode reset has occurred between the anchor and step h. The added loss is

L_\rmOL=(1)/(|S|)∑_t∈S(∑ₕ₌₁^Hb_t,h ℓ_ω(yₜ₊ₕ;sg[z̃ₕ,uₕ]))/(\max(1,∑ₕ₌₁^Hb_t,h)).

(5)

Here ℓ_ω is the backbone reward-prediction loss. We use H=15, anchors every four replay steps and weight 1. The stop-gradient boundary makes this term train only the reward head, leaving representation, dynamics and motion learning under their existing objectives. The posterior reward loss is retained; Appendix A illustrates both training paths.

Perceptual implementation.

A landmark detector and visual odometry maintain sparse target positions and agent pose. The read-out contains a known flag, sine/cosine bearing, log-distance and log-age. These perception networks are trained on separate calibration trajectories with simulator labels, then frozen; deployment uses images and actions. Memory Maze adds image-based heading correction, and MiniWorld models lateral motion. Every arm encodes and reconstructs the same memory observation and shares the same front end within an experiment. Appendix A details calibration, state updates and storage.

4 Experimental setup

Tasks and training.

The principal learned-control tests use multi-goal Memory Maze [38] at 9×9 and 13×13, and a MiniWorld [9]9×9 implementation with different rendering and kinematics. The DreamerV3-based agent uses the 12M-parameter configuration, 16 environments and a 2M-transition replay capacity. All policies train from scratch. Memory Maze endpoints are 1M interactions, with twelve initialization labels at 9×9 and six at 13×13; MiniWorld uses twelve initialization labels and a 2M endpoint. Each policy is evaluated on 48 common layout/target/spawn identities. Episode budgets are 1,000 actions for both 9×9 implementations and 3,000 for 13×13. Concentration, tactile simulation and real tactile frames test complementary stages of the framework (Sec. 6).

Six integration choices.

Table 1 names arms by their components. “Held” and “evolved” refer to direct read-outs during imagination. All arms have the same memory information in observation encoding, matched head dimensions and common initial parameters within a label. Zero-filled direct slots preserve parameter counts. The six-arm design is used at 9×9 and in MiniWorld; the 13×13 experiment trains the four non-held arms. “Evolved” supplies the evolving read-out to the policy and value only, without reward access or the open-loop loss.

Comparisons and inference.

The full-method contrast is EPM minus Evolved; reward access is EPM minus Evolved+OL; OL alone is Evolved+OL minus Evolved. The held arms measure reward access under holding. Return differences use paired two-sided 95% t intervals over initialization labels, with positive-label counts and sign-flip sensitivity analyses in the appendix. Each task is inferred separately; secondary contrasts are not multiplicity-adjusted. Budgets and primary endpoints are fixed before evaluation. Interaction budgets count policy training and exclude the shared offline perception calibration.

Reward-anticipation probes.

Every arm is tested on common histories from EPM and Evolved+OL policies, with equal source-policy weight. We compare visible targets (VIS) with remembered, out-of-view targets whose arrival is anticipated by explicit state (MEM and RA). RA is evaluated per model, so the retained event subsets can differ. Net reward anticipation A subtracts predicted mass in non-arrival windows from mass around first arrivals, weighting eligible horizon bins equally. It is not an accuracy or probability. The memory deficit is D=A_\rmVIS-A_\rmMEM∩RA; Appendix C gives the full definitions.

5 Perceptual history improves learning and control

5.1 The complete method improves control

On the larger 13×13 task, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 for the policy/value-only interface (Evolved) on the same front end. The gain is 7.00 [3.80, 10.21], positive on all six initialization labels. Against observation-only memory access, the gain is 16.19 [12.67, 19.72]: the same perceptual information is more useful when it participates directly in imagined prediction and learning. The 9×9 experiment independently gives 6.08 [4.46, 7.71] over Evolved, positive on all twelve labels.

The second visual implementation tests the learning design with different rendering and planar motion. In MiniWorld at 2M, EPM reaches 21.83 versus 18.09 for Evolved: +3.74 [2.51, 4.97], positive on all twelve labels. The complete method also exceeds observation-only access in each experiment. Figure 2 shows learning progress, and Table 2 gives endpoint returns and component effects.

5.2 What do the components contribute?

Reward access.

Under common open-loop training, EPM exceeds Evolved+OL by 5.51 [4.46, 6.57] on 9×9 and 11.39 [7.89, 14.89] on 13×13, positive on every label. In MiniWorld, this increment is 1.00 [-0.04, 2.03] at 2M and remains unresolved. Thus the complete method improves control across all three tasks, with the reward-access contribution established in both Memory Maze sizes.

Action-dependent evolution.

With common OL and no direct reward access, evolution improves return over holding by 2.51 [1.36, 3.66] on 9×9 and 2.31 [1.10, 3.52] in MiniWorld. Reward access under holding lowers return by 5.10 [3.86, 6.34] and 15.15 [12.36, 17.95], respectively; Held+R+OL reaches 3.37 in MiniWorld. Both reward-access arms use transition-aligned replay inputs; holding changes the rollout-side read-out. Access-by-evolution interactions are 10.61 and 16.15; the latter mainly reflects the held arm’s degradation. These controls distinguish executing remembered relations from repeatedly supplying an unchanged read-out.

Open-loop supervision.

Without direct reward access, OL gives +0.57 [-1.55, 2.70] on 9×9, -4.39 [-8.16, -0.61] on 13×13, and +2.74 [1.16, 4.33] in MiniWorld. The large 13×13 reward-access gain occurs where OL alone lowers return. Appendix B provides full contrast tables.

5.3 Remembered facts inform predicted rewards

For Memory Maze 9×9, reward access raises remembered-arrival anticipation from 0.154 to 0.587. The paired increment is 0.434 [0.376, 0.491], positive on 12/12 labels. Visible anticipation also increases, from 0.482 to 0.679; the memory deficit decreases from 0.329 to 0.092, a paired reduction of 0.237 [0.211, 0.264]. The larger increase on remembered arrivals narrows the deficit beyond the overall rise in anticipation.

In MiniWorld, remembered-arrival anticipation rises from 0.447 to 0.787: +0.341 [0.283, 0.398], again positive on 12/12 labels. Visible anticipation rises from 0.582 to 0.860, and the deficit falls by 0.063 [0.024, 0.102]. Across both visual implementations, the interface increases predicted reward at remembered arrivals and narrows the gap to visible arrivals, consistent with remembered facts reaching reward prediction.

5.4 Comparison with DreamerV3 and R2I

We compare with native DreamerV3 and R2I, and with R2I supplied with the same perception stream and maintained state (Table 3). A six-label experiment uses visual odometry without heading correction and a direct policy/value interface. It reaches 11.17 at 1M, versus 5.93 with memory accessed only through observation encoding: +5.24 [1.05, 9.43]. Appendix E gives all checkpoints. Table 3 separates this setting from the heading-corrected experiments.

This direct-interface agent has higher mean return than native DreamerV3 at 1M (2.90) and native R2I at 3M (6.74). R2I with the front end and maintained state reaches 9.36 at 3M; the training-seed difference from 11.17 is unresolved. With the shared heading-corrected front end, Evolved reaches 23.37 and EPM 30.37.

6 Remembered facts and physical interaction

The following instances test complementary stages: respecting facts during imagined training, carrying state through lost contact, and retaining real sensory content for later use.

6.1 Remembered facts improve imagined-policy training

ConcentrationHard [34] gives a discrete instance of the same question. A key–value memory stores observed card identities. During imagination, a simulator executes the public game rules while retaining those identities and sampling unknown cards. A matched control uses the same rules but resamples all identities. The policy is optimized entirely on imagined rollouts from public-observation prefixes, then deployed in the real game.

Retaining remembered facts yields deployed returns of 0.475, 0.367 and 0.490 over three training seeds, compared with 0.147, 0.181 and 0.027 when all identities are resampled. Real-environment training gives 0.541, 0.520 and 0.542 (256 evaluation episodes per policy). The supplied rule simulator differs from the neural navigation model, but the comparison isolates a shared methodological point: the futures used for training should respect the facts already acquired by the agent.

6.2 Tactile history supports future branches and recovery

In Tactile Gym 2.0 [33], an estimator writes object-relative state from tactile observations while contact is available. Kinematic updates carry this state after contact is lost and advance it along candidate actions. On twelve previously unexposed worlds, explicit evolution reduces pre-contact prediction error by 0.51 mm [0.28, 0.73] and raises agreement with the best executed branch from 0.02 to 0.64.

We next test recovery choices after a retreat and sideways excursion. A chooser evaluates 128 fixed open-loop paths using an evolved state and a fitted outcome model, then hands over to a feedback law at re-contact. On 48 new worlds with varying excursion lengths, it achieves 34.80 mm of progress per recovery window, versus 24.33 mm for a state-free command selected by excursion side. The primary difference is 10.47 [8.65, 12.29] mm, positive on 46/48 worlds. It also exceeds a held-action reference by 10.32 [8.64, 12.00] mm and a command table indexed by side and excursion length by 6.04 [4.43, 7.66] mm (Fig. 4).

A constant-start dead-reckoning reference reaches 35.46 mm; evolved minus this reference is -0.65 [-2.02, 0.71] mm and remains unresolved. The results support motion-carried state for candidate-path selection; this comparison does not isolate tactile initialization. Appendix I gives protocols, splits and additional comparisons.

6.3 Real tactile observations survive in compact memory

Real Tactile MNIST contains GelSight Mini images collected with a robot manipulator [41]. We encode contact frames and their positions into eight slots with 48 bytes of payload plus up to 9 bytes of validity and age metadata. A late query asks for digit identity or material at a held-out position. Evaluation uses 100 held-out objects; background subtraction uses a per-round offline background computed from all 256 touches. Figure 5 shows original training-set frames and the held-out query results.

After 32 touches, the byte memory achieves mean identity accuracy 0.417, compared with 0.187 without history and 0.152 with proprioception and the shared image-derived write gate; individual-seed values appear in Fig. 5. Removing content bytes returns accuracy to chance, and larger payloads improve retention. A 128-dimensional, non-quantized GRU reference reaches 0.485. For material queries, the byte memory exceeds this control on two of three seeds, with the third unresolved. Compact memory thus retains useful real sensory content.

7 Discussion and conclusion

Executable perceptual memory gives world models a way to use facts that outlast their immediate observation. Perception maintains the facts, candidate actions advance their local consequences, and reward and behavior-learning interfaces use the resulting state. Control gains in two visual implementations and improved anticipation of remembered arrivals support this connection from perceptual history to imagined learning signals.

The component experiments identify where this connection matters. Action-dependent evolution improves on held read-outs, while open-loop supervision depends on the task and the information supplied to the reward head. The current local navigation state follows a remembered target during short rollouts. Extending it to anticipated observations, target changes and richer contact transitions is a natural direction for the framework.

The symbolic and tactile instances show complementary uses of the same principle: known facts constrain imagined-policy training, carried state supports recovery choices, and compact memory preserves real sensory content. These results motivate world models for Physical AI in which perceptual history remains available as actionable state throughout imagination and learning.

（参考文献见原文。）

disable

Appendix A Implementation and memory accounting

EPM couples explicit perceptual state to neural imagination, reward prediction and actor–critic learning. Its navigation comparisons share the perception front end across all arms. An additional policy/value-only comparison uses visual odometry without heading correction, identified separately below and in Table 3. This appendix specifies the state updates, learning objectives, evaluation protocols and complete results for the reported comparisons.

Real-state update and local projection.

The writer uses a calibrated detector and visual odometry to maintain seen landmarks and the estimated agent pose. A target query returns a known flag, cosine and sine of relative bearing, log-distance, and log-age. Unknown targets gate the geometric slots. The imagination initializer recovers a target vector from this query, starts the local position and yaw at zero, and carries the query age. It does not initialize an entire map rollout. For local position pₕ, yaw ψₕ and target vector v, a predicted translation and rotation produce

pₕ₊₁=pₕ+Rot(ψₕ)d̂ₕ,(6)
ψₕ₊₁=ψₕ+ω̂ₕ,(7)
v^\rmrelₕ₊₁=Rot(-ψₕ₊₁)(v-pₕ₊₁).(8)

The known flag is retained, age advances, and bearing/distance are read from v^\rmrel. The neural model continues to handle dynamics not represented by this local state. The motion head predicts displacement and yaw change from the pre-action latent feature and candidate action; its supervision is the subsequent measured motion.

Perception calibration.

The detector, odometry and heading networks are fitted offline using simulator-derived labels on calibration trajectories, and frozen before policy training. At deployment they read images and actions. Memory Maze’s six-color detector uses pooled 9×9, 11×11 and 13×13 calibration data, with a visibility half-angle of 0.75 radians; odometry is trained on pooled 9×9, 11×11 and 13×13 calibration walks. The heading network learns (\cos4θ,\sin4θ) from a single 64×64 frame, exploiting axis-aligned walls. It uses 87,000 training frames and 15,000 validation frames from separate 9×9 calibration episodes, with 30 epochs, batch size 256 and Adam at initial learning rate 10⁻³ with cosine decay. After integrating odometry, the writer corrects yaw to the predicted heading on the nearest 90^∘ branch. No heading correction is applied inside imagination, where no images are available. MiniWorld uses a separately calibrated detector and a three-output odometry network for forward, lateral and angular displacement, trained on calibration layouts excluded from policy training and evaluation. It uses no heading correction. Each experiment shares these frozen networks across arms; the reported interaction budgets exclude this offline calibration.

Neural paths and parameter accounting.

Memory Maze uses a 31-value memory observation: six target slots, eighteen detector-stream slots, five read-out slots and two motion slots. MiniWorld adds lateral motion, giving 32 values and a three-output motion head. Every arm encodes and reconstructs the complete observation; absent direct channels are zero-filled. Reward receives five additional slots, continuation retains neural input, and actor, critic, slow critic and replay value consume their assigned read-outs. The trainable runtime groups contain 12,222,441 parameters for Memory Maze and 12,223,211 for MiniWorld, identical across arms within an implementation and excluding fixed perception networks. The five reward-input slots account for 1,280 weights, present in every arm. Batches contain 16 sequences of length 64, the training ratio is 32, the imagination horizon is 15, and the return horizon is 333. Gradients from the additional open-loop reward loss update only the reward head (Fig. 6).

Memory storage.

The sparse visual state’s serialized payload occupies 48 bytes. The neural recurrent state separately occupies 8,224 bytes (8,192 for deterministic float32 state and 32 stochastic indices), while visual odometry retains the previous 64×64×3 image, or 12,288 bytes. Network parameters and replay are additional storage components. The real-tactile memory contains 48 payload bytes and up to 9 bytes of validity and age bookkeeping.

Appendix B Control experiments and complete contrasts

Component design.

Table 1 defines arms by their direct policy/value access, direct reward access and open-loop reward loss. Every arm receives the same memory observation; holding and evolution refer to imagination. Both reward-access arms use transition-aligned replay inputs. The access-by-evolution interaction is measured under common OL training. Reward access without OL is not a tested cell.

Training runs and evaluation checkpoints.

Memory Maze 9×9 uses twelve initialization labels and 13×13 uses six, each evaluated at 250k, 500k and the 1M endpoint. MiniWorld uses twelve labels, evaluated at 1M and its 2M endpoint. Each return averages 48 fixed layout/target/spawn identities. Tables 4–6 give all pre-specified contrasts, paired 95% t intervals, counts of positive labels and exact two-sided sign-flip sensitivity analyses; Table 7 gives label-level returns. The reward-access contrast is the designated primary analysis at 9×9; the remaining contrasts are pre-specified secondary analyses. Inference is separate for each experiment; shared arms make contrasts dependent. The 13×13 experiment trains all four non-held arms from scratch. Label-level endpoint returns are indexed within each experiment.

MiniWorld endpoint.

MiniWorld’s reward-access difference is 2.18 [0.68, 3.68] at 1M and 1.00 [-0.04, 2.03] at the pre-specified 2M endpoint. At 2M, Evolved+OL minus Observation+OL is 0.09 [-0.84, 1.03], while Evolved+OL minus Held+OL is 2.31 [1.10, 3.52]. The pre-specified joint criterion, which requires EPM to exceed both Evolved+OL and Observation+OL with resolved intervals, is not met in MiniWorld because the first difference is unresolved; the difference from Observation+OL is 1.09 [0.02, 2.17]. The complete-method contrast against Evolved is a separate pre-specified comparison.

Appendix C Reward-anticipation evaluation

The evaluation filters each recorded episode with real observations and actions, then rolls the prior along recorded continuations for 15 steps. Predictions average four stochastic rollouts. Every tested arm reads common histories from the EPM and Evolved+OL source policies at the endpoint; estimates aggregate windows within episodes and give the two sources equal weight. VIS denotes a truly visible target at the anchor. MEM denotes a non-visible target that is known in memory, with bearing error at most 0.5 radians. A MEM event satisfies RA when the stepped read-out anticipates arrival: at the step before the first reward, its predicted distance is at most the task’s reach distance plus one forward step (0.2 cells). RA uses each tested model’s predicted motion, so MEM-and-RA subsets can differ across arms even on the same histories. The paired contrasts compare conditional anticipation scores, not pointwise errors on identical events. Simulator truth defines diagnostic strata and is not policy input. Later rewards after a target switch are excluded from the first-arrival contrast.

For a first reward at horizon index k, event mass sums predicted reward at k-1 through k+1. Non-arrival mass is the predicted horizon total scaled to three steps. Their difference is net anticipation A. Eligible horizon bins (1–5, 6–10, 11–15) have at least five distinct events in VIS and the compared memory set and receive equal weight. The assessability rule requires twenty distinct VIS and twenty MEM-and-RA events per cell; all twelve labels are assessable in each experiment, with no exclusions. A can exceed one and is neither a probability nor an accuracy. Table 8 gives all-arm levels; the pre-specified paired contrast is EPM minus Evolved+OL for A_\rmMEM∩RA. Secondary differences in A_\rmVIS are 0.196 [0.148, 0.244] in Memory Maze and 0.278 [0.215, 0.340] in MiniWorld. The corresponding increases in the per-label ratio A_\rmMEM∩RA/A_\rmVIS are 0.547 [0.495, 0.599] and 0.146 [0.097, 0.195]. Ratios accompany absolute levels rather than replacing them.

Appendix D MiniWorld implementation

The MiniWorld task uses the maze layout generator, target identities and action budget of the navigation protocol, with its own renderer and wall-sliding kinematics. Each environment maintains an independent scene display list. Planar odometry includes forward, lateral and angular displacement. All arms use independent training runs from scratch, matched initialization within each label, and the same 1,000-action episode budget.

Appendix E Policy/value-only memory interface

This comparison uses six initialization labels, common initial weights and identical parameter counts across the evolved, held and observation-only arms. Visual odometry without heading correction supplies the same memory observations to all arms; direct read-outs enter policy and value heads, and reward training uses posterior neural features. Evaluation pairs the same 48 maze identities across arms and masking modes. Tables 9–11 give all checkpoints and per-label outcomes. Paired t intervals and sign-flip sensitivity analyses use training labels as the unit. The primary sequence tests evolved against observation-only at 500k, then 1M; other contrasts are secondary and unadjusted.

Masking removes the target read-out from the observation vector and its direct path while retaining the remaining observation history and neural state. At 1M, the evolved arm’s additional masking loss over observation-only is positive under both the paired t interval and sign-flip analysis. Its dependence contrast against held remains unresolved by the t interval (Table 10).

Appendix F Alternative state updates

Advancing age versus geometry.

A clock-only comparison, on the front end without heading correction, increments memory age during imagination while holding bearing and distance at the anchor. Table 12 reports evolved, held and clock-only arms at all three budgets on six initialization labels and 48 common evaluation mazes. At 1M, evolved geometry exceeds clock-only on all six labels. The evolved–held difference is positive on five labels, with a seed-level bootstrap interval crossing zero. Thus this comparison distinguishes spatial updates from merely advancing the clock, while the main six-arm experiments evaluate evolution under the reward-learning design.
