一句话：记忆不是静态快照——动作会改变这些记住的事实的含义。

要点：

  • 需求很具体：物理智能体必须在**可见性或接触丢失之后**，仍然用得上此前看到或摸到的东西
  • 难在语义会变：它们的动作会**改变这些被记住事实的含义**，所以记忆不能是静态快照
  • EPM（可执行感知记忆）是一个世界模型框架：在想象过程中，让**显式的感知状态**与神经潜动态并行推进，并用其不断演化的读出去支撑奖励预测、价值估计与策略学习

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」在智能体侧的版本：显式状态 + 神经动态并行。它对 AI NPC 的直接含义是——NPC 得有「记得住且会变」的世界认知，而不是每帧重新看一遍画面。

中文摘要：物理智能体必须在可见性或接触丢失之后，仍然能够使用此前看到或触摸到的东西；而这些被记住事实的含义又会随智能体的动作而改变，因此记忆不能是静态快照。这篇提出「可执行感知记忆」（EPM），一个世界模型框架：在想象过程中，让显式的感知状态与神经潜动态并行推进，并利用不断演化的读出结果去支撑奖励预测、价值估计与策略学习。换句话说，记忆不只是一份存档，而是一个参与决策、并随行动更新的可执行结构——这也正是「显式状态 + 神经动态」这一分工在智能体侧的体现。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Perception into Imagination:
Executable Memory for World Models

Abstract

Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze 13×13, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on 9×9 and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.

1 Introduction

A robot can lose sight of a landmark when it turns, or lose tactile contact with an object when it withdraws. What it previously perceived remains useful, but the implications change with its actions: the landmark acquires a new bearing, and the remembered contact a new relative position. For Physical AI, using perception therefore requires both preserving facts and reasoning about their consequences in possible futures.

World models provide a setting for this reasoning: they predict action consequences and train behaviors on imagined trajectories [17, 19, 18, 21, 23]. Recurrent states encode history, while spatial memories and maps maintain explicit structure [36, 8, 29]. A further question is how maintained facts enter the futures used for learning: their relations to the agent change along a rollout, and these changes must inform predicted rewards and values as well as actions.

We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM). A perceptual writer maintains explicit state during real interaction. At an imagination anchor, a local state is initialized from that history and advanced using candidate actions and predicted motion. Its read-out complements the neural latent state in reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning (Fig. 1). A remembered fact can thus affect both the action under consideration and the return target used to learn that action.

The learning interface connects this joint state to the signals that train behavior. In our DreamerV3 implementation, a transition-aligned read-out refers to the fact relevant to each reward, before the next observation writes new evidence or changes the goal. An additional open-loop loss trains the reward head on prior rollouts of recorded actions. Together, these inputs and objectives make remembered relations available when learning rewards from real transitions and predicting them in imagination.

EPM improves control over a policy/value-only memory interface on a common front end in Memory Maze 9×9 and 13×13, and in MiniWorld. At 13×13, it reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 for that interface and 14.18 for observation-only memory access. Controlled probes in both visual implementations show stronger reward anticipation at remembered, out-of-view arrivals. Comparisons with DreamerV3 and R2I establish the approach’s competitive context. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames test the same perception–memory–decision principle through complementary tasks.

We make three contributions. First, we formulate executable perceptual memory: explicit perceptual state that candidate actions advance alongside neural world-model dynamics, with its read-outs available throughout imagination. Second, we connect these read-outs to reward and actor–critic learning through transition-aligned reward inputs and open-loop supervision. Third, matched-information comparisons establish control gains and conditional component effects in two visual implementations, while symbolic and tactile tasks test complementary uses of persistent facts.

2 Related work

World models and learning through imagination.

World Models [17], PlaNet [19] and Dreamer [18, 20, 21] learn predictive representations for planning or imagined behavior learning. Value Prediction Networks [35], MuZero [42] and TD-MPC2 [23] emphasize reward and value predictions for control. Dreamer 4 [22], iVideoGPT [44], Navigation World Models [4], V-JEPA 2 [3] and Cosmos [1] extend predictive modeling toward video and physical interaction. Multi-step objectives shape latent dynamics and belief states [19, 14]; DreamSmooth studies reward prediction under sparse rewards [28]. EPM connects persistent perceptual facts to the predicted rewards and values used for learning.

Memory under partial observability.

Transformer policies [37], structured sequence models [15], S4WM [11] and R2I [40] strengthen neural memory. Long-context video models preserve past observations [39, 46, 45]; concurrent TT-MBRL encodes episode memory in model parameters at test time [6]. DIACRITIC studies recurrent memory sufficient to reproduce expert behavior [31]. Cognitive Mapping and Planning [16], Neural Map [36], Active Neural SLAM [8] and MemoNav [29] organize spatial history; Memoir retrieves history using imagined futures [47]. GTM-SM couples spatial memory to agent dynamics [12], and FloWM transforms latent memory with self-motion and object motion [32]. Concurrent ScanDreamer advances pose over a frozen map and analytically computes selected reward and termination signals [13]. EPM instead supplies executed fact read-outs to a learned reward model, using transition-aligned and open-loop training. Our comparisons hold the memory observation common and isolate how its read-outs enter imagination and learning.

Structured dynamics and grounded prediction.

Interaction Networks [5], SE3-Nets [7] and structured world models [27] exploit object and geometric structure. Code world models [10] and Programmable World Model [25] express transitions as executable structure. SearchWorld grounds search in spatial values [26]; DreamLedger uses execution outcomes to assess reliance on model predictions [30]. EPM specifies how perceptually maintained facts are executed and read by reward and behavior-learning interfaces.

Touch as persistent perceptual evidence.

Optical tactile sensors recover local geometry and contact information [48]. Tactile Gym [33], Taxim [43] and TacSL [2] support simulation and learning, while Tactile MNIST [41] supplies real observations for active perception. Visuo-tactile world models improve object permanence in predicted rollouts [24]. We study how tactile information persists beyond contact: explicit state advances along candidate motions, and compact sensory memory preserves content for later queries.

3 Executable perceptual memory

3.1 Persistent facts and action-dependent relations

Consider a partially observed process with observations oₜ, actions aₜ, rewards yₜ and an optional goal gₜ. We represent history by a neural state zₜ and explicit perceptual state mₜ. The latter stores quantities with defined persistence and update rules: landmark estimates, object-relative poses or observed card identities. At interaction time, their values are estimated from the agent’s observation stream. Privileged simulator state is not supplied to the policy.

Real interaction combines state propagation with a perceptual write:

mₜ=W (C(mₜ₋₁,δₜ),E(oₜ)), uₜ=R(mₜ,gₜ).

(1)

Here E extracts sensory evidence, δₜ is measured motion, C carries the stored state, and W incorporates new evidence. The query R gives a task-relevant read-out uₜ. A landmark may remain fixed in world coordinates while its bearing changes with the agent’s pose. This distinction lets the model preserve a fact while executing its consequences under movement.

3.2 Joint imagination

At a real anchor t, the posterior initializes z̃₀, and a projection of history initializes local state m̃₀=P(mₜ,gₜ). The policy acts on their joint read-out. Each imagined step advances both components:

ãₕ∼π_ψ(·|z̃ₕ,uₕ),(2)
z̃ₕ₊₁∼p_θ(·|z̃ₕ,ãₕ),
δ̂ₕ=G_θ(z̃ₕ,ãₕ),
m̃ₕ₊₁=F(m̃ₕ,δ̂ₕ,ãₕ), uₕ₊₁=R(m̃ₕ₊₁,gₜ).

The neural model learns dynamics from experience; the executable update applies candidate actions to selected history. The paths interact through policy actions and predicted motion. The neural transition is conditioned on the latent state and action.

In navigation, P extracts the current target’s relative geometry and age. Predicted translation and rotation advance this local relation; new observations and target switches are outside that short-rollout update. A shared motion head learns the subsequent odometry measurement from the pre-action neural feature and action with a squared-error objective. Motion predictions used by F are stopped-gradient. In the tactile instance, the carried quantity is object-relative pose; in Concentration, known identities constrain a simulator of the public rules. The framework specifies where executable structure enters, while each instance defines the structure it can propagate.

3.3 From imagined facts to learning signals

The navigation method supplies [z̃ₕ,uₕ] to both the reward head q_ω and actor–critic. Continuation c_θ reads neural features alone:

ŷₕ=q_ω(z̃ₕ,uₕ), ĉₕ=c_θ(z̃ₕ), v̂ₕ=v_ξ(z̃ₕ,uₕ).

(3)

Predicted rewards, continuation and bootstrapped values form the usual Dreamer returns. The explicit state therefore informs the learning target as well as the behavior being optimized. Policy, critic, slow critic and replay value computation all retain direct read-out access.

Aligning facts with rewards.

Reward yₜ₊₁ is produced by action aₜ. Its replay-side read-out must refer to that transition, before the new observation writes evidence or switches the target. We obtain it by advancing the preceding memory with measured motion:

ūₜ₊₁=R (F(P(mₜ,gₜ),δₜ₊₁,aₜ),gₜ).

(4)

The posterior reward loss pairs (zₜ₊₁,ūₜ₊₁) with yₜ₊₁. At episode starts and at the first replay-sequence position, the additional slots are zeroed. In imagination, the head instead uses the read-out advanced with predicted motion along the imagined trajectory.

Training rewards on open-loop futures.

From replay posterior anchors t∈S, we roll the prior along the recorded actions for H steps without further observations, and propagate the local memory in the same way. Let b_t,h indicate that no episode reset has occurred between the anchor and step h. The added loss is

L_\rmOL=(1)/(|S|)∑_t∈S(∑ₕ₌₁^Hb_t,h ℓ_ω(yₜ₊ₕ;sg[z̃ₕ,uₕ]))/(\max(1,∑ₕ₌₁^Hb_t,h)).

(5)

Here ℓ_ω is the backbone reward-prediction loss. We use H=15, anchors every four replay steps and weight 1. The stop-gradient boundary makes this term train only the reward head, leaving representation, dynamics and motion learning under their existing objectives. The posterior reward loss is retained; Appendix A illustrates both training paths.

Perceptual implementation.

A landmark detector and visual odometry maintain sparse target positions and agent pose. The read-out contains a known flag, sine/cosine bearing, log-distance and log-age. These perception networks are trained on separate calibration trajectories with simulator labels, then frozen; deployment uses images and actions. Memory Maze adds image-based heading correction, and MiniWorld models lateral motion. Every arm encodes and reconstructs the same memory observation and shares the same front end within an experiment. Appendix A details calibration, state updates and storage.

4 Experimental setup

Tasks and training.

The principal learned-control tests use multi-goal Memory Maze [38] at 9×9 and 13×13, and a MiniWorld [9]9×9 implementation with different rendering and kinematics. The DreamerV3-based agent uses the 12M-parameter configuration, 16 environments and a 2M-transition replay capacity. All policies train from scratch. Memory Maze endpoints are 1M interactions, with twelve initialization labels at 9×9 and six at 13×13; MiniWorld uses twelve initialization labels and a 2M endpoint. Each policy is evaluated on 48 common layout/target/spawn identities. Episode budgets are 1,000 actions for both 9×9 implementations and 3,000 for 13×13. Concentration, tactile simulation and real tactile frames test complementary stages of the framework (Sec. 6).

Six integration choices.

Table 1 names arms by their components. “Held” and “evolved” refer to direct read-outs during imagination. All arms have the same memory information in observation encoding, matched head dimensions and common initial parameters within a label. Zero-filled direct slots preserve parameter counts. The six-arm design is used at 9×9 and in MiniWorld; the 13×13 experiment trains the four non-held arms. “Evolved” supplies the evolving read-out to the policy and value only, without reward access or the open-loop loss.

Comparisons and inference.

The full-method contrast is EPM minus Evolved; reward access is EPM minus Evolved+OL; OL alone is Evolved+OL minus Evolved. The held arms measure reward access under holding. Return differences use paired two-sided 95% t intervals over initialization labels, with positive-label counts and sign-flip sensitivity analyses in the appendix. Each task is inferred separately; secondary contrasts are not multiplicity-adjusted. Budgets and primary endpoints are fixed before evaluation. Interaction budgets count policy training and exclude the shared offline perception calibration.

Reward-anticipation probes.

Every arm is tested on common histories from EPM and Evolved+OL policies, with equal source-policy weight. We compare visible targets (VIS) with remembered, out-of-view targets whose arrival is anticipated by explicit state (MEM and RA). RA is evaluated per model, so the retained event subsets can differ. Net reward anticipation A subtracts predicted mass in non-arrival windows from mass around first arrivals, weighting eligible horizon bins equally. It is not an accuracy or probability. The memory deficit is D=A_\rmVIS-A_\rmMEM∩RA; Appendix C gives the full definitions.

5 Perceptual history improves learning and control

5.1 The complete method improves control

On the larger 13×13 task, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 for the policy/value-only interface (Evolved) on the same front end. The gain is 7.00 [3.80, 10.21], positive on all six initialization labels. Against observation-only memory access, the gain is 16.19 [12.67, 19.72]: the same perceptual information is more useful when it participates directly in imagined prediction and learning. The 9×9 experiment independently gives 6.08 [4.46, 7.71] over Evolved, positive on all twelve labels.

The second visual implementation tests the learning design with different rendering and planar motion. In MiniWorld at 2M, EPM reaches 21.83 versus 18.09 for Evolved: +3.74 [2.51, 4.97], positive on all twelve labels. The complete method also exceeds observation-only access in each experiment. Figure 2 shows learning progress, and Table 2 gives endpoint returns and component effects.

5.2 What do the components contribute?

Reward access.

Under common open-loop training, EPM exceeds Evolved+OL by 5.51 [4.46, 6.57] on 9×9 and 11.39 [7.89, 14.89] on 13×13, positive on every label. In MiniWorld, this increment is 1.00 [-0.04, 2.03] at 2M and remains unresolved. Thus the complete method improves control across all three tasks, with the reward-access contribution established in both Memory Maze sizes.

Action-dependent evolution.

With common OL and no direct reward access, evolution improves return over holding by 2.51 [1.36, 3.66] on 9×9 and 2.31 [1.10, 3.52] in MiniWorld. Reward access under holding lowers return by 5.10 [3.86, 6.34] and 15.15 [12.36, 17.95], respectively; Held+R+OL reaches 3.37 in MiniWorld. Both reward-access arms use transition-aligned replay inputs; holding changes the rollout-side read-out. Access-by-evolution interactions are 10.61 and 16.15; the latter mainly reflects the held arm’s degradation. These controls distinguish executing remembered relations from repeatedly supplying an unchanged read-out.

Open-loop supervision.

Without direct reward access, OL gives +0.57 [-1.55, 2.70] on 9×9, -4.39 [-8.16, -0.61] on 13×13, and +2.74 [1.16, 4.33] in MiniWorld. The large 13×13 reward-access gain occurs where OL alone lowers return. Appendix B provides full contrast tables.

5.3 Remembered facts inform predicted rewards

For Memory Maze 9×9, reward access raises remembered-arrival anticipation from 0.154 to 0.587. The paired increment is 0.434 [0.376, 0.491], positive on 12/12 labels. Visible anticipation also increases, from 0.482 to 0.679; the memory deficit decreases from 0.329 to 0.092, a paired reduction of 0.237 [0.211, 0.264]. The larger increase on remembered arrivals narrows the deficit beyond the overall rise in anticipation.

In MiniWorld, remembered-arrival anticipation rises from 0.447 to 0.787: +0.341 [0.283, 0.398], again positive on 12/12 labels. Visible anticipation rises from 0.582 to 0.860, and the deficit falls by 0.063 [0.024, 0.102]. Across both visual implementations, the interface increases predicted reward at remembered arrivals and narrows the gap to visible arrivals, consistent with remembered facts reaching reward prediction.

5.4 Comparison with DreamerV3 and R2I

We compare with native DreamerV3 and R2I, and with R2I supplied with the same perception stream and maintained state (Table 3). A six-label experiment uses visual odometry without heading correction and a direct policy/value interface. It reaches 11.17 at 1M, versus 5.93 with memory accessed only through observation encoding: +5.24 [1.05, 9.43]. Appendix E gives all checkpoints. Table 3 separates this setting from the heading-corrected experiments.

This direct-interface agent has higher mean return than native DreamerV3 at 1M (2.90) and native R2I at 3M (6.74). R2I with the front end and maintained state reaches 9.36 at 3M; the training-seed difference from 11.17 is unresolved. With the shared heading-corrected front end, Evolved reaches 23.37 and EPM 30.37.

6 Remembered facts and physical interaction

The following instances test complementary stages: respecting facts during imagined training, carrying state through lost contact, and retaining real sensory content for later use.

6.1 Remembered facts improve imagined-policy training

ConcentrationHard [34] gives a discrete instance of the same question. A key–value memory stores observed card identities. During imagination, a simulator executes the public game rules while retaining those identities and sampling unknown cards. A matched control uses the same rules but resamples all identities. The policy is optimized entirely on imagined rollouts from public-observation prefixes, then deployed in the real game.

Retaining remembered facts yields deployed returns of 0.475, 0.367 and 0.490 over three training seeds, compared with 0.147, 0.181 and 0.027 when all identities are resampled. Real-environment training gives 0.541, 0.520 and 0.542 (256 evaluation episodes per policy). The supplied rule simulator differs from the neural navigation model, but the comparison isolates a shared methodological point: the futures used for training should respect the facts already acquired by the agent.

6.2 Tactile history supports future branches and recovery

In Tactile Gym 2.0 [33], an estimator writes object-relative state from tactile observations while contact is available. Kinematic updates carry this state after contact is lost and advance it along candidate actions. On twelve previously unexposed worlds, explicit evolution reduces pre-contact prediction error by 0.51 mm [0.28, 0.73] and raises agreement with the best executed branch from 0.02 to 0.64.

We next test recovery choices after a retreat and sideways excursion. A chooser evaluates 128 fixed open-loop paths using an evolved state and a fitted outcome model, then hands over to a feedback law at re-contact. On 48 new worlds with varying excursion lengths, it achieves 34.80 mm of progress per recovery window, versus 24.33 mm for a state-free command selected by excursion side. The primary difference is 10.47 [8.65, 12.29] mm, positive on 46/48 worlds. It also exceeds a held-action reference by 10.32 [8.64, 12.00] mm and a command table indexed by side and excursion length by 6.04 [4.43, 7.66] mm (Fig. 4).

A constant-start dead-reckoning reference reaches 35.46 mm; evolved minus this reference is -0.65 [-2.02, 0.71] mm and remains unresolved. The results support motion-carried state for candidate-path selection; this comparison does not isolate tactile initialization. Appendix I gives protocols, splits and additional comparisons.

6.3 Real tactile observations survive in compact memory

Real Tactile MNIST contains GelSight Mini images collected with a robot manipulator [41]. We encode contact frames and their positions into eight slots with 48 bytes of payload plus up to 9 bytes of validity and age metadata. A late query asks for digit identity or material at a held-out position. Evaluation uses 100 held-out objects; background subtraction uses a per-round offline background computed from all 256 touches. Figure 5 shows original training-set frames and the held-out query results.

After 32 touches, the byte memory achieves mean identity accuracy 0.417, compared with 0.187 without history and 0.152 with proprioception and the shared image-derived write gate; individual-seed values appear in Fig. 5. Removing content bytes returns accuracy to chance, and larger payloads improve retention. A 128-dimensional, non-quantized GRU reference reaches 0.485. For material queries, the byte memory exceeds this control on two of three seeds, with the third unresolved. Compact memory thus retains useful real sensory content.

7 Discussion and conclusion

Executable perceptual memory gives world models a way to use facts that outlast their immediate observation. Perception maintains the facts, candidate actions advance their local consequences, and reward and behavior-learning interfaces use the resulting state. Control gains in two visual implementations and improved anticipation of remembered arrivals support this connection from perceptual history to imagined learning signals.

The component experiments identify where this connection matters. Action-dependent evolution improves on held read-outs, while open-loop supervision depends on the task and the information supplied to the reward head. The current local navigation state follows a remembered target during short rollouts. Extending it to anticipated observations, target changes and richer contact transitions is a natural direction for the framework.

The symbolic and tactile instances show complementary uses of the same principle: known facts constrain imagined-policy training, carried state supports recovery choices, and compact memory preserves real sensory content. These results motivate world models for Physical AI in which perceptual history remains available as actionable state throughout imagination and learning.

（参考文献见原文。）

disable

Appendix A Implementation and memory accounting

EPM couples explicit perceptual state to neural imagination, reward prediction and actor–critic learning. Its navigation comparisons share the perception front end across all arms. An additional policy/value-only comparison uses visual odometry without heading correction, identified separately below and in Table 3. This appendix specifies the state updates, learning objectives, evaluation protocols and complete results for the reported comparisons.

Real-state update and local projection.

The writer uses a calibrated detector and visual odometry to maintain seen landmarks and the estimated agent pose. A target query returns a known flag, cosine and sine of relative bearing, log-distance, and log-age. Unknown targets gate the geometric slots. The imagination initializer recovers a target vector from this query, starts the local position and yaw at zero, and carries the query age. It does not initialize an entire map rollout. For local position pₕ, yaw ψₕ and target vector v, a predicted translation and rotation produce

pₕ₊₁=pₕ+Rot(ψₕ)d̂ₕ,(6)
ψₕ₊₁=ψₕ+ω̂ₕ,(7)
v^\rmrelₕ₊₁=Rot(-ψₕ₊₁)(v-pₕ₊₁).(8)

The known flag is retained, age advances, and bearing/distance are read from v^\rmrel. The neural model continues to handle dynamics not represented by this local state. The motion head predicts displacement and yaw change from the pre-action latent feature and candidate action; its supervision is the subsequent measured motion.

Perception calibration.

The detector, odometry and heading networks are fitted offline using simulator-derived labels on calibration trajectories, and frozen before policy training. At deployment they read images and actions. Memory Maze’s six-color detector uses pooled 9×9, 11×11 and 13×13 calibration data, with a visibility half-angle of 0.75 radians; odometry is trained on pooled 9×9, 11×11 and 13×13 calibration walks. The heading network learns (\cos4θ,\sin4θ) from a single 64×64 frame, exploiting axis-aligned walls. It uses 87,000 training frames and 15,000 validation frames from separate 9×9 calibration episodes, with 30 epochs, batch size 256 and Adam at initial learning rate 10⁻³ with cosine decay. After integrating odometry, the writer corrects yaw to the predicted heading on the nearest 90^∘ branch. No heading correction is applied inside imagination, where no images are available. MiniWorld uses a separately calibrated detector and a three-output odometry network for forward, lateral and angular displacement, trained on calibration layouts excluded from policy training and evaluation. It uses no heading correction. Each experiment shares these frozen networks across arms; the reported interaction budgets exclude this offline calibration.

Neural paths and parameter accounting.

Memory Maze uses a 31-value memory observation: six target slots, eighteen detector-stream slots, five read-out slots and two motion slots. MiniWorld adds lateral motion, giving 32 values and a three-output motion head. Every arm encodes and reconstructs the complete observation; absent direct channels are zero-filled. Reward receives five additional slots, continuation retains neural input, and actor, critic, slow critic and replay value consume their assigned read-outs. The trainable runtime groups contain 12,222,441 parameters for Memory Maze and 12,223,211 for MiniWorld, identical across arms within an implementation and excluding fixed perception networks. The five reward-input slots account for 1,280 weights, present in every arm. Batches contain 16 sequences of length 64, the training ratio is 32, the imagination horizon is 15, and the return horizon is 333. Gradients from the additional open-loop reward loss update only the reward head (Fig. 6).

Memory storage.

The sparse visual state’s serialized payload occupies 48 bytes. The neural recurrent state separately occupies 8,224 bytes (8,192 for deterministic float32 state and 32 stochastic indices), while visual odometry retains the previous 64×64×3 image, or 12,288 bytes. Network parameters and replay are additional storage components. The real-tactile memory contains 48 payload bytes and up to 9 bytes of validity and age bookkeeping.

Appendix B Control experiments and complete contrasts

Component design.

Table 1 defines arms by their direct policy/value access, direct reward access and open-loop reward loss. Every arm receives the same memory observation; holding and evolution refer to imagination. Both reward-access arms use transition-aligned replay inputs. The access-by-evolution interaction is measured under common OL training. Reward access without OL is not a tested cell.

Training runs and evaluation checkpoints.

Memory Maze 9×9 uses twelve initialization labels and 13×13 uses six, each evaluated at 250k, 500k and the 1M endpoint. MiniWorld uses twelve labels, evaluated at 1M and its 2M endpoint. Each return averages 48 fixed layout/target/spawn identities. Tables 4–6 give all pre-specified contrasts, paired 95% t intervals, counts of positive labels and exact two-sided sign-flip sensitivity analyses; Table 7 gives label-level returns. The reward-access contrast is the designated primary analysis at 9×9; the remaining contrasts are pre-specified secondary analyses. Inference is separate for each experiment; shared arms make contrasts dependent. The 13×13 experiment trains all four non-held arms from scratch. Label-level endpoint returns are indexed within each experiment.

MiniWorld endpoint.

MiniWorld’s reward-access difference is 2.18 [0.68, 3.68] at 1M and 1.00 [-0.04, 2.03] at the pre-specified 2M endpoint. At 2M, Evolved+OL minus Observation+OL is 0.09 [-0.84, 1.03], while Evolved+OL minus Held+OL is 2.31 [1.10, 3.52]. The pre-specified joint criterion, which requires EPM to exceed both Evolved+OL and Observation+OL with resolved intervals, is not met in MiniWorld because the first difference is unresolved; the difference from Observation+OL is 1.09 [0.02, 2.17]. The complete-method contrast against Evolved is a separate pre-specified comparison.

Appendix C Reward-anticipation evaluation

The evaluation filters each recorded episode with real observations and actions, then rolls the prior along recorded continuations for 15 steps. Predictions average four stochastic rollouts. Every tested arm reads common histories from the EPM and Evolved+OL source policies at the endpoint; estimates aggregate windows within episodes and give the two sources equal weight. VIS denotes a truly visible target at the anchor. MEM denotes a non-visible target that is known in memory, with bearing error at most 0.5 radians. A MEM event satisfies RA when the stepped read-out anticipates arrival: at the step before the first reward, its predicted distance is at most the task’s reach distance plus one forward step (0.2 cells). RA uses each tested model’s predicted motion, so MEM-and-RA subsets can differ across arms even on the same histories. The paired contrasts compare conditional anticipation scores, not pointwise errors on identical events. Simulator truth defines diagnostic strata and is not policy input. Later rewards after a target switch are excluded from the first-arrival contrast.

For a first reward at horizon index k, event mass sums predicted reward at k-1 through k+1. Non-arrival mass is the predicted horizon total scaled to three steps. Their difference is net anticipation A. Eligible horizon bins (1–5, 6–10, 11–15) have at least five distinct events in VIS and the compared memory set and receive equal weight. The assessability rule requires twenty distinct VIS and twenty MEM-and-RA events per cell; all twelve labels are assessable in each experiment, with no exclusions. A can exceed one and is neither a probability nor an accuracy. Table 8 gives all-arm levels; the pre-specified paired contrast is EPM minus Evolved+OL for A_\rmMEM∩RA. Secondary differences in A_\rmVIS are 0.196 [0.148, 0.244] in Memory Maze and 0.278 [0.215, 0.340] in MiniWorld. The corresponding increases in the per-label ratio A_\rmMEM∩RA/A_\rmVIS are 0.547 [0.495, 0.599] and 0.146 [0.097, 0.195]. Ratios accompany absolute levels rather than replacing them.

Appendix D MiniWorld implementation

The MiniWorld task uses the maze layout generator, target identities and action budget of the navigation protocol, with its own renderer and wall-sliding kinematics. Each environment maintains an independent scene display list. Planar odometry includes forward, lateral and angular displacement. All arms use independent training runs from scratch, matched initialization within each label, and the same 1,000-action episode budget.

Appendix E Policy/value-only memory interface

This comparison uses six initialization labels, common initial weights and identical parameter counts across the evolved, held and observation-only arms. Visual odometry without heading correction supplies the same memory observations to all arms; direct read-outs enter policy and value heads, and reward training uses posterior neural features. Evaluation pairs the same 48 maze identities across arms and masking modes. Tables 9–11 give all checkpoints and per-label outcomes. Paired t intervals and sign-flip sensitivity analyses use training labels as the unit. The primary sequence tests evolved against observation-only at 500k, then 1M; other contrasts are secondary and unadjusted.

Masking removes the target read-out from the observation vector and its direct path while retaining the remaining observation history and neural state. At 1M, the evolved arm’s additional masking loss over observation-only is positive under both the paired t interval and sign-flip analysis. Its dependence contrast against held remains unresolved by the t interval (Table 10).

Appendix F Alternative state updates

Advancing age versus geometry.

A clock-only comparison, on the front end without heading correction, increments memory age during imagination while holding bearing and distance at the anchor. Table 12 reports evolved, held and clock-only arms at all three budgets on six initialization labels and 48 common evaluation mazes. At 1M, evolved geometry exceeds clock-only on all six labels. The evolved–held difference is positive on five labels, with a seed-level bootstrap interval crossing zero. Thus this comparison distinguishes spatial updates from merely advancing the clock, while the main six-arm experiments evaluate evolution under the reward-learning design.

item.title: Genex 把「AI 做游戏」做成桌面 IDE：UE/Unity/Godot/Roblox/Three.js 都能进，插件市场可装 Blender/Tripo/Meshy ｜ genex-games/genex-desktop
item.description:
一句话：不锁引擎、不锁模型：多 agent 混用主 agent/worker/reviewer，还能全本地跑。

要点：

  • 覆盖面上不挑引擎：可在 **Unreal Engine、Unity、Godot、Roblox Studio 与 Three.js** 里构建；模型侧支持 Claude Code、Codex、Antigravity、Cursor、Grok、OpenCode、OpenRouter，也支持 **Ollama / LM Studio / llama.cpp 的本地模型**
  • 架构上是多 agent：主 agent、worker 与 reviewer 可以**混用不同模型**；内置游戏开发工具（Blender、Tripo、Meshy、Uthana、ElevenLabs、fal），并声称「一句话搞定服务端权威的多人联机」，可发布到 Web/Mac/Windows/Linux
  • 扩展靠插件：连 Blender 工具本身都是插件；`npm run plugin:new` 脚手架 + `plugin:doctor` 检查，可本地加载、从 GitHub 安装，或提交到 Marketplace 供所有 Genex 用户安装

Open-source desktop app for AI-native game dev. Agents set up the engine, build your game and play-test it by themselves.

Download Platform Download macOS (Apple Silicon) Genex.dmg Linux (x64) .deb, .rpm or .zip from the latest release. The .deb and .rpm add the Genex package repository, so your system's updates (Software Updater, apt, dnf) bring every later version Windows (x64), preview Genex-Setup.exe. Not signed yet: if Windows warns, choose More info, then Run anyway

Genex is early: expect rough edges, and tell us about them in issues.

What it does

→ Build in Unreal Engine, Unity, Godot, Roblox Studio or Three.js → Any AI: Claude Code, Codex (ChatGPT), Antigravity, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode and OpenRouter → Or local models: Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp → Multi-agent: mix models across the main agent, workers and reviewers → Built-in game dev tools: Blender, Tripo, Meshy, Uthana, ElevenLabs, fal → Server-authoritative multiplayer in one prompt → Publish to Web, Mac, Windows and Linux

Tip

Have a tool your games need? Build a plugin and put it in the Genex Marketplace for everyone.

Contributing

You need macOS on Apple Silicon, Git and Node 24.

git clone https://github.com/genex-games/genex-desktop.git cd genex-desktop nvm install && nvm use # Node 24, from .nvmrc npm ci npm run studio:dev -- start --profile first-run --fixture app-basics

The fixture runs the app with scripted models and sample games, so it needs no account. Read CONTRIBUTING.md before you open a pull request; coding agents start at AGENTS.md.

Build a plugin

Plugins give Genex's agents new tools: an asset generator, an engine bridge, a service your game talks to. The Blender and Genex tools that ship with the app are plugins too. From a Genex checkout:

npm run plugin:new -- my-plugin --out ~/studio-plugins # scaffold it from the example npm run plugin:doctor -- ~/studio-plugins/my-plugin # check it the way Genex will Try it: in the app, Plugins → Add → Load local plugin… and pick the folder. Share it: push it to a public GitHub repository and publish a release for each version. Anyone can install it from there with Plugins → Add → Install from GitHub…. List it: open a pull request to genex-plugins. A maintainer reviews it, and it appears in every Genex app's Marketplace.

The plugin guide covers tools, panels, settings and accounts.

Documentation Product overview: what the app does, with a page per feature Developer field guide: run commands and where data lives Release operations: packaging, signing and publishing a release Code signing policy

Free code signing provided by SignPath.io, certificate by SignPath Foundation.

Windows builds are signed only when GitHub Actions builds them from this repository's source, and a maintainer approves each release before it is signed. Until that signing is in place, Windows builds ship unsigned as a preview; every release lists each file's SHA-256 in SHA256SUMS.

Committers and reviewers: members of genex-games Approvers: owners of genex-games

Privacy: what Genex stores and sends is in its privacy policy; connected providers, plugins and services have their own policies.

item.title: 从成片反推可编辑的三维走位：MAVE 把影片镜头变成能改的 3D 布置，还带了 50 个镜头的评测集 ｜ MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
item.description:
一句话：手工从参考视频重建 3D 走位成本太高，创作者用不上，配对训练数据也做不出来。

要点：

  • 价值链条：动画化的 3D 走位（blockout）支撑预演，并为视频生成提供**结构条件**；但从参考视频手工重建它们代价很高
  • 后果是双向的：创作者用不上，而且**配对训练数据也做不出来**
  • 这篇同时给了评测与方桘：**MAVEBench**（50 个电影镜头、416 个关键帧，评相机运动、空间布局与角色站位）与 **MAVE**，一个视频到 3D 走位的重建方法

为什么值得看：走位（blockout）是影视与关卡设计里最通用的沟通媒介。把它从视频里自动反推出来且可编辑，等于把「参考片 → 可改的场景」这一步打通——这同时也是视频生成需要的结构条件，一举两得。

中文摘要：动画化的三维走位（blockout）既服务于预演，又能为视频生成提供结构条件，但要从参考视频手工重建它们代价极高，结果既让创作者难以使用，也使配对训练数据难以生产。这篇同时提供评测与方桘：MAVEBench 是一个包含 50 个电影镜头、416 个关键帧的基准，用于评估相机运动、空间布局与角色站位；MAVE 则是一个从视频重建可编辑三维走位的方法。把「参考片」自动转成「可改的场景」，既打开了创作者的工作流，也为视频生成补上了缺失的结构条件。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots

Abstract

Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5--41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only $0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout–video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available.111https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE

1 Introduction

An animated 3D blockout represents a shot using simple geometry, stand-in characters, and a camera. Its editable structure lets creators adjust camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking for previsualization [19]. Recent video generation methods use 3D layouts, scene geometry, and human motion as structural guidance [41, 4, 35, 13, 1, 42]. Rendering an editable blockout provides a practical way to translate scene-level edits into such guidance. This workflow faces two related bottlenecks. For creators, manually reconstructing a blockout from a reference video requires time and 3D production expertise [21, 15]. For model training, producing blockouts that match target videos is costly, limiting the scale of paired data [41, 4]. As shown in Fig.1, automatically reconstructing blockouts from existing videos can provide editable scenes for creators and aligned blockout–video pairs for training. This requires efficient, faithful, and scalable reconstruction.

However, two gaps remain in video-to-blockout reconstruction. First, existing video reconstruction benchmarks focus on indoor scans of furnished spaces [36], which differ substantially from film shots with expressive camera motion, staged character interactions, and precisely timed actions. A dedicated benchmark is needed to assess reconstruction fidelity across these cinematic dimensions. Second, although agents can inspect videos and operate Blender to build scenes [36, 53], their judgments of geometric improvements can be unreliable [24]. Character animation adds further difficulty, requiring faithful poses, trajectories, and timing throughout the shot.

We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking in video-to-blockout reconstruction. It contains 50 single shots from 50 films and 416 keyframes sampled at approximately 1.5-second intervals, including shot endpoints. Camera references, depth pseudo ground truth, and human annotations enable quantitative comparison between reconstructed Blender scenes and the source videos. We also report runtime and API cost to assess efficiency.

Recent advances in visual geometry recovery [25, 39] and world-grounded human motion estimation [44, 33] provide a foundation for grounding reconstruction in measured observations. We propose MAVE to ground agentic construction in measured observations and explicit checks. Metric Observation first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. Agentic Modeling then uses this evidence and the source video to construct the environment from named, editable primitives. Recovered cameras and human poses remain fixed, with constrained adjustments for human scale and support alignment. Evidence-Based Verification reports depth conflicts, missing structural coverage, and inconsistent human–environment relationships to guide scene refinement. On MAVEBench, MAVE achieves an overall score of up to 76.1, improving on the corresponding vanilla baselines by 27.5–41.1 points across three agents. With DeepSeek-1017, MAVE achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only $0.054 per shot, surpassing the strongest vanilla baseline (GPT-6.1 Sol, 48.6) while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%.

Using MAVE, we construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout–video pairs for public release. Each reconstructed scene is rendered with the recovered camera trajectory to produce a blockout video aligned frame by frame with the source, providing paired data for training blockout-conditioned video generation models. The reconstructed scenes also let creators adapt a reference shot in Blender by changing the viewpoint and revising character paths. Creators can preview these variants and render them as blockout videos to condition video generation.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    MAVEBench, a benchmark for quantitative evaluation of camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking in video-to-blockout reconstruction.

  • •

    MAVE, a framework combining metric observation, agentic modeling, and evidence-based verification to reconstruct editable blockouts.

  • •

    MAVEData-3K, 3,000 blockout–video pairs for public release, with applications to previsualization editing and blockout-conditioned video generation.

    • 2 Benchmark

    2.1 Task Formulation

    Given a single film shot V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₁^N of 3–20 s featuring people, where N denotes the total number of frames, the task is to reconstruct an editable 3D blockout scene B and render it into a corresponding blockout video V̂:

    B=(ℂ,G,H)=M(V), V̂=R(B),

    		(1)

    where M denotes the video-to-blockout reconstruction process, and R renders the reconstructed scene using the recovered camera trajectory to reproduce the original shot in a blockout representation.

    The blockout scene consists of three components: the shot camera ℂ={(Kₜ,Rₜ,tₜ)}ₜ₌₁^N, specifying the camera intrinsics and extrinsics at each frame; the greybox scene G, represented by a set of named geometric primitives, such as boxes, cylinders, and planes; and the stand-in characters H={hᵏₜ}, where each person k is represented by a rigged mannequin with a pose defined at every frame t.

    The rendered blockout video V̂ is required to match the input video in resolution, frame rate, and frame count, establishing a frame-aligned video pair (V,V̂). The underlying 3D scene must remain editable, allowing users to modify the camera, scene geometry, and character poses.

    2.2 Data Collection and Annotation

    MAVEBench contains 50 single shots from 50 films, covering diverse camera movements, human actions, spatial relationships, and multi-person configurations. We sample 416 keyframes at approximately 1.5-second intervals, including shot endpoints. Reference cameras are obtained through cross-validation of multiple reconstruction methods, with manually annotated static-object tracks supporting ORE evaluation. Depth pseudo ground truth is constructed by combining DA3 [25], π³[43], and VGGT [39] predictions with geometric consistency filtering. Person identities and masks are initialized by SAM 3 [5] and manually corrected. Fig.2 shows annotation examples. Shot selection, annotation procedures, and filtering details are provided in the supplementary material.

    2.3 Evaluation Protocol

    We evaluate camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking directly from the submitted .blend files. For each shot, we render instance and depth maps using the camera in the reconstructed scene at 1.5 s intervals, yielding 416 keyframes in total. Metrics are computed for each shot and uniformly averaged across shots.

    Camera Motion.

    We evaluate camera motion using Object Reprojection Error (ORE)↓[7] and Relative Rotation and Translation Accuracy at 15^∘ (RRA@15 and RTA@15)↑[40, 39]. ORE measures cross-frame reprojection consistency of static objects without reference camera trajectories and is evaluated on all 50 shots. RRA@15 and RTA@15 measure the fractions of frame pairs whose relative rotation and translation direction, respectively, fall within 15^∘ of the reference camera trajectories.

    Spatial Layout.

    We evaluate relative depth ordering using ordinal accuracy [6]. For each keyframe, we sample 40k pixel pairs and measure the fraction whose predicted depths preserve the ground-truth ordering. Ties and missing reconstructed geometry count as errors.

    Character Blocking.

    We render character silhouettes with scene occlusion. We report HOTA↑[28], including its detection (DetA) and association (AssA) components, using keyframes as frames and box IoU as the similarity measure. HOTA captures missing, spurious, and identity-switched characters. We further evaluate character silhouettes using Mask IoU↑[32], which measures the overlap between rendered and ground-truth masks. Within each shot, annotated persons are matched to proxies via Hungarian matching [23] based on accumulated bounding-box IoU. We average Mask IoU over all person–keyframe instances, assigning zero to unmatched instances.

    Overall Score.

    The overall score is the mean of the three axis scores multiplied by 100. The camera score is the average of 1-\min(1,ORE/τ), RRA@15, and RTA@15 over the available metrics for each shot, where τ=0.168 approximates the ORE of a static camera. The depth score is ordinal accuracy, while the character score is the average of HOTA and Mask IoU. The overall score is the mean of the three axis scores.

    Efficiency.

    We report mean API cost and wall-clock runtime per shot, from reconstruction start to Blender scene completion, excluding final video rendering.

    3 Method

    To reduce the capability requirements and costs of agentic scene construction, we propose a structured framework for 3D blockout reconstruction, as shown in Fig.3. The framework first recovers the camera trajectory and metric character geometry in a shared 3D coordinate system. An LLM-based agent then iteratively constructs the environment, editing the scene and verifying its geometry against the input video to produce a coherent, editable 3D scene.

    3.1 Metric Observation

    Given an input video, we recover video-aligned camera and human representations, denoted by ℂ and H, respectively, in a metric coordinate system. We also extract geometric evidence D to support subsequent scene construction and agentic reasoning.

    Camera and human recovery.

    We first apply DA3 [25] to uniformly sampled keyframes to jointly estimate depth maps, camera intrinsics, and camera poses in a shared coordinate system. We interpolate the camera poses and intrinsics to obtain the full video trajectory. Meanwhile, SAM 3 [5] segments and tracks people throughout the video, providing frame-wise person masks and bounding boxes. Given these masks, bounding boxes, and the corresponding DA3 camera intrinsics, SAM 3D Body [49] estimates metric 3D human poses in the camera coordinate system. This produces video-aligned camera and human representations ℂ and H.

    Metric scene alignment.

    We first align the scale of DA3 depth with the metric human estimates from SAM 3D Body [30]. For each person i in keyframe j, we estimate the corresponding visible-surface depths zᵇᵒᵈʸ_i,j and z^DA3_i,j from the projected human meshes and DA3 depth maps, respectively [30, 47]. The global scale factor is computed as

    s=*median_i,j(zᵇᵒᵈʸ_i,j/z^DA3_i,j).

    		(2)

    We apply s to the DA3 depth maps and camera translations to obtain a metric scene representation.

    Gravity alignment provides a consistent reference for world-space human motion [33]. We estimate the scene up direction u^⋆ by combining geometric and orientation cues:

    u^⋆=\arg\min_∥u∥=1∑_h∈{g,c}ψ((∠(u,nₕ))/(σₕ))+(∠(u,c)²)/(σ_c²)(3)
    +∑_wψ((\arcsin|u^⊤n_w|)/(σ_w))+ψ((∠(u,b))/(σ_b)).

    Here, n_g and n_c denote ground and ceiling normals, n_w denotes vertical-surface normals, b is the human upright direction, and c is the camera up direction. The robust penalty ψ reduces the influence of unreliable observations.

    Finally, we construct a unified scene coordinate system with u^⋆ as its positive z-axis. We fit a ground plane from the static scene point cloud and place the origin at the projection of the first camera center onto this plane. The horizontal axes are initialized from the first camera orientation and rotated around the z-axis to align with the dominant Manhattan directions [9] estimated from static scene normals.

    Human placement.

    After scene alignment, we place each person using DA3 depth. We estimate the neck depth d̄_i,t from the aligned depth within the person mask and compute a per-frame position factor [55]:

    f_i,t=d̄_i,t/zᵇ_i,t, mᵢ=medianₜf_i,t.

    		(4)

    where zᵇ_i,t is the neck depth predicted by SAM 3D Body. Let J_i,t denote its predicted 3D body keypoints and Jⁿᵉᶜᵏ_i,t the neck keypoint. We place the human in the camera coordinate system as

    P_i,t=f_i,tJⁿᵉᶜᵏ_i,t+mᵢ(J_i,t-Jⁿᵉᶜᵏ_i,t).

    		(5)

    Here, f_i,t adjusts the neck position along its camera ray to match the DA3 depth, while the temporally constant mᵢ scales the body around the neck, preserving a consistent human height throughout the video. The resulting poses are then transformed into the scene coordinate system.

    Geometric evidence extraction.

    We back-project the aligned DA3 depth maps into the scene coordinate system to construct a static point cloud ℚ, excluding dynamic human regions and unreliable depth observations. We then assign semantic labels to the retained points using Mask2Former [8] and aggregate them spatially to extract wall segments W, support layers L, and ceiling regions U. Together with camera and human information, these observations form the geometric evidence set

    D={ℚ,W,L,U,ℂ,H}.

    		(6)

    This evidence provides geometric and spatial references for subsequent agentic scene construction and verification.

    3.2 Agentic Modeling

    Scene initialization.

    We initialize the scene with the recovered cameras and human representations, leaving the environment geometry empty:

    B₀=(ℂ,∅,H).

    		(7)

    Scene construction.

    Given the source video and geometric evidence D, the agent constructs the environment using editable parametric primitives:

    σ=(κ,c,d,θ,τ,ν),

    		(8)

    where κ, c, d, and θ denote the primitive type, center, dimensions, and orientation, while τ and ν specify its semantic class and name. Complex structures combine multiple primitives [37, 51]. At each iteration, Blender executes an agent-generated edit program eₙ to update the scene:

    Bₙ=Apply(Bₙ₋₁,eₙ).

    		(9)

    Camera trajectories and human poses remain fixed, while each human track has a single scale parameter λₖ that jointly controls its physical size and camera distance while preserving its image projection. The scale remains constant throughout the video.

    Human-environment alignment.

    The video constrains human poses and image projections but does not uniquely determine their metric scale [54, 52]. We parameterize each human track with a single scale factor λₖ, which scales the entire trajectory about the corresponding camera centers:

    P^′_k,t=oₜ+λₖ(P_k,t-oₜ).

    		(10)

    This transformation preserves image projection while scaling the person’s height and camera distance [16]. A single λₖ is shared across all frames.

    The agent determines λₖ through three operations: (1) support-based placement, which aligns the feet with a specified scene primitive; (2) height-based placement, which sets λₖ=H^⋆/Hₖ given an estimated physical height H^⋆; and (3) direct assignment. Since the same scale factor governs both human height and support alignment, the resulting height provides an additional check on the reconstructed geometry. Inconsistent constraints prompt the agent to reconsider the scene geometry or human interpretation. The agent can also remove entire tracks or invalid temporal segments identified as non-human objects or tracking failures, without modifying the remaining poses.

    Closed-loop modeling.

    Following iterative code–render–inspect workflows for agentic graphics [53, 21], we organize scene construction into a query–edit–verify loop. The agent inspects the scene, queries evidence, executes edits, and analyzes diagnostic renderings until completion or exhaustion of the time budget. At each iteration, the agent selects an operation according to

    eₙ∼π_LLM(·|T,D,ℝₙ₋₁),

    		(11)

    where T denotes the task description and tool documentation, and ℝₙ₋₁ records previous queries, edits, and verification feedback.

    3.3 Evidence-Based Verification

    Motivated by the limitations of agents’ geometric self-assessment [24], we provide explicit checks against measured scene evidence. After each scene edit, verification tools evaluate the reconstruction against the input video and geometric evidence, reporting inconsistencies through diagnostic feedback. The agent resolves these issues through further edits or explicit justifications. We consider four complementary aspects.

    Video consistency.

    We check whether reconstructed primitives incorrectly occlude surfaces observed in the input video. For each primitive σ, we compare its projected depth with the observed depth across keyframes and quantify potential occlusion violations by measuring the proportion of overlapping pixels where the primitive lies significantly in front of the observed surface:

    φ(σ)=(∑ⱼ|{u∈Ωⱼ∩Ωⱼ^σ:d_σ(u)

    		(12)

    where Ωⱼ and Ωⱼ^σ denote the valid observed pixels and projected primitive region, respectively; dⱼ and d_σ are their depths, and δ is a depth-dependent tolerance. Primitives with substantial violations are flagged for inspection.

    Evidence coverage.

    We assess whether scene primitives spatially cover the geometric measurements in D, including wall segments W, support layers L, and ceiling regions U, subject to geometric proximity constraints. Uncovered or misaligned measurements are reported to the agent for reconstruction or justification based on the source video.

    Human–environment consistency.

    We check body penetration, foot support, and estimated human height to verify the spatial relationships between reconstructed people and scene geometry [17, 52, 48]. The agent uses the reported violations to revise scene geometry, adjust the human scale λₖ, or justify exceptional poses such as jumping or riding. Removed tracks and invalid temporal segments also require explicit justifications.

    Scene completeness.

    Using orbit views, the agent inspects global scene structure, including spatial enclosure, openings, and floating, duplicated, or disconnected geometry. This complements local geometric checks with an assessment of overall structural coherence.

    Submission and output.

    The submission tool checks whether reported issues have been resolved or justified. At the time limit, the latest successful scene is retained with unresolved issues recorded. The final scene is rendered using the recovered cameras:

    Îₜ=Render(B_final;Kₜ,Rₜ,tₜ),V̂={Îₜ}ₜ₌₁^N.

    		(13)

    We deliver the editable scene and its blockout video at the source resolution, frame rate, and frame count, rendering characters only when visible in the source.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We evaluate all 50 shots in MAVEBench following the protocol described in Sec.2.3. Each agent is allocated a 15-minute target runtime, with a hard limit of 30 minutes. The most recent successfully executed scene is used for evaluation. All agents operate with high reasoning effort.

    No Reconstruction renders an empty scene using a static camera. Vanilla Agent allows an LLM agent to construct the scene in Blender using only the input video and a shared task description, without access to the observation, evidence, and verification tools provided by MAVE.

    We evaluate five LLM agents in the Vanilla setting: GPT-6.1 Sol [31], Claude Opus 5.5 [2], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [11], Claude Sonnet 5.5 [3], and Kimi K3.1 Pro [29]. We further evaluate GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 with MAVE.

    4.2 Main Results

    Reconstruction Quality.

    As shown in Tab.1, MAVE consistently improves all three agents, yielding gains of 27.5–41.1 points in overall score. All three outperform the strongest Vanilla result (48.6). The largest gains are observed in camera motion, with score improvements of 0.461–0.688, followed by character blocking (0.190–0.385) and spatial layout (0.121–0.172). Moreover, MAVE benefits weaker agents more, reducing the performance gap among the three agents from 17.0 to 3.4 points.

    Efficiency.

    MAVE achieves substantial quality improvements with comparable API costs (Tab.2). The per-shot API cost changes by at most $0.06 across the three agents. Meanwhile, agent execution time decreases by 42% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 55% for DeepSeek-1017, partially offsetting the additional 1m28s required by Metric Observation. Notably, DeepSeek-1017 with MAVE surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol with Vanilla by 24.6 points in overall score, while reducing API cost by 86% and total runtime by 53%.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    Components.

    We ablate each component using DeepSeek-1017 (Tab.3). All variants retain the recovered cameras, which establish the metric frame shared by depth, geometric evidence, and human placement. Removing camera recovery would disable these components, reducing the method to Vanilla and preventing their individual contributions from being isolated. We fix the cameras and focus on spatial layout and character blocking.

    w/o Geometric Evidence removes the point cloud, depth map, and extracted structural elements (walls, supports, and ceilings), requiring the agent to reconstruct the environment from scratch using only the input video. Pre-placed humans are retained. w/o Human Recovery removes the pre-placed human proxies, requiring the agent to create and pose them independently. w/o Verification removes the verification tools and submission checks.

    Removing geometric evidence reduces OrdAcc by 0.129, while leaving character blocking largely unaffected. Removing human recovery causes the largest overall score drop (12.0 points), with HOTA and Mask IoU decreasing by 0.363 and 0.300, respectively. Verification provides smaller but consistent gains across both axes, improving the overall score by 2.2 points. Together, these results demonstrate the complementary contributions of the three components.

    Time Budget.

    MAVE achieves an overall score of 72.8 with a 5-minute target, close to the best score of 73.2 obtained with the default 15-minute target (Tab.4). Extending the target to 30 minutes brings no further improvement. Moreover, even with a 30-minute target and a 40-minute hard limit, the agent finishes in 10m25s on average, indicating that MAVE achieves strong reconstruction quality without requiring prolonged agent interaction.

    Additional experiments and analyses, including a user study, are provided in the appendix.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：手工从参考视频重建 3D 走位成本太高，创作者用不上，配对训练数据也做不出来。

要点：

  • 价值链条：动画化的 3D 走位（blockout）支撑预演，并为视频生成提供**结构条件**；但从参考视频手工重建它们代价很高
  • 后果是双向的：创作者用不上，而且**配对训练数据也做不出来**
  • 这篇同时给了评测与方桘：**MAVEBench**（50 个电影镜头、416 个关键帧，评相机运动、空间布局与角色站位）与 **MAVE**，一个视频到 3D 走位的重建方法

为什么值得看：走位（blockout）是影视与关卡设计里最通用的沟通媒介。把它从视频里自动反推出来且可编辑，等于把「参考片 → 可改的场景」这一步打通——这同时也是视频生成需要的结构条件，一举两得。

中文摘要：动画化的三维走位（blockout）既服务于预演，又能为视频生成提供结构条件，但要从参考视频手工重建它们代价极高，结果既让创作者难以使用，也使配对训练数据难以生产。这篇同时提供评测与方桘：MAVEBench 是一个包含 50 个电影镜头、416 个关键帧的基准，用于评估相机运动、空间布局与角色站位；MAVE 则是一个从视频重建可编辑三维走位的方法。把「参考片」自动转成「可改的场景」，既打开了创作者的工作流，也为视频生成补上了缺失的结构条件。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots

Abstract

Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5--41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only $0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout–video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available.111https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE

1 Introduction

An animated 3D blockout represents a shot using simple geometry, stand-in characters, and a camera. Its editable structure lets creators adjust camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking for previsualization [19]. Recent video generation methods use 3D layouts, scene geometry, and human motion as structural guidance [41, 4, 35, 13, 1, 42]. Rendering an editable blockout provides a practical way to translate scene-level edits into such guidance. This workflow faces two related bottlenecks. For creators, manually reconstructing a blockout from a reference video requires time and 3D production expertise [21, 15]. For model training, producing blockouts that match target videos is costly, limiting the scale of paired data [41, 4]. As shown in Fig.1, automatically reconstructing blockouts from existing videos can provide editable scenes for creators and aligned blockout–video pairs for training. This requires efficient, faithful, and scalable reconstruction.

However, two gaps remain in video-to-blockout reconstruction. First, existing video reconstruction benchmarks focus on indoor scans of furnished spaces [36], which differ substantially from film shots with expressive camera motion, staged character interactions, and precisely timed actions. A dedicated benchmark is needed to assess reconstruction fidelity across these cinematic dimensions. Second, although agents can inspect videos and operate Blender to build scenes [36, 53], their judgments of geometric improvements can be unreliable [24]. Character animation adds further difficulty, requiring faithful poses, trajectories, and timing throughout the shot.

We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking in video-to-blockout reconstruction. It contains 50 single shots from 50 films and 416 keyframes sampled at approximately 1.5-second intervals, including shot endpoints. Camera references, depth pseudo ground truth, and human annotations enable quantitative comparison between reconstructed Blender scenes and the source videos. We also report runtime and API cost to assess efficiency.

Recent advances in visual geometry recovery [25, 39] and world-grounded human motion estimation [44, 33] provide a foundation for grounding reconstruction in measured observations. We propose MAVE to ground agentic construction in measured observations and explicit checks. Metric Observation first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. Agentic Modeling then uses this evidence and the source video to construct the environment from named, editable primitives. Recovered cameras and human poses remain fixed, with constrained adjustments for human scale and support alignment. Evidence-Based Verification reports depth conflicts, missing structural coverage, and inconsistent human–environment relationships to guide scene refinement. On MAVEBench, MAVE achieves an overall score of up to 76.1, improving on the corresponding vanilla baselines by 27.5–41.1 points across three agents. With DeepSeek-1017, MAVE achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only $0.054 per shot, surpassing the strongest vanilla baseline (GPT-6.1 Sol, 48.6) while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%.

Using MAVE, we construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout–video pairs for public release. Each reconstructed scene is rendered with the recovered camera trajectory to produce a blockout video aligned frame by frame with the source, providing paired data for training blockout-conditioned video generation models. The reconstructed scenes also let creators adapt a reference shot in Blender by changing the viewpoint and revising character paths. Creators can preview these variants and render them as blockout videos to condition video generation.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    MAVEBench, a benchmark for quantitative evaluation of camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking in video-to-blockout reconstruction.

  • •

    MAVE, a framework combining metric observation, agentic modeling, and evidence-based verification to reconstruct editable blockouts.

  • •

    MAVEData-3K, 3,000 blockout–video pairs for public release, with applications to previsualization editing and blockout-conditioned video generation.

    2.1 Task Formulation

    B=(ℂ,G,H)=M(V), V̂=R(B),

    The rendered blockout video V̂ is required to match the input video in resolution, frame rate, and frame count, establishing a frame-aligned video pair (V,V̂). The underlying 3D scene must remain editable, allowing users to modify the camera, scene geometry, and character poses.
