Together with camera and human information, these observations form the geometric evidence set

    D={ℚ,W,L,U,ℂ,H}.

    		(6)

    This evidence provides geometric and spatial references for subsequent agentic scene construction and verification.

    3.2 Agentic Modeling

    Scene initialization.

    We initialize the scene with the recovered cameras and human representations, leaving the environment geometry empty:

    B₀=(ℂ,∅,H).

    		(7)

    Scene construction.

    Given the source video and geometric evidence D, the agent constructs the environment using editable parametric primitives:

    σ=(κ,c,d,θ,τ,ν),

    		(8)

    where κ, c, d, and θ denote the primitive type, center, dimensions, and orientation, while τ and ν specify its semantic class and name. Complex structures combine multiple primitives [37, 51]. At each iteration, Blender executes an agent-generated edit program eₙ to update the scene:

    Bₙ=Apply(Bₙ₋₁,eₙ).

    		(9)

    Camera trajectories and human poses remain fixed, while each human track has a single scale parameter λₖ that jointly controls its physical size and camera distance while preserving its image projection. The scale remains constant throughout the video.

    Human-environment alignment.

    The video constrains human poses and image projections but does not uniquely determine their metric scale [54, 52]. We parameterize each human track with a single scale factor λₖ, which scales the entire trajectory about the corresponding camera centers:

    P^′_k,t=oₜ+λₖ(P_k,t-oₜ).

    		(10)

    This transformation preserves image projection while scaling the person’s height and camera distance [16]. A single λₖ is shared across all frames.

    The agent determines λₖ through three operations: (1) support-based placement, which aligns the feet with a specified scene primitive; (2) height-based placement, which sets λₖ=H^⋆/Hₖ given an estimated physical height H^⋆; and (3) direct assignment. Since the same scale factor governs both human height and support alignment, the resulting height provides an additional check on the reconstructed geometry. Inconsistent constraints prompt the agent to reconsider the scene geometry or human interpretation. The agent can also remove entire tracks or invalid temporal segments identified as non-human objects or tracking failures, without modifying the remaining poses.

    Closed-loop modeling.

    Following iterative code–render–inspect workflows for agentic graphics [53, 21], we organize scene construction into a query–edit–verify loop. The agent inspects the scene, queries evidence, executes edits, and analyzes diagnostic renderings until completion or exhaustion of the time budget. At each iteration, the agent selects an operation according to

    eₙ∼π_LLM(·|T,D,ℝₙ₋₁),

    		(11)

    where T denotes the task description and tool documentation, and ℝₙ₋₁ records previous queries, edits, and verification feedback.

    3.3 Evidence-Based Verification

    Motivated by the limitations of agents’ geometric self-assessment [24], we provide explicit checks against measured scene evidence. After each scene edit, verification tools evaluate the reconstruction against the input video and geometric evidence, reporting inconsistencies through diagnostic feedback. The agent resolves these issues through further edits or explicit justifications. We consider four complementary aspects.

    Video consistency.

    We check whether reconstructed primitives incorrectly occlude surfaces observed in the input video. For each primitive σ, we compare its projected depth with the observed depth across keyframes and quantify potential occlusion violations by measuring the proportion of overlapping pixels where the primitive lies significantly in front of the observed surface:

    φ(σ)=(∑ⱼ|{u∈Ωⱼ∩Ωⱼ^σ:d_σ(u)

    		(12)

    where Ωⱼ and Ωⱼ^σ denote the valid observed pixels and projected primitive region, respectively; dⱼ and d_σ are their depths, and δ is a depth-dependent tolerance. Primitives with substantial violations are flagged for inspection.

    Evidence coverage.

    We assess whether scene primitives spatially cover the geometric measurements in D, including wall segments W, support layers L, and ceiling regions U, subject to geometric proximity constraints. Uncovered or misaligned measurements are reported to the agent for reconstruction or justification based on the source video.

    Human–environment consistency.

    We check body penetration, foot support, and estimated human height to verify the spatial relationships between reconstructed people and scene geometry [17, 52, 48]. The agent uses the reported violations to revise scene geometry, adjust the human scale λₖ, or justify exceptional poses such as jumping or riding. Removed tracks and invalid temporal segments also require explicit justifications.

    Scene completeness.

    Using orbit views, the agent inspects global scene structure, including spatial enclosure, openings, and floating, duplicated, or disconnected geometry. This complements local geometric checks with an assessment of overall structural coherence.

    Submission and output.

    The submission tool checks whether reported issues have been resolved or justified. At the time limit, the latest successful scene is retained with unresolved issues recorded. The final scene is rendered using the recovered cameras:

    Îₜ=Render(B_final;Kₜ,Rₜ,tₜ),V̂={Îₜ}ₜ₌₁^N.

    		(13)

    We deliver the editable scene and its blockout video at the source resolution, frame rate, and frame count, rendering characters only when visible in the source.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We evaluate all 50 shots in MAVEBench following the protocol described in Sec.2.3. Each agent is allocated a 15-minute target runtime, with a hard limit of 30 minutes. The most recent successfully executed scene is used for evaluation. All agents operate with high reasoning effort.

    No Reconstruction renders an empty scene using a static camera. Vanilla Agent allows an LLM agent to construct the scene in Blender using only the input video and a shared task description, without access to the observation, evidence, and verification tools provided by MAVE.

    We evaluate five LLM agents in the Vanilla setting: GPT-6.1 Sol [31], Claude Opus 5.5 [2], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [11], Claude Sonnet 5.5 [3], and Kimi K3.1 Pro [29]. We further evaluate GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 with MAVE.

    4.2 Main Results

    Reconstruction Quality.

    As shown in Tab.1, MAVE consistently improves all three agents, yielding gains of 27.5–41.1 points in overall score. All three outperform the strongest Vanilla result (48.6). The largest gains are observed in camera motion, with score improvements of 0.461–0.688, followed by character blocking (0.190–0.385) and spatial layout (0.121–0.172). Moreover, MAVE benefits weaker agents more, reducing the performance gap among the three agents from 17.0 to 3.4 points.

    Efficiency.

    MAVE achieves substantial quality improvements with comparable API costs (Tab.2). The per-shot API cost changes by at most $0.06 across the three agents. Meanwhile, agent execution time decreases by 42% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 55% for DeepSeek-1017, partially offsetting the additional 1m28s required by Metric Observation. Notably, DeepSeek-1017 with MAVE surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol with Vanilla by 24.6 points in overall score, while reducing API cost by 86% and total runtime by 53%.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    Components.

    We ablate each component using DeepSeek-1017 (Tab.3). All variants retain the recovered cameras, which establish the metric frame shared by depth, geometric evidence, and human placement. Removing camera recovery would disable these components, reducing the method to Vanilla and preventing their individual contributions from being isolated. We fix the cameras and focus on spatial layout and character blocking.

    w/o Geometric Evidence removes the point cloud, depth map, and extracted structural elements (walls, supports, and ceilings), requiring the agent to reconstruct the environment from scratch using only the input video. Pre-placed humans are retained. w/o Human Recovery removes the pre-placed human proxies, requiring the agent to create and pose them independently. w/o Verification removes the verification tools and submission checks.

    Removing geometric evidence reduces OrdAcc by 0.129, while leaving character blocking largely unaffected. Removing human recovery causes the largest overall score drop (12.0 points), with HOTA and Mask IoU decreasing by 0.363 and 0.300, respectively. Verification provides smaller but consistent gains across both axes, improving the overall score by 2.2 points. Together, these results demonstrate the complementary contributions of the three components.

    Time Budget.

    MAVE achieves an overall score of 72.8 with a 5-minute target, close to the best score of 73.2 obtained with the default 15-minute target (Tab.4). Extending the target to 30 minutes brings no further improvement. Moreover, even with a 30-minute target and a 40-minute hard limit, the agent finishes in 10m25s on average, indicating that MAVE achieves strong reconstruction quality without requiring prolonged agent interaction.

    Additional experiments and analyses, including a user study, are provided in the appendix.

item.title: 把解码器省掉：DWD 让微调后的 DiT 用一个线性头直接出像素，去噪头不再兼任「解码」 ｜ Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
一句话：潜扩散依赖解码器把潜变量映射回像素，多一层复杂度也多一层推理成本。

要点：

  • 成本来源：潜扩散模型依赖**解码器**把去噪后的潜变量映射到像素，这既增加复杂度也增加推理开销
  • DWD 让微调后的扩散 transformer 通过一个**线性头**直接产出最终像素；与以往方法不同，它把两种角色**分开**：原来的去噪头继续驱动采样，另一个线性头负责输出像素
  • 这种分离避免了「去噪输出必须同时是最终像素」带来的约束

为什么值得看：解码器是潜扩散管线里最后一块不可控的开销，还可能带来颜色与细节损失。用线性头直接出像素，等于把「潜空间 ↔ 像素」这条链路简化到底——与 11-15 期 PixVid「提到像素空间」是同一方向的另一条实现。

中文摘要：潜扩散模型依赖一个解码器把去噪后的潜变量映射回像素，这一步既增加了模型的复杂度，也带来额外的推理开销。这篇提出「无解码器解码」（DWD）：让经过微调的扩散 transformer 通过一个线性头直接产生最终像素。与以往方法的关键区别在于角色分离——原先的去噪头继续负责驱动采样过程，而另设的线性头专门负责输出像素，从而避免「去噪输出必须同时充当最终像素」所带来的约束。这与把视频扩散整体提到像素空间的做法方向一致，但改动面更小。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers

Abstract

Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

1 Introduction

Latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023)] is the dominant recipe for image and video generation [(Esser et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024; Z-Image Team et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025)]. Typically, a diffusion transformer (DiT) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] generates in a compressed latent space, and a convolutional decoder [(Kingma & Welling, 2014; Esser et al., 2021)] maps the latents to pixels. The decoder complicates deployment and can add substantial inference cost. For example, on H100, generating a 5-second video with a 4-step Wan 1.3B model [(Zheng et al., 2026b)] takes 2.8 seconds for sampling and another 1.9 seconds for decoding, adding about 70% overhead. Recent work obtains much faster decoders with comparable quality [(Zhu et al., 2026; Kang & Kwak, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026)], suggesting that the decoder is largely redundant. This raises the question: what is the minimal network architecture for producing final pixels from a latent diffusion model?

We show that a simple linear head can replace the decoder while improving pixel quality. Our method, Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), finetunes a pretrained latent DiT by adding a linear output head (the DWD head) in parallel with the DiT’s original output layer (the denoising head). The denoising head continues to drive denoising steps, then the DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step only.

The dual-head separation distinguishes DWD from previous approaches, whose denoising output leads to final pixels: latent models decode it, pixel models output it directly. This couples pixel fidelity to denoising, causing a tradeoff between detail rendering and denoiser learnability [(Yao et al., 2025; Skorokhodov et al., 2025)]. DWD decouples the two roles: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses [(Esser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018)], while the denoising head is anchored to the frozen pretrained model to preserve sample content.

The separation is most evident on pixel diffusion models, where the denoising head already predicts the final output. These predictions smooth fine detail because they estimate conditional means under ℓ₂ loss. Applying perceptual losses directly to them [(Lin & Yang, 2023; Berrada Ifriqi et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026b)] risks collapsing sample diversity, as our shared-head ablation fails to improve FID (Table 1). In contrast, a separate head improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43.

We evaluate DWD across latent and pixel generators on ImageNet, text-to-image, and video generation (Fig. 1). Removing the decoder improves nearly all FID metrics across tested latent image models. On Wan [(Wang et al., 2025)] video, warping error drops by 23%, with visibly less detail distortion and flickering. On text-to-image pixel diffusion, DWD recovers photorealistic textures.

To summarize, we show that:

  • •

    A latent DiT needs no decoder: finetuning its last few blocks with an additional linear head suffices, reducing inference cost, improving ImageNet FIDs, and lessening detail distortion and flickering in Wan video.

  • •

    The dual-head separation also improves pixel diffusion models, producing better texture detail in text-to-image generation and a state-of-the-art ImageNet FID of 1.43 among pixel flow models.

    • 2 Related Work

    Latent-space diffusion. VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)] trains autoencoders with reconstruction, perceptual [(Zhang et al., 2018)], and adversarial [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] losses, and LDM [(Rombach et al., 2022)] uses this perceptual compression to reduce diffusion cost. VA-VAE [(Yao et al., 2025)], REPA-E [(Leng et al., 2025)], and RAE [(Zheng et al., 2026a)] address the gap between reconstruction quality and diffusability. DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025)] and Qwen-Image-VAE-2.0 [(Zhang et al., 2026)] increase spatial compression while preserving reconstruction fidelity. SSDD [(Vallaeys et al., 2025)] and PiD [(Lu et al., 2026)] replace conventional decoders with distilled pixel diffusion models. PiD and LTX-Video [(HaCohen et al., 2024)] also stop latent sampling early, letting the decoder complete the remaining denoising. [Zhang et al. (2024)] improve latent generators by applying losses to images produced through the VAE decoder. These approaches retain a standalone decoding network. DWD instead produces the final pixels through a linear head on the existing DiT, reusing its last-layer tokens and computation without an extra decoder.

    Pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion models denoise directly in pixel space without an autoencoder. They overcome difficulties in high-resolution generation through multiscale architectures and specialized output pathways [(Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a)], or improved prediction targets [(Li & He, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Zirvi et al., 2026)]. AsymFlow [(Chen et al., 2026a)] and L2P [(Chen et al., 2026d)] finetune pretrained latent models to perform denoising in pixel space, altering the flow trajectory and sample content (see Appendix B.4 for a comparison). In contrast, DWD preserves the original latent trajectory rather than converting the model to pixel diffusion. DWD finetuning is also more efficient, since only the last few transformer blocks and output heads are updated with shallow backpropagation, whereas latent-to-pixel conversion must backpropagate through the entire network to adapt to pixel-space inputs.

    3 Decoding Without a Decoder

    A pretrained latent DiT’s last-layer tokens already encode rich pixel information [(Gan et al., 2025; Akarken et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c)]: a least-squares linear projection recovers most of the image structure before any finetuning (Fig. 3). DWD exploits this by appending a linear head that produces final pixels directly from these tokens, bypassing the decoder at inference (Fig. 2(b)). Separating the pixel readout from the denoising output lets each be trained with its own objective: pixel quality losses for the DWD head, and trajectory anchoring to preserve denoising behavior.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    We describe latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)] using the flow matching convention [(Lipman et al., 2023)]. A pretrained autoencoder encodes an image or video x into a latent representation z₀. The forward process mixes the latent z₀ with Gaussian noise to form zₜ=(1-t)z₀+tε, where ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t∈[0,1] denotes diffusion time. A flow model (zₜ,t,c)↦û trains a network with extra conditioning c to estimate the conditional mean of velocity u\coloneqqε-z₀, using an ℓ₂ flow matching loss. At inference, the model uses this velocity to progressively transform Gaussian noise into a denoised latent sample ẑ₀, running from t=1 toward t=0[(Song et al., 2021; Liu, 2022; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023)]. Finally, the decoder maps ẑ₀ to the final image or video x.

    For the models studied here, the denoising network is a diffusion transformer (DiT) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024)], which processes tokenized noisy latent zₜ with multiple transformer blocks [(Vaswani et al., 2017)], and feeds the last-layer tokens h (after normalization and modulation) to a linear output head that produces a patch-wise denoising prediction. This is the denoising head, shown in Fig. 2(a).

    3.2 DWD head

    Our goal is to produce final pixels from a pretrained latent DiT without a decoder, subject to two constraints: minimal additional computation, and preservation of the pretrained denoising trajectory.

    A linear probe shows that the last-layer tokens h already support pixel reconstruction without finetuning, more accurately than probing the denoised latents ẑ₀, as shown in Fig. 3. The remaining reconstruction mismatch can be addressed by finetuning the DiT. This inspires us to adopt a simple linear DWD head that maps each token to a pixel patch:

    x̂ᵢ=Linear(hᵢ)=Whᵢ+b,

    		(1)

    where W and b are learnable weights and bias, and x̂ᵢ is the pixel patch corresponding to token hᵢ. This design places the DWD head in parallel with the denoising head, both reading the same last-layer tokens. The linear head is the minimal form of this separate pixel output, which can optionally be extended with a lightweight convolutional refiner (Appendix A.1). The predicted patches are then assembled into the final image or video x̂, with color space conversion where needed (Appendix A).

    Efficiency. By reusing the DiT’s nonlinear computation, the linear head is a lightweight readout with negligible cost for common pixel patch sizes. Pixel patch size follows the combined downsampling factor of the autoencoder and tokenizer. The most common spatial factor of 16 gives a 16×16×3 patch per token. For video models, an additional temporal factor of 4 expands each patch to four frames. For most tested models, the total number of output dimensions per token stays below the DiT’s hidden dimension.

    Separating denoising and pixel outputs. DWD achieves trajectory preservation and pixel rendering through a clear separation of outputs: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses, while the denoising head drives sampling and is anchored to the pretrained model (Sec. 3.3). This dual-head separation distinguishes our work from prior diffusion-based image and video generators, where the denoising output serves as a bottleneck pathway to final pixels.

    Final-step pixel rendering. The DWD head is only used at the final denoiser evaluation step, where the DiT input t is small but nonzero. The nonzero timestep is important: treating DiT–DWD as a latent decoder at t=0 substantially worsens quality (Sec. 4.1), while the t>0 noise gives the pixel head freedom to create detail that the denoised latent would have smoothed away. Classifier-free guidance [(Ho & Salimans, 2021)] is not used in the final step since its role is to steer the trajectory, whereas our final step does not advance the trajectory.

    3.3 Finetuning

    We finetune the last K transformer blocks (typically K=4–8 for large text-conditioned models, see Appendix A for details), both output heads, and the last modulation, keeping the prefix frozen. The timestep embedding MLP is shared across all blocks, so we duplicate its weights for the adapted blocks, allowing their modulations to be fully tuned without disturbing the frozen prefix. This restricts backpropagation to the end of the network and retains most pretrained parameters, making training up to 3× faster than full backpropagation.

    The training objective combines pixel quality with trajectory anchoring:

    L=Lₚᵢₓ+λLₜᵣₐⱼ,

    		(2)

    where λ is the trajectory anchoring weight (Appendix A). Both terms use noisy inputs zₜ encoded from real image data x, but their timesteps t are sampled separately to match the roles of the two outputs. The two losses are backpropagated before one optimizer step on accumulated gradients, so the last-layer tokens adapt for pixel quality while the denoising head’s prediction remains anchored to the pretrained model. The full training loop is shown in Algorithm 1.

    Pixel quality. The DWD head predicts the clean image under the L1 reconstruction, LPIPS perceptual, and adversarial objectives commonly used to train autoencoders [(Esser et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018; Goodfellow et al., 2014)]:

    Lₚᵢₓ=𝔼_x,z,c,t∼pₚᵢₓ[∥x̂-x∥₁+LPIPS(x̂,x)+ℓ_adv(x̂)],

    		(3)

    where pₚᵢₓ is typically uniform over [0.0,0.1] before timestep shifting [(Esser et al., 2024)], matching the small-t regime where the DWD head operates at inference. Following [Zheng et al. (2026a)] and [Singh et al. (2026)], the adversarial term uses the StyleGAN-T discriminator [(Sauer et al., 2023)] with adaptive gradient balancing, and is switched on only in the last stage of training (Appendix A).

    Trajectory anchoring. To preserve the pretrained denoising behavior as the final blocks adapt, we match the denoising head’s prediction to that of a frozen copy of the original model. Let û and û^ref denote the adapted and frozen reference velocity predictions for the same input. We minimize

    Lₜᵣₐⱼ=𝔼_x,z,c,t∼pₜᵣₐⱼ[∥û-û^ref∥₂²],

    		(4)

    where pₜᵣₐⱼ is typically uniform over [0.04,1.0] before timestep shifting, covering the intermediate denoising steps. Both the original and finetuned models share a single forward pass through the frozen prefix: only the final K blocks and output components run separately, avoiding two full-model passes.

    3.4 Extension to pixel diffusion and few-step models

    Pixel diffusion models. The quality benefit of the dual-head separation is most pronounced on pixel diffusion models, which have no decoder to confound the comparison. We still add a DWD head in parallel with the denoising head, treating pixel denoising the same as the latent case. The training objectives are unchanged except for a stronger anchoring weight. Fewer tunable blocks and a shorter training schedule suffice, since the DiT already has pixel knowledge. Details are in Appendix A.

    Few-step latent models. Few-step distilled models [(Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Sauer et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026c)] are the practical frontier of fast generation, where the fixed decoding cost takes a proportionally larger share of inference time. Validating DWD here therefore has direct practical significance. A simple adaptation is to adjust pₚᵢₓ and pₜᵣₐⱼ to cover new ranges around the timesteps used by the few-step sampler. More variants are discussed in Appendix B.2 and B.5.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 ImageNet generation

    We show that DWD consistently improves FID across both latent and pixel baselines. We then ablate the separate head design and show that fusing the two heads degrades quality despite the same training losses, and also study the effect of head capacity and final timestep.

    Setup. We test two latent models, SiT-XL/2-REPA [(Ma et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025)] with the SD-VAE decoder [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and SiT-XL/2-REPA-E [(Leng et al., 2025)] with its end-to-end tuned E2E-VA-VAE decoder [(Yao et al., 2025)], and two pixel models, JiT-H/16 [(Li & He, 2026)] and AnisoFlow-H/16 [(Zirvi et al., 2026)]. DWD extensions are finetuned on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], with training schedules detailed in Appendix A.2. We report FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and Inception Score (IS) [(Salimans et al., 2016)] under the ADM evaluation protocol [(Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021)].

    Improvement over latent diffusion baselines. Removing the decoder improves both latent baselines (Table 1): FID improves from 1.38 to 1.36 for REPA and from 1.12 to 1.06 for REPA-E, with IS improving as well. The two baselines use different latent spaces and decoders, yet a linear head improves on both. Removing the decoder also saves 622 decoder GFLOPs for REPA, 2.6× the cost of a single denoiser evaluation, and 252 decoder GFLOPs for REPA-E.

    Improvement over pixel diffusion baselines. The pixel models have no decoder to remove, so DWD only adds a second output trained with pixel quality losses. As shown in Table 1, DWD improves JiT from 1.90 to 1.85 FID and AnisoFlow from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models, while raising IS by 3–5 points. This also narrows the FID gap between pixel and latent models on ImageNet.

    Separate head vs. shared head. The pixel-model gains have two sources: the pixel quality losses, which latent decoders are trained with but pixel models normally lack, and the separate head that receives them. The w/o separate head rows in Table 1 isolate the latter by fusing the two heads in both training and inference, so the denoising head receives both pixel losses and trajectory anchoring at their respective timesteps, with everything else unchanged. This degrades baseline FID (1.55 to 1.71 for AnisoFlow), so the losses alone do not account for the gain. The degradation reflects a conflict: the ℓ₂ denoising loss favors mode coverage, whereas LPIPS and adversarial losses favor perceptual quality but collapse diversity (better IS but worse FID than the baseline). Trajectory anchoring cannot fully counteract this interference, so the pixel losses need a separate head.

    Linear vs. convolutional head. We ablate the capacity of the linear DWD head by adding a small convolutional residual refiner conditioned on the linear prediction and the last-layer tokens (DWD-conv; Appendix A). This extension brings no consistent improvement across the ImageNet models in Table 1. A linear head therefore suffices to obtain the quality gains under our tested settings.

    Nonzero final timestep. Fig. 4 sweeps the final timestep at which the DWD head is evaluated. Quality degrades toward t=0, where the input is the fully denoised state a decoder would receive, and recovers at a small positive timestep. This shows that the DWD head needs a partially denoised input to produce high-quality pixels, rather than mimicking a decoder applied to a clean state.

    4.2 Text-to-image generation

    We show that DWD replaces the decoder with matched quality on latent baselines, including a few-step distilled model, and recovers photorealistic texture detail on the pixel baseline. We also ablate the adversarial loss to show that it is not critical on text-to-image generation.

    Setup. We test two latent models built on FLUX.2 klein 9B [(Black Forest Labs, 2025)], the 32-step Base model and its distilled 4-step variant, and one pixel model, AnisoFlow-L/16-T2I [(Zirvi et al., 2026)] (0.9B). All DWD extensions are finetuned on public real-image datasets [(Wang et al., 2026a; Desai et al., 2021; Schuhmann et al., 2022)] at mixed aspect ratios. We evaluate at 1024×1024 on COCO-10k [(Lin et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2024)] (FID, patch FID (pFID) [(Lin et al., 2024)], HPSv3 [(Ma et al., 2025)], HPSv2.1 [(Wu et al., 2023)]), OneIG-Bench [(Chang et al., 2025)], and LongText-Bench [(Wu et al., 2025)]. Training and sampling details are in Appendix A.

    Decoder removal without quality loss. On FLUX.2 klein Base, DWD and the baseline are effectively tied on every metric in Table 2, and same-seed samples are nearly indistinguishable (Fig. 5(a)). This is expected: the FLUX.2 latent is much wider than those of other VAEs, with 128 latent dimensions per token for a 768-dimensional pixel patch, compared with 64 for a 3072-dimensional patch in Wan, so decoding from it is easy, leaving little room for improvement. The result nevertheless shows that a linear head can replace it, removing 10.47 TFLOPs of decoder computation per image.

    Compatibility with few-step model. The distilled 4-step FLUX.2 klein tests the few-step regime, where the decoder takes a larger share of the total inference cost. With only the timestep ranges adjusted (Appendix A.2), DWD is again effectively tied with the baseline in Table 2 and visually indistinguishable in Fig. 5(a), even though its final step operates at a much larger timestep (t=0.7 after shifting) than in the 32-step model.

    Improved detail over pixel diffusion baseline. Pixel diffusion models tend to fall short of latent models in very fine texture, even with very large denoisers [(Cai et al., 2026)] or AnisoFlow’s improved parameterization [(Zirvi et al., 2026)]. With a linear head and 3k finetuning iterations, DWD recovers photorealistic skin, hair, foliage, and cloud detail while preserving composition (Fig. 1(b), Fig. 4(b), Fig. 5(b)). The gain also shows up in the low-level metrics in Table 2: COCO FID improves from 28.86 to 27.54 and pFID from 36.59 to 32.26, the latter showing a more significant improvement due to its sensitivity to fine detail. The remaining higher-level metrics are effectively tied, as the trajectory is preserved.

    Adversarial loss. Without the adversarial loss (Table 2), FLUX.2 klein and AnisoFlow’s DWD extensions stay close to full DWD on most metrics, except that pFID worsens more noticeably, though still close to or outperforming the baseline. The adversarial loss is thus helpful but not critical, in line with recent decoder research that drops it [(Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026)].

    4.3 Text-to-video generation

    We apply DWD to the Wan2.1 14B video model, where each token must predict 4 frames rather than a single image patch. Despite this harder setting, DWD not only removes the decoder but visibly reduces distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by at least 23%.

    Setup. We finetune Wan2.1 T2V 14B [(Wang et al., 2025)] on Vchitect T2V DataVerse [(Fan et al., 2025)] clips at mixed 360p, 480p, and 720p resolutions, all downsampled from sources of at least 720p to obtain sharper real pixels (Appendix A.2). We evaluate 81-frame 832×480 generations on extended VBench prompts [(Huang et al., 2024)] from [Huang et al. (2025)] and report warping error [(Lai et al., 2018)], frame-level HPSv3 and HPSv2.1, and seven VBench quality dimensions. For both the baseline and DWD, we additionally evaluate a quantized model with FP8 weights and activations (W8A8) and 8-bit SageAttention2 kernels [(Zhang et al., 2025)], which better reflects efficient deployment settings.

    Decoder removal with reduced distortion and flickering. DWD removes the 0.28-PFLOP Wan decoder and replaces it with a linear head at negligible cost (Table 3), while also improving visual quality. The baseline decoder distorts fine detail such as small text and dense structures, and the distortion changes from frame to frame, which appears as flicker (Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 6). With the decoder removed, the linear DWD head keeps these details stable and legible, noticeably reducing flickering (see the project page for video comparisons). Warping error captures this artifact directly: it aligns consecutive frames by optical flow, masks occlusions, and measures the remaining photometric error, which DWD reduces by 23% (1.52 to 1.18) in Table 3. VBench’s temporal flickering score is less suitable here, since it is the raw pixel difference between consecutive frames without accounting for residual motion, and it saturates near its maximum for both models. The remaining VBench dimensions and HPS metrics are effectively tied, except for a slightly lower dynamic degree, though qualitative results show no visible motion reduction. A decoder finetuned on the same data with the same pixel losses reduces warping error only to 1.39 (Table 3 and Appendix B.1), so most of the gain comes from DWD rather than from the training data.

    8-bit inference. Quantization degrades the baseline noticeably (warping error 1.52 to 1.69) but barely affects DWD (1.18 to 1.20), widening the warping error gap to 29% in Table 3. The other metrics follow the same pattern as under BF16. The DWD extension is thus robust to reduced-precision inference, and the quality gain over the decoder is larger in the deployment setting.

    5 Conclusion

    DWD replaces the decoder with a linear pixel head on the diffusion transformer, finetuning only the last few blocks and output heads. Across latent image and video generators, DWD preserves or improves pixel quality while removing the decoder entirely. On video, this visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering. On pixel diffusion models, a separate DWD head recovers photorealistic texture that the denoising head oversmooths. The broader lesson is that final pixel prediction should be separated from intermediate denoising, so that pixel-space objectives can improve quality without interfering with the sampling trajectory.

    Limitations. The DWD quality gain shrinks when the decoder is already strong, as on FLUX.2. We have not proved that the linear head is sufficient for spatial patch sizes beyond 16×16 pixels, where a stronger head like DWD-conv may be needed. Also, we have not tuned the pixel losses per model, leaving potential room for improvement.

    AI Use Statement

    In this work, we used generative AI tools (LLM-based assistants) to edit the paper for grammar and readability and to accelerate the implementation of our experiments. All AI-assisted work was reviewed and verified by the authors, and we take responsibility for the final content of this paper.

    Reproducibility Statement

    Appendix A gives the implementation details: the head and its initialization (Appendix A.1), the per-model finetuning settings and training data (Appendix A.2 and Table 4), the inference procedure (Appendix A.3), the video evaluation protocol (Appendix A.4), and the parameter and FLOP accounting (Appendix A.5).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    This section complements Sec. 3 with the specifics of the DWD head, finetuning, inference, and evaluation, with per-model settings collected in Table 4.

    A.1 DWD Head

    Output format. The linear head maps each last-layer token to one pixel patch, and the patches are assembled into the image. Image models use 16×16 patches. Wan uses 4×16×16 spatiotemporal patches and a separate 1×16×16 head for the first latent frame, which covers a single pixel frame in the Wan VAE. Following AsymFlow [(Chen et al., 2026a)], latent models and AnisoFlow-L/16-T2I predict pixels in normalized Oklab color space [(Ottosson, 2020)], while the pixel quality losses are applied to the converted RGB values, matching the common autoencoder training recipe. The ImageNet pixel models predict RGB directly, matching their native output.

    Least-squares initialization. The head is initialized by linear regression from last-layer tokens to ground-truth pixel patches. We run the frozen pretrained model on 10k training images with timesteps drawn from pₚᵢₓ, the same distribution used for the pixel losses, and solve the normal equations for the weight and bias jointly. The same procedure produces the probes in Fig. 3, where the latent probe regresses from the denoised latent instead of the tokens.

    Convolutional head (DWD-conv). The DWD-conv ablation keeps the linear head and adds a residual correction, following lightweight super-resolution networks [(Shi et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2018; Ayazoglu, 2021)]: the nonlinear convolutions run at half resolution, a final sub-pixel convolution (pixel shuffle) restores the full resolution, and the branch predicts a residual over a linear base prediction. It packs each 2×2 neighborhood of the linear pixel prediction into channels and refines this packed grid with a convolutional branch. The last-layer tokens are projected through a 128-dimensional bottleneck and expanded into a 32-channel spatial feature map, which is added to a 1×1 projection of the packed pixels. Two residual blocks with 3×3 convolutions and SiLU activations predict the correction through a zero-initialized output convolution, so the head starts as the linear head. For video, the convolutions operate on each frame independently.

中文摘要：潜扩散模型依赖一个解码器把去噪后的潜变量映射回像素，这一步既增加了模型的复杂度，也带来额外的推理开销。这篇提出「无解码器解码」（DWD）：让经过微调的扩散 transformer 通过一个线性头直接产生最终像素。与以往方法的关键区别在于角色分离——原先的去噪头继续负责驱动采样过程，而另设的线性头专门负责输出像素，从而避免「去噪输出必须同时充当最终像素」所带来的约束。这与把视频扩散整体提到像素空间的做法方向一致，但改动面更小。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers

Abstract

Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

1 Introduction

Latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023)] is the dominant recipe for image and video generation [(Esser et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024; Z-Image Team et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025)]. Typically, a diffusion transformer (DiT) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] generates in a compressed latent space, and a convolutional decoder [(Kingma & Welling, 2014; Esser et al., 2021)] maps the latents to pixels. The decoder complicates deployment and can add substantial inference cost. For example, on H100, generating a 5-second video with a 4-step Wan 1.3B model [(Zheng et al., 2026b)] takes 2.8 seconds for sampling and another 1.9 seconds for decoding, adding about 70% overhead. Recent work obtains much faster decoders with comparable quality [(Zhu et al., 2026; Kang & Kwak, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026)], suggesting that the decoder is largely redundant. This raises the question: what is the minimal network architecture for producing final pixels from a latent diffusion model?

We show that a simple linear head can replace the decoder while improving pixel quality. Our method, Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), finetunes a pretrained latent DiT by adding a linear output head (the DWD head) in parallel with the DiT’s original output layer (the denoising head). The denoising head continues to drive denoising steps, then the DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step only.

The dual-head separation distinguishes DWD from previous approaches, whose denoising output leads to final pixels: latent models decode it, pixel models output it directly. This couples pixel fidelity to denoising, causing a tradeoff between detail rendering and denoiser learnability [(Yao et al., 2025; Skorokhodov et al., 2025)]. DWD decouples the two roles: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses [(Esser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018)], while the denoising head is anchored to the frozen pretrained model to preserve sample content.

The separation is most evident on pixel diffusion models, where the denoising head already predicts the final output. These predictions smooth fine detail because they estimate conditional means under ℓ₂ loss. Applying perceptual losses directly to them [(Lin & Yang, 2023; Berrada Ifriqi et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026b)] risks collapsing sample diversity, as our shared-head ablation fails to improve FID (Table 1). In contrast, a separate head improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43.

We evaluate DWD across latent and pixel generators on ImageNet, text-to-image, and video generation (Fig. 1). Removing the decoder improves nearly all FID metrics across tested latent image models. On Wan [(Wang et al., 2025)] video, warping error drops by 23%, with visibly less detail distortion and flickering. On text-to-image pixel diffusion, DWD recovers photorealistic textures.

To summarize, we show that:

  • •

    A latent DiT needs no decoder: finetuning its last few blocks with an additional linear head suffices, reducing inference cost, improving ImageNet FIDs, and lessening detail distortion and flickering in Wan video.

  • •

    The dual-head separation also improves pixel diffusion models, producing better texture detail in text-to-image generation and a state-of-the-art ImageNet FID of 1.43 among pixel flow models.

    • 2 Related Work

    Latent-space diffusion. VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)] trains autoencoders with reconstruction, perceptual [(Zhang et al., 2018)], and adversarial [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] losses, and LDM [(Rombach et al., 2022)] uses this perceptual compression to reduce diffusion cost. VA-VAE [(Yao et al., 2025)], REPA-E [(Leng et al., 2025)], and RAE [(Zheng et al., 2026a)] address the gap between reconstruction quality and diffusability. DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025)] and Qwen-Image-VAE-2.0 [(Zhang et al., 2026)] increase spatial compression while preserving reconstruction fidelity. SSDD [(Vallaeys et al., 2025)] and PiD [(Lu et al., 2026)] replace conventional decoders with distilled pixel diffusion models. PiD and LTX-Video [(HaCohen et al., 2024)] also stop latent sampling early, letting the decoder complete the remaining denoising. [Zhang et al. (2024)] improve latent generators by applying losses to images produced through the VAE decoder. These approaches retain a standalone decoding network. DWD instead produces the final pixels through a linear head on the existing DiT, reusing its last-layer tokens and computation without an extra decoder.

    Pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion models denoise directly in pixel space without an autoencoder. They overcome difficulties in high-resolution generation through multiscale architectures and specialized output pathways [(Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a)], or improved prediction targets [(Li & He, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Zirvi et al., 2026)]. AsymFlow [(Chen et al., 2026a)] and L2P [(Chen et al., 2026d)] finetune pretrained latent models to perform denoising in pixel space, altering the flow trajectory and sample content (see Appendix B.4 for a comparison). In contrast, DWD preserves the original latent trajectory rather than converting the model to pixel diffusion. DWD finetuning is also more efficient, since only the last few transformer blocks and output heads are updated with shallow backpropagation, whereas latent-to-pixel conversion must backpropagate through the entire network to adapt to pixel-space inputs.

    3 Decoding Without a Decoder

    A pretrained latent DiT’s last-layer tokens already encode rich pixel information [(Gan et al., 2025; Akarken et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c)]: a least-squares linear projection recovers most of the image structure before any finetuning (Fig. 3). DWD exploits this by appending a linear head that produces final pixels directly from these tokens, bypassing the decoder at inference (Fig. 2(b)). Separating the pixel readout from the denoising output lets each be trained with its own objective: pixel quality losses for the DWD head, and trajectory anchoring to preserve denoising behavior.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    We describe latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)] using the flow matching convention [(Lipman et al., 2023)]. A pretrained autoencoder encodes an image or video x into a latent representation z₀. The forward process mixes the latent z₀ with Gaussian noise to form zₜ=(1-t)z₀+tε, where ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t∈[0,1] denotes diffusion time. A flow model (zₜ,t,c)↦û trains a network with extra conditioning c to estimate the conditional mean of velocity u\coloneqqε-z₀, using an ℓ₂ flow matching loss. At inference, the model uses this velocity to progressively transform Gaussian noise into a denoised latent sample ẑ₀, running from t=1 toward t=0[(Song et al., 2021; Liu, 2022; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023)]. Finally, the decoder maps ẑ₀ to the final image or video x.

    For the models studied here, the denoising network is a diffusion transformer (DiT) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024)], which processes tokenized noisy latent zₜ with multiple transformer blocks [(Vaswani et al., 2017)], and feeds the last-layer tokens h (after normalization and modulation) to a linear output head that produces a patch-wise denoising prediction. This is the denoising head, shown in Fig. 2(a).

    3.2 DWD head

    Our goal is to produce final pixels from a pretrained latent DiT without a decoder, subject to two constraints: minimal additional computation, and preservation of the pretrained denoising trajectory.

    A linear probe shows that the last-layer tokens h already support pixel reconstruction without finetuning, more accurately than probing the denoised latents ẑ₀, as shown in Fig. 3. The remaining reconstruction mismatch can be addressed by finetuning the DiT. This inspires us to adopt a simple linear DWD head that maps each token to a pixel patch:

    x̂ᵢ=Linear(hᵢ)=Whᵢ+b,

    		(1)

    where W and b are learnable weights and bias, and x̂ᵢ is the pixel patch corresponding to token hᵢ. This design places the DWD head in parallel with the denoising head, both reading the same last-layer tokens. The linear head is the minimal form of this separate pixel output, which can optionally be extended with a lightweight convolutional refiner (Appendix A.1). The predicted patches are then assembled into the final image or video x̂, with color space conversion where needed (Appendix A).

    Efficiency. By reusing the DiT’s nonlinear computation, the linear head is a lightweight readout with negligible cost for common pixel patch sizes. Pixel patch size follows the combined downsampling factor of the autoencoder and tokenizer. The most common spatial factor of 16 gives a 16×16×3 patch per token. For video models, an additional temporal factor of 4 expands each patch to four frames. For most tested models, the total number of output dimensions per token stays below the DiT’s hidden dimension.

    Separating denoising and pixel outputs. DWD achieves trajectory preservation and pixel rendering through a clear separation of outputs: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses, while the denoising head drives sampling and is anchored to the pretrained model (Sec. 3.3). This dual-head separation distinguishes our work from prior diffusion-based image and video generators, where the denoising output serves as a bottleneck pathway to final pixels.

    Final-step pixel rendering. The DWD head is only used at the final denoiser evaluation step, where the DiT input t is small but nonzero. The nonzero timestep is important: treating DiT–DWD as a latent decoder at t=0 substantially worsens quality (Sec. 4.1), while the t>0 noise gives the pixel head freedom to create detail that the denoised latent would have smoothed away. Classifier-free guidance [(Ho & Salimans, 2021)] is not used in the final step since its role is to steer the trajectory, whereas our final step does not advance the trajectory.

    3.3 Finetuning

    We finetune the last K transformer blocks (typically K=4–8 for large text-conditioned models, see Appendix A for details), both output heads, and the last modulation, keeping the prefix frozen. The timestep embedding MLP is shared across all blocks, so we duplicate its weights for the adapted blocks, allowing their modulations to be fully tuned without disturbing the frozen prefix. This restricts backpropagation to the end of the network and retains most pretrained parameters, making training up to 3× faster than full backpropagation.

    The training objective combines pixel quality with trajectory anchoring:

    L=Lₚᵢₓ+λLₜᵣₐⱼ,

    		(2)

    where λ is the trajectory anchoring weight (Appendix A). Both terms use noisy inputs zₜ encoded from real image data x, but their timesteps t are sampled separately to match the roles of the two outputs. The two losses are backpropagated before one optimizer step on accumulated gradients, so the last-layer tokens adapt for pixel quality while the denoising head’s prediction remains anchored to the pretrained model. The full training loop is shown in Algorithm 1.

    Pixel quality. The DWD head predicts the clean image under the L1 reconstruction, LPIPS perceptual, and adversarial objectives commonly used to train autoencoders [(Esser et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018; Goodfellow et al., 2014)]:

    Lₚᵢₓ=𝔼_x,z,c,t∼pₚᵢₓ[∥x̂-x∥₁+LPIPS(x̂,x)+ℓ_adv(x̂)],

    		(3)

    where pₚᵢₓ is typically uniform over [0.0,0.1] before timestep shifting [(Esser et al., 2024)], matching the small-t regime where the DWD head operates at inference. Following [Zheng et al. (2026a)] and [Singh et al. (2026)], the adversarial term uses the StyleGAN-T discriminator [(Sauer et al., 2023)] with adaptive gradient balancing, and is switched on only in the last stage of training (Appendix A).

    Trajectory anchoring. To preserve the pretrained denoising behavior as the final blocks adapt, we match the denoising head’s prediction to that of a frozen copy of the original model. Let û and û^ref denote the adapted and frozen reference velocity predictions for the same input. We minimize

    Lₜᵣₐⱼ=𝔼_x,z,c,t∼pₜᵣₐⱼ[∥û-û^ref∥₂²],

    		(4)

    where pₜᵣₐⱼ is typically uniform over [0.04,1.0] before timestep shifting, covering the intermediate denoising steps. Both the original and finetuned models share a single forward pass through the frozen prefix: only the final K blocks and output components run separately, avoiding two full-model passes.

    3.4 Extension to pixel diffusion and few-step models

    Pixel diffusion models. The quality benefit of the dual-head separation is most pronounced on pixel diffusion models, which have no decoder to confound the comparison. We still add a DWD head in parallel with the denoising head, treating pixel denoising the same as the latent case. The training objectives are unchanged except for a stronger anchoring weight. Fewer tunable blocks and a shorter training schedule suffice, since the DiT already has pixel knowledge. Details are in Appendix A.

    Few-step latent models. Few-step distilled models [(Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Sauer et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026c)] are the practical frontier of fast generation, where the fixed decoding cost takes a proportionally larger share of inference time. Validating DWD here therefore has direct practical significance. A simple adaptation is to adjust pₚᵢₓ and pₜᵣₐⱼ to cover new ranges around the timesteps used by the few-step sampler. More variants are discussed in Appendix B.2 and B.5.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 ImageNet generation

    We show that DWD consistently improves FID across both latent and pixel baselines. We then ablate the separate head design and show that fusing the two heads degrades quality despite the same training losses, and also study the effect of head capacity and final timestep.

    Setup. We test two latent models, SiT-XL/2-REPA [(Ma et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025)] with the SD-VAE decoder [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and SiT-XL/2-REPA-E [(Leng et al., 2025)] with its end-to-end tuned E2E-VA-VAE decoder [(Yao et al., 2025)], and two pixel models, JiT-H/16 [(Li & He, 2026)] and AnisoFlow-H/16 [(Zirvi et al., 2026)]. DWD extensions are finetuned on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], with training schedules detailed in Appendix A.2. We report FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and Inception Score (IS) [(Salimans et al., 2016)] under the ADM evaluation protocol [(Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021)].

    Improvement over latent diffusion baselines. Removing the decoder improves both latent baselines (Table 1): FID improves from 1.38 to 1.36 for REPA and from 1.12 to 1.06 for REPA-E, with IS improving as well. The two baselines use different latent spaces and decoders, yet a linear head improves on both. Removing the decoder also saves 622 decoder GFLOPs for REPA, 2.6× the cost of a single denoiser evaluation, and 252 decoder GFLOPs for REPA-E.

    Improvement over pixel diffusion baselines. The pixel models have no decoder to remove, so DWD only adds a second output trained with pixel quality losses. As shown in Table 1, DWD improves JiT from 1.90 to 1.85 FID and AnisoFlow from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models, while raising IS by 3–5 points. This also narrows the FID gap between pixel and latent models on ImageNet.

    Separate head vs. shared head. The pixel-model gains have two sources: the pixel quality losses, which latent decoders are trained with but pixel models normally lack, and the separate head that receives them. The w/o separate head rows in Table 1 isolate the latter by fusing the two heads in both training and inference, so the denoising head receives both pixel losses and trajectory anchoring at their respective timesteps, with everything else unchanged. This degrades baseline FID (1.55 to 1.71 for AnisoFlow), so the losses alone do not account for the gain. The degradation reflects a conflict: the ℓ₂ denoising loss favors mode coverage, whereas LPIPS and adversarial losses favor perceptual quality but collapse diversity (better IS but worse FID than the baseline). Trajectory anchoring cannot fully counteract this interference, so the pixel losses need a separate head.

    Linear vs. convolutional head. We ablate the capacity of the linear DWD head by adding a small convolutional residual refiner conditioned on the linear prediction and the last-layer tokens (DWD-conv; Appendix A). This extension brings no consistent improvement across the ImageNet models in Table 1. A linear head therefore suffices to obtain the quality gains under our tested settings.

    Nonzero final timestep. Fig. 4 sweeps the final timestep at which the DWD head is evaluated. Quality degrades toward t=0, where the input is the fully denoised state a decoder would receive, and recovers at a small positive timestep. This shows that the DWD head needs a partially denoised input to produce high-quality pixels, rather than mimicking a decoder applied to a clean state.

    4.2 Text-to-image generation

    We show that DWD replaces the decoder with matched quality on latent baselines, including a few-step distilled model, and recovers photorealistic texture detail on the pixel baseline. We also ablate the adversarial loss to show that it is not critical on text-to-image generation.

    Setup. We test two latent models built on FLUX.2 klein 9B [(Black Forest Labs, 2025)], the 32-step Base model and its distilled 4-step variant, and one pixel model, AnisoFlow-L/16-T2I [(Zirvi et al., 2026)] (0.9B). All DWD extensions are finetuned on public real-image datasets [(Wang et al., 2026a; Desai et al., 2021; Schuhmann et al., 2022)] at mixed aspect ratios. We evaluate at 1024×1024 on COCO-10k [(Lin et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2024)] (FID, patch FID (pFID) [(Lin et al., 2024)], HPSv3 [(Ma et al., 2025)], HPSv2.1 [(Wu et al., 2023)]), OneIG-Bench [(Chang et al., 2025)], and LongText-Bench [(Wu et al., 2025)]. Training and sampling details are in Appendix A.

    Decoder removal without quality loss. On FLUX.2 klein Base, DWD and the baseline are effectively tied on every metric in Table 2, and same-seed samples are nearly indistinguishable (Fig. 5(a)). This is expected: the FLUX.2 latent is much wider than those of other VAEs, with 128 latent dimensions per token for a 768-dimensional pixel patch, compared with 64 for a 3072-dimensional patch in Wan, so decoding from it is easy, leaving little room for improvement. The result nevertheless shows that a linear head can replace it, removing 10.47 TFLOPs of decoder computation per image.

    Compatibility with few-step model. The distilled 4-step FLUX.2 klein tests the few-step regime, where the decoder takes a larger share of the total inference cost. With only the timestep ranges adjusted (Appendix A.2), DWD is again effectively tied with the baseline in Table 2 and visually indistinguishable in Fig. 5(a), even though its final step operates at a much larger timestep (t=0.7 after shifting) than in the 32-step model.

    Improved detail over pixel diffusion baseline. Pixel diffusion models tend to fall short of latent models in very fine texture, even with very large denoisers [(Cai et al., 2026)] or AnisoFlow’s improved parameterization [(Zirvi et al., 2026)]. With a linear head and 3k finetuning iterations, DWD recovers photorealistic skin, hair, foliage, and cloud detail while preserving composition (Fig. 1(b), Fig. 4(b), Fig. 5(b)). The gain also shows up in the low-level metrics in Table 2: COCO FID improves from 28.86 to 27.54 and pFID from 36.59 to 32.26, the latter showing a more significant improvement due to its sensitivity to fine detail. The remaining higher-level metrics are effectively tied, as the trajectory is preserved.

    Adversarial loss. Without the adversarial loss (Table 2), FLUX.2 klein and AnisoFlow’s DWD extensions stay close to full DWD on most metrics, except that pFID worsens more noticeably, though still close to or outperforming the baseline. The adversarial loss is thus helpful but not critical, in line with recent decoder research that drops it [(Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026)].

    4.3 Text-to-video generation

    We apply DWD to the Wan2.1 14B video model, where each token must predict 4 frames rather than a single image patch. Despite this harder setting, DWD not only removes the decoder but visibly reduces distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by at least 23%.

    Setup. We finetune Wan2.1 T2V 14B [(Wang et al., 2025)] on Vchitect T2V DataVerse [(Fan et al., 2025)] clips at mixed 360p, 480p, and 720p resolutions, all downsampled from sources of at least 720p to obtain sharper real pixels (Appendix A.2). We evaluate 81-frame 832×480 generations on extended VBench prompts [(Huang et al., 2024)] from [Huang et al. (2025)] and report warping error [(Lai et al., 2018)], frame-level HPSv3 and HPSv2.1, and seven VBench quality dimensions. For both the baseline and DWD, we additionally evaluate a quantized model with FP8 weights and activations (W8A8) and 8-bit SageAttention2 kernels [(Zhang et al., 2025)], which better reflects efficient deployment settings.

    Decoder removal with reduced distortion and flickering. DWD removes the 0.28-PFLOP Wan decoder and replaces it with a linear head at negligible cost (Table 3), while also improving visual quality. The baseline decoder distorts fine detail such as small text and dense structures, and the distortion changes from frame to frame, which appears as flicker (Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 6). With the decoder removed, the linear DWD head keeps these details stable and legible, noticeably reducing flickering (see the project page for video comparisons). Warping error captures this artifact directly: it aligns consecutive frames by optical flow, masks occlusions, and measures the remaining photometric error, which DWD reduces by 23% (1.52 to 1.18) in Table 3. VBench’s temporal flickering score is less suitable here, since it is the raw pixel difference between consecutive frames without accounting for residual motion, and it saturates near its maximum for both models. The remaining VBench dimensions and HPS metrics are effectively tied, except for a slightly lower dynamic degree, though qualitative results show no visible motion reduction. A decoder finetuned on the same data with the same pixel losses reduces warping error only to 1.39 (Table 3 and Appendix B.1), so most of the gain comes from DWD rather than from the training data.

    8-bit inference. Quantization degrades the baseline noticeably (warping error 1.52 to 1.69) but barely affects DWD (1.18 to 1.20), widening the warping error gap to 29% in Table 3. The other metrics follow the same pattern as under BF16. The DWD extension is thus robust to reduced-precision inference, and the quality gain over the decoder is larger in the deployment setting.

    5 Conclusion

    DWD replaces the decoder with a linear pixel head on the diffusion transformer, finetuning only the last few blocks and output heads. Across latent image and video generators, DWD preserves or improves pixel quality while removing the decoder entirely. On video, this visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering. On pixel diffusion models, a separate DWD head recovers photorealistic texture that the denoising head oversmooths. The broader lesson is that final pixel prediction should be separated from intermediate denoising, so that pixel-space objectives can improve quality without interfering with the sampling trajectory.

    Limitations. The DWD quality gain shrinks when the decoder is already strong, as on FLUX.2. We have not proved that the linear head is sufficient for spatial patch sizes beyond 16×16 pixels, where a stronger head like DWD-conv may be needed. Also, we have not tuned the pixel losses per model, leaving potential room for improvement.

    AI Use Statement

    In this work, we used generative AI tools (LLM-based assistants) to edit the paper for grammar and readability and to accelerate the implementation of our experiments. All AI-assisted work was reviewed and verified by the authors, and we take responsibility for the final content of this paper.

    Reproducibility Statement

    Appendix A gives the implementation details: the head and its initialization (Appendix A.1), the per-model finetuning settings and training data (Appendix A.2 and Table 4), the inference procedure (Appendix A.3), the video evaluation protocol (Appendix A.4), and the parameter and FLOP accounting (Appendix A.5).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    This section complements Sec. 3 with the specifics of the DWD head, finetuning, inference, and evaluation, with per-model settings collected in Table 4.

    A.1 DWD Head

    Output format. The linear head maps each last-layer token to one pixel patch, and the patches are assembled into the image. Image models use 16×16 patches. Wan uses 4×16×16 spatiotemporal patches and a separate 1×16×16 head for the first latent frame, which covers a single pixel frame in the Wan VAE. Following AsymFlow [(Chen et al., 2026a)], latent models and AnisoFlow-L/16-T2I predict pixels in normalized Oklab color space [(Ottosson, 2020)], while the pixel quality losses are applied to the converted RGB values, matching the common autoencoder training recipe. The ImageNet pixel models predict RGB directly, matching their native output.

    Least-squares initialization. The head is initialized by linear regression from last-layer tokens to ground-truth pixel patches. We run the frozen pretrained model on 10k training images with timesteps drawn from pₚᵢₓ, the same distribution used for the pixel losses, and solve the normal equations for the weight and bias jointly. The same procedure produces the probes in Fig. 3, where the latent probe regresses from the denoised latent instead of the tokens.

    Convolutional head (DWD-conv). The DWD-conv ablation keeps the linear head and adds a residual correction, following lightweight super-resolution networks [(Shi et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2018; Ayazoglu, 2021)]: the nonlinear convolutions run at half resolution, a final sub-pixel convolution (pixel shuffle) restores the full resolution, and the branch predicts a residual over a linear base prediction. It packs each 2×2 neighborhood of the linear pixel prediction into channels and refines this packed grid with a convolutional branch. The last-layer tokens are projected through a 128-dimensional bottleneck and expanded into a 32-channel spatial feature map, which is added to a 1×1 projection of the packed pixels. Two residual blocks with 3×3 convolutions and SiLU activations predict the correction through a zero-initialized output convolution, so the head starts as the linear head. For video, the convolutions operate on each frame independently.

    A.2 Finetuning
