为什么值得看：数字人与角色的质量瓶颈常常不在建模，而在贴图分辨率：1K 反照率在特写下必然糊，位移分辨率不够则轮廓就假。把超分按「UV 统计 + 高度场误差」专门调优，比拿通用照片超分硬套靠谱得多。

中文摘要：基于物理的面部资产在电影级特写中需要 4K 的反照率与位移贴图，但生成式管线通常只产出 1K 分辨率。直接把摄影超分模型套过来并不合适：面部 UV 贴图具有领域特有的统计特性，而位移贴图是一个标量高度场，其误差会直接扭曲几何形状。这篇因此提出一个针对该领域调优的扩散超分器，把面部资产贴图做 4 倍放大（1024 到 4096）。对数字人与角色资产管线，这解决的是「特写一放大就糊、轮廓一细看就假」这个最实际的瓶颈。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps

© cc

Abstract.

Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4× (1024→4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.

Keywords:

facial assets, UV texture maps, displacement maps, texture super-resolution, diffusion models, domain adaptation ††cc-license: by-nc-nd

1. Introduction

In modern digital-human workflows, physically based facial assets are represented by spatially registered UV maps, including an albedo map for diffuse surface color and a displacement map for mesoscopic geometry such as pores, fine expression lines, and micro-wrinkles. Close-up rendering requires these maps at 4K resolution, yet generative pipelines often produce only 1K outputs that must be upscaled before production use.

Applying an off-the-shelf image super-resolution (SR) model to these maps is a poor fit. Albedo UV layouts contain seams, charts, and near-uniform regions whose statistics differ substantially from natural photographs. More fundamentally, displacement is a single-channel scalar height field dominated by high-frequency skin micro-structure, so photographic SR models can hallucinate visually plausible but geometrically incorrect relief.

We address this mismatch through lightweight in-domain adaptation rather than a new SR architecture. For each modality, we adapt a frozen SDXL latent-diffusion backbone [(Podell et al., 2024; Rombach et al., 2022)] as an image-to-image upscaler using LoRA modules [(Hu et al., 2022)] on the UNet and a Tile ControlNet [(Zhang et al., 2023)] conditioned on the low-resolution map. This preserves the input structure while restoring domain-specific pore- and wrinkle-scale detail, with particular benefit for displacement, where generic photographic priors are most mismatched.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for facial UV assets that handles both RGB albedo and scalar displacement using lightweight adaptation of a frozen backbone.

  • •

    A modality-specific displacement formulation that preserves the native geometric range in the latent path while providing a [0,1] image condition to the Tile ControlNet.

  • •

    A held-out evaluation showing sharper, more perceptually faithful 4K facial asset maps than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers.

    • 2. Related Work

    Image super-resolution and diffusion priors.

    Single-image super-resolution has moved from CNN- and GAN-based restorers to diffusion priors: Real-ESRGAN [(Wang et al., 2021)] uses adversarial training with synthetic degradations, while SR3 [(Saharia et al., 2023)], StableSR [(Wang et al., 2024)], and DiffBIR [(Lin et al., 2024)] synthesize detail from generative priors. Their natural-image assumptions, however, are mismatched to our setting: facial UV asset maps contain seams, charts, and non-photographic statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field rather than an RGB appearance map. We keep the pretrained-prior advantage of diffusion SR while adapting it to this production asset domain.

    Controllable and parameter-efficient diffusion.

    Latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and SDXL [(Podell et al., 2024)] provide strong high-resolution image priors, ControlNet [(Zhang et al., 2023)] adds spatial conditioning for image-to-image refinement, and LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] enables lightweight backbone adaptation. We combine these in a targeted way: a frozen SDXL prior, Tile ControlNet to preserve the low-resolution UV structure, and per-modality LoRA adapters specializing the model for albedo and displacement.

    UV texture and material-map generation.

    Recent work applies 2D generative priors to UV-space texture and material synthesis [(Richardson et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Youwang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024)], and DECA [(Feng et al., 2021)] stresses the role of UV-space facial appearance and mesoscopic detail. Most closely, PBR-SR [(Chen et al., 2025)] super-resolves PBR texture maps through a zero-shot differentiable-rendering optimization loop; we instead target facial albedo and displacement with a lightweight in-domain upscaler that needs no per-asset optimization at inference.

    3. Method

    Our goal is to super-resolve a facial UV map from 1024×1024 to 4096×4096 (4×) for both albedo and displacement; we train one model per modality. Given a low-resolution map y, we bilinearly upsample it to the target resolution, ỹ=U(y), and refine it with a domain-tuned image-to-image diffusion model rather than synthesizing from scratch.

    3.1. Image-to-image diffusion upscaler

    We use a pretrained SDXL [(Podell et al., 2024)] latent-diffusion backbone [(Rombach et al., 2022)] as a frozen generative prior, with its base UNet weights, VAE, and text encoders frozen and adaptation performed only through low-rank (LoRA) modules [(Hu et al., 2022)]. At training time, the ground-truth high-resolution map x is VAE-encoded to z₀; we sample a timestep t, add noise to obtain zₜ, and train the LoRA-adapted UNet to predict the added noise, conditioned on the aligned upsampled input. At inference time, we instead encode ỹ, add noise to a start step determined by the image-to-image strength, and denoise from there, so the model refines ỹ rather than generating from noise. A Tile ControlNet [(Zhang et al., 2023)], initialized from pretrained Tile weights with frozen base weights and trained rank-16 LoRA adapters, supplies spatial conditioning from ỹ. This keeps the output tied to the input UV layout while the diffusion prior restores in-domain detail.

    3.2. Handling albedo and displacement

    Albedo is a three-channel RGB map in [0,1], encoded using the standard VAE preprocessing that maps it to [-1,1]. Displacement is a single-channel scalar height field: a fixed global scale maps it to [-1,1], after which it is replicated across three channels for the image VAE. We avoid per-image photographic normalization so that the latent input preserves the field’s scalar range and ordering. Because the pretrained Tile ControlNet expects a [0,1] image condition, we separately remap the displacement field to [0,1] for conditioning. Displacement therefore uses one representation for latent denoising and another for spatial conditioning. After decoding, the three predicted channels are averaged into a scalar map and remapped to the original range.

    3.3. Training and inference details

    We train for 5,000 steps with an L₁ noise-prediction loss under Min-SNR weighting (γ=5), using AdamW, an effective batch size of 8, and a cosine learning-rate schedule (300 warmup steps, peak 5×10⁻⁴, floor 10⁻⁵). The UNet uses rank-64 LoRA adapters, while the Tile ControlNet uses rank-16 adapters at conditioning scale 0.5. Each 4096² target is paired with a 1024² input obtained by area-downsampling the 4K map by 4. To make 4K training tractable, we cache each map’s VAE latent posterior and sample a 128² latent tile per step, corresponding to a 1024² pixel region, together with the aligned crop from the upsampled input, so the VAE is not invoked during training. At inference, we refine ỹ with 50 DPM-Solver++ steps at strength 0.5 and no classifier-free guidance. Tiled VAE encoding and decoding process the full 4096² map, while the UNet denoises the full latent in one pass, avoiding sliding-window seams.

    3.4. Albedo chroma preservation

    For production albedo, we add a deterministic post-decode step to preserve captured surface color. We convert the decoded albedo and upsampled low-resolution input to CIELAB, retain the decoded luminance (L), replace its opponent-color channels (a,b) with those of the input, and convert back to RGB. Because chromatic variation is dominated by low frequencies, this anchors surface color to the captured reference while retaining synthesized luminance detail. This step applies only to albedo.

    4. Results

    Evaluation protocol.

    We evaluate on 100 held-out maps disjoint from training, super-resolving each modality from 1024² to 4096² against 4K ground-truth maps from a 28-camera 12MP rig. For albedo, we report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. For displacement, we also report a detail-band score. After subtracting a Gaussian-smoothed version of each map (σ=2 px at 4096), we measure the predicted-to-ground-truth detail-energy ratio (1.0 = correct magnitude) and Pearson correlation with the ground-truth detail band (1.0 = perfect structural agreement).

    Baselines.

    We compare each modality against bilinear upsampling, which initializes our pipeline; Real-ESRGAN [(Wang et al., 2021)]; and the pretrained Stable Diffusion ×4 upscaler [(Rombach et al., 2022)]. Both learned baselines are used off-the-shelf, isolating the benefit of domain tuning. Displacement is mapped to [0,1] and replicated across three channels. All albedo methods use the same CIELAB chroma-preservation step (Sec. 3.4).

    Quantitative results.

    Table 1 confirms that off-the-shelf super-resolvers are poorly matched to this asset domain. Real-ESRGAN underperforms bilinear on standard fidelity metrics for both modalities, suppressing albedo detail and distorting fine displacement relief. SD (×4) restores more high-frequency content, but its grainy, off-domain texture produces the weakest albedo scores (LPIPS 0.49, SSIM 0.77). Ours reduces perceptual error and more closely matches the captured appearance (Fig. 3).

    PSNR and SSIM provide limited discrimination because their low-frequency bias rewards smooth interpolation. Ours remains comparable to bilinear on these metrics (albedo 35.7/0.94; displacement 35.9/0.91 vs. 36.2/0.93), while reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08. For displacement, bilinear preserves alignment (correlation 0.61) but recovers only 46% of ground-truth detail energy. Off-the-shelf models overshoot the energy magnitude (1.15–1.26) with lower correlation (0.33–0.36). Ours recovers nearly the correct energy (97%) while preserving bilinear-level alignment (0.61). Since the 1K input does not determine skin micro-structure, these results demonstrate structural consistency rather than pixel-exact pore reconstruction.

    5. Discussion and Conclusion

    We presented a domain-specific latent-diffusion upscaler that super-resolves facial albedo and displacement maps from 1024×1024 to 4096×4096 by adapting a frozen SDXL backbone with lightweight LoRA modules and a Tile ControlNet conditioned on the low-resolution input. Faithful 4× upscaling needs no custom SR architecture: in-domain adaptation with modality-specific handling produces sharper, more faithful 4K asset maps than off-the-shelf photograph-trained super-resolvers, particularly for scalar displacement, and outputs render-ready maps in the asset UV layout without per-asset optimization. The contribution is this domain recipe—image-to-image initialization, Tile ControlNet, and scalar displacement handling—not a new super-resolution architecture.

    Limitations.

    Our evaluation uses held-out maps from a single capture pipeline at a fixed 4× factor; robustness across capture conditions, scan qualities, and other scale factors remains untested, and a different factor would require retraining. We train separate models for albedo and displacement and do not treat specular, roughness, or normal maps, nor do we enforce cross-map consistency beyond the shared UV layout. Because a 1K input does not uniquely determine skin micro-structure, recovered displacement is structurally consistent rather than pixel-exact. We target production upscaling of 1K generative or archived maps; cinematic VFX close-ups may still need artist review.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Single-image super-resolution has moved from CNN- and GAN-based restorers to diffusion priors: Real-ESRGAN [(Wang et al., 2021)] uses adversarial training with synthetic degradations, while SR3 [(Saharia et al., 2023)], StableSR [(Wang et al., 2024)], and DiffBIR [(Lin et al., 2024)] synthesize detail from generative priors. Their natural-image assumptions, however, are mismatched to our setting: facial UV asset maps contain seams, charts, and non-photographic statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field rather than an RGB appearance map. We keep the pretrained-prior advantage of diffusion SR while adapting it to this production asset domain.

    Controllable and parameter-efficient diffusion.

    Latent diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and SDXL [(Podell et al., 2024)] provide strong high-resolution image priors, ControlNet [(Zhang et al., 2023)] adds spatial conditioning for image-to-image refinement, and LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] enables lightweight backbone adaptation. We combine these in a targeted way: a frozen SDXL prior, Tile ControlNet to preserve the low-resolution UV structure, and per-modality LoRA adapters specializing the model for albedo and displacement.

    UV texture and material-map generation.

    Recent work applies 2D generative priors to UV-space texture and material synthesis [(Richardson et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Youwang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024)], and DECA [(Feng et al., 2021)] stresses the role of UV-space facial appearance and mesoscopic detail. Most closely, PBR-SR [(Chen et al., 2025)] super-resolves PBR texture maps through a zero-shot differentiable-rendering optimization loop; we instead target facial albedo and displacement with a lightweight in-domain upscaler that needs no per-asset optimization at inference.

    3. Method

    Our goal is to super-resolve a facial UV map from 1024×1024 to 4096×4096 (4×) for both albedo and displacement; we train one model per modality. Given a low-resolution map y, we bilinearly upsample it to the target resolution, ỹ=U(y), and refine it with a domain-tuned image-to-image diffusion model rather than synthesizing from scratch.

    3.1. Image-to-image diffusion upscaler

    We use a pretrained SDXL [(Podell et al., 2024)] latent-diffusion backbone [(Rombach et al., 2022)] as a frozen generative prior, with its base UNet weights, VAE, and text encoders frozen and adaptation performed only through low-rank (LoRA) modules [(Hu et al., 2022)]. At training time, the ground-truth high-resolution map x is VAE-encoded to z₀; we sample a timestep t, add noise to obtain zₜ, and train the LoRA-adapted UNet to predict the added noise, conditioned on the aligned upsampled input. At inference time, we instead encode ỹ, add noise to a start step determined by the image-to-image strength, and denoise from there, so the model refines ỹ rather than generating from noise. A Tile ControlNet [(Zhang et al., 2023)], initialized from pretrained Tile weights with frozen base weights and trained rank-16 LoRA adapters, supplies spatial conditioning from ỹ. This keeps the output tied to the input UV layout while the diffusion prior restores in-domain detail.

    3.2. Handling albedo and displacement

    Albedo is a three-channel RGB map in [0,1], encoded using the standard VAE preprocessing that maps it to [-1,1]. Displacement is a single-channel scalar height field: a fixed global scale maps it to [-1,1], after which it is replicated across three channels for the image VAE. We avoid per-image photographic normalization so that the latent input preserves the field’s scalar range and ordering. Because the pretrained Tile ControlNet expects a [0,1] image condition, we separately remap the displacement field to [0,1] for conditioning. Displacement therefore uses one representation for latent denoising and another for spatial conditioning. After decoding, the three predicted channels are averaged into a scalar map and remapped to the original range.

    3.3. Training and inference details

    We train for 5,000 steps with an L₁ noise-prediction loss under Min-SNR weighting (γ=5), using AdamW, an effective batch size of 8, and a cosine learning-rate schedule (300 warmup steps, peak 5×10⁻⁴, floor 10⁻⁵). The UNet uses rank-64 LoRA adapters, while the Tile ControlNet uses rank-16 adapters at conditioning scale 0.5. Each 4096² target is paired with a 1024² input obtained by area-downsampling the 4K map by 4. To make 4K training tractable, we cache each map’s VAE latent posterior and sample a 128² latent tile per step, corresponding to a 1024² pixel region, together with the aligned crop from the upsampled input, so the VAE is not invoked during training. At inference, we refine ỹ with 50 DPM-Solver++ steps at strength 0.5 and no classifier-free guidance. Tiled VAE encoding and decoding process the full 4096² map, while the UNet denoises the full latent in one pass, avoiding sliding-window seams.

    3.4. Albedo chroma preservation

    For production albedo, we add a deterministic post-decode step to preserve captured surface color. We convert the decoded albedo and upsampled low-resolution input to CIELAB, retain the decoded luminance (L), replace its opponent-color channels (a,b) with those of the input, and convert back to RGB. Because chromatic variation is dominated by low frequencies, this anchors surface color to the captured reference while retaining synthesized luminance detail. This step applies only to albedo.

    4. Results

    Evaluation protocol.

    We evaluate on 100 held-out maps disjoint from training, super-resolving each modality from 1024² to 4096² against 4K ground-truth maps from a 28-camera 12MP rig. For albedo, we report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. For displacement, we also report a detail-band score. After subtracting a Gaussian-smoothed version of each map (σ=2 px at 4096), we measure the predicted-to-ground-truth detail-energy ratio (1.0 = correct magnitude) and Pearson correlation with the ground-truth detail band (1.0 = perfect structural agreement).

    Baselines.

    We compare each modality against bilinear upsampling, which initializes our pipeline; Real-ESRGAN [(Wang et al., 2021)]; and the pretrained Stable Diffusion ×4 upscaler [(Rombach et al., 2022)]. Both learned baselines are used off-the-shelf, isolating the benefit of domain tuning. Displacement is mapped to [0,1] and replicated across three channels. All albedo methods use the same CIELAB chroma-preservation step (Sec. 3.4).

    Quantitative results.

    Table 1 confirms that off-the-shelf super-resolvers are poorly matched to this asset domain. Real-ESRGAN underperforms bilinear on standard fidelity metrics for both modalities, suppressing albedo detail and distorting fine displacement relief. SD (×4) restores more high-frequency content, but its grainy, off-domain texture produces the weakest albedo scores (LPIPS 0.49, SSIM 0.77). Ours reduces perceptual error and more closely matches the captured appearance (Fig. 3).

    PSNR and SSIM provide limited discrimination because their low-frequency bias rewards smooth interpolation. Ours remains comparable to bilinear on these metrics (albedo 35.7/0.94; displacement 35.9/0.91 vs. 36.2/0.93), while reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08. For displacement, bilinear preserves alignment (correlation 0.61) but recovers only 46% of ground-truth detail energy. Off-the-shelf models overshoot the energy magnitude (1.15–1.26) with lower correlation (0.33–0.36). Ours recovers nearly the correct energy (97%) while preserving bilinear-level alignment (0.61). Since the 1K input does not determine skin micro-structure, these results demonstrate structural consistency rather than pixel-exact pore reconstruction.

    5. Discussion and Conclusion

    We presented a domain-specific latent-diffusion upscaler that super-resolves facial albedo and displacement maps from 1024×1024 to 4096×4096 by adapting a frozen SDXL backbone with lightweight LoRA modules and a Tile ControlNet conditioned on the low-resolution input. Faithful 4× upscaling needs no custom SR architecture: in-domain adaptation with modality-specific handling produces sharper, more faithful 4K asset maps than off-the-shelf photograph-trained super-resolvers, particularly for scalar displacement, and outputs render-ready maps in the asset UV layout without per-asset optimization. The contribution is this domain recipe—image-to-image initialization, Tile ControlNet, and scalar displacement handling—not a new super-resolution architecture.

    Limitations.

    Our evaluation uses held-out maps from a single capture pipeline at a fixed 4× factor; robustness across capture conditions, scan qualities, and other scale factors remains untested, and a different factor would require retraining. We train separate models for albedo and displacement and do not treat specular, roughness, or normal maps, nor do we enforce cross-map consistency beyond the shared UV layout. Because a 1K input does not uniquely determine skin micro-structure, recovered displacement is structurally consistent rather than pixel-exact. We target production upscaling of 1K generative or archived maps; cinematic VFX close-ups may still need artist review.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 动作数据里没有力：ForceBody 把「带力矩不确定性的力」和参数化人体动作配对起来 ｜ ForceBody: Force-Paired Parametric Body Motion with Torque Uncertainty
item.description:
一句话：力和力矩驱动人体运动，但学习式动作管线里通常根本没有它们。

要点：

  • 缺口：力与力矩是驱动人体运动的本源，在生物力学、机器人与**物理感知动画**里都关键，但在基于学习的动作重建与生成管线里**通常缺失**
  • 已有带力标注的数据集也不够用：其配对的动作序列与现代学习管线使用的**参数化人体模型不兼容**；此外既有数据集在关节力矩的获取方式上也有局限
  • ForceBody 因此提供「配对的力 + 参数化人体动作」，并把**力矩不确定性**一并标注

为什么值得看：物理感知动画要「有重量感」，就必须有力。把力与参数化人体（SMPL 系）对齐、还带不确定性，这条补的是数据基础——没有它，物理驱动角色只能靠手调。

中文摘要：力与力矩是驱动物体运动的根本量，在生物力学、机器人学以及物理感知的动画中都至关重要，然而在基于学习的运动重建与生成管线里，它们通常是缺失的。已有部分数据集提供力标注，但其配对的动作序列与现代学习管线所用的参数化人体模型并不兼容；此外这些数据集在关节力矩的获取方式上也存在局限。ForceBody 因此提供与力配对参数化人体运动，并同时标注力矩的不确定性。对希望让角色动作「有重量感」的物理驱动动画来说，这条补的是数据基础——缺少力的标注，控制器只能靠手调增益。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

ForceBody: Force-Paired Parametric Body Motion with Torque Uncertainty

Abstract

Forces and torques drive human motion, central to biomechanics, robotics, and physics-aware animation, yet they are often absent from learning-based motion pipelines for body reconstruction and generation. Some motion datasets provide force annotations, but the paired motion sequences are incompatible with the parametric body models used in modern learning pipelines. In addition, existing datasets typically obtain joint torques through inverse dynamics, which is inherently sensitive to the quality of the input kinematics; however, they do not quantify the reliability of these torque estimates. We close this gap with ForceBody, the first dataset to bring ground truth force supervision into a parametric body representation, shipped with per-sample torque uncertainty. ForceBody pairs the SKEL body model with ground reaction forces and inverse-dynamics joint torques across 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects. Each torque label is paired with a per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotation obtained by Monte Carlo sampling through the inverse dynamics pipeline. We benchmark six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) on ground reaction force and joint torque prediction from SKEL motion. As one example use of the released uncertainty, finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces the MAE of joint torque estimation by 5%. Code and data are at https://github.com/DominoAI-Lab/ForceBody-NeurIPS-ED-2026.

1 Introduction

Capturing human motion in 3D body pose and shape has become increasingly prevalent with recent advances in computer vision, computer graphics, and deep learning [49, 36, 44]. Nonetheless, the forces, including joint torques and ground reaction forces (GRF), that produce the motion are primarily absent from the estimation. These physical signals are critical to applications ranging from biomechanical assessment [11, 13] to exoskeleton and prosthetic design [22] and sports performance analysis [12]. Concurrent efforts tackle this limitation by incorporating dynamics into learning-based motion estimation, but progress is bottlenecked on two fronts. On the training side, dynamics is typically incorporated via external simulators rather than end-to-end learning. On the evaluation side, metrics rely on kinematic surrogate of physics plausibility, e.g., motion smoothness [47], motion replay stability [50], rather than the dynamic quantities themselves. Both limitations trace to the same root cause: real-world force annotations are unavailable in parametric body representations. Closing this gap requires a force-paired parametric body dataset, where forces are derived from measurements, in a form learning-based body motion pipelines can directly consume.

The AddBiomechanics (AddB) dataset [42, 41] is the largest publicly available collection of human motion paired with measured GRF and inverse-dynamics torques, aggregating 15 sources of motion-and-force data. Its motion, however, is provided as marker trajectories (i.e., 3D positions of motion-capture markers placed on the body) rather than the parametric body parameters (e.g., SMPL [20], SKEL [15]) native to motion reconstruction and generation pipelines. Prior attempts to pair parametric body models with physical labels remain limited. GroundLink [8] provides force-plate-measured GRF alongside SMPL motion but is small in scale and does not include joint torques. ImDy [18] applies physics simulation to SMPL motion from AMASS [21] to produce forces and torques at scale, but its labels are simulator outputs rather than physically measured. As a result, no existing dataset offers measured forces in a parametric body representation.

The reliability of torque annotations poses a further challenge. Joint torques cannot be directly measured. They are computed through inverse dynamics from motion kinematics and external forces such as GRF [43]. Inverse dynamics is inherently sensitive to kinematic noise: small positional perturbations at the input can propagate and yield large deviations in estimated torques [37, 31, 32]. This uncertainty is intrinsic to any dataset that derives torques from inverse dynamics, AddBiomechanics [42] included. Yet no existing force dataset releases per-sample torque reliability annotations.

This paper presents ForceBody (see Fig. 1), a large-scale dataset that aligns biomechanical force measurements from AddBiomechanics [41] with a parametric body model, and provides uncertainty annotations for every torque label. Our contributions are:

  • •

    A force-paired parametric body dataset. ForceBody comprises 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects, with per-trial SKEL poses, per-subject body shape parameters, and associated measured GRF and joint torques. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset to pair large-scale measured forces with a parametric body model.

  • •

    Per-sample uncertainty annotations. We provide per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotations for every joint torque label, derived from Monte Carlo sampling through inverse dynamics. This makes ForceBody the first force dataset to ship with annotated uncertainty.

  • •

    Reference baselines for force prediction. We evaluate six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) on the tasks of ground reaction force and joint torque prediction from SKEL motion. As one example use of our uncertainty annotation, finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces joint torque MAE by 5%.

    • 2 Related Work

    Datasets with Force Annotation

    Motion datasets vary widely in the type and scale of physical supervision they provide. We compare existing datasets along three factors: the parametric body model, the availability of force supervision, and the scale (Tab. 1). These factors are rarely satisfied simultaneously. AddBiomechanics [42] offers force-plate-measured GRF and inverse-dynamics torques at scale, but its motion is released as marker trajectories rather than parametric body parameters. ImDy [18] reaches scale in a parametric representation but its forces come from physics simulation. At smaller scale, UnderPressure [24] and VidSole [14] do not use a parametric body model, while GroundLink [8] adopts SMPL-X [27] but does not provide joint torques. None of these datasets, however, measures the reliability of its force annotations.

    Beyond force-paired data, parallel lines of work pair parametric motion with biomechanical skeletal anatomy or muscle activations. BioAMASS [15] fits SKEL [15], a biomechanically grounded body model, to AMASS sequences, but provides no force supervision. Compared to SMPL, SKEL replaces non-anatomical joints with biomechanically grounded ones. Since per-joint torques are meaningful only on anatomically grounded joints, we adopt SKEL as the parametric body model. Other work pairs parametric motion with muscle activations, either measured via sEMG (Muscles in Action [2]) or simulated via OpenSim (MInT [33]). These address a different layer of physical supervision.

    Uncertainty Analysis of Inverse Dynamics

    Inverse-dynamics uncertainty has been studied through Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis [32, 37, 31] that perturbs body segment parameters, joint centers, or marker placements to characterize how kinematic noise propagates into torque estimates. These studies establish the methodological foundation but are confined to single-subject, single-trial demonstrations. AddBiomechanics [42] reports aggregate, but not per-sample, pipeline uncertainty. We close this gap by performing Monte Carlo uncertainty estimation through the inverse-dynamics pipeline for every trial, producing a per-frame, per-joint label uncertainty σ_τ for each torque label.

    Dynamics in Human Motion Modeling

    Existing work has leveraged dynamics for improving motion estimation and generation, which falls into two broad categories. Simulation-based methods embed human models in a physics simulator and apply learned control to ensure the motion complies with physical laws [28, 29, 46, 45]. Constraint-based methods integrate physics-derived losses or priors to enhance the physical plausibility of kinematic estimation [34, 48, 47]. All these methods primarily enforce physics laws without grounding in the underlying biomechanical forces, making it difficult to quantitatively evaluate their physical validity. ForceBody provides this grounding: it can be directly used by these pipelines for both training and validation against measured dynamics.

    A separate line of work on modeling dynamics focuses on regressing forces from kinematics under supervised learning, ranging from task-specific gait models [26, 25] to large-scale approaches [18, 19, 42, 35]. These methods primarily estimate forces from sparse marker trajectories [26, 25, 35], incompatible with dense parametric body models in vision pipelines. Other methods support SMPL [8, 18] but inherit its biomechanical limitations, small scale, or reliance on simulated forces. ForceBody addresses these limitations by providing large-scale, measured force supervision directly on SKEL.

    3 Dataset

    Dataset statistics. ForceBody contains 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames at 100 Hz, 26.9 hours) of 140 subjects (75 male, 55 female, 10 unreported; height 1.73±0.09 m, mass 68.8±11.5 kg, BMI 22.8±2.8 kg/m2) spanning walking, running, jumping, sit-to-stand, stair climbing, and mixed daily activities (see Fig. 2). The dataset is dominated by walking and running (93.5% of trials), with detailed activity and source distribution provided in the Appendix. We adopt a subject-level split stratified by body size, activity, and source, with 121 training subjects (9,472 trials, 24 hours) and 19 disjoint test subjects (914 trials, 3 hours).

    Released components. Each trial in ForceBody contains: (1) SKEL parameters (pose θ, shape β, global translation t); (2) measured ground reaction forces (GRFs) with their centers of pressure (CoP), the 2D point on the force plate at which the GRF acts; (3) inverse-dynamics joint torques τ, both inherited from AddB; and (4) per-frame, per-joint uncertainty σ_τ on the torques.

    To achieve this, we re-express AddBiomechanics’ measurement-grounded force data in the SKEL parametric body model and accompany every torque label with a Monte Carlo uncertainty estimated through the same inverse-dynamics pipeline that produced the labels. We first describe the SKEL motion fitting pipeline in Sec. 3.1, then the uncertainty annotation of inverse-dynamics torque in Sec. 3.2. Lastly, we show the fitting results and validity of force and SKEL motion pairing in Sec. 3.3.

    3.1 SKEL Motion Fitting

    Why SKEL. We choose SKEL [15] as the parametric body model for ForceBody for two reasons. First, SKEL inherits the 46-DOF biomechanical skeleton (BSM) from the OpenSim community, providing anatomically grounded joint axes that are required for valid inverse-dynamics interpretation of the inherited torque labels. Second, SKEL is fitted inside SMPL bodies, exposing the same surface mesh and shape space as SMPL-based encoders, decoders, and motion priors, which form the dominant system for human motion learning.

    Problem setting. Each AddBiomechanics trial provides motion in the OpenSim Rajagopal skeleton [30], encoded as T frames of joint angles together with anatomical joint centers, bone segments, and optical marker trajectories. Our task is to recover a single SKEL shape β∈ℝ¹⁰per subject along with per-frame pose θₜ∈ℝ⁴⁶ and global translation tₜ∈ℝ³ that reproduce the recorded motion under the SKEL kinematic model. Because SKEL is a full-body model, we use only AddB’s full-body recordings; the half-body subset lacks the upper-body data needed for fitting.

    From Rajagopal kinematics to SKEL parameters. This recovery is underdetermined. AddB exposes only 20 joints (37 DOFs) while SKEL has 24 joints (46 DOFs), so 9 SKEL DOFs at the spine, scapula, and humerus have no direct AddB counterpart and must be recovered through the kinematic chain. Of the 20 AddB joints, 15 have anatomically equivalent counterparts in SKEL (pelvis, bilateral hip, knee, ankle, MTP, elbow, radioulnar, and wrist; Fig. 3), and serve as direct joint-position supervision. Our fitting recovers β once per subject and then {θₜ,tₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ for each trial. Our pipeline adapts the SKEL fitting of Keller et al.[15] to AddB, with bone-length and temporal regularizers added to handle the marker and joint layout differences.

    Stage 1. We estimate one shape β∈ℝ¹⁰ per subject by matching SKEL bone lengths to the subject’s AddB bone lengths, together with terms for the recorded height and body mass. A single shape per subject keeps the body identical across all trials of that person.β is then frozen for Stage 2. Stage 2. With β fixed, we optimize the per-frame pose θₜ∈ℝ⁴⁶ and translation tₜ∈ℝ³ using two positional supervisions: (i) a joint-position loss on the 15 directly matched joints (Fig. 3), and (ii) a marker loss that aligns SKEL mesh vertices to the observed optical markers via the SMPL→AddB vertex correspondence [15]. We additionally apply anatomical regularizers on under-constrained joints (spine, scapula, humerus) and a temporal smoothness term on velocity and acceleration. Source recordings span 61–250 Hz, so we standardize them to 100 Hz and use only AddB’s IK output (excluding force-based refinement) to prevent force leakage into kinematic inputs [35]. The full loss formulation, hyperparameters, and preprocessing details are provided in Appendix B.

    3.2 Per-Sample Torque Uncertainty

    For each trial, AddBiomechanics provides joint torques τₜ alongside the captured kinematics. τₜ is not observed but computed by inverse dynamics from joint kinematics qₜ and the measured GRF λₜ. Inverse dynamics propagates kinematic noise nonlinearly into the output torques [32, 37]. We accompany every released τₜ with a per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotation σ_τ,t.

    We obtain σ_τ by Monte Carlo sampling through the same OpenSim inverse-dynamics solver that produced the inherited torques. At each frame we perturb the AddB joint angles with band-limited Gaussian noise ε ∼ ℕ(0,σ_q²I) at the 20 direct DOFs spanning the 14 major joints (bilateral hip, knee, ankle, MTP, elbow, radioulnar, wrist), feed each perturbed pose back through the solver with GRF λₜ held fixed, and report the per-DOF sample mean μ_τ and standard deviation σ_τ over N samples. The full algorithm is in Appendix C. We set σ_q = 1.6^∘, matching the average joint-angle RMSE that AddB reports for its inverse-kinematics pass on synthetic walking data [41], so that the perturbations match the noise level the released kinematics actually carry. Because AddB reports only an aggregate angle error and does not release per-DOF noise levels, we apply σ_q uniformly to all 20 direct DOFs as an isotropic approximation. We use N = 1,000 samples per frame. The standard error of σ̂_τ shrinks from 7.1% at N = 100 to 3.2% at N = 500 and 2.2% at N = 1,000, beyond which further increases offer marginal returns. Of the 10,386 trials, we exclude 1,654 (15.9%) with missing GRF labels or coverage below 50%, leaving 8,732 trials with released σ_τ.

    Fig. 4 visualizes the per-joint MC histograms for one representative frame from a Carter2023 [1] running trial. As an aggregate-level sanity check, the median released σ_τ on walking trials is approximately 0.10 %BW·h, on the same order as the 0.15 %BW·h walking-torque error AddBiomechanics reports for its own pipeline [41]. Across the 14 direct joints, the released σ_τ spans about three orders of magnitude (Tab. 2(a)). The distal upper-body joints (radioulnar, wrist) sit at the bottom of the range, since they only swing light distal segments and the same angle perturbation changes very little torque. The elbow sits in the middle of the range. Lower-body proximal joints (hip, knee) sit at the top of the range, since they carry the entire body weight through the longest lever arms, so a small angle perturbation moves a large torque. The toe joint (MTP) is the lower-body exception, with a σ_τ comparable to the upper-body distal joints. More detailed analyses on per-activity and per-source breakdowns are in Appendix D.

    Beyond joint-level patterns, the relative ratio σ_τ/|τ| is motion dependent (Tab. 2(b)). Dynamic motions yield smaller relative uncertainty (around 0.4 in jumping and 0.5 in running) than near-static ones (around 1.3 in standing), with sit-to-stand and walking falling in between. Across all trials, σ_τ/|τ| is strongly anti-correlated with both joint-velocity RMS (Spearman ρ =-0.85) and joint-torque RMS (Spearman ρ =-0.81). The high ratio in static activities reflects the small underlying |τ| (∼0.017 Nm/kg) rather than inflated σ_τ.

    3.3 Pairing Torques with SKEL Motions

    ForceBody is not just a fitting dataset; its value rests on the pairing between fitted SKEL motion and inherited torque. We assess the validity of our pairing along two axes: motion fidelity with AddB (Motion Fitting Quality) and consistency between SKEL-derived and AddB torques (Torque Consistency).

    Motion Fitting Quality. The released SKEL fits track the AddB kinematics closely. Mean per-joint Euclidean error is 21.6 mm overall. We also report standard physical plausibility metrics: foot sliding (1.23 mm) and ground penetration (1.17 mm). For acceleration, Fig. 5 compares finite-difference angular acceleration between AddB and our SKEL fits on walking, running, and jumping trials. The two curves stay on top of each other across all panels with Pearson correlation between 0.97 and 1.00, so the fit captures the underlying acceleration profile rather than only matching frame-level joint positions. Fig. 6 shows SKEL meshes, internal skeletons, joint-torque heatmaps, and measured GRF arrows for one trial of each major activity (running, sit-to-stand, drop jump, tai chi, ballet high leg, and soccer kick), illustrating the released motions across range of behaviors covered. Per-joint and physical plausibility statistics are tabulated in Appendix F.

    Torque Consistency. To verify the SKEL fit at the torque level, we feed the fitted SKEL kinematics through the same OpenSim inverse-dynamics pipeline that produced τ, obtaining a SKEL-derived torque τ_SKEL. Fig. 7 compares τ_SKEL with the inherited τ against the τ±σ_τ band on representative running and sit-to-stand trials; τ_SKEL tracks τ closely, indicating that the SKEL fit recovers torque-level dynamics consistent with the inherited labels. Across the trials with released σ_τ (8,455 of 8,732 after an inverse-kinematics residual check), the median per-trial RMSE between τ_SKEL and τ is 0.31, 0.20, and 0.04 Nm/kg at the hip, knee, and ankle. τ_SKEL falls inside the τ±σ_τ band on 89%, 83%, and 89% of the frames at these joints. The gap is the largest in running (hip RMSE 0.38 Nm/kg) and smallest in standing (hip RMSE 0.03 Nm/kg, 99% inside the band at hip and knee). Upper-body joints show lower coverage (41 to 64%), where the SKEL and Rajagopal joint axes differ the most (Fig. 3).

    4 Experiments

    We use ForceBody to study two questions. Firstly, does ForceBody’s parametric representation match the predictive utility of AddBiomechanics’ Rajagopal-based pipelines? (Sec. 4.1) Secondly, what level of torque prediction performance can be achieved on ForceBody, and how can the released uncertainty annotation be used? (Sec. 4.2).

    4.1 Comparison with AddB

    Following AddBiomechanics’ baseline protocol [42], we predict per-foot ground reaction force (GRF) and per-foot ground reaction moment (GRM) from SKEL poses θ. For comparison, we train MLP and GLN, the architectures used by AddB [42], on ForceBody. Both pipelines take as input the same underlying motion, expressed in different parametric representations: The AddB baselines use Rajagopal joint kinematics from AddBiomechanics, while our models use SKEL joint kinematics fitted on the same trials. As shown in Tab. 3, across matched architectures, ForceBody-trained models perform on par with their AddB-trained counterparts. The SKEL parametric representation thus supports force prediction at AddB-level performance.

    4.2 Reference Baselines for Torque Prediction

    Joint Torque Prediction

    Given a sequence of SKEL pose parameters q_1:T and shape parameters β, the model predicts the AddB inverse-dynamics torque τ_1:T at every frame, mass-normalized to Nm/kg. We evaluate on the 14 anatomical joints (20 DOFs) with a direct SKEL correspondence, and compare six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) trained on ForceBody. We report errors separately on the upper body, the lower body, and as an overall All joints mean, using RMSE, MAE, and Pearson correlation. Each baseline is fully supervised on the released torque annotations. All six backbones produce plausible torque predictions (Tab. 4), and Mamba2 performs the best. Adding the parametric body inputs (SKEL β, body mass, and height) tothe pose doesnotreducethe error, while adding pose and rootvelocitiesandaccelerations raises the All joints PCC from 0.67 to 0.76 (Appendix I). Detailed training settings and the input feature ablation are in Appendix G and I.

    Torque Prediction with Uncertainty-guidance

    To demonstrate one use of the released per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotations, we enhance the torque prediction model with an uncertainty-aware loss that assigns each training window a loss weight computed from its mean σ_τ[49]. Following recent force and dynamics prediction models [35, 33], we adopt a Transformer backbone. Compared to its performance without uncertainty (Tab. 5), we improve the All joints RMSE from 0.155 to 0.149 Nm/kg (-4%), MAE from 0.107 to 0.101 Nm/kg (-5%), and PCC from 0.760 to 0.772 (+2%), averaged over three seeds, with gains on both upper- and lower-body joint groups. Because the only change is the per-sample loss weight, the gain comes from the σ_τ annotation alone. These results lay a foundation for further uncertainty-aware methods that the community can build on top of ForceBody.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented ForceBody, the first large-scale dataset to pair measured ground reaction force (GRF) and inverse-dynamics torques with the SKEL parametric body, and the first to release per-frame, per-joint Monte Carlo uncertainty for every torque label σ_τ. Benchmarking GRF prediction against the AddBiomechanics baselines and joint-torque prediction across six architectures shows that ForceBody enables direct, end-to-end learning of physical signals on a parametric body. As one example use of the released σ_τ, fine-tuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting yields gains across joint groups. Together, ForceBody opens a path toward force-grounded, uncertainty-aware modeling of human dynamics.

    One limitation of our work lies in the representational capacity. The current fitting stage uses SKEL as the parametric body model. Atypical body shapes outside the SKEL shape space can be addressed by extending our pipeline to new parametric models with different shape spaces. The released σ_τ models joint-angle noise only and does not cover GRF and CoP errors, segment inertia, or the axis mismatch between SKEL and the Rajagopal model. The data are dominated by walking and running (Appendix A), so results on rare activities rest on few trials.

要点：

  • 缺口：力与力矩是驱动人体运动的本源，在生物力学、机器人与**物理感知动画**里都关键，但在基于学习的动作重建与生成管线里**通常缺失**
  • 已有带力标注的数据集也不够用：其配对的动作序列与现代学习管线使用的**参数化人体模型不兼容**；此外既有数据集在关节力矩的获取方式上也有局限
  • ForceBody 因此提供「配对的力 + 参数化人体动作」，并把**力矩不确定性**一并标注

为什么值得看：物理感知动画要「有重量感」，就必须有力。把力与参数化人体（SMPL 系）对齐、还带不确定性，这条补的是数据基础——没有它，物理驱动角色只能靠手调。

中文摘要：力与力矩是驱动物体运动的根本量，在生物力学、机器人学以及物理感知的动画中都至关重要，然而在基于学习的运动重建与生成管线里，它们通常是缺失的。已有部分数据集提供力标注，但其配对的动作序列与现代学习管线所用的参数化人体模型并不兼容；此外这些数据集在关节力矩的获取方式上也存在局限。ForceBody 因此提供与力配对参数化人体运动，并同时标注力矩的不确定性。对希望让角色动作「有重量感」的物理驱动动画来说，这条补的是数据基础——缺少力的标注，控制器只能靠手调增益。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-18

本期推送：2026-11-19

ForceBody: Force-Paired Parametric Body Motion with Torque Uncertainty

Abstract

Forces and torques drive human motion, central to biomechanics, robotics, and physics-aware animation, yet they are often absent from learning-based motion pipelines for body reconstruction and generation. Some motion datasets provide force annotations, but the paired motion sequences are incompatible with the parametric body models used in modern learning pipelines. In addition, existing datasets typically obtain joint torques through inverse dynamics, which is inherently sensitive to the quality of the input kinematics; however, they do not quantify the reliability of these torque estimates. We close this gap with ForceBody, the first dataset to bring ground truth force supervision into a parametric body representation, shipped with per-sample torque uncertainty. ForceBody pairs the SKEL body model with ground reaction forces and inverse-dynamics joint torques across 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects. Each torque label is paired with a per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotation obtained by Monte Carlo sampling through the inverse dynamics pipeline. We benchmark six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) on ground reaction force and joint torque prediction from SKEL motion. As one example use of the released uncertainty, finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces the MAE of joint torque estimation by 5%. Code and data are at https://github.com/DominoAI-Lab/ForceBody-NeurIPS-ED-2026.

1 Introduction

Capturing human motion in 3D body pose and shape has become increasingly prevalent with recent advances in computer vision, computer graphics, and deep learning [49, 36, 44]. Nonetheless, the forces, including joint torques and ground reaction forces (GRF), that produce the motion are primarily absent from the estimation. These physical signals are critical to applications ranging from biomechanical assessment [11, 13] to exoskeleton and prosthetic design [22] and sports performance analysis [12]. Concurrent efforts tackle this limitation by incorporating dynamics into learning-based motion estimation, but progress is bottlenecked on two fronts. On the training side, dynamics is typically incorporated via external simulators rather than end-to-end learning. On the evaluation side, metrics rely on kinematic surrogate of physics plausibility, e.g., motion smoothness [47], motion replay stability [50], rather than the dynamic quantities themselves. Both limitations trace to the same root cause: real-world force annotations are unavailable in parametric body representations. Closing this gap requires a force-paired parametric body dataset, where forces are derived from measurements, in a form learning-based body motion pipelines can directly consume.

The AddBiomechanics (AddB) dataset [42, 41] is the largest publicly available collection of human motion paired with measured GRF and inverse-dynamics torques, aggregating 15 sources of motion-and-force data. Its motion, however, is provided as marker trajectories (i.e., 3D positions of motion-capture markers placed on the body) rather than the parametric body parameters (e.g., SMPL [20], SKEL [15]) native to motion reconstruction and generation pipelines. Prior attempts to pair parametric body models with physical labels remain limited. GroundLink [8] provides force-plate-measured GRF alongside SMPL motion but is small in scale and does not include joint torques. ImDy [18] applies physics simulation to SMPL motion from AMASS [21] to produce forces and torques at scale, but its labels are simulator outputs rather than physically measured. As a result, no existing dataset offers measured forces in a parametric body representation.

The reliability of torque annotations poses a further challenge. Joint torques cannot be directly measured. They are computed through inverse dynamics from motion kinematics and external forces such as GRF [43]. Inverse dynamics is inherently sensitive to kinematic noise: small positional perturbations at the input can propagate and yield large deviations in estimated torques [37, 31, 32]. This uncertainty is intrinsic to any dataset that derives torques from inverse dynamics, AddBiomechanics [42] included. Yet no existing force dataset releases per-sample torque reliability annotations.

This paper presents ForceBody (see Fig. 1), a large-scale dataset that aligns biomechanical force measurements from AddBiomechanics [41] with a parametric body model, and provides uncertainty annotations for every torque label. Our contributions are:

  • •

    A force-paired parametric body dataset. ForceBody comprises 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects, with per-trial SKEL poses, per-subject body shape parameters, and associated measured GRF and joint torques. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset to pair large-scale measured forces with a parametric body model.

  • •

    Per-sample uncertainty annotations. We provide per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotations for every joint torque label, derived from Monte Carlo sampling through inverse dynamics. This makes ForceBody the first force dataset to ship with annotated uncertainty.

  • •

    Reference baselines for force prediction. We evaluate six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) on the tasks of ground reaction force and joint torque prediction from SKEL motion. As one example use of our uncertainty annotation, finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces joint torque MAE by 5%.

    • 2 Related Work

    Datasets with Force Annotation

    Motion datasets vary widely in the type and scale of physical supervision they provide. We compare existing datasets along three factors: the parametric body model, the availability of force supervision, and the scale (Tab. 1). These factors are rarely satisfied simultaneously. AddBiomechanics [42] offers force-plate-measured GRF and inverse-dynamics torques at scale, but its motion is released as marker trajectories rather than parametric body parameters. ImDy [18] reaches scale in a parametric representation but its forces come from physics simulation. At smaller scale, UnderPressure [24] and VidSole [14] do not use a parametric body model, while GroundLink [8] adopts SMPL-X [27] but does not provide joint torques. None of these datasets, however, measures the reliability of its force annotations.

    Beyond force-paired data, parallel lines of work pair parametric motion with biomechanical skeletal anatomy or muscle activations. BioAMASS [15] fits SKEL [15], a biomechanically grounded body model, to AMASS sequences, but provides no force supervision. Compared to SMPL, SKEL replaces non-anatomical joints with biomechanically grounded ones. Since per-joint torques are meaningful only on anatomically grounded joints, we adopt SKEL as the parametric body model. Other work pairs parametric motion with muscle activations, either measured via sEMG (Muscles in Action [2]) or simulated via OpenSim (MInT [33]). These address a different layer of physical supervision.

    Uncertainty Analysis of Inverse Dynamics

    Inverse-dynamics uncertainty has been studied through Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis [32, 37, 31] that perturbs body segment parameters, joint centers, or marker placements to characterize how kinematic noise propagates into torque estimates. These studies establish the methodological foundation but are confined to single-subject, single-trial demonstrations. AddBiomechanics [42] reports aggregate, but not per-sample, pipeline uncertainty. We close this gap by performing Monte Carlo uncertainty estimation through the inverse-dynamics pipeline for every trial, producing a per-frame, per-joint label uncertainty σ_τ for each torque label.

    Dynamics in Human Motion Modeling

    Existing work has leveraged dynamics for improving motion estimation and generation, which falls into two broad categories. Simulation-based methods embed human models in a physics simulator and apply learned control to ensure the motion complies with physical laws [28, 29, 46, 45]. Constraint-based methods integrate physics-derived losses or priors to enhance the physical plausibility of kinematic estimation [34, 48, 47]. All these methods primarily enforce physics laws without grounding in the underlying biomechanical forces, making it difficult to quantitatively evaluate their physical validity. ForceBody provides this grounding: it can be directly used by these pipelines for both training and validation against measured dynamics.

    A separate line of work on modeling dynamics focuses on regressing forces from kinematics under supervised learning, ranging from task-specific gait models [26, 25] to large-scale approaches [18, 19, 42, 35]. These methods primarily estimate forces from sparse marker trajectories [26, 25, 35], incompatible with dense parametric body models in vision pipelines. Other methods support SMPL [8, 18] but inherit its biomechanical limitations, small scale, or reliance on simulated forces. ForceBody addresses these limitations by providing large-scale, measured force supervision directly on SKEL.

    3 Dataset

    Dataset statistics. ForceBody contains 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames at 100 Hz, 26.9 hours) of 140 subjects (75 male, 55 female, 10 unreported; height 1.73±0.09 m, mass 68.8±11.5 kg, BMI 22.8±2.8 kg/m2) spanning walking, running, jumping, sit-to-stand, stair climbing, and mixed daily activities (see Fig. 2). The dataset is dominated by walking and running (93.5% of trials), with detailed activity and source distribution provided in the Appendix. We adopt a subject-level split stratified by body size, activity, and source, with 121 training subjects (9,472 trials, 24 hours) and 19 disjoint test subjects (914 trials, 3 hours).

    Released components. Each trial in ForceBody contains: (1) SKEL parameters (pose θ, shape β, global translation t); (2) measured ground reaction forces (GRFs) with their centers of pressure (CoP), the 2D point on the force plate at which the GRF acts; (3) inverse-dynamics joint torques τ, both inherited from AddB; and (4) per-frame, per-joint uncertainty σ_τ on the torques.

    To achieve this, we re-express AddBiomechanics’ measurement-grounded force data in the SKEL parametric body model and accompany every torque label with a Monte Carlo uncertainty estimated through the same inverse-dynamics pipeline that produced the labels. We first describe the SKEL motion fitting pipeline in Sec. 3.1, then the uncertainty annotation of inverse-dynamics torque in Sec. 3.2. Lastly, we show the fitting results and validity of force and SKEL motion pairing in Sec. 3.3.

    3.1 SKEL Motion Fitting

    Why SKEL. We choose SKEL [15] as the parametric body model for ForceBody for two reasons. First, SKEL inherits the 46-DOF biomechanical skeleton (BSM) from the OpenSim community, providing anatomically grounded joint axes that are required for valid inverse-dynamics interpretation of the inherited torque labels. Second, SKEL is fitted inside SMPL bodies, exposing the same surface mesh and shape space as SMPL-based encoders, decoders, and motion priors, which form the dominant system for human motion learning.

    Problem setting. Each AddBiomechanics trial provides motion in the OpenSim Rajagopal skeleton [30], encoded as T frames of joint angles together with anatomical joint centers, bone segments, and optical marker trajectories. Our task is to recover a single SKEL shape β∈ℝ¹⁰per subject along with per-frame pose θₜ∈ℝ⁴⁶ and global translation tₜ∈ℝ³ that reproduce the recorded motion under the SKEL kinematic model. Because SKEL is a full-body model, we use only AddB’s full-body recordings; the half-body subset lacks the upper-body data needed for fitting.

    From Rajagopal kinematics to SKEL parameters. This recovery is underdetermined. AddB exposes only 20 joints (37 DOFs) while SKEL has 24 joints (46 DOFs), so 9 SKEL DOFs at the spine, scapula, and humerus have no direct AddB counterpart and must be recovered through the kinematic chain. Of the 20 AddB joints, 15 have anatomically equivalent counterparts in SKEL (pelvis, bilateral hip, knee, ankle, MTP, elbow, radioulnar, and wrist; Fig. 3), and serve as direct joint-position supervision. Our fitting recovers β once per subject and then {θₜ,tₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ for each trial. Our pipeline adapts the SKEL fitting of Keller et al.[15] to AddB, with bone-length and temporal regularizers added to handle the marker and joint layout differences.

    Stage 1. We estimate one shape β∈ℝ¹⁰ per subject by matching SKEL bone lengths to the subject’s AddB bone lengths, together with terms for the recorded height and body mass. A single shape per subject keeps the body identical across all trials of that person.β is then frozen for Stage 2. Stage 2. With β fixed, we optimize the per-frame pose θₜ∈ℝ⁴⁶ and translation tₜ∈ℝ³ using two positional supervisions: (i) a joint-position loss on the 15 directly matched joints (Fig. 3), and (ii) a marker loss that aligns SKEL mesh vertices to the observed optical markers via the SMPL→AddB vertex correspondence [15]. We additionally apply anatomical regularizers on under-constrained joints (spine, scapula, humerus) and a temporal smoothness term on velocity and acceleration. Source recordings span 61–250 Hz, so we standardize them to 100 Hz and use only AddB’s IK output (excluding force-based refinement) to prevent force leakage into kinematic inputs [35]. The full loss formulation, hyperparameters, and preprocessing details are provided in Appendix B.

    3.2 Per-Sample Torque Uncertainty

    For each trial, AddBiomechanics provides joint torques τₜ alongside the captured kinematics. τₜ is not observed but computed by inverse dynamics from joint kinematics qₜ and the measured GRF λₜ. Inverse dynamics propagates kinematic noise nonlinearly into the output torques [32, 37]. We accompany every released τₜ with a per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotation σ_τ,t.

    We obtain σ_τ by Monte Carlo sampling through the same OpenSim inverse-dynamics solver that produced the inherited torques. At each frame we perturb the AddB joint angles with band-limited Gaussian noise ε ∼ ℕ(0,σ_q²I) at the 20 direct DOFs spanning the 14 major joints (bilateral hip, knee, ankle, MTP, elbow, radioulnar, wrist), feed each perturbed pose back through the solver with GRF λₜ held fixed, and report the per-DOF sample mean μ_τ and standard deviation σ_τ over N samples. The full algorithm is in Appendix C. We set σ_q = 1.6^∘, matching the average joint-angle RMSE that AddB reports for its inverse-kinematics pass on synthetic walking data [41], so that the perturbations match the noise level the released kinematics actually carry. Because AddB reports only an aggregate angle error and does not release per-DOF noise levels, we apply σ_q uniformly to all 20 direct DOFs as an isotropic approximation. We use N = 1,000 samples per frame. The standard error of σ̂_τ shrinks from 7.1% at N = 100 to 3.2% at N = 500 and 2.2% at N = 1,000, beyond which further increases offer marginal returns. Of the 10,386 trials, we exclude 1,654 (15.9%) with missing GRF labels or coverage below 50%, leaving 8,732 trials with released σ_τ.

    Fig. 4 visualizes the per-joint MC histograms for one representative frame from a Carter2023 [1] running trial. As an aggregate-level sanity check, the median released σ_τ on walking trials is approximately 0.10 %BW·h, on the same order as the 0.15 %BW·h walking-torque error AddBiomechanics reports for its own pipeline [41]. Across the 14 direct joints, the released σ_τ spans about three orders of magnitude (Tab. 2(a)). The distal upper-body joints (radioulnar, wrist) sit at the bottom of the range, since they only swing light distal segments and the same angle perturbation changes very little torque. The elbow sits in the middle of the range. Lower-body proximal joints (hip, knee) sit at the top of the range, since they carry the entire body weight through the longest lever arms, so a small angle perturbation moves a large torque. The toe joint (MTP) is the lower-body exception, with a σ_τ comparable to the upper-body distal joints. More detailed analyses on per-activity and per-source breakdowns are in Appendix D.

    Beyond joint-level patterns, the relative ratio σ_τ/|τ| is motion dependent (Tab. 2(b)). Dynamic motions yield smaller relative uncertainty (around 0.4 in jumping and 0.5 in running) than near-static ones (around 1.3 in standing), with sit-to-stand and walking falling in between. Across all trials, σ_τ/|τ| is strongly anti-correlated with both joint-velocity RMS (Spearman ρ =-0.85) and joint-torque RMS (Spearman ρ =-0.81). The high ratio in static activities reflects the small underlying |τ| (∼0.017 Nm/kg) rather than inflated σ_τ.

    3.3 Pairing Torques with SKEL Motions

    ForceBody is not just a fitting dataset; its value rests on the pairing between fitted SKEL motion and inherited torque. We assess the validity of our pairing along two axes: motion fidelity with AddB (Motion Fitting Quality) and consistency between SKEL-derived and AddB torques (Torque Consistency).

    Motion Fitting Quality. The released SKEL fits track the AddB kinematics closely. Mean per-joint Euclidean error is 21.6 mm overall. We also report standard physical plausibility metrics: foot sliding (1.23 mm) and ground penetration (1.17 mm). For acceleration, Fig. 5 compares finite-difference angular acceleration between AddB and our SKEL fits on walking, running, and jumping trials. The two curves stay on top of each other across all panels with Pearson correlation between 0.97 and 1.00, so the fit captures the underlying acceleration profile rather than only matching frame-level joint positions. Fig. 6 shows SKEL meshes, internal skeletons, joint-torque heatmaps, and measured GRF arrows for one trial of each major activity (running, sit-to-stand, drop jump, tai chi, ballet high leg, and soccer kick), illustrating the released motions across range of behaviors covered. Per-joint and physical plausibility statistics are tabulated in Appendix F.

    Torque Consistency. To verify the SKEL fit at the torque level, we feed the fitted SKEL kinematics through the same OpenSim inverse-dynamics pipeline that produced τ, obtaining a SKEL-derived torque τ_SKEL. Fig. 7 compares τ_SKEL with the inherited τ against the τ±σ_τ band on representative running and sit-to-stand trials; τ_SKEL tracks τ closely, indicating that the SKEL fit recovers torque-level dynamics consistent with the inherited labels. Across the trials with released σ_τ (8,455 of 8,732 after an inverse-kinematics residual check), the median per-trial RMSE between τ_SKEL and τ is 0.31, 0.20, and 0.04 Nm/kg at the hip, knee, and ankle. τ_SKEL falls inside the τ±σ_τ band on 89%, 83%, and 89% of the frames at these joints. The gap is the largest in running (hip RMSE 0.38 Nm/kg) and smallest in standing (hip RMSE 0.03 Nm/kg, 99% inside the band at hip and knee). Upper-body joints show lower coverage (41 to 64%), where the SKEL and Rajagopal joint axes differ the most (Fig. 3).

    4 Experiments

    We use ForceBody to study two questions. Firstly, does ForceBody’s parametric representation match the predictive utility of AddBiomechanics’ Rajagopal-based pipelines? (Sec. 4.1) Secondly, what level of torque prediction performance can be achieved on ForceBody, and how can the released uncertainty annotation be used? (Sec. 4.2).

    4.1 Comparison with AddB

    Following AddBiomechanics’ baseline protocol [42], we predict per-foot ground reaction force (GRF) and per-foot ground reaction moment (GRM) from SKEL poses θ. For comparison, we train MLP and GLN, the architectures used by AddB [42], on ForceBody. Both pipelines take as input the same underlying motion, expressed in different parametric representations: The AddB baselines use Rajagopal joint kinematics from AddBiomechanics, while our models use SKEL joint kinematics fitted on the same trials. As shown in Tab. 3, across matched architectures, ForceBody-trained models perform on par with their AddB-trained counterparts. The SKEL parametric representation thus supports force prediction at AddB-level performance.

    4.2 Reference Baselines for Torque Prediction

    Joint Torque Prediction

    Given a sequence of SKEL pose parameters q_1:T and shape parameters β, the model predicts the AddB inverse-dynamics torque τ_1:T at every frame, mass-normalized to Nm/kg. We evaluate on the 14 anatomical joints (20 DOFs) with a direct SKEL correspondence, and compare six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) trained on ForceBody. We report errors separately on the upper body, the lower body, and as an overall All joints mean, using RMSE, MAE, and Pearson correlation. Each baseline is fully supervised on the released torque annotations. All six backbones produce plausible torque predictions (Tab. 4), and Mamba2 performs the best. Adding the parametric body inputs (SKEL β, body mass, and height) tothe pose doesnotreducethe error, while adding pose and rootvelocitiesandaccelerations raises the All joints PCC from 0.67 to 0.76 (Appendix I). Detailed training settings and the input feature ablation are in Appendix G and I.

    Torque Prediction with Uncertainty-guidance

    To demonstrate one use of the released per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotations, we enhance the torque prediction model with an uncertainty-aware loss that assigns each training window a loss weight computed from its mean σ_τ[49]. Following recent force and dynamics prediction models [35, 33], we adopt a Transformer backbone. Compared to its performance without uncertainty (Tab. 5), we improve the All joints RMSE from 0.155 to 0.149 Nm/kg (-4%), MAE from 0.107 to 0.101 Nm/kg (-5%), and PCC from 0.760 to 0.772 (+2%), averaged over three seeds, with gains on both upper- and lower-body joint groups. Because the only change is the per-sample loss weight, the gain comes from the σ_τ annotation alone. These results lay a foundation for further uncertainty-aware methods that the community can build on top of ForceBody.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented ForceBody, the first large-scale dataset to pair measured ground reaction force (GRF) and inverse-dynamics torques with the SKEL parametric body, and the first to release per-frame, per-joint Monte Carlo uncertainty for every torque label σ_τ. Benchmarking GRF prediction against the AddBiomechanics baselines and joint-torque prediction across six architectures shows that ForceBody enables direct, end-to-end learning of physical signals on a parametric body. As one example use of the released σ_τ, fine-tuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting yields gains across joint groups. Together, ForceBody opens a path toward force-grounded, uncertainty-aware modeling of human dynamics.

    One limitation of our work lies in the representational capacity. The current fitting stage uses SKEL as the parametric body model. Atypical body shapes outside the SKEL shape space can be addressed by extending our pipeline to new parametric models with different shape spaces. The released σ_τ models joint-angle noise only and does not cover GRF and CoP errors, segment inertia, or the axis mismatch between SKEL and the Rajagopal model. The data are dominated by walking and running (Appendix A), so results on rare activities rest on few trials.

    ForceBody aggregates motion trials from ten public motion-capture datasets included in AddBiomechanics [42]. After applying the quality-based filter (Appendix E), the released dataset spans 140 subjects, 10,386 trials, and approximately 26.9 hours of recorded motion. Table 6 summarizes the per-source composition: trial and subject counts, the male/female/unreported breakdown, mean±std subject height and mass, and the dominant activity type.
